tocqueville.chapter_summary: Utilité de connaître le point de départ des peuples pour comprendre leur état social et leurs lois. -- L'Amérique est le seul pays où l'on ait pu apercevoir clairement le point de départ d'un grand peuple. -- En quoi tous les hommes qui vinrent peupler l'Amérique anglaise se ressemblaient. -- En quoi ils différaient. -- Remarque applicable à tous les Européens qui vinrent s'établir sur le rivage du Nouveau-Monde. -- Colonisation de la Virginie. -- _Id._ de la Nouvelle-Angleterre. -- Caractère original des premiers habitants de la Nouvelle-Angleterre. -- Leur arrivée. -- Leurs premières lois. -- Contrat social. -- Code pénal emprunté à la législation de Moïse. -- Ardeur religieuse. -- Esprit républicain. -- Union intime de l'esprit de religion et de l'esprit de liberté.
translation: A man is born; his earliest years pass obscurely, amid the pleasures or the labors of childhood. He grows; manhood begins; at last the doors of the world open to receive him; he comes into contact with his fellows. Only then is he studied for the first time, and one supposes one can see forming in him the seeds of the vices and virtues of his maturity.
This, if I am not mistaken, is a great error.

Go back further; examine the child even in his mother's arms; watch the outer world reflect itself for the first time upon the still dim mirror of his intelligence; consider the first examples that strike his eye; listen to the first words that awaken in him the sleeping powers of thought; witness, finally, the first struggles he must sustain — and only then will you understand the source of the prejudices, the habits, the passions that are to govern his life. The man is, so to speak, entire in the swaddling-clothes of his cradle.
Something analogous occurs in nations. Peoples always bear the marks of their origins. The circumstances that attended their birth and aided their development affect all the rest of their course.

If we could trace societies back to their elements, and examine the first records of their history, I do not doubt that we should find there the first cause of the prejudices, the habits, the dominant passions — of everything, in short, that makes up what is called the national character; we should encounter explanations of usages that today seem at odds with the reigning mores; of laws that seem opposed to recognized principles; of incoherent opinions met with here and there in society, like those fragments of broken chains that still sometimes hang from the vaults of an old building and support nothing. The destiny of certain peoples whom an unknown force seems to be drawing toward some end of which they themselves are ignorant would thus be explained. But up to now the facts have been wanting for such a study; the analytical spirit has come to nations only as they aged, and when at last they thought to contemplate their cradle, time had already wrapped it in cloud, and ignorance and pride had surrounded it with fables behind which the truth lay hidden.
[Translator's note: mores — Tocqueville's term for the habits, dispositions, and moral character of a people; no English equivalent captures its full range.]

America is the only country in which one has been able to witness the natural and tranquil development of a society, and in which it has been possible to specify the influence exerted by the point of departure upon the future of the States.

By the time the peoples of Europe descended on the shores of the New World, the traits of their national character were already firmly set; each had a distinct physiognomy; and since they had already reached that degree of civilization which leads men to study themselves, they have handed down to us a faithful picture of their opinions, their mores, and their laws. The men of the fifteenth century are nearly as well known to us as those of our own. America therefore shows us in broad daylight what the ignorance or the barbarism of earlier ages has hidden from view.

Near enough to the founding of the American societies to know their elements in detail, far enough from that time to be able to judge what those seeds have produced, the men of our day seem destined to see further than their predecessors into human affairs. Providence has placed within our reach a torch which our fathers lacked, and has allowed us to discern, in the destiny of nations, first causes that the obscurity of the past concealed from them.

When, after carefully studying the history of America, one examines its political and social condition with care, one is deeply persuaded of this truth: that there is not an opinion, not a habit, not a law — I might say not an event — that the point of departure does not readily explain. Those who read this book will therefore find in the present chapter the germ of what is to follow, and the key to nearly the whole work.

The emigrants who came, at different periods, to occupy the territory now covered by the American Union differed from one another in many respects; their aims were not the same, and they governed themselves by different principles.
Yet these men had certain traits in common, and they were all in an analogous situation.

The bond of language is perhaps the strongest and most durable that can unite men. All the emigrants spoke the same tongue; they were all children of the same people. Born in a country which the strife of parties had agitated for centuries, and where the factions had been obliged, each in turn, to place themselves under the protection of the laws, their political education had been formed in this rough school, and one found more notions of rights, more principles of true liberty current among them than among most of the peoples of Europe. By the time of the first emigrations, communal government — that fertile seed of free institutions — had already entered deeply into English habits, and with it the dogma of the sovereignty of the people had made its way into the very midst of the Tudor monarchy.

This was the time of the religious quarrels that have shaken the Christian world. England had hurled herself with a kind of fury into that new career. The character of her inhabitants, always grave and reflective, had become austere and disputatious. Learning had grown greatly in these intellectual struggles; the mind had received a deeper cultivation there. While men were busy talking religion, mores had grown purer. All these general traits of the nation were found, more or less, in the physiognomy of those of her sons who had come to seek a new future on the opposite shores of the Ocean.

A further observation, to which we shall have occasion to return, applies not only to the English but also to the French, the Spanish, and all the Europeans who came successively to settle on the shores of the New World. All the new European colonies contained, if not the full development, at least the seed of a complete democracy. Two causes led to this result: one may say that, in general, at their departure from the mother country, the emigrants had no notion of any superiority among themselves. The fortunate and the powerful do not, as a rule, go into exile, and poverty and misfortune are the best guarantors of equality known among men. It happened, however, on several occasions, that great lords crossed to America in the wake of political or religious quarrels. Laws were passed there to establish a hierarchy of ranks, but it was soon perceived that the American soil utterly rejected the territorial aristocracy. It was seen that to clear this stubborn land nothing less was required than the constant, self-interested effort of the proprietor himself. The ground prepared, its yield turned out to be insufficient to enrich both master and farmer at once. The land was therefore broken up, naturally, into small holdings which the proprietor alone cultivated. Now, it is to the land that aristocracy is fastened, it is to the soil that it clings and on which it leans; it is not privileges alone that establish it, it is not birth that constitutes it — it is landed property, transmitted by inheritance. A nation may exhibit immense fortunes and great miseries; but if those fortunes are not territorial, one sees within it the poor and the rich; there is, properly speaking, no aristocracy.

All the English colonies, therefore, at the time of their birth, bore a strong family resemblance to one another. All, from the outset, seemed destined to display the development of liberty — not the aristocratic liberty of their mother country, but the bourgeois and democratic liberty of which the history of the world had not yet offered any complete model.
Within this general tint, however, very strong shadings could be discerned, which need to be shown.
In the great Anglo-American family one may distinguish two principal offshoots which, to the present, have grown without entirely merging — one in the south, the other in the north.

Virginia received the first English colony. The emigrants arrived there in 1607. Europe at that time was still strangely preoccupied with the idea that gold and silver mines constitute the wealth of nations: a baneful idea which has impoverished the European nations that gave themselves over to it, and destroyed more men in America, than war and all the bad laws together. Gold-seekers, then, were sent to Virginia[20], men without resources and without discipline, whose restless and turbulent spirit troubled the infancy of the colony[21] and made its progress uncertain. There followed the artisans and farmers, a more moral and tranquil race, but one which rose at almost no point above the level of the lower classes of England[22]. No noble thought, no immaterial design presided over the founding of the new establishments. The colony was hardly created before slavery was introduced into it[23]; that was the cardinal fact destined to exert an immense influence on the character, the laws, and the whole future of the South.

Slavery, as we shall explain later, dishonors labor; it introduces idleness into society, and with idleness, ignorance and pride, poverty and luxury. It enervates the powers of the intellect and lulls human activity to sleep. The influence of slavery, combined with the English character, explains the mores and the social condition of the South.
Upon this same English ground, in the North, very different shadings appeared. Here I must be allowed some detail.

It is in the English colonies of the North — better known under the name of the New England States[24] — that the two or three principal ideas which today form the basis of the social theory of the United States were combined.

The principles of New England first spread to the neighboring states; thence they reached, by gradual steps, the most distant ones, and at last, if I may so put it, they *penetrated* the entire confederation. They now exert their influence beyond its borders, over the whole American world. The civilization of New England has been like those fires kindled on high places which, having spread their warmth around them, still tinge with their light the furthest horizon.
The founding of New England presented a new spectacle; everything in it was singular and original.

Almost all colonies have had for their first inhabitants men without education and without resources, whom poverty and bad conduct drove out of the country that had seen them born, or else greedy speculators and industrial entrepreneurs. There are colonies that cannot claim even such an origin: Santo Domingo was founded by pirates, and in our own day, the courts of England take charge of peopling Australia.

The emigrants who came to settle on the shores of New England all belonged to the comfortable classes of the mother country. Their gathering on American soil offered, from the start, the singular phenomenon of a society in which there were neither great lords nor common people, and, so to speak, neither poor nor rich. There was, proportionately, a greater mass of enlightenment spread among these men than within any European nation of our day. All of them — perhaps without a single exception — had received a fairly advanced education, and several had made themselves known in Europe by their talents and their learning. The other colonies had been founded by adventurers without families; the emigrants of New England brought with them admirable elements of order and morality; they went into the wilderness accompanied by their wives and children. But what distinguished them above all from every other group was the very purpose of their enterprise. It was not necessity that compelled them to leave their country; they left behind there a social position to be regretted and assured means of subsistence; nor did they cross over to the New World to better their condition or increase their wealth; they tore themselves away from the sweetness of home to obey a purely intellectual need; by exposing themselves to the inevitable miseries of exile, they sought to make *an idea* triumph.

The emigrants — or, as they so aptly called themselves, the *pilgrims* — belonged to that English sect to which the austerity of its principles had given the name of Puritan. Puritanism was not only a religious doctrine; on several points it merged with the most absolute democratic and republican theories. Hence its most dangerous adversaries. Persecuted by the government of the mother country, wounded in the rigor of their principles by the daily course of the society in which they lived, the Puritans sought out a land so barbarous and so abandoned by the world that they might still be permitted to live in their own fashion there and to pray to God in liberty.
A few citations will make the spirit of these pious adventurers better known than anything we could add of our own.

Nathaniel Morton, the historian of the early years of New England, opens his subject thus[25]: "I have always thought," he says, "that it was a sacred duty for us, whose fathers received so many and so memorable tokens of divine goodness in the establishment of this colony, to perpetuate the memory of it in writing. What we have seen, and what has been told us by our fathers, we must make known to our children, so that the generations to come may learn to praise the Lord; so that the lineage of Abraham His servant, and the sons of Jacob His chosen, may always keep the memory of the miraculous works of God (*Ps.* CV, 5, 6). They must know how the Lord brought His vine into the wilderness; how He planted it and drove away the heathen from it; how He prepared a place for it, drove deep its roots, and then let it spread and cover the land afar (*Ps.* LXXX, 15, 13); and not only that, but how He led His people to His holy tabernacle and established them upon the mountain of His inheritance (*Exod.* XV, 13). These things must be known, so that God may receive the honor due to Him, and that some rays of His glory may fall upon the venerable names of the saints whom He used as His instruments."
It is impossible to read this opening without being penetrated, in spite of oneself, by a religious and solemn impression; one seems to breathe in it an air of antiquity, a kind of biblical perfume.

The conviction that animates the writer raises his language. In your eyes, as in his, it is no longer a small band of adventurers going to seek their fortune across the seas; it is the seed of a great people that God is laying with His own hands upon a predestined land.
The author goes on, and paints the departure of the first emigrants in this manner[26]:

"Thus," he says, "did they leave that town (Delft-Haven) which had been for them a place of rest; yet they were calm; they knew they were pilgrims and strangers here below. They did not cleave to the things of the earth, but lifted their eyes toward heaven, their dear homeland, where God had prepared for them His holy city. They came at last to the port where the ship awaited them. A great number of friends who could not depart with them had at least wished to follow them that far. The night passed without sleep; it passed in outpourings of friendship, in pious discourse, in expressions full of a true Christian tenderness. The next day they went on board; their friends wished to accompany them even there; and it was then that deep sighs were heard, that tears were seen flowing from every eye, that long embraces and ardent prayers were heard, by which even strangers felt themselves moved. The signal for departure being given, they fell to their knees, and their pastor, raising to heaven eyes full of tears, commended them to the mercy of the Lord. They took leave at last of one another, and pronounced that farewell which, for many of them, was to be the last."

The emigrants numbered about one hundred and fifty, men, women, and children together. Their aim was to found a colony on the banks of the Hudson; but, after wandering long upon the Ocean, they were finally forced to land on the barren coasts of New England, on the spot where the town of Plymouth now stands. The rock on which the pilgrims stepped ashore is still pointed out[27].
"But before going further," says the historian I have already quoted, "let us consider for a moment the present condition of this poor people, and admire the goodness of God who saved them[28].

"They had now crossed the vast Ocean, they were arriving at the goal of their voyage, but they saw no friends to receive them, no dwelling to offer them shelter; it was the middle of winter, and those who know our climate know how harsh our winters are, and what furious storms then sweep our coasts. In such a season it is hard to cross known country, much more to settle on new shores. Around them appeared only a hideous and desolate wilderness, full of wild animals and savage men, of whose ferocity and number they knew nothing. The earth was frozen; the soil was covered with forests and brushwood. The whole had a barbarous aspect. Behind them they saw only the immense Ocean which separated them from the civilized world. For a little peace and hope they could turn their eyes only upward."

It must not be supposed that the piety of the Puritans was merely speculative, or that it stood apart from the conduct of human affairs. Puritanism, as I have said above, was almost as much a political theory as a religious doctrine. Hardly had the emigrants landed on this inhospitable shore which Nathaniel Morton has just described, when their first care was to organize themselves as a society. They at once passed an act which read[29]:

"We, whose names follow, who, for the glory of God, the advancement of the Christian faith, and the honor of our country, have undertaken to establish the first colony on these distant shores, do agree by these presents, by mutual and solemn consent, and before God, to form ourselves into a body of political society, in order to govern ourselves and to labor to fulfill our purposes; and by virtue of this contract, we agree to promulgate laws, acts, and ordinances, and to institute, according to need, magistrates to whom we promise submission and obedience."

This was happening in 1620. From that time on, the emigration did not cease. The religious and political passions which tore the British empire throughout the reign of Charles I drove fresh swarms of sectaries each year to the shores of America. In England, the focus of Puritanism continued to lie in the middle classes; and it was from the middle classes that most of the emigrants came. The population of New England grew rapidly, and while the hierarchy of ranks still classified men despotically in the mother country, the colony presented more and more the new spectacle of a society homogeneous in all its parts. Democracy, such as antiquity had not dared to dream of, broke free, full-grown and fully armed, from the midst of the old feudal society.

Content to be rid of seeds of disorder and elements of fresh revolutions, the English government watched this large emigration without displeasure. It even favored it with all its power, and seemed scarcely concerned with the destiny of those who came to American soil to seek refuge from the harshness of its laws. One might have said that it regarded New England as a region given over to the dreams of imagination, a place to be left to the free experiments of innovators.

The English colonies — and this was one of the principal causes of their prosperity — have always enjoyed more internal liberty and more political independence than the colonies of other peoples; but nowhere was this principle of liberty more fully applied than in the States of New England.
It was then generally admitted that the lands of the New World belonged to the European nation which had first discovered them.

In this way almost the entire coast of North America became an English possession toward the end of the sixteenth century. The means used by the British government to people these new domains were of various kinds: in certain cases the king submitted a portion of the New World to a governor of his choosing, charged with administering the country in his name and under his immediate orders[30]; this is the colonial system adopted in the rest of Europe. At other times he conceded to a single man or to a company the ownership of certain portions of country[31]. All civil and political powers were then concentrated in the hands of one or several individuals who, under the supervision and control of the crown, sold the land and governed the inhabitants. A third system, finally, consisted in granting to a certain number of emigrants the right to form themselves into a political society under the patronage of the mother country, and to govern themselves in everything not contrary to her laws.
This mode of colonization, so favorable to liberty, was put in practice only in New England[32].
As early as 1628[33], a charter of this nature was granted by Charles I to emigrants who came to found the colony of Massachusetts.

But, in general, charters were not granted to the New England colonies until long after their existence had become an accomplished fact. Plymouth, Providence, New Haven, the State of Connecticut, and that of Rhode Island[34] were founded without the cooperation and, in a sense, without the knowledge of the mother country. The new inhabitants, without denying the supremacy of the metropolis, did not draw the source of their powers from her; they constituted themselves, and it was only thirty or forty years afterward, under Charles II, that a royal charter came to legalize their existence.

It is therefore often difficult, on reading the first historical and legislative records of New England, to perceive the tie that binds the emigrants to the land of their ancestors. They are seen at every moment performing acts of sovereignty; they appoint their magistrates, make peace and war, set down police regulations, give themselves laws as if they answered to God alone[35].

Nothing is at once more singular and more instructive than the legislation of this period; it is there above all that one finds the key to the great social riddle which the United States present to the world today.
Among these records we shall single out, as one of the most characteristic, the code of laws which the small State of Connecticut gave itself in 1650[36].
The legislators of Connecticut[37] turn first to penal laws; and to compose them they conceive the strange idea of drawing from the sacred texts:
"Whoever shall worship any God other than the Lord," they begin, "shall be put to death."
Ten or twelve provisions of the same nature follow, taken *verbatim* from Deuteronomy, Exodus, and Leviticus.

Blasphemy, sorcery, adultery[38], rape, are punished by death; an insult given by a son to his parents is struck with the same penalty. Thus was the legislation of a rude and half-civilized people transferred into a society whose mind was enlightened and whose mores were mild: with the result that nowhere has the death penalty been more lavishly assigned by the laws, nor applied to fewer offenders.

The legislators, in this body of penal laws, are above all concerned with maintaining moral order and good mores in society; in this way they enter constantly into the domain of conscience, and there is hardly a sin that they fail to bring under the magistrate's censure. The reader will have noticed with what severity these laws struck adultery and rape. Plain commerce between unmarried persons is sternly repressed. The judge is left the right to inflict on the guilty one of three penalties: a fine, the lash, or marriage[39]; and if we are to believe the registers of the old New Haven courts, prosecutions of this sort were not rare; under the date of May 1, 1660, one finds a judgment imposing a fine and reprimand upon a young girl accused of having spoken some indiscreet words and of having allowed herself to be kissed[40]. The code of 1650 abounds in preventive measures. Idleness and drunkenness are severely punished[41]. Tavern-keepers may not supply more than a certain quantity of wine to each customer; the fine or the lash represses a simple lie when it may do harm[42]. Elsewhere the legislator, forgetting entirely the great principles of religious liberty he himself was claiming in Europe, compels attendance at divine service by fear of fines[43], and goes so far as to strike with severe penalties[44], and often with death, Christians who wish to worship God in any form other than his own[45]. At times, finally, the regulatory ardor that possesses him leads him to occupy himself with concerns most unworthy of him. Thus one finds in the same code a law that forbids the use of tobacco[46]. It must not, however, be forgotten that these bizarre or tyrannical laws were not imposed; that they were voted by the free concurrence of all those interested in them, and that the mores were even more austere and more puritanical than the laws. In the year 1649, a solemn association formed in Boston whose purpose was to prevent the worldly luxury of long hair[47] (*E*).

Such excesses, no doubt, do dishonor to the human spirit; they attest the inferiority of our nature, which, incapable of seizing firmly upon the true and the just, is reduced most often to choosing only between two extremes.

Beside this penal legislation, so strongly imprinted with the narrow sectarian spirit and with all the religious passions that persecution had inflamed and that still fermented in the depths of men's souls, stands placed — and in some sense chained together with it — a body of political laws which, drafted two hundred years ago, still seems far in advance of the spirit of liberty of our own age.

The general principles on which modern constitutions rest — those principles which most Europeans of the seventeenth century barely comprehended, and which were then only incompletely triumphant in Great Britain — are all recognized and established by the laws of New England: the people's participation in public affairs, the free voting of taxes, the responsibility of the agents of power, individual liberty and trial by jury, are there established as fact and without dispute.
These generative principles receive there an application and a development which no nation of Europe has yet ventured to give them.

In Connecticut, the electoral body consisted, from the outset, of the whole body of citizens, and this is readily understood[48]. Among this nascent people there reigned at the time an almost perfect equality of fortunes, and a still greater equality of minds[49].
In Connecticut, at that time, all the agents of the executive power were elected, including the governor of the State[50].

Citizens above the age of sixteen were obliged to bear arms; they formed a national militia which appointed its own officers, and which had to be ready at all times to march for the defense of the country[51].

It is in the laws of Connecticut, as in all those of New England, that one sees the birth and the development of that communal independence which still forms in our day, as it were, the principle and the life of American liberty.
Among most of the nations of Europe, political existence began in the upper regions of society and was communicated little by little, and always incompletely, to the various parts of the body social.
In America, on the contrary, one may say that the township was organized before the county, the county before the State, the State before the Union.

In New England, by 1650, the township is completely and definitively constituted. Around the township as an individual entity, interests, passions, duties, and rights gather and attach themselves firmly. Within the township one sees reign a real political life, active, fully democratic and republican. The colonies still recognize the supremacy of the metropolis; monarchy is the law of the State, but already the republic is fully alive within the township.

The township appoints its magistrates of every kind; it taxes itself; it assesses and levies the tax upon itself[52]. In the New England township the principle of representation is not admitted. It is in the public square and within the general assembly of the citizens that, as at Athens, affairs touching the common interest are handled.
When one carefully studies the laws promulgated during this first age of the American republics, one is struck by the legislator's grasp of government and by his advanced theories.

He plainly has a higher and more complete idea of society's duties toward its members than did the European legislators of that time, and he imposes on it obligations from which it still escaped elsewhere. In the States of New England, from the outset, the lot of the poor is secured[53]; severe measures are taken for the upkeep of the roads, and officials are appointed to supervise them[54]; the townships have public registers in which the results of general deliberations, deaths, marriages, and the births of citizens are inscribed[55]; clerks are charged with keeping these registers[56]; officers are entrusted with administering vacant successions, others with overseeing the boundaries of estates; several have as their principal function the maintenance of public tranquility in the township[57].

The law enters into a thousand particulars to anticipate and meet a host of social needs of which, even in our own day in France, one has only a confused sense. But it is in the provisions relating to public education that, from the very beginning, the original character of American civilization shows itself in its full light.

"Whereas," runs the law, "Satan, the enemy of the human race, finds in the ignorance of men his most powerful weapons, and whereas it is important that the lights brought by our fathers should not remain buried in their tombs; — whereas the education of children is one of the first interests of the State, with the assistance of the Lord...[58]" There follow provisions creating schools in every township and requiring the inhabitants, under penalty of heavy fines, to tax themselves for their support. Higher schools are founded in the same way in the more populous districts. The municipal magistrates are to see to it that parents send their children to the schools; they have the right to impose fines upon those who refuse; and if resistance continues, the society then puts itself in the place of the family, takes hold of the child, and removes from the fathers the rights that nature had given them but which they so ill knew how to use[59]. The reader will doubtless have noticed the preamble of these ordinances: in America, it is religion that leads to enlightenment; it is the observance of divine laws that leads man to liberty.

When, after casting this rapid glance at American society in 1650, one examines the condition of Europe — and particularly of the continent — at the same period, one is struck with a profound astonishment: on the continent of Europe, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, absolute royalty was triumphing everywhere upon the ruins of the oligarchic and feudal liberty of the Middle Ages. In the bosom of that brilliant and literary Europe, perhaps the idea of rights had never been more thoroughly disregarded; never had peoples lived less of a political life; never had notions of true liberty less occupied men's minds; and it was then that these same principles, unknown to the nations of Europe or despised by them, were proclaimed in the wilderness of the New World, and became the future emblem of a great people. The boldest theories of the human spirit were put into practice in this society so humble in appearance, with which no statesman would then have deigned to concern himself; left to the originality of its own nature, the imagination of man improvised there a legislation without precedent. In the bosom of that obscure democracy, which had not yet brought forth either generals or philosophers or great writers, a man could rise before a free people and offer, to the acclaim of all, this fine definition of liberty:

"Let us not be mistaken as to what we ought to understand by our independence. There is, in fact, a kind of corrupt liberty whose use is common to animals as well as to man, and which consists in doing whatever pleases one. This liberty is the enemy of all authority; it bears all rules impatiently; with it, we become inferior to ourselves; it is the enemy of truth and of peace; and God thought it His duty to rise up against it! But there is a civil and moral liberty which finds its strength in union, and which it is the very mission of authority to protect: it is the liberty of doing without fear all that is just and good. This holy liberty we must defend at every hazard, and, if need be, expose our lives for it[60]."

I have said enough to set in its true light the character of Anglo-American civilization. It is the product (and this point of departure must be kept constantly before the mind) of two perfectly distinct elements, which elsewhere have often been at war with each other, but which in America have been brought, so to speak, to incorporate themselves one with the other and to combine marvelously. I mean *the spirit of religion* and *the spirit of liberty*.
The founders of New England were at once ardent sectaries and exalted innovators. Held in the narrowest bonds of certain religious beliefs, they were free of all political prejudice.
From this come two distinct, but not contrary, tendencies, whose trace is easy to find everywhere — in mores as in laws.

Men sacrifice to a religious opinion their friends, their family, and their country; one would think them absorbed in the pursuit of that intellectual good which they have come to buy at so high a price. Yet one sees them seeking, with an almost equal ardor, material riches and moral satisfactions, heaven in the other world, and well-being and liberty in this one.
Under their hand, political principles, laws, and human institutions seem malleable things, which can be turned and combined at will.

Before them, the barriers that had imprisoned the society into which they were born give way; the old opinions which for centuries had directed the world vanish; an almost boundless career, a horizonless field opens before them: the human spirit rushes in; it traverses it in every direction; but, arrived at the limits of the political world, it stops of its own accord; it lays down, trembling, the use of its most formidable faculties; it abjures doubt; it renounces the need to innovate; it abstains even from lifting the veil of the sanctuary; it bows with respect before truths which it accepts without discussion.

Thus, in the moral world, everything is classified, coordinated, foreseen, decided in advance. In the political world, everything is agitated, contested, uncertain; in the one, passive obedience, though voluntary; in the other, independence, contempt of experience, and jealousy of all authority.
Far from harming one another, these two tendencies, in appearance so opposed, march in concert and seem to lend each other mutual support.

Religion sees in civil liberty a noble exercise of man's faculties; in the political world, a field given over by the Creator to the efforts of the intellect. Free and powerful within its sphere, satisfied with the place reserved for it, it knows that its empire is the better established for ruling only by its own forces and dominating, unaided, over hearts.

Liberty sees in religion the companion of its struggles and its triumphs; the cradle of its infancy, the divine source of its rights. It considers religion as the safeguard of mores; mores as the guarantee of laws and as the pledge of its own duration (*F*).
REASONS FOR CERTAIN SINGULARITIES PRESENTED BY THE LAWS AND CUSTOMS OF THE ANGLO-AMERICANS.
Some remnants of aristocratic institutions in the midst of the most complete democracy. — Why? — One must distinguish carefully between what is of Puritan origin and what is of English origin.

The reader must not draw too general or too absolute consequences from what precedes. The social condition, the religion, and the mores of the first emigrants no doubt exerted an immense influence on the destiny of their new homeland. Nevertheless, it did not lie within their power to found a society whose point of departure was located entirely within themselves; no man can wholly detach himself from the past; it happened that they mingled, whether voluntarily or unawares, with the ideas and usages proper to them, other usages and other ideas drawn from their upbringing and from the national traditions of their country.
When one would know and judge the Anglo-Americans of our day, one must therefore carefully distinguish between what is of Puritan origin and what is of English origin.

One often encounters in the United States laws or customs that stand in contrast with everything around them. These laws appear drafted in a spirit opposed to the dominant spirit of American legislation; these mores seem contrary to the whole social state. If the English colonies had been founded in an age of darkness, or if their origin were already lost in the night of time, the problem would be insoluble.
I shall cite a single example to make my meaning clear.

The civil and criminal legislation of the Americans knows only two means of action: *imprisonment* or *bail*. The first step in any proceeding consists in obtaining bail from the defendant, or, if he refuses, in having him incarcerated; afterward the validity of the claim or the gravity of the charges is debated.
It is plain that such legislation is directed against the poor, and favors only the rich.
The poor man does not always find bail, even in civil matters; and if he is forced to await justice in prison, his enforced inactivity soon reduces him to misery.

The rich man, on the contrary, always manages to escape imprisonment in civil matters; what is more, if he has committed a crime, he readily escapes the punishment that should reach him: having furnished bail, he disappears. One may therefore say that for him all the penalties the law inflicts come down to fines[61]. What could be more aristocratic than such a legislation?
In America, however, it is the poor who make the law, and they ordinarily reserve for themselves the greatest advantages of society.

The explanation of this phenomenon must be sought in England: the laws of which I speak are English[62]. The Americans have not changed them, though they are repugnant to the whole of their legislation and to the mass of their ideas.

The thing a people changes least, after its usages, is its civil legislation. Civil laws are familiar only to lawyers — that is, to those who have a direct interest in maintaining them as they are, good or bad, for the reason that they know them. The bulk of the nation scarcely knows them at all; it sees them act only in particular cases, grasps their tendency with difficulty, and submits to them without thinking about them.
I have cited one example; I could have pointed out many others.
The picture which American society presents is, if I may so put it, covered with a democratic layer, beneath which one sees, from time to time, the old colors of the aristocracy showing through.

paragraphs: The charter granted by the Crown of England in 1609 provided, among other clauses, that the colonists would pay to the Crown one-fifth of the produce of the gold and silver mines. See *Life of Washington*, by Marshall, vol. 1, pp. 18–66.

A great part of the new colonists, says Stith (*History of Virginia*), were dissolute young men of family whom their parents had shipped off to save them from an ignominious fate; former servants, fraudulent bankrupts, debauchees, and others of that sort, more fit to pillage and destroy than to consolidate the establishment, made up the rest. Seditious leaders easily drew this troop into every kind of extravagance and excess. See, on the history of Virginia, the following works: *History of Virginia from the first Settlements in the year 1624, by Smith.* *History of Virginia, by William Stith.* *History of Virginia from the earliest period, by Beverly*, translated into French in 1807.
It was only later that a certain number of wealthy English proprietors came to settle in the colony.
Slavery was introduced around the year 1620 by a Dutch ship which landed twenty negroes on the shores of the James River. See *Chalmers*.
The States of New England are those situated east of the Hudson; they are today six in number: 1° Connecticut; 2° Rhode Island; 3° Massachusetts; 4° Vermont; 5° New Hampshire; 6° Maine.
*New-England's Memorial*, p. 14; Boston, 1826. See also *Hutchinson's History*, vol. 2, p. 440.
*New-England's Memorial*, p. 22.

This rock has become an object of veneration in the United States. I have seen fragments of it carefully preserved in several cities of the Union. Does this not show clearly that the power and grandeur of man lie wholly in his soul? Here is a stone which the feet of a few wretches touched for a moment, and the stone becomes famous; it draws the gaze of a great people; its fragments are venerated, its dust is shared far and wide. What has become of the thresholds of so many palaces? Who concerns himself with them?
*New-England's Memorial*, p. 33.

The emigrants who created the State of Rhode Island in 1638, those who established themselves at New Haven in 1637, the first inhabitants of Connecticut in 1639, and the founders of Providence in 1640, all began equally by drafting a social contract which was submitted to the approval of all interested parties. *Pitkin's History*, pp. 42 and 47.
This was the case of the State of New York.
Maryland, the Carolinas, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey were such cases. See *Pitkin's History*, vol. 1, pp. 11–31.

See in the work entitled *Historical collection of state papers and other authentic documents intended as materials for an history of the United States of America, by Ebenezer Hazard, printed at Philadelphia MDCCXCII*, a great number of documents valuable for their content and authenticity, relating to the earliest age of the colonies — among others, the various charters granted them by the Crown of England, as well as the first acts of their governments. See also the analysis Mr. Story, justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, gives of all these charters in the introduction to his Commentary on the Constitution of the United States. It appears from all these documents that the principles of representative government and the outward forms of political liberty were introduced into all the colonies almost from their birth. These principles had received greater development in the north than in the south, but they existed everywhere.
See *Pitkin's History*, p. 35, vol. 1. See *the History of the colony of Massachusetts, by Hutchinson*, vol. 1, p. 9.

The inhabitants of Massachusetts, in establishing their criminal and civil laws, procedures, and courts of justice, had departed from the usages followed in England: in 1650, the king's name did not yet appear at the head of judicial writs. See Hutchinson, vol. 1, p. 452.
*Code of 1650*, p. 28 (Hartford 1830).

See also in Hutchinson's history, vol. 1, pp. 435–456, the analysis of the penal code adopted in 1648 by the colony of Massachusetts; this code is drafted on principles analogous to that of Connecticut.

Adultery was likewise punished with death by the law of Massachusetts, and Hutchinson, vol. 1, p. 441, says that several persons did in fact suffer death for this crime; he relates in this connection a curious anecdote which dates from the year 1663. A married woman had had a love affair with a young man; she became a widow and married him; several years passed: the public at last coming to suspect the intimacy that had once existed between the spouses, they were prosecuted criminally; they were thrown into prison, and it was nearly the case that they were both condemned to death.

*Code of 1650*, p. 48. It seems that judges sometimes pronounced these various penalties cumulatively, as may be seen in a decree handed down in 1643 (p. 114, *New-Haven antiquities*), which orders that Margaret Bedfort, convicted of having engaged in reprehensible acts, shall undergo the penalty of the lash, and that she shall be enjoined to marry Nicholas Jemmings, her accomplice.
*New-Haven antiquities*, p. 104. See also in Hutchinson's History, vol. 1, p. 435, several judgments as extraordinary as that one.
*Id.*

This was not peculiar to Connecticut. See among others the law passed September 13, 1644, in Massachusetts, condemning Anabaptists to banishment. *Historical collection of state papers*, vol. 1, p. 538. See also the law published October 14, 1656, against the Quakers: "Whereas," runs the law, "there has just arisen an accursed sect of heretics called Quakers..." There follow provisions condemning to a very heavy fine any captains of vessels who bring Quakers into the country. Quakers who succeed in entering will be whipped and shut up in a prison for hard labor. Those who defend their opinions will first be fined, then condemned to prison, and driven from the province. Same collection, vol. 1, p. 630.
In the penal law of Massachusetts, a Catholic priest who sets foot in the colony after having been driven out is punished with death.
*New-England's Memorial*, 316.
Constitution of 1638, p. 17.

As early as 1645, the general assembly of Rhode Island declared unanimously that the government of the State was a democracy, and that power rested with the body of free men, who alone had the right to make the laws and to oversee their execution. *Code of 1650*, p. 70.
*Pitkin's History*, p. 47.
Constitution of 1638, p. 12.
