J'imagine que quand la Chine sera ouverte aux Européens, ceux-ci y trouveront le plus beau modèle de centralisation administrative qui existe dans l'univers.

Un écrivain de talent qui, dans une comparaison entre les finances des États-Unis et celles de la France, a prouvé que l'esprit ne pouvait pas toujours suppléer à la connaissance des faits, reproche avec raison aux Américains l'espèce de confusion qui règne dans leurs budgets communaux, et après avoir donné le modèle d'un budget départemental de France, il ajoute: «Grâce à la centralisation, création admirable d'un grand homme, les budgets municipaux, d'un bout du royaume à l'autre, ceux des grandes villes comme ceux des plus humbles communes, ne présentent pas moins d'ordre et de méthode.» Voilà certes un résultat que j'admire; mais je vois la plupart de ces communes françaises, dont la comptabilité est si parfaite, plongées dans une profonde ignorance de leurs vrais intérêts, et livrées à une apathie si invincible, que la société semble plutôt y végéter qu'y vivre; d'un autre côté, j'aperçois dans ces mêmes communes américaines, dont les budgets ne sont pas dressés sur des plans méthodiques, ni surtout uniformes, une population éclairée, active, entreprenante; j'y contemple la société toujours en travail. Ce spectacle m'étonne; car à mes yeux le but principal d'un bon gouvernement est de produire le bien-être des peuples et non d'établir un certain ordre au sein de leur misère. Je me demande donc s'il ne serait pas possible d'attribuer à la même cause la prospérité de la commune américaine et le désordre apparent de ses finances, la détresse de la commune de France et le perfectionnement de son budget. En tous cas, je me défie d'un bien que je trouve mêlé à tant de maux, et je me console aisément d'un mal qui est compensé par tant de bien.

translation: In the following chapter, we propose to examine the form of government founded in America on the principle of the sovereignty of the people: what its means of action are, what its difficulties, advantages, and dangers.

A first difficulty presents itself. The United States have a complex constitution. One observes there two distinct societies, engaged in one another and, if I may so put it, nested one inside the other. One sees two governments wholly separate and almost independent: the first habitual and indefinite, answering to the daily needs of society; the second exceptional and circumscribed, applying only to certain general interests. They are, in a word, twenty-four small sovereign nations, whose aggregate forms the great body of the Union.

To examine the Union before studying the State is to set out on a road strewn with obstacles. The federal form of government in the United States appeared last. It was only a modification of the republic, a summary of political principles already diffused throughout the whole society before it, and subsisting there independently of it. The federal government, moreover, as I have just said, is only an exception; the government of the States is the common rule. A writer who tried to show the whole of such a picture before having shown its details would necessarily fall into obscurities or repetitions.

The great political principles that govern American society today were born and developed in the *State*; this cannot be doubted. It is therefore the State one must know to have the key to all the rest.

The States that make up the American Union today all present, as to the outward aspect of their institutions, the same spectacle. Political and administrative life is concentrated there in three centers of action, which might be compared to the various nerve centers that move the human body.
At the first level is the *township*; above it the *county*; and finally the *State*.
ON THE COMMUNAL SYSTEM IN AMERICA.

Why the author begins his examination of political institutions with the commune. — The commune is found among all peoples. — The difficulty of establishing and preserving communal liberty. — Its importance. — Why the author has chosen the communal organization of New England as the principal object of his examination.
It is not by chance that I examine the commune first.
The commune is the only association so well rooted in nature that wherever men are gathered together a commune forms of itself.

Communal society therefore exists among all peoples, whatever their customs and laws. Man makes kingdoms and creates republics; the commune seems to come directly from the hands of God. But while the commune has existed as long as there have been men, communal liberty is a rare and fragile thing. A people can always establish great political assemblies, because there is usually a certain number of men among them in whom enlightenment makes up, to some extent, for the lack of experience in affairs. The commune is composed of coarser elements, which often resist the action of the legislator. The difficulty of founding the independence of the communes, far from diminishing as nations grow more enlightened, increases with their enlightenment. A highly civilized society tolerates only with reluctance the experiments of communal liberty; it revolts at the sight of its many missteps, and despairs of success before having reached the experiment's final result.

Of all liberties, that of the townships, which is so difficult to establish, is also the most exposed to the encroachments of power. Left to themselves, township institutions could hardly contend against an enterprising and strong government; to defend themselves successfully, they must have attained their full development and have become interwoven with the ideas and habits of the nation. Thus, so long as township liberty has not entered into *mores*, it is easy to destroy, and it can enter into *mores* only after having long subsisted in the laws.

Communal liberty thus escapes, so to speak, the effort of man. It is rarely created; it is born, in a sense, of itself. It develops almost in secret within a half-barbarous society. It is the continual action of laws and mores, of circumstances, and above all of time, that succeeds in consolidating it. Of all the nations of the European continent, one can say there is not a single one that knows it.

And yet it is in the commune that the strength of free peoples resides. Communal institutions are to liberty what primary schools are to learning; they put it within reach of the people; they give them a taste for its peaceful use and accustom them to its exercise. Without communal institutions, a nation can give itself a free government, but it does not have the spirit of liberty. Passing passions, the interests of a moment, the chances of circumstance can give it the outward forms of independence; but despotism, driven back into the interior of the social body, sooner or later reappears at the surface.

To make the reader well understand the general principles on which the political organization of the commune and the county rest in the United States, I thought it useful to take a particular State as a model; to examine in detail what takes place there, and then to cast a rapid glance over the rest of the country.
I have chosen one of the States of New England.

The commune and the county are not organized in the same manner in all parts of the Union; yet it is easy to see that throughout the Union almost the same principles have presided over the formation of both.

Now it has seemed to me that these principles received in New England a more considerable development, and reached more distant consequences, than anywhere else. They therefore stand out there, so to speak, in higher relief, and lend themselves more readily to the foreigner's observation.

The communal institutions of New England form a complete and regular whole. They are old; they are strong by their laws, stronger still by their mores; they exercise a prodigious influence on the whole of society.
On all these grounds they deserve to attract our regard.
COMPASS OF THE COMMUNE.

The New England commune (*Township*) stands midway between the French canton and the French commune. It contains, in general, from two to three thousand inhabitants[67]; it is therefore not so extensive that all its inhabitants do not share more or less the same interests, and, on the other hand, it is populous enough that one can always be sure of finding within it the elements of a good administration.
COMMUNAL POWERS IN NEW ENGLAND.

The people, the source of all powers in the commune as elsewhere. — They transact the principal affairs themselves. — No municipal council. — The greater part of the communal authority concentrated in the hands of the *select-men*. — How the select-men act. — General assembly of the inhabitants of the commune (*Town-Meeting*). — Enumeration of all the communal officers. — Obligatory and salaried functions.

In the commune as everywhere else, the people are the source of social powers, but nowhere do they exercise their power more directly. The people in America are a master to be pleased to the outermost limits of the possible.

In New England, the majority acts through representatives when the general affairs of the State must be transacted. This had to be so; but in the commune, where legislative and governmental action stands closer to the governed, the principle of representation is not admitted. There is no municipal council; the body of electors, after having named its magistrates, directs them itself in everything that is not the pure and simple execution of the laws of the State[68].
This order of things is so contrary to our ideas, and so opposed to our habits, that it is necessary to furnish some examples here so that it may be properly understood.

The public functions are extremely numerous and much divided in the commune, as we shall see below; nevertheless the greater part of the administrative powers is concentrated in the hands of a small number of individuals elected each year, who are called select-men[69].

The general laws of the State have imposed on the select-men a certain number of obligations. They do not need the authorization of their constituents to fulfill them, and they cannot escape them without incurring personal responsibility. The law of the State charges them, for example, with drawing up, in their commune, the electoral lists; if they fail to do so, they make themselves guilty of an offense. But in all those matters left to the direction of the communal power, the select-men are the executors of the popular will, as among us the mayor is the executor of the deliberations of the municipal council. Most often they act on their private responsibility, and in practice merely follow out the consequences of principles the majority has previously laid down. But if they wish to introduce any change whatever into the established order, if they desire to undertake some new enterprise, they must go back to the source of their power. Suppose it is a matter of establishing a school: the select-men call the whole body of electors together on a given day, at a place fixed in advance; there they explain the need that is making itself felt; they set forth the means of meeting it, the money to be spent, the site to be chosen. The assembly, consulted on all these points, adopts the principle, fixes the place, votes the tax, and places the execution of its will in the hands of the select-men.

The select-men alone have the right to call the communal meeting (*town-meeting*), but they may be required to do so. If ten property owners conceive a new project and wish to submit it to the assent of the commune, they may demand a general convocation of the inhabitants; the select-men are obliged to comply, retaining only the right to preside over the assembly[70].

These political mores, these social usages are surely far removed from our own. I have at this moment no wish to judge them or to disclose the hidden causes that produce and quicken them; I limit myself to setting them out.

The select-men are elected every year in April or May. The communal assembly chooses at the same time a host of other municipal officers[71], assigned to certain important administrative details. Some, under the name of assessors, are to lay the tax; others, called collectors, are to gather it in. An officer called constable is charged with keeping order, watching over public places, and seeing to the material execution of the laws. Another, called the town clerk, registers all the deliberations and keeps note of the acts of civil status. A treasurer keeps the communal funds. Add to these officers an overseer of the poor, whose duty, very difficult to fulfill, is to see to the execution of legislation relating to the indigent; school committeemen, who direct public instruction; surveyors of highways, who take charge of all the details of the great and small road-system; and you will have the list of the principal agents of communal administration. But the division of functions does not stop there. One finds, among the municipal officers[72], parish commissioners who are to regulate the expenses of public worship; inspectors of several kinds, some charged with directing the citizens' efforts in case of fire; others with watching over the harvests; still others with provisionally settling the disputes that may arise over fences; and still others with overseeing the measuring of wood, or inspecting weights and measures.

There are in all nineteen principal functions in the commune. Each inhabitant is compelled, under penalty of fine, to accept these various functions; but on the other hand most of them are paid, so that poor citizens may devote their time to them without suffering loss. Moreover, the American system is not to give the officers a fixed salary. In general, each act of their office has a price, and they are compensated only in proportion to what they have done.
ON COMMUNAL EXISTENCE.

Each man is the best judge of what concerns him alone. — Corollary of the principle of the sovereignty of the people. — How the American communes apply these doctrines. — The New England commune, sovereign in all that pertains only to itself, subject in all the rest. — The obligation of the commune toward the State. — In France, the government lends its agents to the commune. — In America, the commune lends its own to the government.

I have said before that the principle of the sovereignty of the people hovers over the whole political system of the Anglo-Americans. Each page of this book will disclose some new application of that doctrine.
Among nations where the dogma of the sovereignty of the people prevails, every individual forms an equal portion of the sovereign and participates equally in the government of the State.
Each individual is therefore presumed as enlightened, as virtuous, as strong as any other of his fellows.
Why then does he obey society, and what are the natural limits of this obedience?

He obeys society not because he is inferior to those who direct it, or less capable than another man of governing himself; he obeys society because union with his fellows seems to him useful, and because he knows that this union cannot exist without a regulating power.

In all that concerns the duties of citizens toward one another, then, he has become a subject. In all that concerns himself alone, he has remained master: he is free, and accountable for his actions only to God. From this comes the maxim that the individual is the best, as he is the only, judge of his particular interest, and that society has the right to direct his actions only when it feels itself harmed by what he does, or when it has need to call upon his assistance.

This doctrine is universally admitted in the United States. I shall examine elsewhere what general influence it exercises even upon the ordinary actions of life; but at this moment I am speaking of the communes.
The commune, taken as a whole and in relation to the central government, is only an individual like another, to which the theory I have just laid out applies.

Communal liberty in the United States flows, therefore, from the very dogma of the sovereignty of the people; all the American republics have, more or less, recognized this independence; but among the peoples of New England, circumstances have particularly favored its development.

In that part of the Union, political life arose within the communes themselves; one could almost say that, at its origin, each of them was an independent nation. When later the kings of England claimed their share of sovereignty, they confined themselves to taking the central power. They left the commune in the state in which they found it; the communes of New England are now subjects, but at the outset they were not, or were barely so. They did not receive their powers; rather, they appear to have surrendered, in favor of the State, a portion of their independence — an important distinction, which the reader must keep in mind.
The communes are in general subject to the State only when it is a matter of an interest that I shall call *social*, that is to say, one they share with others.

In all that pertains to them alone, the communes have remained independent bodies; and among the inhabitants of New England, there is not one, I think, who would acknowledge in the government of the State the right to intervene in the direction of purely communal interests.

One sees, then, the communes of New England buy and sell, attack and defend themselves in the courts, burden their budget or relieve it, without any administrative authority whatever dreaming of opposing them[73].

As for social duties, they are bound to discharge them. Thus if the State needs money, the commune is not free to grant or refuse its concurrence[74]. If the State wishes to open a road, the commune is not free to close its territory to it. If it makes a police regulation, the commune must carry it out. If it wishes to organize instruction on a uniform plan throughout the country, the commune is bound to set up the schools required by the law[75]. We shall see, when we speak of administration in the United States, how and by whom the communes, in all these various cases, are compelled to obedience. Here I only wish to establish the existence of the obligation. The obligation is strict, but the government of the State, in imposing it, only decrees a principle; for its execution, the commune in general returns to all its rights of individuality. Thus the tax is, it is true, voted by the legislature, but it is the commune that apportions and collects it; the existence of a school is imposed, but it is the commune that builds it, pays for it, and runs it.
In France, the State's tax-collector levies the communal taxes; in America, the commune's tax-collector levies the State's tax.

Thus, with us, the central government lends its agents to the commune; in America, the commune lends its officers to the government. That alone makes one understand to what degree the two societies differ.
ON THE COMMUNAL SPIRIT IN NEW ENGLAND.

Why the New England commune attracts the affection of those who inhabit it. — The difficulty of creating a communal spirit in Europe. — Communal rights and duties combining in America to form that spirit. — The fatherland has more physiognomy in the United States than elsewhere. — How the communal spirit manifests itself in New England. — What happy effects it produces there.
In America, there exist not only communal institutions but also a communal spirit that sustains and quickens them.

The New England commune unites two advantages that wherever they are found vividly excite men's interest: independence and power. It acts, it is true, within a circle from which it cannot stray, but its movements within that circle are free. This independence alone would already give it a real importance, even if its population and extent did not assure it.

One must be persuaded that the affections of men in general are drawn only to where there is strength. Love of country is never long seen to prevail in a conquered land. The inhabitant of New England is attached to his commune not so much because he was born there as because he sees in that commune a free and strong corporation of which he is a part, and which is worth the trouble of trying to direct.

It often happens in Europe that the rulers themselves regret the absence of the communal spirit; for everyone agrees that the communal spirit is a great element of order and of public tranquility; but they do not know how to produce it. By making the commune strong and independent, they fear they will divide the social power and expose the State to anarchy. Now, take from the commune its strength and independence, and you will never find there anything but administered subjects and no citizens.

Note, moreover, an important fact: the New England commune is so constituted that it can serve as a hearth for vivid affections, and at the same time there is nothing beside it that strongly draws the ambitious passions of the human heart.

The county officers are not elected, and their authority is restricted. The State itself has only secondary importance; its existence is obscure and tranquil. Few men, in order to obtain the right to administer it, will agree to leave the center of their interests and disturb their existence.

The federal government confers power and glory upon those who direct it; but the men to whom it is given to influence its destinies are very few. The presidency is a high magistracy which one hardly reaches before an advanced age; and when one arrives at the other federal offices of a high order, it is in a manner by chance, and after having already made oneself famous in another career. Ambition cannot take them as the permanent goal of its efforts. It is in the commune, at the center of the ordinary relations of life, that the desire for esteem, the need for real interests, the taste for power and noise come to be concentrated. These passions, which so often trouble society, change their character when they can be exercised thus near the domestic hearth and in a sense within the family.

See with what art, in the American commune, care has been taken — if I may so put it — to *scatter* power, in order to interest more people in the public thing. Beyond the electors called from time to time to perform acts of government, how many varied functions, how many different magistrates, all of whom, within the circle of their attributions, represent the powerful corporation in whose name they act! How many men thus exploit communal power for their own benefit and take an interest in it for themselves!

The American system, while it shares municipal power among a great number of citizens, is also not afraid to multiply communal duties. In the United States it is thought, with reason, that love of country is a kind of worship to which men become attached by its practices.

In this way communal life makes itself felt, so to speak, at every moment; it manifests itself each day by the discharge of a duty or by the exercise of a right. This political existence imparts to society a continual but at the same time peaceful movement, which stirs it without troubling it.

Americans become attached to their town for a reason analogous to that which makes mountain dwellers love their country. Among them the fatherland has marked and characteristic features; it has more physiognomy than elsewhere.

The communes of New England have, in general, a happy existence. Their government is to their taste as well as of their choosing. Amid the profound peace and material prosperity that reign in America, the organs of municipal life are few. The direction of communal interests is easy. Moreover, the political education of the people was long ago completed — or rather, they arrived already instructed on the soil they occupy. In New England the division of ranks does not exist even in memory; no portion of the commune is therefore tempted to oppress the other, and the injustices, which strike only isolated individuals, are lost in the general contentment. Even were the government to present defects — and certainly it is easy to point them out — they do not strike the eye, because the government really emanates from the governed, and it is enough for it to move along after a fashion for a kind of paternal pride to protect it. Besides, they have nothing to compare it with. England once reigned over the colonies as a whole, but the people always directed communal affairs. The sovereignty of the people in the commune is therefore not only an old state but a primitive one.

The inhabitant of New England is attached to his commune because it is strong and independent; he takes an interest in it because he shares in directing it; he loves it because he has nothing in it to complain of regarding his lot. In it he places his ambition and his future; he involves himself in each of the incidents of communal life. In this restricted sphere within his reach, he tries his hand at governing society; he accustoms himself to the forms without which liberty proceeds only by revolutions, takes their spirit into himself, develops a taste for order, comes to understand the harmony of powers, and gathers at last clear and practical ideas about the nature of his duties and the extent of his rights.
OF THE COUNTY IN NEW ENGLAND.
The New England county, analogous to the French *arrondissement*. — Created with a purely administrative interest in view. — Has no representation. — Is administered by non-elective officers.

The American county has much in common with the French *arrondissement*. An arbitrary boundary has been traced for it, as for the latter; it forms a body whose various parts have no necessary tie among themselves, and to which no affection, no memory, no community of existence attaches. It is created only with a purely administrative interest in view.

The commune was too small in extent for the administration of justice to be enclosed within it. The county therefore forms the first judicial center. Each county has a court of justice[76], a sheriff to execute the decrees of the tribunals, and a prison to contain the criminals.

There are needs felt in nearly equal measure by all the communes of a county; it was natural that a central authority should be charged with providing for them. In Massachusetts, this authority resides in the hands of a certain number of magistrates designated by the governor of the State on the advice[77] of his council[78].

The administrators of the county have only a limited and exceptional power, which applies only to a very small number of cases provided for in advance. The State and the commune suffice for the ordinary course of things. These administrators do no more than draw up the county budget; the legislature votes it[79]. There is no assembly that directly or indirectly represents the county.
The county, then, has, properly speaking, no political existence.

One observes in most American constitutions a twofold tendency that leads legislators to divide the executive power and to concentrate the legislative power. The New England commune has, in itself, a principle of existence of which it cannot be stripped; but this life would have to be created fictively in the county, and the usefulness of doing so has not been felt. All the communes united have only one representation, the State, the center of all the national powers; outside the communal and the national action, one may say there are only individual forces.
OF ADMINISTRATION IN NEW ENGLAND.

In America, one does not see the administration. — Why. — Europeans think to found liberty by taking from the social power some of its rights; Americans, by dividing its exercise. — Almost all administration, properly so called, is contained within the commune, and divided among the communal officers. — One sees no trace of an administrative hierarchy, either in the commune or above it. — Why this is so. — How it nevertheless comes about that the State is administered in a uniform manner. — Who is charged with making the administrations of the commune and the county obey the law. — Of the introduction of judicial power into administration. — Consequence of the principle of election extended to all officers. — Of the justice of the peace in New England. — By whom appointed. — Administers the county. — Secures the administration of the communes. — Court of sessions. — How it acts. — Who brings cases before it. — The right of inspection and complaint, scattered like all the administrative functions. — Informers encouraged by the sharing of fines.

What strikes the European most as he travels through the United States is the absence of what we call government or administration. In America one sees written laws; one perceives their daily execution; everything moves around you, and nowhere does one discover the motor. The hand that directs the social machine escapes one at every moment.

Nevertheless, just as all peoples are obliged, in order to express their thoughts, to have recourse to certain grammatical forms constitutive of human languages, so all societies, in order to subsist, are constrained to submit to a certain measure of authority, without which they fall into anarchy. This authority may be distributed in different ways, but it must always be found somewhere.
There are two ways to lessen the force of authority in a nation.

The first is to weaken power at its very source, by taking from society the right or the capacity to defend itself in certain cases: to weaken authority in this fashion is, in general, what is called in Europe founding liberty.

There is a second way to lessen the action of authority: this consists not in stripping society of some of its rights, or in paralyzing its efforts, but in dividing the use of its forces among several hands; in multiplying officers, attributing to each of them all the power he needs to do what he is intended to execute. Among certain peoples, this division of social powers may still lead to anarchy; in itself, however, it is not anarchic. By dividing authority in this way, one renders its action, it is true, less irresistible and less dangerous, but one does not destroy it.

The revolution in the United States was produced by a mature and reflective taste for liberty, and not by a vague and undefined instinct of independence. It did not rest on passions for disorder; on the contrary, it advanced together with the love of order and of legality.

In the United States, then, it has not been pretended that man in a free country has the right to do everything; on the contrary, more varied social obligations have been imposed on him than elsewhere. They have not had the idea of attacking the power of society at its source and of disputing its rights; they have confined themselves to dividing its exercise. In this way they sought to bring it about that authority should be great and the officer small, in order that society might continue to be well regulated and yet remain free.
There is no country in the world where the law speaks so absolute a language as in America, and there is none either where the right to apply it is divided among so many hands.

The administrative power in the United States offers nothing in its constitution that is either central or hierarchical; that is why one does not see it. The power exists, but one does not know where to find its representative.
We have seen above that the communes of New England were not under tutelage. They take care, then, of their own particular interests themselves.
It is also the municipal officers who, most often, are charged with seeing to the execution of the general laws of the State, or with executing them themselves[80].

Independently of the general laws, the State sometimes makes general police regulations; but ordinarily it is the communes and the communal officers who, jointly with the justices of the peace and according to local needs, regulate the details of social existence, and promulgate the prescriptions relating to public health, good order, and the morals of the citizens[81].
Finally, it is the municipal officers who, of themselves and without needing any external impulse, provide for those unforeseen needs that societies often experience[82].
It results from what we have just said that in Massachusetts the administrative power is almost entirely enclosed within the commune[83]; but it is there divided among many hands.
In the French commune there is, properly speaking, only one administrative officer, the mayor.
We have seen that there are at least nineteen of them in the New England commune.

These nineteen officers generally do not depend on one another. The law has carefully traced a circle of action around each of these magistrates. Within that circle they are all-powerful in fulfilling the duties of their office, and they answer to no communal authority.

If one looks beyond the commune, one barely sees the trace of an administrative hierarchy. It sometimes happens that the county officers reform the decision taken by the communes or by the communal magistrates[84]; but in general one may say that the administrators of the county do not have the right to direct the conduct of the administrators of the commune[85]. They command them only in things that have to do with the county.

The magistrates of the commune and those of the county are bound, in a very small number of cases provided for in advance, to communicate the results of their operations to the officers of the central government[86]. But the central government is not represented by any single man charged with making general police regulations or ordinances for the execution of the laws; with habitually communicating with the administrators of the county and the commune; with inspecting their conduct, directing their acts, and punishing their faults.
There is, therefore, nowhere a center to which the rays of administrative power converge.
How, then, is it managed that society is conducted on a more or less uniform plan? How can one make the counties and their administrators, the communes and their officers, obey?

In the States of New England, the legislative power extends to more objects than among us. The legislator penetrates, so to speak, into the very heart of administration; the law descends to minute details; it prescribes at once the principles and the means of applying them; it thus encloses the secondary bodies and their administrators within a multitude of strict and rigorously defined obligations.

It follows that, if all the secondary bodies and all the officers conform to the law, society proceeds in a uniform manner in all its parts; but it remains to know how one can force the secondary bodies and their officers to conform to the law.
One may say, generally speaking, that society has at its disposal only two means to oblige officers to obey the laws:
It can entrust to one of them the discretionary power to direct all the others and to dismiss them in case of disobedience;
Or it can charge the courts with inflicting judicial penalties on offenders.
One is not always free to take one or the other of these means.

The right to direct the officer presupposes the right to dismiss him if he does not follow the orders transmitted to him, or to raise him in rank if he fulfills all his duties with zeal. Now, one can neither dismiss nor promote an elected magistrate. It is in the nature of elective functions to be irrevocable until the end of the mandate. In reality, the elected magistrate has nothing to expect or to fear except from the electors, when all the public functions are the product of election. There can therefore exist no true hierarchy among the officers, since one cannot unite in the same man the right to give orders and the right to repress disobedience effectively, and since one cannot join to the power of commanding that of rewarding and punishing.
The peoples who introduce election into the secondary workings of their government are therefore necessarily led to make great use of judicial penalties as a means of administration.

This is not apparent at first glance. Rulers regard it as a first concession to make the functions elective, and as a second concession to subject the elected magistrate to the rulings of judges. They equally dread these two innovations; and since they are more pressed to make the first than the second, they grant election to the officer and leave him independent of the judge. And yet one of these two measures is the only counterweight one can give to the other. Take care: an elective power not subjected to a judicial power escapes sooner or later from all control, or is destroyed. Between the central power and the elected administrative bodies, only the courts can serve as intermediary. They alone can force the elected officer to obedience without violating the right of the elector.

The extension of the judicial power in the political world ought therefore to be correlative with the extension of the elective power. If these two things do not go together, the State ends by falling into anarchy or into servitude.
It has been remarked at all times that judicial habits prepared men rather poorly for the exercise of administrative power.
The Americans took from their fathers, the English, the idea of an institution that has no analogue in what we know on the continent of Europe: that of the justices of the peace.

The justice of the peace stands midway between the man of the world and the magistrate, the administrator and the judge. He is an enlightened citizen, but not necessarily versed in the knowledge of the laws. So he is charged only with policing society — something that demands more good sense and uprightness than learning. The justice of the peace brings into administration, when he takes part in it, a certain taste for forms and for publicity, which makes him a most inconvenient instrument for despotism; but he does not show himself there the slave of those legal superstitions that make magistrates little capable of governing.

The Americans have made the institution of justices of the peace their own, while removing the aristocratic character that distinguished it in the mother country. The governor of Massachusetts[87] appoints, in every county, a certain number of justices of the peace, whose functions are to last seven years[88].
Moreover, from among these justices of the peace he designates three who form, in each county, what is called the *court of sessions*.

The justices of the peace take part individually in the public administration. Sometimes they are charged, concurrently with elected officers, with certain administrative acts[89]; sometimes they form a tribunal before which the magistrates summarily accuse the citizen who refuses to obey, or the citizen denounces the offenses of the magistrates. But it is in the court of sessions that the justices of the peace exercise the most important of their administrative functions.
The court of sessions meets twice a year in the seat of the county. It is the body that, in Massachusetts, is charged with maintaining the greater number[90] of the public officers in obedience[91].
One must bear in mind that in Massachusetts the court of sessions is at once an administrative body, properly so called, and a political tribunal.

We have said that the county had only an administrative existence. It is the court of sessions that itself directs the small number of interests pertaining at the same time to several communes, or to all the communes of the county at once, and which therefore cannot be charged to any one of them in particular[92].

When it is a matter of the county, then, the duties of the court of sessions are purely administrative; and if it often introduces into its manner of proceeding the forms of justice, it is only a means of informing itself[93] and a guarantee it gives to those it administers. But when the administration of the communes must be assured, it acts almost always as a judicial body, and only in a few rare cases as an administrative body.
The first difficulty that presents itself is to make the commune itself, an almost independent power, obey the general laws of the State.

We have seen that the communes are required to appoint each year a certain number of magistrates who, under the name of assessors, apportion the tax. A commune attempts to escape the obligation of paying the tax by not appointing the assessors. The court of sessions condemns it to a heavy fine[94]. The fine is collected from the persons of all the inhabitants. The sheriff of the county, an officer of justice, executes the decree. Thus in the United States power seems jealous to hide itself carefully from view. The administrative command almost always veils itself under the judicial mandate; it is only the more powerful for it, having on its side the nearly irresistible force that men accord to the legal form.

This procedure is easy to follow and is understood without difficulty. What is demanded of the commune is, in general, clear and definite; it consists in a simple, non-complex fact, in a principle and not an application of detail[95]. But the difficulty begins when it is a matter of making not the commune but the communal officers obey.
All the reprehensible actions a public officer can commit fall, in the end, into one of these categories:
He can do, without ardor and without zeal, what the law commands of him.
He can fail to do what the law commands of him.
And finally, he can do what the law forbids him.
A court cannot reach the conduct of an officer except in the last two cases. There must be a positive and assessable fact to serve as the basis of judicial action.
Thus, if the select-men fail to fulfill the formalities required by the law in case of a communal election, they may be condemned to a fine[96].
But when the public officer fulfills his duty without intelligence; when he obeys the prescriptions of the law without ardor and without zeal, he is entirely beyond the reach of a judicial body.

The court of sessions, even when invested with its administrative attributions, is powerless in this case to compel him to fulfill all his obligations. Only the fear of dismissal can prevent these quasi-offenses, and the court of sessions is not the source of the communal powers; it cannot dismiss officers it does not appoint.

To make certain, moreover, that there is negligence and lack of zeal, one would have to exercise continual surveillance over the inferior officer. Now, the court of sessions sits only twice a year; it does not inspect, it judges the reprehensible facts that are brought before it.
The arbitrary power to dismiss public officers alone can guarantee, on their part, that kind of enlightened and active obedience which judicial repression cannot impose upon them.
In France, we look for this last guarantee in the *administrative hierarchy*; in America, it is sought in *election*.
To sum up in a few words what I have just set forth:
If the public officer of New England commits a *crime* in the exercise of his functions, the ordinary courts are *always* called upon to do justice on him.

If he commits an *administrative fault*, a purely administrative tribunal is charged with punishing him, and when the matter is serious or urgent, the judge does what the officer ought to have done[97].

Finally, if the same officer makes himself guilty of one of those imperceptible offenses that human justice can neither define nor measure, he appears annually before a tribunal without appeal, which can suddenly reduce him to impotence; his power escapes him along with his mandate.
This system surely contains great advantages in itself, but it encounters in its execution a practical difficulty that must be pointed out.

I have already remarked that the administrative tribunal, called the court of sessions, did not have the right to inspect the communal magistrates; it can act, to use a term of law, only when a matter has been brought before it. There lies the delicate point of the system.

The Americans of New England have not instituted any prosecuting office attached to the court of sessions[98], and one may understand that it would have been difficult for them to establish one. Had they confined themselves to placing a prosecuting magistrate in the seat of each county, without giving him agents in the communes, why would this magistrate have been better informed of what was happening in the county than the members of the court of sessions themselves? If they had given him agents in each commune, they would have centralized in his hands the most formidable of powers, that of administering judicially. Besides, laws are the daughters of habits, and nothing of the kind existed in English legislation.
The Americans have therefore divided the right of inspection and complaint as they have all the other administrative functions.

The members of the grand jury are required by the terms of the law to inform the court before which they act of offenses of every kind that may be committed in their county[99]. There are certain great administrative offenses that the ordinary prosecutor must pursue *ex officio*[100]; most often, the obligation of having offenders punished is imposed on the fiscal officer charged with collecting the proceeds of the fine; thus the communal treasurer is charged with prosecuting most of the administrative offenses committed under his eyes.
But it is above all to private interest that American legislation appeals[101]; it is the great principle one finds again and again in studying the laws of the United States.
American legislators show little confidence in human honesty; but they always suppose man to be intelligent. They therefore rely most often on personal interest for the execution of the laws.
When an individual is positively and presently injured by an administrative offense, one understands indeed that personal interest will guarantee the complaint.

But it is easy to foresee that, in the case of a legal prescription which, while useful to society, is not of an utility presently felt by any individual, each will hesitate to take the role of accuser. In this way, and by a kind of tacit accord, the laws might well fall into desuetude.
Reduced to this extremity by their system, the Americans are obliged to interest the informers by calling them in certain cases to a share of the fines[102].
A dangerous means, which secures the execution of the laws by degrading mores.
Above the magistrates of the county there is, properly speaking, no administrative power, but only a governmental power.
GENERAL IDEAS ON ADMINISTRATION IN THE UNITED STATES.

In what the States of the Union differ from one another by their system of administration. — Communal life less active and less complete as one descends toward the south. — The power of the magistrate then becomes greater, that of the elector smaller. — Administration passes from the commune to the county. — States of New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania. — Administrative principles applicable to the whole Union. — Election of public officers or irremovability of their functions. — Absence of hierarchy. — Introduction of judicial means into administration.
I announced before that, after examining in detail the constitution of the commune and the county in New England, I would cast a general glance over the rest of the Union.
There are communes and a communal life in every State; but in none of the confederated States does one meet with a commune identically like that of New England.

As one descends toward the south, one perceives that communal life becomes less active; the commune has fewer magistrates, fewer rights, fewer duties; the population does not exercise so direct an influence on affairs; the communal assemblies are less frequent and extend to fewer objects. The power of the elected magistrate is therefore comparatively greater and that of the elector smaller; the communal spirit is less awake and less powerful[103].

These differences begin to be perceptible in the State of New York; they are already very evident in Pennsylvania; but they become less striking as one advances toward the northwest. Most of the emigrants who go to found the States of the northwest come from New England, and they carry the administrative habits of the mother country into their adopted country. The commune of Ohio has much in common with the commune of Massachusetts.

We have seen that in Massachusetts the principle of public administration is found in the commune. The commune is the hearth where men's interests and affections come together. But it ceases to be so as one descends toward States where enlightenment is not so universally diffused, and where, consequently, the commune offers fewer guarantees of wisdom and fewer elements of administration. As one moves away from New England, then, communal life passes, so to speak, to the county. The county becomes the great administrative center and forms the intermediary power between the government and the ordinary citizens.

I have said that in Massachusetts the affairs of the county are directed by the court of sessions. The court of sessions is composed of a certain number of magistrates named by the governor and his council. The county has no representation, and its budget is voted by the national legislature.

In the great State of New York, on the contrary, in the State of Ohio, and in Pennsylvania, the inhabitants of each county elect a certain number of deputies; the gathering of these deputies forms an assembly representative of the county[104].

The county assembly possesses, within certain limits, the right of taxing the inhabitants; it constitutes, in this respect, a true legislature; it is at the same time the body that administers the county, directs in many cases the administration of the communes, and confines their powers within much narrower limits than in Massachusetts.

Such are the principal differences that the constitution of the commune and the county presents in the various confederated States. If I wished to go down to the details of the means of execution, I would have many other dissimilarities still to point out. But my goal is not to give a course in American administrative law.

I have said enough, I think, to give an understanding of the general principles on which administration in the United States rests. These principles are variously applied; they yield more or fewer consequences depending on the locality; but at bottom they are everywhere the same. The laws vary; their physiognomy changes; one and the same spirit animates them.

The commune and the county are not everywhere constituted in the same way; but one can say that the organization of the commune and the county in the United States rests everywhere on this same idea: that each man is the best judge of what concerns himself alone, and the most capable of providing for his particular needs. The commune and the county are therefore charged with watching over their special interests. The State governs; it does not administer. One meets exceptions to this principle, but not a contrary principle.
The first consequence of this doctrine has been to have all the administrators of the commune and county chosen by the inhabitants themselves, or at least chosen exclusively from among them.

The administrators being everywhere elected, or at least irremovable, it has followed that nowhere has it been possible to introduce the rules of hierarchy. There have therefore been almost as many independent officers as there are functions. The administrative power has thus been disseminated into a multitude of hands.

The administrative hierarchy existing nowhere, and the administrators being elected and irremovable until the end of their mandate, the obligation has followed of introducing the courts more or less into administration. Hence the system of fines, by means of which the secondary bodies and their representatives are compelled to obey the laws. One finds this system from one end of the Union to the other.
Moreover, the power to repress administrative offenses, or to perform administrative acts when needed, has not been granted in all the States to the same judges.
The Anglo-Americans drew the institution of justices of the peace from a common source; one finds it in all the States. But they have not always made the same use of it.

Everywhere the justices of the peace take part in the administration of the communes and counties[105], either by administering themselves or by repressing certain administrative offenses; but in most States the most serious of these offenses are submitted to the ordinary courts.

Thus, then: election of the administrative officers, or irremovability of their functions; absence of administrative hierarchy; introduction of judicial means into the secondary government of society — such are the principal traits by which one recognizes American administration, from Maine to the Floridas.
There are some States in which one begins to perceive the traces of an administrative centralization. The State of New York is the most advanced in this direction.

In the State of New York, the officers of the central government exercise, in certain cases, a sort of surveillance and control over the conduct of the secondary bodies[106]. In certain others, they form a kind of court of appeal for deciding affairs[107]. In the State of New York, judicial penalties are less employed than elsewhere as an administrative means. The right to prosecute administrative offenses is also placed there in fewer hands[108].

The same tendency is slightly noticeable in some other States[109]. But in general one may say that the salient character of public administration in the United States is to be prodigiously decentralized.
OF THE STATE.
I have spoken of the communes and of administration; it remains for me to speak of the State and of the government.

Here I may hasten, without fear of not being understood; what I have to say is already laid out in written constitutions which anyone can easily procure[110]. These constitutions themselves rest on a simple and rational theory.
Most of the forms they indicate have been adopted by all constitutional peoples; they have thus become familiar to us.
I have therefore only to give a brief exposition here. Later I shall try to judge what I am going to describe.
LEGISLATIVE POWER OF THE STATE.
Division of the legislative body into two chambers. — Senate. — House of Representatives. — Different attributions of these two bodies.
The legislative power of the State is entrusted to two assemblies; the first generally bears the name of senate.
The senate is habitually a legislative body; but sometimes it becomes an administrative and judicial body.

It takes part in administration in several ways, according to the various constitutions[111]; but it is by participating in the choice of officers that it ordinarily penetrates the sphere of the executive power.
It participates in the judicial power by ruling on certain political offenses, and also sometimes by deciding certain civil cases[112].
Its members are always few in number.

The other branch of the legislature, generally called the house of representatives, takes no part in the administrative power, and shares in the judicial power only by accusing public officers before the senate.
The members of the two chambers are subject, almost everywhere, to the same conditions of eligibility. Both are elected in the same way and by the same citizens.

The only difference between them is that the mandate of the senators is in general longer than that of the representatives. The latter rarely remain in office more than a year; the former usually sit for two or three years.

By granting the senators the privilege of being named for several years, and renewing them in series, the law has taken care to maintain within the legislators a nucleus of men already accustomed to affairs, who may exercise a useful influence on the newcomers.

By dividing the legislative body into two branches, the Americans did not, then, mean to create a hereditary assembly and another elective; they did not intend to make one of them an aristocratic body and the other a representative of democracy; their goal was not, either, to give in the first a support to power, while leaving to the second the interests and passions of the people.

To divide the legislative force, thereby to slow the movement of political assemblies, and to create a court of appeal for the revision of the laws — such are the only advantages that flow from the present constitution of two chambers in the United States.

Time and experience have brought home to the Americans that, even when reduced to these advantages, the division of legislative powers is still a necessity of the first order. Alone among all the united republics, Pennsylvania had first tried to establish a single assembly. Franklin himself, carried away by the logical consequences of the dogma of the sovereignty of the people, had taken part in this measure. It was soon necessary to change the law and to constitute the two chambers. The principle of the division of the legislative power thus received its final consecration; one may henceforth consider as a demonstrated truth the necessity of sharing legislative action among several bodies. This theory, almost unknown to the ancient republics, introduced into the world almost by chance, like most great truths, ignored by several modern peoples, has finally passed as an axiom into the political science of our day.
OF THE EXECUTIVE POWER OF THE STATE.
What the governor is in an American State. — What position he occupies vis-à-vis the legislature. — What his rights and duties are. — His dependence on the people.
The executive power of the State has the governor for its representative.
It is not by chance that I have used the word representative. The governor of the State does indeed represent the executive power; but he exercises only some of its rights.

The supreme magistrate called the governor is placed beside the legislature as a moderator and a counsellor. He is armed with a suspensive veto which allows him to arrest or at least to slow its movements at his discretion. He sets before the legislative body the needs of the country, and makes known the means he judges useful to employ to meet them; he is the natural executor of its will in all undertakings that concern the whole nation[113]. In the absence of the legislature, he must take all measures fit to safeguard the State from violent shocks and unforeseen dangers.
The governor unites in his hands all the military power of the State. He is the commander of the militia and chief of the armed force.

When the power of opinion, which men have agreed to grant to the law, is set at naught, the governor advances at the head of the material force of the State; he breaks resistance and restores the accustomed order.

Moreover, the governor does not enter into the administration of the communes and the counties, or at least he takes part in it only very indirectly through the appointment of justices of the peace, whom he cannot afterward dismiss[114].
The governor is an elective magistrate. Care is generally taken to elect him only for one or two years, so that he always remains in strict dependence on the majority that produced him.
OF THE POLITICAL EFFECTS OF ADMINISTRATIVE DECENTRALIZATION IN THE UNITED STATES.

Distinction to be established between governmental centralization and administrative centralization. — In the United States, no administrative centralization, but very great governmental centralization. — Some unfortunate effects that result in the United States from the extreme administrative decentralization. — Administrative advantages of this order of things. — The force that administers society, less regulated, less enlightened, less learned, far greater than in Europe. — Political advantages of the same order of things. — In the United States, the fatherland makes itself felt everywhere. — Support that the governed lend to the government. — Provincial institutions more necessary as the social state becomes more democratic. — Why.
Centralization is a word repeated incessantly in our day, and whose meaning, in general, nobody tries to make precise.
There exist, however, two very distinct kinds of centralization, which it is important to know well.
Certain interests are common to all parts of the nation, such as the framing of general laws and the relations of the people with foreigners.
Other interests are special to certain parts of the nation, such as, for example, communal enterprises.
To concentrate in one same place or in one same hand the power of directing the first is to found what I shall call governmental centralization.
To concentrate in the same manner the power of directing the second is to found what I shall call administrative centralization.

There are points at which these two kinds of centralization come to merge. But by taking, in their general sweep, the objects that fall more particularly into the domain of each, one easily distinguishes them.

One understands that governmental centralization acquires an immense force when it joins itself to administrative centralization. In this way it accustoms men to make a complete and continual abstraction from their own will; to obey not once and on one point but in everything and every day. Not only does it then subdue them by force, but it also takes them by their habits; it isolates them and then seizes them one by one in the common mass.
These two kinds of centralization lend each other a mutual help, they attract one another; but I could not bring myself to believe that they are inseparable.

Under Louis XIV, France saw the greatest governmental centralization that can be conceived, since the same man made the general laws and had the power to interpret them, represented France abroad, and acted in her name. *L'État, c'est moi*, he said; and he was right.
And yet under Louis XIV there was much less administrative centralization than in our day.

In our own time, we see a power, England, in which governmental centralization is carried to a very high degree: the State seems to move there like one man; at its will it raises immense masses, gathers them, and brings to bear at any point it wishes the whole effort of its power.
England, which has done such great things for the last fifty years, has no administrative centralization.
For my part, I cannot conceive that a nation can live, much less prosper, without a strong governmental centralization.

But I think that administrative centralization is fit only to enervate the peoples who submit to it, because it tends ceaselessly to diminish among them the spirit of the city. Administrative centralization succeeds, it is true, in gathering at a given time, and in a given place, all the available forces of the nation, but it harms the reproduction of forces. It makes them triumph on the day of battle, and in the long run diminishes their power. It can thus contribute admirably to the passing greatness of one man, but not to the durable prosperity of a people.

Let us take care: when one says that a State cannot act because it has no centralization, one almost always speaks, without knowing it, of governmental centralization. The German Empire, it is repeated, has never been able to draw from its forces all the use possible. Agreed. But why? Because national force has never been centralized in it; because the State has never been able to make its general laws obeyed; because the separate parts of this great body have always had the right or the possibility of refusing their concurrence to the depositaries of the common authority, even in matters that concerned all the citizens; in other words, because there was no governmental centralization. The same remark applies to the Middle Ages: what produced all the miseries of feudal society was that the power not only to administer but to govern was shared among a thousand hands and broken up in a thousand ways; the absence of all governmental centralization then prevented the nations of Europe from advancing energetically toward any goal.

We have seen that in the United States there is no administrative centralization. One barely finds a trace of hierarchy there. Decentralization has been pushed there to a degree that no European nation could endure, I think, without a deep uneasiness, and which even produces unfortunate effects in America. But in the United States governmental centralization exists to the highest degree. It would be easy to prove that the national power is more concentrated there than in any of the old monarchies of Europe. Not only is there in each State only one body that makes the laws; not only is there in it only one power that can create political life around it; but care has generally been taken not to gather there numerous district or county assemblies, for fear that those assemblies might be tempted to overstep their administrative attributions and hamper the workings of the government. In America, the legislature of each State has before it no power capable of resisting it. Nothing can stop it in its course — neither privileges nor local immunity, nor personal influence, nor even the authority of reason, for it represents the majority, which claims to be the sole organ of reason. It has therefore no other limits, in its action, than its own will. Beside it, and at its hand, is placed the representative of the executive power, who, with the help of material force, is to constrain the malcontents to obedience.
Weakness is found only in certain details of governmental action.

The American republics have no permanent armed force to suppress minorities; but the minorities have never been reduced, up to the present, to making war, and the need of an army has not yet been felt. The State most often uses the officers of the commune or the county to act upon the citizens. Thus, for example, in New England, it is the commune's assessor who apportions the tax; the commune's collector who levies it; the commune's treasurer who forwards the proceeds to the public treasury, and the complaints that arise are submitted to the ordinary courts. Such a manner of collecting the tax is slow and cumbersome; it would hamper at every moment the workings of a government that had great pecuniary needs. It is, in general, to be desired that, for all that is essential to its life, a government should have its own officers, chosen by it, removable by it, and rapid forms of proceeding. But it will always be easy for the central power, organized as it is in America, to introduce, as needs arise, more energetic and more efficacious means of action.

It is not, then, as is often repeated, because there is no centralization in the United States that the republics of the New World will perish; far from being insufficiently centralized, one may affirm that the American governments are too much so; I shall prove it later. The legislative assemblies engulf each day some fragment of the governmental powers; they tend to gather them all to themselves, as the Convention had done. The social power, thus centralized, changes hands ceaselessly, because it is subordinated to the popular power. It often happens that it lacks wisdom and foresight, because it can do everything. There lies the danger for it. It is therefore on account of its very strength, and not as a result of its weakness, that it is threatened with perishing one day.
Administrative decentralization produces in America several different effects.

We have seen that the Americans had almost entirely isolated the administration from the government; in this they seem to me to have overstepped the limits of sound reason; for order, even in secondary matters, is still a national interest[115].

The State having no administrative officers of its own, set in fixed posts on the various points of its territory, to which it might give a common impulse, it follows that the State rarely attempts to establish general police regulations. Now, the need for such regulations is keenly felt. The European often notices their absence. The appearance of disorder that reigns on the surface persuades him, at first sight, that there is complete anarchy in society; only by examining the depths of things does he undeceive himself.

Certain undertakings concern the whole State, and yet cannot be carried out, because there is no national administration to direct them. Abandoned to the care of the communes and the counties, surrendered to elected and temporary agents, they produce no result, or produce nothing durable.

The partisans of centralization in Europe maintain that the governmental power administers localities better than they could administer themselves: that may be true, when the central power is enlightened and the localities are not, when it is active and they are inert, when it has the habit of acting and they the habit of obeying. It is also to be understood that the more centralization increases, the more this double tendency grows, and the more capacity on the one hand and incapacity on the other become evident.
But I deny that it is so when the people are enlightened, awake to their interests, and accustomed to think upon them as they are in America.
I am persuaded, on the contrary, that in that case the collective force of the citizens will always be more potent in producing social well-being than the authority of the government.

I admit that it is difficult to point with certainty to the means of awakening a sleeping people, to give it passions and enlightenment it does not have; to persuade men that they must attend to their own affairs is, I do not deny, an arduous undertaking. It would often be less difficult to interest them in the details of the etiquette of a court than in the repair of their common house.
But I think also that when the central administration pretends to replace entirely the free concurrence of those primarily concerned, it deceives itself or means to deceive you.

A central power, however enlightened, however learned one may imagine it, cannot by itself embrace all the details of the life of a great people. It cannot, because such a task exceeds human capacities. When it wishes by its own care alone to create and set in motion so many varied mechanisms, it contents itself with a very incomplete result, or wears itself out in useless efforts.

Centralization succeeds easily, it is true, in subjecting men's outward actions to a certain uniformity that one comes in the end to love for its own sake, independently of the things to which it is applied; like those devotees who adore the statue, forgetting the divinity it represents. Centralization manages without trouble to impress a regular gait upon current affairs; to govern with skill the details of social policing; to repress slight disorders and small offenses; to maintain society in a *status quo* that is properly neither decay nor progress; to keep in the social body a kind of administrative drowsiness which the administrators are accustomed to call good order and public tranquility[116]. It excels, in a word, in preventing, not in doing. When it is a matter of stirring society deeply, or of impressing on it a rapid course, its force abandons it. As soon as its measures require the concurrence of individuals, one is then quite surprised at the weakness of that immense machine; it suddenly finds itself reduced to impotence.

It sometimes happens then that centralization tries, in despair, to call the citizens to its aid; but it says to them: You will act as I wish, as long as I wish, and exactly in the sense I wish. You will take charge of these details without aspiring to direct the whole; you will work in the dark, and you will judge my work later by its results. It is not on such conditions that one obtains the concurrence of the human will. It requires liberty in its movements, responsibility in its acts. Man is so made that he prefers to stand still than to walk without independence toward a goal he does not know.
I will not deny that in the United States one often regrets not finding those uniform rules which seem ceaselessly to watch over each of us.
One meets there from time to time with great examples of social insouciance and incuria. Here and there appear coarse blotches that seem in complete discord with the surrounding civilization.
Useful enterprises that demand continual care and rigorous exactness to succeed often end by being abandoned; for in America as elsewhere the people proceed by momentary efforts and sudden impulses.

The European, accustomed to finding always at hand an officer who meddles in nearly everything, accommodates himself with difficulty to the different workings of communal administration. In general one may say that the small details of social policing, which make life sweet and convenient, are neglected in America; but the essential guarantees for man in society exist there as much as anywhere else. Among the Americans, the force that administers the State is far less regulated, less enlightened, less learned, but a hundred times greater than in Europe. There is no country in the world where men make, on the whole, so many efforts to create social well-being. I know of no people that has succeeded in establishing schools so numerous and so effective; places of worship more in harmony with the religious needs of the inhabitants; communal roads better maintained. One must not, then, look in the United States for uniformity and permanence of views, minute care for details, perfection of administrative procedures[117]; what one finds there is the image of force, somewhat savage, it is true, but full of power; of life, accompanied by accidents, but also by movement and effort.

I will admit, moreover, if anyone wishes, that the villages and counties of the United States would be more usefully administered by a central authority placed far from them, which would remain a stranger to them, than by officers drawn from their midst. I will grant, if pressed, that there would reign more security in America, that a wiser and more judicious use would be made of social resources, if the administration of the whole country were concentrated in a single hand. The *political* advantages that the Americans draw from the system of decentralization would still make me prefer it to the contrary system.

What does it matter to me, after all, that there should be an authority always on its feet, watching that my pleasures be tranquil, flying ahead of my steps to ward off every danger, without my even needing to think of it; if this authority, at the same time as it removes the slightest thorns in my path, is absolute master of my liberty and my life; if it monopolizes movement and existence to such a degree that everything must languish around it when it languishes, that everything must sleep when it sleeps, that everything must perish if it dies?

There are nations of Europe in which the inhabitant regards himself as a kind of settler, indifferent to the destiny of the place he inhabits. The greatest changes occur in his country without his concurrence; he does not even know precisely what has happened; he suspects it; he has heard the event told by chance. What is more, the fortune of his village, the policing of his street, the fate of his church and parsonage do not touch him; he thinks all these things concern him in no way, and that they belong to a powerful stranger called the government. For himself, he enjoys these goods as a usufructuary, without spirit of ownership and without any idea of improvement. This self-disinterest goes so far that, if his own safety or that of his children is finally compromised, instead of seeking to ward off the danger, he folds his arms to wait for the whole nation to come to his aid. This man, moreover, though he has made so complete a sacrifice of his free will, loves obedience no more than another. He submits, it is true, to the good pleasure of a clerk; but he likes to defy the law like a defeated enemy as soon as force withdraws. So one sees him oscillate ceaselessly between servitude and license.

When nations have reached this point, they must modify their laws and their mores, or they will perish, for the source of public virtues is, as it were, dried up: one finds there still subjects, but no longer citizens.

I say that such nations are prepared for conquest. If they do not disappear from the scene of the world, it is because they are surrounded by nations similar or inferior to themselves; it is because there still remains in their bosom a sort of undefinable instinct of country, some unthinking pride in the name it bears, some vague recollection of past glory, which, without attaching itself precisely to anything, is enough to imprint on them at need a conservative impulse.

One would be wrong to take comfort in the thought that certain peoples have made prodigious efforts to defend a fatherland in which they lived, so to speak, as strangers. Look closely, and you will see that religion was almost always then their principal mainspring.
The duration, the glory, or the prosperity of the nation had become for them sacred dogmas, and in defending their fatherland they were also defending that holy city of which they were all citizens.

The Turkish populations have never taken any part in the direction of the affairs of society; they have nevertheless accomplished immense undertakings, so long as they saw the triumph of Mahomet's religion in the conquests of the sultans. Today their religion is fading away; despotism alone remains to them: they fall.

Montesquieu, in attributing to despotism a force of its own, did it, I think, an honor it did not deserve. Despotism, by itself, can maintain nothing that is durable. When one looks closely, one perceives that what long made absolute governments prosper was religion and not fear.

One will never meet, whatever one does, with any real power among men except in the free concurrence of wills. Now, there is in the world only patriotism, or religion, that can make the universality of citizens march for long toward the same goal.

It does not lie within the power of laws to rekindle beliefs that are dying; but it does lie within the power of laws to interest men in the destinies of their country. It is within the power of laws to awaken and direct that vague instinct of country which never abandons the heart of man, and, by binding it to the thoughts, the passions, the habits of each day, to make of it a reflective and durable sentiment. And let it not be said that it is too late to attempt it; nations do not grow old in the same manner as men. Each generation born in their bosom is like a new people offering itself to the hand of the legislator.

What I most admire in America is not the *administrative* effects of decentralization, but its *political* effects. In the United States, the fatherland makes itself felt everywhere. It is an object of concern from the village up to the whole Union. The inhabitant becomes attached to each of his country's interests as to his own. He glories in the glory of the nation; in the successes she obtains he believes he recognizes his own work, and he rises with them; he rejoices in the general prosperity from which he profits. He has for his fatherland a sentiment analogous to that which one feels for one's family, and it is still by a kind of egoism that he takes an interest in the State.
