Often the European sees in the public officer only force; the American sees in him right. One may say, then, that in America man never obeys man, but justice or the law.

So he has formed of himself an opinion often exaggerated, but almost always salutary. He trusts without fear in his own strength, which seems to him sufficient for everything. A private individual conceives the idea of some enterprise; even were this enterprise to have a direct bearing on the well-being of society, it does not occur to him to address himself to the public authority to obtain its concurrence. He makes his plan known, offers to carry it out, calls individual forces to the aid of his own, and struggles hand to hand against every obstacle. Often, no doubt, he succeeds less well than the State would in his place; but in the long run, the general result of all individual undertakings far exceeds what the government could do.

Because the administrative authority is placed beside the administered, and represents them in a sense themselves, it excites neither jealousy nor hatred. Because its means of action are limited, each feels he cannot rely on it alone.

Thus, when the administrative power intervenes within the circle of its attributions, it does not find itself abandoned to itself as in Europe. One does not believe that the duties of private persons have ceased because the representative of the public has come to act. Each, on the contrary, guides, supports, and upholds him.

The action of individual forces joining itself to the action of social forces, one often arrives at doing what the most concentrated and most energetic administration would be in no condition to execute (*I*).
I could cite many facts in support of what I am putting forward; but I would rather take only one, and choose the one I know best.
In America, the means placed at the disposal of authority for discovering crimes and pursuing criminals are few.

There is no administrative police; passports are unknown. The judicial police, in the United States, cannot be compared to ours; the officers of the prosecution are few; they do not always have the initiative of pursuit; the inquiry is rapid and oral. I doubt, however, that in any country crime escapes punishment so seldom.
The reason is that everyone believes himself concerned to furnish the proofs of the offense and to seize the offender.

During my stay in the United States I saw the inhabitants of a county in which a great crime had been committed form spontaneously committees with the aim of pursuing the guilty man and handing him over to the courts.

In Europe the criminal is an unfortunate man fighting to steal his head away from the agents of power; the population is, so to speak, a spectator at the struggle. In America he is an enemy of the human race, and he has all humanity against him.
I believe provincial institutions useful to all peoples; but none seems to me to have a more real need of these institutions than that whose social state is democratic.
In an aristocracy, one is always sure of maintaining a certain order in the midst of liberty.
The rulers having much to lose, order is a matter of great interest to them.
One can equally say that in an aristocracy the people are sheltered from the excesses of despotism, because there are always organized forces ready to resist the despot.
A democracy without provincial institutions possesses no guarantee against such ills.
How can a multitude be made to bear liberty in great matters when it has not learned to use it in small ones?
How resist tyranny in a country where each individual is weak, and where individuals are united by no common interest?
Those who fear license, and those who dread absolute power, must therefore equally desire the gradual development of provincial liberties.
I am convinced, moreover, that there are no nations more exposed to falling under the yoke of administrative centralization than those whose social state is democratic.
Several causes concur to this result, but among them this one:

The permanent tendency of these nations is to concentrate all governmental power in the hands of the only power that directly represents the people, because beyond the people one no longer perceives anything but equal individuals merged in a common mass.

Now, when one and the same power is already invested with all the attributes of government, it is very difficult for it not to seek to penetrate into the details of administration, and it does not fail in the long run to find an opportunity to do so. We have witnessed this among ourselves.
There were, in the French Revolution, two movements in opposite directions which must not be confused: one favorable to liberty, the other favorable to despotism.

Under the old monarchy, the king alone made the law; below the sovereign power were placed some half-destroyed remains of provincial institutions. These provincial institutions were incoherent, ill-ordered, often absurd. In the hands of the aristocracy they had sometimes been instruments of oppression.

The Revolution declared itself at once against royalty and against the provincial institutions. It confounded in a single hatred everything that had preceded it, absolute power and what could temper its rigors; it was at once republican and centralizing.

This double character of the French Revolution is a fact of which the friends of absolute power have taken hold with great care. When you see them defending administrative centralization, do you suppose they are laboring on behalf of despotism? Not at all: they are defending one of the great conquests of the Revolution (*K*). In this way one can remain popular and an enemy of the rights of the people; a hidden servant of tyranny and an avowed lover of liberty.
I have visited the two nations that have developed to the highest degree the system of provincial liberties, and I have listened to the voice of the parties that divide these nations.

In America I found men who secretly aspired to destroy the democratic institutions of their country. In England I found others who openly attacked the aristocracy; I did not meet a single one who did not regard provincial liberty as a great good.
I saw, in these two countries, the ills of the State imputed to an infinity of various causes, but never to communal liberty.

I heard the citizens attribute the greatness or the prosperity of their country to a multitude of reasons; but I heard them all place in the first rank, and classify at the head of all other advantages, provincial liberty.

Shall I believe that men so divided by nature that they cannot agree on religious doctrines or on political theories, fall into agreement on a single fact — the one they are best able to judge, since it passes each day before their eyes — and that this fact is in error?
It is only the peoples who have few or no provincial institutions who deny their utility; that is to say, only those who have no knowledge of the thing speak ill of it.

paragraphs: The number of communes in the State of Massachusetts in 1830 was 305; the number of inhabitants was 610,014; which gives an average of about 2,000 inhabitants per commune.

The same rules are not applicable to the large communes. These have in general a mayor and a municipal body divided into two branches; but this is an exception which must be authorized by a law. See the law of 22 February 1822, regulating the powers of the city of Boston. *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 2, p. 588. This applies to the large cities. It also frequently happens that the small towns are subject to a particular administration. There were in 1832 104 communes administered in this manner in the State of New York (*William's-Register*).

Three are elected in the smallest communes, nine in the largest. See *The Town officer*, p. 186. See also the principal laws of Massachusetts relating to the select-men: Law of 20 February 1786, vol. 1, p. 219;—of 24 February 1796, vol. 1, p. 488;—7 March 1801, vol. 2, p. 45;—16 June 1795, vol. 1, p. 475;—12 March 1808, vol. 2, p. 186;—28 February 1787, vol. 1, p. 302;—22 June 1797, vol. 1, p. 539.
See *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 1, p. 150; law of 22 March 1796.
*Ibid.*

All these officers really exist in practice. For the details of the functions of all these communal officers, see the book entitled *Town officer, by Isaac Goodwin*; *Worcester*, 1827; and the collection of the general laws of Massachusetts in 3 vols. Boston, 1823.
See *Laws of Massachusetts*, law of 23 March 1796, vol. 1, p. 250.
*Ibid.*, law of 20 February 1786, vol. 1, p. 217.
See the same collection, law of 25 June 1789, and 8 March 1827, vol. 1, p. 367, and vol. 3, p. 179.
See the law of 14 February 1821, *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 1, p. 551.
See the law of 20 February 1819, *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 2, p. 494.
The governor's council is an elective body.
See the law of 2 November 1791, *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 1, p. 61.

See the *Town officer*, particularly under the words *select-men*, *assessors*, *collectors*, *schools*, *surveyors of highways*... One example among a thousand: the State forbids traveling without a motive on Sunday. It is the *tythingmen*, communal officers, who are specially charged with seeing to the execution of the law. See the law of 8 March 1792, *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 1, p. 410. The select-men draw up the electoral lists for the election of the governor, and transmit the result of the vote to the secretary of the republic. Law of 24 February 1796, *id.*, vol. 1, p. 488.

Example: the *select-men* authorize the construction of sewers, designate the places where slaughterhouses may be made, and where certain kinds of trade whose proximity is harmful may be carried on. See the law of 7 June 1785, vol. 1, p. 193.
Example: the *select-men* watch over public health in the case of contagious diseases, and take the necessary measures jointly with the justices of the peace. Law of 22 June 1797, vol. 1, p. 539.

I say *almost*, because there are several incidents of communal life that are regulated either by the justices of the peace in their individual capacity, or by the justices of the peace assembled as a body at the seat of the county. Example: it is the justices of the peace who grant licenses. See the law of 28 February 1787, vol. 1, p. 297.

Example: a license is granted only to those who present a certificate of good conduct given by the select-men. If the select-men refuse to give this certificate, the person may complain to the justices of the peace assembled in court of session, and the latter may grant the license. See the law of 12 March 1808, vol. 2, p. 136. The communes have the right to make regulations (*by-laws*), and to enforce these regulations by fines whose rate is fixed; but these regulations must be approved by the court of sessions. See the law of 23 March 1786, vol. 1, p. 284.

In Massachusetts the administrators of the county are often called upon to assess the acts of the administrators of the commune; but it will be seen below that they engage in this examination as a judicial power, and not as an administrative authority.
Example: the communal committees of schools are required annually to make a report on the state of the school to the secretary of the republic. See the law of 10 March 1827, vol. 3, p. 183.
We shall see below what the governor is; I must say at present that the governor represents the executive power of the whole State.
See the constitution of Massachusetts, ch. II, section I, paragraph 9; ch. III, paragraph 3.

One example among many: a stranger arrives in a commune from a country ravaged by a contagious disease. He falls ill. Two justices of the peace may, with the advice of the select-men, order the sheriff of the county to transport him elsewhere and to watch over him. Law of 23 June 1797, vol. 1, p. 540. In general, the justices of the peace intervene in all the important acts of administrative life, and give them a semi-judicial character.

I say *the greater number*, because indeed certain administrative offenses are referred to the ordinary courts. Example: when a commune refuses to provide the funds necessary for its schools, or to appoint the committee of schools, it is condemned to a very considerable fine. It is the court called *supreme judicial court*, or the court of *common pleas*, that pronounces this fine. See law of 10 March 1827, vol. 3, p. 190. *Id.* When a commune fails to provide stores of munitions of war. Law of 21 February 1822, vol. 2, p. 570.

The justices of the peace take part, in their individual capacity, in the government of the communes and counties. The most important acts of communal life are generally performed only with the concurrence of one of them.

The objects that have to do with the county, and with which the court of sessions concerns itself, may be reduced to these: 1º the erection of prisons and courts of justice; 2º the draft of the budget of the county (it is the legislature of the State that votes it); 3º the apportionment of these taxes thus voted; 4º the distribution of certain patents; 5º the laying out and repair of the county roads.
Thus, when a road is in question, the court of sessions decides almost all the difficulties of execution with the help of the jury.
See law of 20 February 1786, vol. 1, p. 117.

There is an indirect means of making the commune obey. The communes are bound by law to keep their roads in good condition. If they neglect to vote the funds required for this maintenance, the communal magistrate in charge of the roads is then authorized to levy the necessary money on his own. As he is himself responsible to private persons for the bad state of the roads, and may be sued by them before the court of sessions, one is assured that he will use against the commune the extraordinary right the law gives him. Thus, by threatening the officer, the court of sessions forces the commune to obedience. See the law of 5 March 1787, vol. 2, p. 305.
Law of Massachusetts, vol. 2, p. 45.

Example: if a commune persists in not appointing assessors, the court of sessions appoints them, and the magistrates thus chosen are invested with the same powers as elected magistrates. See the law cited above of 20 February 1787.
I say *attached to the court of sessions*. There is a magistrate who fulfills near the ordinary courts some of the functions of the prosecution.
The grand jurors are required, for example, to inform the courts of the bad state of the roads. Law of Massachusetts, vol. 1, p. 308.
If, for example, the treasurer of the county does not furnish his accounts. Law of Massachusetts, vol. 1, p. 406.

One example among a thousand: a private person damages his vehicle or injures himself on a poorly maintained road; he has the right to claim damages before the court of sessions from the commune or the county charged with the road. Law of Massachusetts, vol. 1, p. 309.

In case of invasion or insurrection, when the communal officers neglect to furnish the militia with the necessary supplies and munitions, the commune may be condemned to a fine of 200 to 500 dollars (1,000 to 2,780 francs). One conceives well that in such a case it may happen that no one has the interest or the desire to take the role of accuser. So the law adds: "All citizens shall have the right to prosecute the punishment of such offenses, and half of the fine shall belong to the prosecutor." See law of 6 March 1810, vol. 2, p. 236. The same provision is found very frequently in the laws of Massachusetts. Sometimes it is not the private person whom the law incites in this way to prosecute the public officers; it is the officer whom it encourages in this way to have the disobedience of private persons punished. Example: an inhabitant refuses to do the share of work assigned to him on a great road. The surveyor of the roads must prosecute him; and if he secures his condemnation, half of the fine returns to him. See the laws cited above, vol. 1, p. 308.

For the details, see *The Revised statutes* of the State of New York, in part I, ch. XI, entitled *Of the powers, duties and privileges of towns.* Of the rights, obligations and privileges of the communes, vol. 1, p. 336-364. See in the collection entitled *Digest of the laws of Pensylvania*, the words *Assessors*, *Collectors*, *Constables*, *Overseers of the poor*, *Supervisor of highway*. And in the collection entitled *Acts of a general nature of the state of Ohio*, the law of 25 February 1834, relating to the communes, p. 412. And then the particular provisions relating to the various communal officers, such as: *Township's Clerks*, *Trustees*, *Overseers of the poor*, *Fence-Viewers*, *Appraisers of property*, *Township's Treasure*, *Constables*, *Supervisors of highways*.

See *Revised statutes of the state of New-York*, part I, ch. XI, vol. 1, p. 340. *Id.*, ch. XII; *Id.*, p. 336. *Id.*, *Acts of the state of Ohio*. Law of 25 February 1824, relating to the county commissioners, p. 262. See *Digest of the laws of Pensylvania*, under the words *County-States, and levies*, p. 170. In the State of New York, each commune elects one deputy, and this same deputy participates at the same time in the administration of the county and that of the commune.

There are even States in the South where the magistrates of the county-courts are charged with all the details of administration. See *The Statute of the state of Tennessee* under the articles *Judiciary*, *Taxes*...

Example: the direction of public instruction is centralized in the hands of the government. The legislature names the members of the University, called regents; the governor and lieutenant-governor of the State are necessarily part of it. (*Revised statutes*, vol. 1, p. 456.) The regents of the University visit the colleges and academies every year, and make an annual report to the legislature; their oversight is not illusory, for these particular reasons: the colleges, in order to become constituted bodies (corporations) that can buy, sell, and possess, need a charter; now this charter is granted by the legislature only on the advice of the regents. Each year the State distributes to the colleges and academies the interest from a special fund created for the encouragement of studies. It is the regents who distribute this money. See ch. XV, Public Instruction, *Revised statutes*, vol. 1, p. 455. Each year the commissioners of public schools are required to send a report on the situation to the superintendent of the republic. *Id.*, p. 488. A similar report must be made to him annually on the number and state of the poor. *Id.*, p. 681.

When someone considers himself injured by certain acts emanating from the commissioners of schools (these are communal officers), he can appeal to the superintendent of primary schools, whose decision is final. *Revised statutes*, vol. 1, p. 487. One finds here and there, in the laws of the State of New York, provisions analogous to those I have just cited as examples. But in general these attempts at centralization are weak and unproductive. In giving the great officers of the State the right to oversee and to direct the inferior agents, they have not been given the right to reward or punish them. The same man is almost never charged at once with giving the order and with repressing disobedience; he has therefore the right to command, but not the capacity to make himself obeyed. In 1830, the superintendent of schools, in his annual report to the legislature, complained that several commissioners of schools had not, in spite of his notices, transmitted to him the accounts they owed him. "If this omission is repeated," he added, "I shall be reduced to prosecuting them, under the terms of the law, before the competent tribunals."

Example: the officer of the prosecution in each county (*district-attorney*) is charged with pursuing the recovery of all fines amounting to more than 50 dollars, unless the right has been expressly given by the law to another magistrate. *Revised statutes*, part I, ch. X, vol. 1, p. 383.

There are several traces of administrative centralization in Massachusetts. Example: the committees of the communal schools are required to make a report each year to the secretary of state. *Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 1, p. 367.
See, at the end of the volume, the text of the constitution of New York.
In Massachusetts, the senate is not invested with any administrative function.
As in the State of New York. See the constitution at the end of the volume.

In practice, it is not always the governor who carries out the undertakings the legislature has conceived; it often happens that the latter, at the same time that it votes a principle, names special agents to oversee its execution.
In several States, the justices of the peace are not named by the governor.

The authority that represents the State, even when it does not administer itself, ought not, I think, to divest itself of the right to inspect local administration. Suppose, for example, that an agent of the government, placed in a fixed post in each county, could refer to the judicial power offenses committed in the communes and in the county; would not order be more uniformly observed, without local independence being compromised? Now, nothing of the kind exists in America. Above the courts of the counties there is nothing; and these courts are, so to speak, only by chance brought to take cognizance of the administrative offenses they are to repress.

China seems to me to offer the most perfect emblem of the kind of social well-being that a very centralized administration can furnish to the peoples who submit to it. Travelers tell us that the Chinese have tranquility without happiness, industry without progress, stability without strength, and material order without public morality. With them, society always proceeds well enough, never very well. I imagine that when China is opened to the Europeans, they will find there the finest model of administrative centralization that exists in the universe.

A writer of talent who, in a comparison between the finances of the United States and those of France, has shown that wit cannot always make up for knowledge of the facts, reproaches the Americans, with reason, for the kind of confusion that reigns in their communal budgets, and after having given the model of a departmental budget of France, he adds: "Thanks to centralization, the admirable creation of a great man, the municipal budgets, from one end of the kingdom to the other, those of the great cities as well as those of the humblest communes, present no less order and method." That is surely a result I admire; but I see most of these French communes, whose accounting is so perfect, plunged in a deep ignorance of their true interests, and given over to such an invincible apathy that society seems rather to vegetate there than to live; on the other hand, I perceive in these same American communes, whose budgets are not drawn up on methodical plans, nor above all on uniform ones, a population enlightened, active, enterprising; I behold there a society always at work. This spectacle astonishes me; for in my eyes the principal goal of a good government is to produce the well-being of peoples and not to establish a certain order in the midst of their misery. I ask myself, therefore, whether it would not be possible to attribute to the same cause both the prosperity of the American commune and the apparent disorder of its finances, the distress of the French commune and the perfection of its budget. In any case, I distrust a good that I find mingled with so many ills, and I easily console myself for an ill that is compensated by so much good.

items.title: DU POUVOIR JUDICIAIRE AUX ÉTATS-UNIS ET DE SON ACTION SUR LA SOCIÉTÉ POLITIQUE
paragraphs: J'ai cru devoir consacrer un chapitre à part au pouvoir judiciaire. Son importance politique est si grande qu'il m'a paru que ce serait la diminuer aux yeux des lecteurs que d'en parler en passant.

Il y a eu des confédérations ailleurs qu'en Amérique; on a vu des républiques autre part que sur les rivages du Nouveau-Monde; le système représentatif est adopté dans plusieurs États de l'Europe; mais je ne pense pas que jusqu'à présent aucune nation du monde ait constitué le pouvoir judiciaire de la même manière que les Américains.

Ce qu'un étranger comprend avec le plus de peine, aux États-Unis, c'est l'organisation judiciaire. Il n'y a pour ainsi dire pas d'événement politique dans lequel il n'entende invoquer l'autorité du juge; et il en conclut naturellement qu'aux États-Unis le juge est une des premières puissances politiques. Lorsqu'il vient ensuite à examiner la constitution des tribunaux, il ne leur découvre, au premier abord, que des attributions et des habitudes judiciaires. À ses yeux, le magistrat ne semble jamais s'introduire dans les affaires publiques que par hasard; mais ce même hasard revient tous les jours.

Lorsque le parlement de Paris faisait des remontrances et refusait d'enregistrer un édit; lorsqu'il faisait citer lui-même à sa barre un fonctionnaire prévaricateur, on apercevait à découvert l'action politique du pouvoir judiciaire. Mais rien de pareil ne se voit aux États-Unis.
Les Américains ont conservé au pouvoir judiciaire tous les caractères auxquels on a coutume de le reconnaître. Ils l'ont exactement renfermé dans le cercle où il a l'habitude de se mouvoir.

Le premier caractère de la puissance judiciaire, chez tous les peuples, est de servir d'arbitre. Pour qu'il y ait lieu à action de la part des tribunaux, il faut qu'il y ait contestation. Pour qu'il y ait juge, il faut qu'il y ait procès. Tant qu'une loi ne donne pas lieu à une contestation, le pouvoir judiciaire n'a donc point occasion de s'en occuper. Il existe, mais il ne la voit pas. Lorsqu'un juge, à propos d'un procès, attaque une loi relative à ce procès, il étend le cercle de ses attributions, mais il n'en sort pas, puisqu'il lui a fallu, en quelque sorte, juger la loi pour arriver à juger le procès. Lorsqu'il prononce sur une loi, sans partir d'un procès, il sort complétement de sa sphère, et il pénètre dans celle du pouvoir législatif.

Le second caractère de la puissance judiciaire est de prononcer sur des cas particuliers et non sur des principes généraux. Qu'un juge, en tranchant une question particulière, détruise un principe général, par la certitude où l'on est que, chacune des conséquences de ce même principe étant frappée de la même manière, le principe devient stérile, il reste dans le cercle naturel de son action. Mais que le juge attaque directement le principe général, et le détruise sans avoir en vue un cas particulier, il sort du cercle où tous les peuples se sont accordés à l'enfermer. Il devient quelque chose de plus important, de plus utile peut-être qu'un magistrat, mais il cesse de représenter le pouvoir judiciaire.

Le troisième caractère de la puissance judiciaire est de ne pouvoir agir que quand on l'appelle, ou, suivant l'expression légale, quand elle est saisie. Ce caractère ne se rencontre point aussi généralement que les deux autres. Je crois cependant que, malgré les exceptions, on peut le considérer comme essentiel. De sa nature, le pouvoir judiciaire est sans action; il faut le mettre en mouvement pour qu'il se remue. On lui dénonce un crime, et il punit le coupable; on l'appelle à redresser une injustice, et il la redresse; on lui soumet un acte, et il l'interprète; mais il ne va pas de lui-même poursuivre les criminels, rechercher l'injustice et examiner les faits. Le pouvoir judiciaire ferait en quelque sorte violence à cette nature passive, s'il prenait de lui-même l'initiative et s'établissait en censeur des lois.

Les Américains ont conservé au pouvoir judiciaire ces trois caractères distinctifs. Le juge américain ne peut prononcer que lorsqu'il y a litige. Il ne s'occupe jamais que d'un cas particulier; et, pour agir, il doit toujours attendre qu'on l'ait saisi.
Le juge américain ressemble donc parfaitement aux magistrats des autres nations. Cependant, il est revêtu d'un immense pouvoir politique.
D'où vient cela? Il se meut dans le même cercle et se sert des mêmes moyens que les autres juges; pourquoi possède-t-il une puissance que ces derniers n'ont pas?

La cause en est dans ce seul fait: les Américains ont reconnu aux juges le droit de fonder leurs arrêts sur la _constitution_ plutôt que sur les _lois_. En d'autres termes, ils leur ont permis de ne point appliquer les lois qui leur paraîtraient inconstitutionnelles.

Je sais qu'un droit semblable a été quelquefois réclamé par les tribunaux d'autres pays; mais il ne leur a jamais été concédé. En Amérique, il est reconnu par tous les pouvoirs; on ne rencontre ni un parti, ni même un homme qui le conteste.
L'explication de ceci doit se trouver dans le principe même des constitutions américaines.
En France, la constitution est une oeuvre immuable ou censée telle. Aucun pouvoir ne saurait y rien changer: telle est la théorie reçue (_L_).

En Angleterre, on reconnaît au parlement le droit de modifier la constitution. En Angleterre, la constitution peut donc changer sans cesse, ou plutôt elle n'existe point. Le parlement, en même temps qu'il est corps législatif, est corps constituant (_M_).
En Amérique, les théories politiques sont plus simples et plus rationnelles.

Une constitution américaine n'est point censée immuable comme en France; elle ne saurait être modifiée par les pouvoirs ordinaires de la société, comme en Angleterre. Elle forme une oeuvre à part, qui, représentant la volonté de tout le peuple, oblige les législateurs comme les simples citoyens, mais qui peut être changée par la volonté du peuple, suivant des formes qu'on a établies, et dans des cas qu'on a prévus.
En Amérique, la constitution peut donc varier; mais, tant qu'elle existe, elle est l'origine de tous les pouvoirs. La force prédominante est en elle seule.
Il est facile de voir en quoi ces différences doivent influer sur la position et sur les droits du corps judiciaire dans les trois pays que j'ai cités.

Si, en France, les tribunaux pouvaient désobéir aux lois, sur le fondement qu'ils les trouvent inconstitutionnelles, le pouvoir constituant serait réellement dans leurs mains, puisque seuls ils auraient le droit d'interpréter une constitution dont nul ne pourrait changer les termes. Ils se mettraient donc à la place de la nation et domineraient la société, autant du moins que la faiblesse inhérente au pouvoir judiciaire leur permettrait de le faire.

Je sais qu'en refusant aux juges le droit de déclarer les lois inconstitutionnelles, nous donnons indirectement au corps législatif le pouvoir de changer la constitution, puisqu'il ne rencontre plus de barrière légale qui l'arrête. Mais mieux vaut encore accorder le pouvoir de changer la constitution du peuple à des hommes qui représentent imparfaitement les volontés du peuple, qu'à d'autres qui ne représentent qu'eux-mêmes.

Il serait bien plus déraisonnable encore de donner aux juges anglais le droit de résister aux volontés du corps législatif, puisque le parlement, qui fait la loi, fait également la constitution, et que, par conséquent, on ne peut, en aucun cas, appeler une loi inconstitutionnelle quand elle émane des trois pouvoirs.
Aucun de ces deux raisonnements n'est applicable à l'Amérique.

Aux États-Unis, la constitution domine les législateurs comme les simples citoyens. Elle est donc la première des lois, et ne saurait être modifiée par une loi. Il est donc juste que les tribunaux obéissent à la constitution, préférablement à toutes les lois. Ceci tient à l'essence même du pouvoir judiciaire: choisir entre les dispositions légales celles qui l'enchaînent le plus étroitement, est, en quelque sorte, le droit naturel du magistrat.

En France, la constitution est également la première des lois, et les juges ont un droit égal à la prendre pour base de leurs arrêts; mais, en exerçant ce droit, ils ne pourraient manquer d'empiéter sur un autre plus sacré encore que le leur: celui de la société au nom de laquelle ils agissent. Ici la raison ordinaire doit céder devant la raison d'État.

En Amérique, où la nation peut toujours, en changeant sa constitution, réduire les magistrats à l'obéissance, un semblable danger n'est pas à craindre. Sur ce point, la politique et la logique sont donc d'accord, et le peuple ainsi que le juge y conservent également leurs priviléges.

Lorsqu'on invoque, devant les tribunaux des États-Unis, une loi que le juge estime contraire à la constitution, il peut donc refuser de l'appliquer. Ce pouvoir est le seul qui soit particulier au magistrat américain, mais une grande influence politique en découle.

Il est, en effet, bien peu de lois qui soient de nature à échapper pendant long-temps à l'analyse judiciaire; car il en est bien peu qui ne blessent un intérêt individuel, et que des plaideurs ne puissent ou ne doivent invoquer devant les tribunaux.

Or, du jour où le juge refuse d'appliquer une loi dans un procès, elle perd à l'instant une partie de sa force morale. Ceux qu'elle a lésés sont alors avertis qu'il existe un moyen de se soustraire à l'obligation de lui obéir: les procès se multiplient, et elle tombe dans l'impuissance. Il arrive alors l'une de ces deux choses: le peuple change sa constitution ou la législature rapporte sa loi.

Les Américains ont donc confié à leurs tribunaux un immense pouvoir politique; mais en les obligeant à n'attaquer les lois que par des moyens judiciaires, ils ont beaucoup diminué les dangers de ce pouvoir.

Si le juge avait pu attaquer les lois d'une façon théorique et générale; s'il avait pu prendre l'initiative et censurer le législateur, il fût entré avec éclat sur la scène politique; devenu le champion ou l'adversaire d'un parti, il eût appelé toutes les passions qui divisent le pays à prendre part à la lutte. Mais quand le juge attaque une loi dans un débat obscur et sur une application particulière, il dérobe en partie l'importance de l'attaque aux regards du public. Son arrêt n'a pour but que de frapper un intérêt individuel; la loi ne se trouve blessée que par hasard.

D'ailleurs, la loi ainsi censurée n'est pas détruite: sa force morale est diminuée, mais son effet matériel n'est point suspendu. Ce n'est que peu à peu, et sous les coups répétés de la jurisprudence, qu'enfin elle succombe.

De plus, on comprend sans peine qu'en chargeant l'intérêt particulier de provoquer la censure des lois, en liant intimement le procès fait à la loi au procès fait à un homme, on s'assure que la législation ne sera pas légèrement attaquée. Dans ce système, elle n'est plus exposée aux agressions journalières des partis. En signalant les fautes du législateur, on obéit à un besoin réel: on part d'un fait positif et appréciable, puisqu'il doit servir de base à un procès.
Je ne sais si cette manière d'agir des tribunaux américains, en même temps qu'elle est la plus favorable à l'ordre public, n'est pas aussi la plus favorable à la liberté.

Si le juge ne pouvait attaquer les législateurs que de front, il y a des temps où il craindrait de le faire; il en est d'autres où l'esprit de parti le pousserait chaque jour à l'oser. Ainsi il arriverait que les lois seraient attaquées quand le pouvoir dont elles émanent serait faible, et qu'on s'y soumettrait sans murmurer quand il serait fort; c'est-à-dire que souvent on attaquerait les lois lorsqu'il serait le plus utile de les respecter, et qu'on les respecterait quand il deviendrait facile d'opprimer en leur nom.

Mais le juge américain est amené malgré lui sur le terrain de la politique. Il ne juge la loi que parce qu'il a à juger un procès, et il ne peut s'empêcher de juger le procès. La question politique qu'il doit résoudre se rattache à l'intérêt des plaideurs, et il ne saurait refuser de la trancher sans faire un déni de justice. C'est en remplissant les devoirs étroits imposés à la profession du magistrat, qu'il fait l'acte du citoyen. Il est vrai que, de cette manière, la censure judiciaire, exercée par les tribunaux sur la législation, ne peut s'étendre sans distinction à toutes les lois, car il en est qui ne peuvent jamais donner lieu à cette sorte de contestation nettement formulée qu'on nomme un procès. Et lorsqu'une pareille contestation est possible, on peut encore concevoir qu'il ne se rencontre personne qui veuille en saisir les tribunaux.
Les Américains ont souvent senti cet inconvénient, mais ils ont laissé le remède incomplet, de peur de lui donner, dans tous les cas, une efficacité dangereuse.

Resserré dans ses limites, le pouvoir accordé aux tribunaux américains de prononcer sur l'inconstitutionnalité des lois, forme encore une des plus puissantes barrières qu'on ait jamais élevées contre la tyrannie des assemblées politiques.
AUTRES POUVOIRS ACCORDÉS AUX JUGES AMÉRICAINS.

Aux États-Unis tous les citoyens ont le droit d'accuser les fonctionnaires publics devant les tribunaux ordinaires. -- Comment ils usent de ce droit. -- Art. 75 de la constitution française de l'an VIII. -- Les Américains et les Anglais ne peuvent comprendre le sens de cet article.

Je ne sais si j'ai besoin de dire que chez un peuple libre, comme les Américains, tous les citoyens ont le droit d'accuser les fonctionnaires publics devant les juges ordinaires, et que tous les juges ont le droit de condamner les fonctionnaires publics, tant la chose est naturelle.

Ce n'est pas accorder un privilége particulier aux tribunaux que de leur permettre de punir les agents du pouvoir exécutif, quand ils violent la loi. C'est leur enlever un droit naturel que de le leur défendre.
Il ne m'a pas paru qu'aux États-Unis, en rendant tous les fonctionnaires responsables des tribunaux, on eût affaibli les ressorts du gouvernement.
Il m'a semblé, au contraire, que les Américains, en agissant ainsi, avaient augmenté le respect qu'on doit aux gouvernants, ceux-ci prenant beaucoup plus de soin d'échapper à la critique.

Je n'ai point observé, non plus, qu'aux États-Unis on intentât beaucoup de procès politiques, et je me l'explique sans peine. Un procès est toujours, quelle que soit sa nature, une entreprise difficile et coûteuse. Il est aisé d'accuser un homme public dans les journaux, mais ce n'est pas sans de graves motifs qu'on se décide à le citer devant la justice. Pour poursuivre juridiquement un fonctionnaire, il faut donc avoir un juste motif de plainte; et les fonctionnaires ne fournissent guère un semblable motif quand ils craignent d'être poursuivis.
Ceci ne tient pas à la forme républicaine qu'ont adoptée les Américains, car la même expérience peut se faire tous les jours en Angleterre.

Ces deux peuples n'ont pas cru avoir assuré leur indépendance, en permettant la mise en jugement des principaux agents du pouvoir. Ils ont pensé que c'était bien plutôt par de petits procès, mis chaque jour à la portée des moindres citoyens, qu'on parvenait à garantir la liberté, que par de grandes procédures auxquelles on n'a jamais recours ou qu'on emploie trop tard.

Dans le moyen-âge, où il était très difficile d'atteindre les criminels, quand les juges en saisissaient quelques uns, il leur arrivait souvent d'infliger à ces malheureux d'affreux supplices; ce qui ne diminuait pas le nombre des coupables. On a découvert depuis qu'en rendant la justice tout à la fois plus sûre et plus douce, on la rendait en même temps plus efficace.
Les Américains et les Anglais pensent qu'il faut traiter l'arbitraire et la tyrannie comme le vol: faciliter la poursuite et adoucir la peine.

En l'an VIII de la république française, il parut une constitution dont l'art. 75 était ainsi conçu: «Les agents du gouvernement, autres que les ministres, ne peuvent être poursuivis, pour des faits relatifs à leurs fonctions, qu'en vertu d'une décision du Conseil d'État; en ce cas, la poursuite a lieu devant les tribunaux ordinaires.»
La constitution de l'an VIII passa, mais non cet article, qui resta après elle; et on l'oppose, chaque jour encore, aux justes réclamations des citoyens.
J'ai souvent essayé de faire comprendre le sens de cet art. 75 à des Américains ou à des Anglais, et il m'a toujours été très difficile d'y parvenir.

Ce qu'ils apercevaient d'abord, c'est que le Conseil d'État, en France, étant un grand tribunal fixé au centre du royaume, il y avait une sorte de tyrannie à renvoyer préliminairement devant lui tous les plaignants.

Mais quand je cherchais à leur faire comprendre que le Conseil d'État n'était point un corps judiciaire, dans le sens ordinaire du mot, mais un corps administratif, dont les membres dépendaient du roi; de telle sorte que le roi, après avoir souverainement commandé à l'un de ses serviteurs, appelé préfet, de commettre une iniquité, pouvait commander souverainement à un autre de ses serviteurs, appelé conseiller d'État, d'empêcher qu'on ne fît punir le premier; quand je leur montrais le citoyen, lésé par l'ordre du prince, réduit à demander au prince lui-même l'autorisation d'obtenir justice, ils refusaient de croire à de semblables énormités, et m'accusaient de mensonge et d'ignorance.

Il arrivait souvent, dans l'ancienne monarchie, que le parlement décrétait de prise de corps le fonctionnaire public qui se rendait coupable d'un délit. Quelquefois l'autorité royale, intervenant, faisait annuler la procédure. Le despotisme se montrait alors à découvert, et, en obéissant, on ne se soumettait qu'à la force.
Nous avons donc bien reculé du point où étaient arrivés nos pères; car nous laissons faire, sous couleur de justice, et consacrer au nom de la loi, ce que la violence seule leur imposait.

tocqueville.chapter_summary: Les Anglo-Américains ont conservé au pouvoir judiciaire tous les caractères qui le distinguent chez les autres peuples. -- Cependant ils en ont fait un grand pouvoir politique. -- Comment. -- En quoi le système judiciaire des Anglo-Américains diffère de tous les autres. -- Pourquoi les juges américains ont le droit de déclarer les lois inconstitutionnelles. -- Comment les juges américains usent de ce droit. -- Précautions prises par le législateur pour empêcher l'abus de ce droit.
translation: I thought it necessary to devote a separate chapter to the judicial power. Its political importance is so great that to speak of it in passing seemed to me a way of diminishing it in the reader's eyes.

Confederations have existed outside America; republics have been seen elsewhere than on the shores of the New World; the representative system has been adopted in several European states; but I do not think that, up to the present, any nation in the world has constituted its judicial power in the same manner as the Americans.

What a foreigner finds most difficult to understand in the United States is the organization of the judiciary. There is scarcely a political event in which he does not hear the authority of the judge invoked; and he naturally concludes that in the United States the judge is one of the foremost political powers. When he then comes to examine the constitution of the courts, at first glance he finds in them only judicial powers and judicial habits. In his eyes the magistrate seems never to enter public affairs except by accident—yet that same accident recurs every day.

When the Parlement of Paris issued remonstrances and refused to register an edict, or when it summoned a corrupt official before its bar, the political action of the judicial power was openly visible. Nothing of the kind is seen in the United States.
The Americans have preserved in their judiciary all the characteristics by which it is customarily recognized. They have confined it precisely within the sphere in which it habitually moves.

The first characteristic of judicial power, among all peoples, is to serve as arbiter. For the courts to act, there must be a dispute. For there to be a judge, there must be a case. As long as a law gives rise to no dispute, the judicial power has no occasion to concern itself with it. It exists, but it does not see the law. When a judge, in the course of a case, challenges a law relevant to that case, he extends the circle of his functions—but he does not leave it, since he was in some sense obliged to judge the law in order to reach a judgment in the case. When he rules on a law without proceeding from a case, he steps entirely outside his sphere and enters that of the legislative power.

The second characteristic of judicial power is that it pronounces on particular cases and not on general principles. Suppose a judge, in settling a particular question, destroys a general principle—because it is certain that each of the consequences flowing from that same principle will be struck down in the same way, the principle becomes sterile. The judge remains within the natural bounds of his action. But should the judge attack a general principle directly, and destroy it without any particular case in view, he steps outside the circle within which all peoples have agreed to confine him. He becomes something more important—perhaps more useful—than a magistrate; but he has ceased to represent the judicial power.

The third characteristic of judicial power is that it can only act when it is called upon, or, to use the legal expression, when it has been seized of a matter. This characteristic is not found as universally as the other two. I believe, however, that despite exceptions it may be considered essential. By its nature the judicial power is inert; it must be set in motion before it will move. A crime is brought before it, and it punishes the guilty; it is called upon to redress an injustice, and it redresses it; a document is submitted to it, and it interprets it. But it does not of itself pursue criminals, seek out injustice, or examine the facts. The judicial power would in some sense do violence to its passive nature if it were to take the initiative on its own and set itself up as a censor of the laws.

The Americans have preserved these three distinctive characteristics in their judiciary. The American judge may only pronounce when there is a dispute. He concerns himself only with particular cases; and in order to act, he must always wait until a matter has been brought before him.
The American judge thus resembles, in every respect, the magistrates of other nations. And yet he is clothed with an immense political power.
How does this come about? He moves within the same circle and employs the same means as other judges; why does he possess a power that they do not?

The cause lies in this single fact: the Americans have recognized in their judges the right to base their rulings on the *constitution* rather than on the *laws*. In other words, they have permitted judges to decline to apply laws that appear to them unconstitutional.

I am aware that a similar right has sometimes been claimed by the courts of other countries; but it has never been conceded to them. In America it is recognized by all the powers of government; one encounters neither a party nor even a single individual who contests it.
The explanation must be found in the very principle underlying the American constitutions.
In France, the constitution is an immutable work, or is held to be such. No power can change it—that is the received theory (*L*).

In England, Parliament is recognized as having the right to alter the constitution. In England, therefore, the constitution can change at any time—or rather, it does not exist at all. Parliament, as a legislative body, is at the same time a constituent body (*M*).
In America, political theories are simpler and more rational.

An American constitution is not held to be immutable, as in France; nor can it be modified by the ordinary powers of society, as in England. It forms a work apart which, representing the will of the whole people, binds legislators as well as ordinary citizens, but which can be changed by the will of the people according to forms established and circumstances foreseen in advance.
In America, therefore, the constitution may vary; but as long as it exists, it is the source of all powers. The predominant force resides in it alone.
It is easy to see how these differences must affect the position and the rights of the judiciary in the three countries I have named.

If, in France, the courts could disobey the laws on the grounds that they found them unconstitutional, the constituent power would effectively reside in their hands, since they alone would have the right to interpret a constitution whose terms no one could alter. They would thus place themselves in the nation's position and would dominate society—at least to the extent that the inherent weakness of the judicial power would allow them to do so.

I know that by denying judges the right to declare laws unconstitutional, we indirectly give the legislature the power to change the constitution, since it no longer encounters any legal barrier to stop it. But it is still better to give the power to change the people's constitution to men who imperfectly represent the people's will than to others who represent no one but themselves.

It would be far more unreasonable still to give English judges the right to resist the will of the legislature, since Parliament, which makes the law, also makes the constitution, and consequently no law can in any case be called unconstitutional when it proceeds from all three powers.
Neither of these two lines of reasoning applies to America.

In the United States, the constitution governs legislators as well as ordinary citizens. It is therefore the first of the laws, and cannot be modified by any law. It is therefore right that the courts should obey the constitution in preference to all other laws. This follows from the very essence of the judicial power: to choose among the applicable legal provisions the one that binds it most strictly is, in some sense, the magistrate's natural right.

In France, the constitution is likewise the first of the laws, and judges have an equal right to take it as the basis of their rulings; but in exercising that right, they could not fail to encroach upon another right still more sacred than their own: that of the society in whose name they act. Here ordinary reason must yield before *raison d'État*.

In America, where the nation can always, by changing its constitution, bring the magistrates back to obedience, no such danger is to be feared. On this point, policy and logic are therefore in agreement, and the people as well as the judge each preserve their privileges.

When a law is invoked before the courts of the United States that the judge considers contrary to the constitution, he may therefore refuse to apply it. This power is the only one peculiar to the American magistrate, but a great political influence flows from it.

Indeed, there are very few laws by their nature capable of escaping judicial scrutiny for long; for there are very few that do not injure some individual interest and that litigants cannot or should not invoke before the courts.

Now, from the day on which a judge refuses to apply a law in a case before him, that law instantly loses a part of its moral force. Those it has wronged are notified that a means exists of evading the obligation to obey it; cases multiply, and the law falls into impotence. One of two things then occurs: the people change the constitution, or the legislature repeals the law.
The Americans have thus entrusted to their courts an immense political power; but by requiring them to attack the laws only by judicial means, they have greatly reduced the dangers of that power.

Had the judge been able to attack laws in a theoretical and general way—had he been able to take the initiative and act as censor of the legislature—he would have entered the political arena with a flourish: becoming the champion or the adversary of a party, he would have summoned all the passions dividing the country to join the struggle. But when the judge attacks a law in an obscure proceeding and in a particular application, he partly conceals the importance of the attack from the public eye. His ruling aims only at affecting one individual interest; the law is wounded only by accident.

Moreover, a law censured in this way is not destroyed: its moral force is diminished, but its material effect is not suspended. It is only gradually, under repeated blows from judicial decisions, that it finally succumbs.

Furthermore, it is easy to see that by placing the burden of challenging the laws upon individual interest, and by tying the case against the law closely to the case against an individual, one ensures that legislation will not be attacked lightly. Under this system it is no longer exposed to the daily assaults of parties. To point out the faults of the legislator, there must be a real need; the challenge must rest on a positive and demonstrable fact, since that fact must serve as the basis of a case.
I do not know whether this way in which American courts operate, while being the most favorable to public order, is not equally the most favorable to liberty.

If the judge could attack legislators only head-on, there are times when he would fear to do so; and there are others when the spirit of party would drive him to dare it every day. The result would be that laws would be attacked when the power from which they emanated was weak, and that they would be submitted to without a murmur when that power was strong—that is to say, laws would often be attacked precisely when it was most useful to respect them, and they would be respected precisely when it was becoming easy to oppress in their name.

But the American judge is drawn onto political ground in spite of himself. He judges the law only because he has a case to judge, and he cannot avoid judging the case. The political question he must resolve is bound up with the interests of the litigants, and he cannot refuse to settle it without committing a denial of justice. It is in fulfilling the strict duties imposed by his profession as a magistrate that he performs the act of a citizen. It is true that, in this way, the judicial censure exercised by the courts over legislation cannot extend without distinction to all laws, for there are some that can never give rise to that sort of clearly formulated dispute which is called a case. And even where such a dispute is possible, one can still conceive that no one will come forward to bring it before the courts.
The Americans have often felt this drawback, but they have left the remedy incomplete, for fear of making it, in all cases, dangerously effective.

Confined within its limits, the power granted to American courts to rule on the unconstitutionality of laws still forms one of the most powerful barriers ever erected against the tyranny of political assemblies.
OTHER POWERS ACCORDED TO AMERICAN JUDGES.

In the United States all citizens have the right to bring public officials before the ordinary courts. — How they exercise this right. — Article 75 of the French constitution of the Year VIII. — Americans and Englishmen cannot grasp the meaning of that article.

I am not sure I need say that among a free people, such as the Americans, all citizens have the right to bring public officials before the ordinary courts, and that all courts have the right to condemn public officials—the thing is so natural.
To allow the courts to punish agents of the executive power when they violate the law is not to grant them a special privilege. To forbid them from doing so is to strip them of a natural right.
It has not seemed to me that in the United States, by making all officials answerable to the courts, the springs of government have been weakened.
On the contrary, it has seemed to me that the Americans, in acting thus, have increased respect for those who govern, since the latter take considerably greater care to avoid criticism.

Nor have I observed that in the United States many political prosecutions are brought, and I can readily explain why. A lawsuit, whatever its nature, is always a difficult and costly undertaking. It is easy enough to accuse a public man in the newspapers; but one does not lightly decide to summon him before a court. To prosecute an official through legal proceedings requires a genuine grievance—and officials rarely furnish such a grievance when they fear being prosecuted.
This has nothing to do with the republican form the Americans have adopted, for the same experience can be had every day in England.

These two peoples have not believed their independence to be secured by permitting the prosecution of the leading agents of power. They have thought that it was rather through small lawsuits, placed every day within the reach of the humblest citizens, that liberty is guaranteed—rather than through great proceedings that are never resorted to, or that are employed too late.

In the Middle Ages, when it was very difficult to reach criminals, judges who managed to seize some of them would often inflict hideous punishments on these wretches—which did not reduce the number of offenders. It was later discovered that by making justice both more certain and more mild, it was made more effective at the same time.
Americans and Englishmen think that arbitrariness and tyranny must be treated like theft: make prosecution easier and reduce the penalty.

In the Year VIII of the French Republic there appeared a constitution whose Article 75 read as follows: "Government agents, other than ministers, may not be prosecuted for acts relating to their duties except by virtue of a decision of the Council of State; in which case the prosecution takes place before the ordinary courts."
The constitution of the Year VIII passed away, but not that article, which outlasted it; and it is still invoked every day against the just grievances of citizens.
I have often tried to explain the meaning of that Article 75 to Americans or Englishmen, and I have always found it very difficult to succeed.

What they first noticed was that the Council of State, in France, being a great tribunal fixed at the center of the kingdom, there was a kind of tyranny in requiring all plaintiffs to appear before it as a preliminary step.

But when I sought to make them understand that the Council of State was not a judicial body, in the ordinary sense of the word, but an administrative body whose members depended on the king — so that the king, after having sovereignly commanded one of his servants, called a prefect, to commit an iniquity, could sovereignly command another of his servants, called a councillor of state, to prevent the first from being punished; when I showed them the citizen, wronged by the prince's order, reduced to asking the prince himself for leave to obtain justice — they refused to believe in such outrages, and accused me of lying or of ignorance.

It often happened, under the old monarchy, that the Parlement issued an arrest warrant against a public official guilty of an offense. Sometimes the royal authority would intervene and have the proceedings quashed. Despotism then showed itself in the open, and in obeying, one submitted to nothing but force.
We have therefore fallen well behind the point our fathers had reached; for we allow to be done under cover of justice, and consecrated in the name of the law, what violence alone imposed upon them.

items.title: DU JUGEMENT POLITIQUE AUX ÉTATS-UNIS
paragraphs: J'entends par jugement politique, l'arrêt que prononce un corps politique momentanément revêtu du droit de juger.

Dans les gouvernements absolus, il est inutile de donner aux jugements des formes extraordinaires: le prince, au nom duquel on poursuit l'accusé, étant maître des tribunaux comme de tout le reste, n'a pas besoin de chercher de garantie ailleurs que dans l'idée qu'on a de sa puissance. La seule crainte qu'il puisse concevoir est qu'on ne garde même pas les apparences extérieures de la justice, et qu'on ne déshonore son autorité en voulant l'affermir.

Mais dans la plupart des pays libres, où la majorité ne peut jamais agir sur les tribunaux, comme le ferait un prince absolu, il est quelquefois arrivé de placer momentanément la puissance judiciaire entre les mains des représentants mêmes de la société. On a mieux aimé y confondre ainsi momentanément les pouvoirs, que d'y violer le principe nécessaire de l'unité du gouvernement. L'Angleterre, la France et les États-Unis ont introduit le jugement politique dans leurs lois: il est curieux d'examiner le parti que ces trois grands peuples en ont tiré.
En Angleterre et en France, la chambre des pairs forme la haute cour criminelle[118] de la nation. Elle ne juge pas tous les délits politiques, mais elle peut les juger tous.

À côté de la chambre des pairs se trouve un autre pouvoir politique, revêtu du droit d'accuser. La seule différence qui existe, sur ce point, entre les deux pays, est celle-ci: en Angleterre, les députés peuvent accuser qui bon leur plaît devant les pairs; tandis qu'en France ils ne peuvent poursuivre de cette manière que les ministres du roi.
Du reste, dans les deux pays, la chambre des pairs trouve à sa disposition toutes les lois pénales pour en frapper les délinquants.
Aux États-Unis, comme en Europe, l'une des deux branches de la législature est revêtue du droit d'accuser, et l'autre du droit de juger. Les représentants dénoncent le coupable, le sénat le punit.

Mais le sénat ne peut être _saisi_ que par les _représentants_, et les représentants ne peuvent accuser devant lui que des _fonctionnaires publics_. Ainsi le sénat a une compétence plus restreinte que la cour des pairs de France, et les représentants ont un droit d'accusation plus étendu que nos députés.

Mais voici la plus grande différence qui existe entre l'Amérique et l'Europe: en Europe, les tribunaux politiques peuvent appliquer toutes les dispositions du Code pénal; en Amérique, lorsqu'ils ont enlevé à un coupable le caractère public dont il était revêtu, et l'ont déclaré indigne d'occuper aucunes fonctions politiques à l'avenir, leur droit est épuisé, et la tâche des tribunaux ordinaires commence.
Je suppose que le président des États-Unis ait commis un crime de haute trahison.
La chambre des représentants l'accuse, les sénateurs prononcent sa déchéance. Il paraît ensuite devant un jury, qui seul peut lui enlever la liberté ou la vie.
Ceci achève de jeter une vive lumière sur le sujet qui nous occupe.

En introduisant le jugement politique dans leurs lois, les Européens ont voulu atteindre les grands criminels, quels que fussent leur naissance, leur rang ou leur pouvoir dans l'État. Pour y parvenir, ils ont réuni momentanément, dans le sein d'un grand corps politique, toutes les prérogatives des tribunaux.

Le législateur s'est transformé alors en magistrat; il a pu établir le crime, le classer et le punir. En lui donnant les droits de juge, la loi lui en a imposé toutes les obligations, et l'a lié à l'observation de toutes les formes de justice.

Lorsqu'un tribunal politique, français ou anglais, a pour justiciable un fonctionnaire public, et qu'il prononce contre lui une condamnation, il lui enlève par le fait ses fonctions, et peut le déclarer indigne d'en occuper aucune à l'avenir; mais ici la destitution et l'interdiction politiques sont une conséquence de l'arrêt et non l'arrêt lui-même.
En Europe, le jugement politique est donc plutôt un acte judiciaire qu'une mesure administrative.
Le contraire se voit aux États-Unis, et il est facile de se convaincre que le jugement politique y est bien plutôt une mesure administrative qu'un acte judiciaire.

Il est vrai que l'arrêt du sénat est judiciaire par la forme; pour le rendre, les sénateurs sont obligés de se conformer à la solennité et aux usages de la procédure. Il est encore judiciaire par les motifs sur lesquels il se fonde; le sénat est en général obligé de prendre pour base de sa décision un délit du droit commun. Mais il est administratif par son objet.

Si le but principal du législateur américain eût été réellement d'armer un corps politique d'un grand pouvoir judiciaire, il n'aurait pas resserré son action dans le cercle des fonctionnaires publics, car les plus dangereux ennemis de l'État peuvent n'être revêtus d'aucune fonction: ceci est vrai, surtout dans les républiques, où la faveur des partis est la première des puissances, et où l'on est souvent d'autant plus fort qu'on n'exerce légalement aucun pouvoir.

Si le législateur américain avait voulu donner à la société elle-même le droit de prévenir les grands crimes, à la manière du juge, par la crainte du châtiment, il aurait mis à la disposition des tribunaux politiques toutes les ressources du Code pénal; mais il ne leur a fourni qu'une arme incomplète, et qui ne saurait atteindre les plus dangereux d'entre les criminels. Car peu importe un jugement d'interdiction politique à celui qui veut renverser les lois elles-mêmes.

Le but principal du jugement politique, aux États-Unis, est donc de retirer le pouvoir à celui qui en fait un mauvais usage, et d'empêcher que ce même citoyen n'en soit revêtu à l'avenir. C'est, comme on le voit, un acte administratif auquel on a donné la solennité d'un arrêt.

En cette matière, les Américains ont donc créé quelque chose de mixte. Ils ont donné à la destitution administrative toutes les garanties du jugement politique, et ils ont ôté au jugement politique ses plus grandes rigueurs.

Ce point fixé, tout s'enchaîne; on découvre alors pourquoi les constitutions américaines soumettent tous les fonctionnaires civils à la juridiction du sénat, et en exemptent les militaires, dont les crimes sont cependant plus à redouter. Dans l'ordre civil, les Américains n'ont pour ainsi dire pas de fonctionnaires révocables: les uns sont inamovibles, les autres tiennent leurs droits d'un mandat qu'on ne peut abroger. Pour leur ôter le pouvoir, il faut donc les juger tous. Mais les militaires dépendent du chef de l'État, qui lui-même est un fonctionnaire civil. En atteignant le chef de l'État, on les frappe tous du même coup[119].
Maintenant, si on en vient à comparer le système européen et le système américain, dans les effets que chacun produit ou peut produire, on découvre des différences non moins sensibles.
En France et en Angleterre, on considère le jugement politique comme une arme extraordinaire, dont la société ne doit se servir que pour se sauver dans les moments de grands périls.

On ne saurait nier que le jugement politique, tel qu'on l'entend en Europe, ne viole le principe conservateur de la division des pouvoirs, et qu'il ne menace sans cesse la liberté et la vie des hommes.

Le jugement politique, aux États-Unis, ne porte qu'une atteinte indirecte au principe de la division des pouvoirs; il ne menace point l'existence des citoyens; il ne plane pas, comme en Europe, sur toutes les têtes, puisqu'il ne frappe que ceux qui, en acceptant des fonctions publiques, se sont soumis d'avance à ses rigueurs.
Il est tout à la fois moins redoutable et moins efficace.
Aussi les législateurs des États-Unis ne l'ont-ils pas considéré comme un remède extrême aux grands maux de la société, mais comme un moyen habituel de gouvernement.

Sous ce point de vue, il exerce peut-être plus d'influence réelle sur le corps social en Amérique qu'en Europe. Il ne faut pas en effet se laisser prendre à l'apparente douceur de la législation américaine, dans ce qui a rapport aux jugements politiques. On doit remarquer, en premier lieu, qu'aux États-Unis le tribunal qui prononce ces jugements est composé des mêmes éléments et soumis aux mêmes influences que le corps chargé d'accuser, ce qui donne une impulsion presque irrésistible aux passions vindicatives des partis. Si les juges politiques, aux États-Unis, ne peuvent prononcer des peines aussi sévères que les juges politiques d'Europe, il y a donc moins de chances d'être acquitté par eux. La condamnation est moins redoutable et plus certaine.

Les Européens, en établissant les tribunaux politiques, ont eu pour principal objet de _punir_ les coupables; les Américains, de leur _enlever le pouvoir_. Le jugement politique, aux États-Unis, est en quelque façon une mesure préventive. On ne doit donc pas y enchaîner le juge dans des définitions criminelles bien exactes.

Rien de plus effrayant que le vague des lois américaines, quand elles définissent les crimes politiques proprement dits. «Les crimes qui motiveront la condamnation du président (dit la constitution des États-Unis, section 4, art. 1er) sont la haute trahison, la corruption, ou autres grands crimes et délits.» La plupart des constitutions d'États sont bien plus obscures encore.

«Les fonctionnaires publics, dit la constitution du Massachusetts, seront condamnés pour la conduite coupable qu'ils auront tenue et pour leur mauvaise administration[120]. Tous les fonctionnaires qui auront mis l'État en danger, par mauvaise administration, corruption, ou autres délits, dit la constitution de Virginie, pourront être accusés par la chambre des députés.» Il y a des constitutions qui ne spécifient aucun crime, afin de laisser peser sur les fonctionnaires publics une responsabilité illimitée[121].
Mais ce qui rend, en cette matière, les lois américaines si redoutables, naît, j'oserai le dire, de leur douceur même.

Nous avons vu qu'en Europe la destitution d'un fonctionnaire, et son interdiction politique, étaient une des conséquences de la peine, et qu'en Amérique c'était la peine même. Il en résulte ceci: en Europe, les tribunaux politiques sont revêtus de droits terribles dont quelquefois ils ne savent comment user; et il leur arrive de ne pas punir, de peur de punir trop. Mais, en Amérique, on ne recule pas devant une peine qui ne fait pas gémir l'humanité: condamner un ennemi politique à mort, pour lui enlever le pouvoir, est aux yeux de tous un horrible assassinat; déclarer son adversaire indigne de posséder ce même pouvoir, et le lui ôter, en lui laissant la liberté et la vie, peut paraître le résultat honnête de la lutte.

Or, ce jugement si facile à prononcer n'en est pas moins le comble du malheur pour le commun de ceux auxquels il s'applique. Les grands criminels braveront sans doute ses vaines rigueurs; les hommes ordinaires verront en lui un arrêt qui détruit leur position, entache leur honneur, et qui les condamne à une honteuse oisiveté pire que la mort.

Le jugement politique, aux États-Unis, exerce donc sur la marche de la société une influence d'autant plus grande qu'elle semble moins redoutable. Il n'agit pas directement sur les gouvernés, mais il rend la majorité entièrement maîtresse de ceux qui gouvernent; il ne donne point à la législature un immense pouvoir qu'elle ne pourrait exercer que dans un jour de crise; il lui laisse prendre une puissance modérée et régulière, dont elle peut user tous les jours. Si la force est moins grande, d'un autre côté l'emploi en est plus commode et l'abus plus facile.

En empêchant les tribunaux politiques de prononcer des peines judiciaires, les Américains me semblent donc avoir prévenu les conséquences les plus terribles de la tyrannie législative, plutôt que la tyrannie elle-même. Et je ne sais si, à tout prendre, le jugement politique, tel qu'on l'entend aux États-Unis, n'est point l'arme la plus formidable qu'on ait jamais remise aux mains de la majorité.
Lorsque les républiques américaines commenceront à dégénérer, je crois qu'on pourra aisément le reconnaître: il suffira de voir si le nombre des jugements politiques augmente (_N_).
La cour des pairs en Angleterre forme en outre le dernier degré de l'appel dans certaines affaires civiles. Voyez Blakstone, liv. III, ch. IV.
Ce n'est pas qu'on puisse ôter à un officier son grade; mais on peut lui enlever son commandement.
Chap. 1, sect. 2, § 8.
Voyez la constitution des Illinois, du Maine, du Connecticut et de la Géorgie.

tocqueville.chapter_summary: Ce que l'auteur entend par jugement politique. -- Comment on comprend le jugement politique en France, en Angleterre, aux États-Unis. -- En Amérique le juge politique ne s'occupe que des fonctionnaires publics. -- Il prononce des destitutions plutôt que des peines. -- Le jugement politique, moyen habituel du gouvernement. -- Le jugement politique, tel qu'on l'entend aux États-Unis, est, malgré sa douceur, et peut-être à cause de sa douceur, une arme très puissante dans les mains de la majorité.
translation: By political judgment I mean the verdict pronounced by a political body momentarily invested with the right to judge.

Under absolute governments there is no point in giving judicial proceedings any extraordinary form: the prince, in whose name the accused is prosecuted, is master of the courts as he is master of all else, and need seek no guarantee beyond the idea men hold of his power. His one fear is that even the outward forms of justice will be abandoned, and his authority disgraced in the very act of being secured.

But in most free countries, where the majority can never act upon the courts as an absolute prince would, it has sometimes happened that judicial power was momentarily placed in the hands of the very representatives of society. The mingling of powers, however brief, was preferred to a breach of that necessary principle, the unity of government. England, France, and the United States have all written political judgment into their laws: it is worth examining what each of these three great peoples has made of it.
In England and in France, the chamber of peers constitutes the high criminal court[118] of the nation. It does not try every political offense, but it can try any.

Alongside the chamber of peers stands another political body, vested with the right to bring charges. On this point the only difference between the two countries is that in England the deputies may impeach whomever they please before the peers, while in France they may proceed in this manner only against the king's ministers.
For the rest, in both countries the chamber of peers has at its disposal the entire body of penal law to bring down upon the guilty.

In the United States, as in Europe, one of the two branches of the legislature is vested with the right to accuse, and the other with the right to judge. The representatives denounce the guilty party; the senate punishes him.

But the senate can only be _seized_ of a case by the _representatives_, and the representatives can only impeach _public officials_ before it. Thus the senate has a narrower competence than the French court of peers, and the representatives a broader right of accusation than our deputies.

But here is the greatest difference between America and Europe: in Europe, the political tribunals may apply every provision of the penal code; in America, once they have stripped the guilty man of his public character and declared him unworthy to hold any political office in the future, their right is exhausted, and the work of the ordinary courts begins.
Suppose the President of the United States to have committed an act of high treason.
The House of Representatives impeaches him; the senators pronounce his removal. He then appears before a jury, which alone can deprive him of liberty or of life.
This casts a sharp light on the subject before us.

In introducing political judgment into their laws, the Europeans meant to reach great criminals whatever their birth, rank, or power in the state. To this end they brought together, within a single great political body, all the prerogatives of the courts.

The legislator thereby turned magistrate; he could define the crime, classify it, and punish it. In conferring on him the rights of a judge, the law imposed all the duties of one, and bound him to observe every form of justice.

When a French or English political tribunal sits in judgment on a public official and condemns him, it strips him of his office by that very act, and may declare him unworthy to hold any office in the future; but here political removal and disqualification are a consequence of the sentence, not the sentence itself.
In Europe, then, political judgment is a judicial act rather than an administrative measure.
The opposite holds in the United States, and one is easily persuaded that political judgment there is an administrative measure rather than a judicial act.

True, the sentence of the senate is judicial in form; in handing it down, the senators are required to observe the solemnities and usages of legal procedure. It is judicial, too, in its grounds; the senate is generally obliged to base its decision on an offense under the common law. But it is administrative in its object.

If the chief aim of the American legislator had really been to arm a political body with great judicial power, he would not have confined its action to public officials, for the most dangerous enemies of the state may hold no office at all: this is especially true in republics, where party favor is the foremost of powers, and where a man is often the stronger for exercising no legal power whatever.

If the American legislator had meant to give society itself the right to forestall great crimes, in the manner of a judge, by the fear of punishment, he would have placed at the disposal of the political tribunals all the resources of the penal code; but he furnished them with only a partial weapon, one that cannot reach the most dangerous of criminals. For a sentence of political disqualification means little to the man who wants to overturn the laws themselves.

The chief aim of political judgment in the United States, then, is to withdraw power from the man who misuses it, and to prevent his being clothed with it again. It is, as we see, an administrative act to which the solemnity of a sentence has been given.

In this matter the Americans have therefore created something hybrid. They have given administrative removal all the guarantees of a political judgment, and they have stripped political judgment of its harshest rigors.

Once this point is fixed, everything follows. We see why the American constitutions place every civil official under the jurisdiction of the senate, while exempting military men, whose crimes are nevertheless the more to be feared. In the civil order, the Americans have, so to speak, no officials who can simply be dismissed: some hold their posts for life, others by a mandate that cannot be revoked. To remove them from power, one must therefore try them all. But military men depend on the head of state, who is himself a civil official. By reaching the head of state, one strikes them all at a single blow[119].
If we now come to compare the European and the American systems in the effects each produces or may produce, the differences we discover are no less striking.
In France and in England, political judgment is regarded as an extraordinary weapon, to be used by society only to save itself in moments of great peril.

It cannot be denied that political judgment, as understood in Europe, violates the conservative principle of the separation of powers, and that it stands as a perpetual threat to the liberty and the lives of men.

In the United States, political judgment touches the principle of the separation of powers only indirectly; it does not threaten the existence of the citizens; it does not hang, as in Europe, over every head, since it falls only on those who, by accepting public office, have submitted in advance to its rigors.
It is at once less to be feared and less effective.
And so the legislators of the United States did not regard it as an extreme remedy for the great evils of society, but as an ordinary instrument of government.

Seen in this light, it perhaps exerts a greater real influence on the body of society in America than in Europe. One must not be deceived by the apparent mildness of American legislation in matters of political judgment.
