_Kent's commentaries_, vol. 1, p. 244. Remarquez que j'ai choisi l'exemple cité plus haut dans des temps postérieurs à l'établissement de la constitution actuelle. Si j'avais voulu remonter à l'époque de la première confédération, j'aurais signalé des faits bien plus concluants encore. Alors il régnait un véritable enthousiasme dans la nation; la révolution était représentée par un homme éminemment populaire, et pourtant, à cette époque, le congrès ne disposait, à proprement parler, de rien. Les hommes et l'argent lui manquaient à tous moments; les plans les mieux combinés par lui échouaient dans l'exécution, et l'Union, toujours sur le point de périr, fut sauvée bien plus par la faiblesse de ses ennemis que par sa propre force.

translation: Up to now I have considered each State as a complete whole, and I have shown the various mechanisms the people set in motion within it, along with the means of action they use. But all these States, which I have treated as independent, are nevertheless required in certain cases to obey a higher authority — that of the Union. The time has come to examine the share of sovereignty conceded to the Union, and to glance briefly at the federal constitution[122].
HISTORY OF THE FEDERAL CONSTITUTION.
Origin of the first Union. — Its weakness. — Congress appeals to the constituent power. — Interval of two years between this moment and the promulgation of the new constitution.

The thirteen colonies that simultaneously threw off the English yoke at the end of the last century had, as I have already said, the same religion, the same language, the same mores, almost the same laws; they were struggling against a common enemy; they therefore had strong reasons to bind themselves closely together and to merge into a single nation.
[Translator's note: mores — Tocqueville's term for the habits, dispositions, and moral character of a people; no English equivalent captures its full range.]

But each of them, having always had a separate existence and a government close at hand, had developed its own interests and habits, and was reluctant to enter a solid and complete union in which its individual importance would disappear into a common one. Hence two opposing tendencies: one that drew the Anglo-Americans toward union, the other toward division.

As long as the war with the mother country lasted, necessity made the principle of union prevail. And though the laws that constituted this union were defective, the common bond held in spite of them[123].

But as soon as peace was concluded, the defects of the legislation came into the open: the State seemed to dissolve all at once. Each colony, having become an independent republic, took hold of full sovereignty. The federal government, condemned to weakness by its very constitution and no longer sustained by the sense of public danger, saw its flag exposed to insult from the great peoples of Europe, while it could not find enough resources to face the Indian nations or to pay the interest on debts contracted during the War of Independence. On the verge of perishing, it officially declared its own impotence and appealed to the constituent power[124].

If America ever rose for a few moments to that high degree of glory where the proud imagination of its inhabitants would ceaselessly have us see her, it was in that supreme moment when the national power had, in a sense, just abdicated its dominion.

That a people should struggle energetically to win its independence is a spectacle every century has been able to furnish. The efforts the Americans made to throw off the English yoke have, moreover, been greatly exaggerated. Separated from their enemies by thirteen hundred leagues of sea, aided by a powerful ally, the United States owed victory to their position far more than to the valor of their armies or the patriotism of their citizens. Who would dare compare the American war to the wars of the French Revolution, and the efforts of the Americans to ours, when France, beset by the attacks of all Europe, without money, without credit, without allies, hurled a twentieth of her population against her enemies, smothering with one hand the fire that was devouring her entrails, and with the other brandishing the torch around her? But what is new in the history of societies is to see a great people, warned by its legislators that the machinery of government is grinding to a halt, turn its gaze upon itself without haste and without fear, sound the depth of the evil, hold itself in check for two full years in order to discover the remedy at leisure, and, once that remedy is identified, submit to it voluntarily without its costing humanity a single tear or a single drop of blood.

When the inadequacy of the first federal constitution made itself felt, the ferment of political passions that the revolution had stirred up was partly calmed, and all the great men it had produced were still alive. That was a double piece of good fortune for America. The small assembly[125] that took upon itself the task of drafting the second constitution included the finest minds and the noblest characters that had ever appeared in the New World. George Washington presided over it.

After long and mature deliberation, this national commission at last offered for the people's adoption the body of organic laws that still governs the Union today. All the States adopted it in turn[126]. The new federal government took office in 1789, after a two-year interregnum. The American revolution thus ended precisely at the moment when ours began.
SUMMARY VIEW OF THE FEDERAL CONSTITUTION.
Division of powers between the federal sovereignty and that of the States. — The government of the States remains the rule; — the federal government, the exception.

A first difficulty had to present itself to the minds of the Americans. They had to divide sovereignty in such a way that the different States making up the Union would continue to govern themselves in everything concerning only their internal prosperity, while the entire nation, represented by the Union, would not cease to form one body and to provide for all its general needs. A complex question, and hard to solve.

It was impossible to fix in advance, exactly and completely, the share of power that should fall to each of the two governments between which sovereignty was to be divided. Who could foresee in advance all the particulars of a people's life?

The duties and rights of the federal government were simple and rather easy to define, because the Union had been formed to meet a few great general needs. The duties and rights of the State government were, by contrast, many and complicated, because that government reached into all the details of social life.

The powers of the federal government were therefore carefully defined, and it was declared that everything not included in the definition fell within the powers of the State government. Thus the State government remained the rule; the federal government was the exception[127].

But since it was foreseen that in practice questions might arise about the exact limits of this exceptional government, and since it would have been dangerous to leave the solution of such questions to the ordinary courts established in the several States by those States themselves, a federal high court[128] was created — a single tribunal, one of whose functions was to maintain, between the two rival governments, the division of powers as the constitution had established it[129].
POWERS OF THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT.

Power granted to the federal government to make peace, to make war, to lay general taxes. — Matters of internal policy with which it may concern itself. — The government of the Union, more centralized on certain points than the royal government was under the old French monarchy.
Peoples in their dealings with one another are only individuals. It is above all in order to appear to advantage before foreigners that a nation needs a single government.
The Union was therefore granted the exclusive right to make peace and war; to conclude commercial treaties; to raise armies and equip fleets[130].
The need for a national government does not make itself felt so imperiously in the conduct of the society's internal affairs.
There are nevertheless certain general interests for which only a general authority can usefully provide.

The Union was given the right to regulate everything relating to the value of money; it was put in charge of the postal service; it was given the right to open the major communications that were to link the various parts of the territory[131].

In general, the government of the various States was considered free within its own sphere; yet it could abuse this independence and, through imprudent measures, compromise the security of the whole Union; for these rare and previously defined cases, the federal government was permitted to intervene in the internal affairs of the States[132]. Thus, while recognizing in each of the confederated republics the power to modify and to change its legislation, it was nevertheless forbidden to pass retroactive laws or to create within itself a body of nobles[133].
Finally, since the federal government had to be able to meet the obligations imposed upon it, it was given the unlimited right to levy taxes[134].

When one attends to the division of powers as the federal constitution has established it; when one examines, on the one hand, the portion of sovereignty the individual States reserved to themselves, and, on the other, the share of power the Union took, one easily discovers that the federal legislators had formed very clear and very accurate ideas of what I have earlier called governmental centralization.

Not only do the United States form a republic, they also form a confederation. Yet the national authority is in some respects more centralized than it was at the same period in several of the absolute monarchies of Europe. I will cite only two examples.

France had thirteen sovereign courts, which most often had the right to interpret the law without appeal. She also possessed certain provinces called *pays d'États*, which, after the sovereign authority charged with representing the nation had ordered the levy of a tax, could refuse their concurrence.

The Union has only a single tribunal to interpret the law, just as it has a single legislature to make it; the tax voted by the representatives of the nation binds every citizen. The Union is thus more centralized on these two essential points than the French monarchy was; and yet the Union is only an assemblage of confederated republics.
In Spain, certain provinces had the power to establish a customs system of their own — a power that by its very essence belongs to national sovereignty.

In America, Congress alone has the right to regulate the commercial relations of the States among themselves. The government of the confederation is therefore more centralized on this point than that of the kingdom of Spain. It is true that in France and in Spain, the royal power, always able to execute by force if need be what the constitution of the kingdom denied it the right to do, in the end came to the same point. But I am speaking here of the theory.
FEDERAL POWERS.
Having enclosed the federal government within a clearly drawn sphere of action, the question was how to set it in motion within that sphere.
LEGISLATIVE POWERS.

Division of the legislative body into two branches. — Differences in the manner of forming the two chambers. — The principle of the independence of the States prevails in the formation of the Senate. — The dogma of national sovereignty, in the composition of the House of Representatives. — Singular effects that result from this — that constitutions are logical only when peoples are young.
In organizing the powers of the Union, the plan already traced by the particular constitution of each of the States was followed on many points.
The federal legislative body of the Union was composed of a Senate and a House of Representatives.
The spirit of conciliation led to different rules being followed in the formation of each of these assemblies.
I have indicated above that, when the federal constitution was to be established, two opposing interests stood facing each other. These two interests gave rise to two opinions.
Some wanted to make the Union a league of independent States, a kind of congress where the representatives of distinct peoples would come to discuss certain points of common interest.

The others wanted to gather all the inhabitants of the former colonies into one and the same people, and to give them a government which, although its sphere was limited, could nevertheless act, within that sphere, as the sole and unique representative of the nation. The practical consequences of these two theories were very different.

Thus, if the task was to organize a league and not a national government, then the majority of States, not the majority of the inhabitants of the Union, would make the law. For each State, large or small, would then retain its character as an independent power, and would enter the Union on a footing of perfect equality.
If, on the contrary, the inhabitants of the United States were taken to form one single people, it was natural that the majority alone of the citizens of the Union should make the law.

One can see that the small States could not agree to the application of this doctrine without entirely abdicating their existence in what concerned federal sovereignty; for from being a co-regulating power, they became an insignificant fraction of a great people. The first system would have given them an unreasonable share of power; the second annulled them.

In this state of affairs there happened what almost always happens when interests run against reasoning: the rules of logic were bent. The legislators adopted a middle term that forcibly reconciled two systems theoretically irreconcilable.
The principle of the independence of the States prevailed in the formation of the Senate; the dogma of national sovereignty, in the composition of the House of Representatives.
Each State was to send two senators to Congress and a certain number of representatives, in proportion to its population[135].

It follows from this arrangement that today the State of New York has forty representatives in Congress and only two senators; the State of Delaware has two senators and only one representative. In the Senate, then, the State of Delaware is the equal of the State of New York; while in the House of Representatives the latter has forty times as much influence as the former. Thus it may happen that the minority of the nation, dominating the Senate, completely paralyzes the will of the majority represented by the other chamber — which is contrary to the spirit of constitutional governments.
All this clearly shows how rare and difficult it is to bind together all the parts of a body of legislation in a logical and rational way.

Time, in any one people, always gives rise in the long run to different interests, and consecrates differing rights. When it is then a question of establishing a general constitution, each of these interests and rights forms so many natural obstacles preventing any political principle from being followed to all its consequences. It is therefore only at the birth of societies that one can be wholly logical in the laws. When you see a people enjoying this advantage, do not hasten to conclude that it is wise; think rather that it is young.

At the time when the federal constitution was formed, there existed as yet among the Anglo-Americans only two positively opposed interests: the interest of particularity for the individual States, the interest of union for the people as a whole; and a compromise had to be reached.
It must nevertheless be acknowledged that this part of the arrangement has not so far produced the evils that might have been feared.

All the States are young; they are close to one another; they have homogeneous mores, ideas, and needs; the difference resulting from their greater or smaller size is not enough to give them sharply opposing interests. The small States have therefore never been seen leaguing themselves in the Senate against the designs of the large ones. Moreover, there is a force so irresistible in the legal expression of the will of an entire people that, when the majority comes to express itself through the House of Representatives, the Senate finds itself quite weak in its presence.

Furthermore, it must not be forgotten that it did not lie with the American legislators to make one and the same nation of the people to whom they wished to give laws. The aim of the federal constitution was not to destroy the existence of the States, but only to restrict it. From the moment, then, that real power was left to these secondary bodies (and it could not be taken from them), the habitual use of coercion to bend them to the will of the majority was renounced in advance. This being so, the introduction of their individual forces into the workings of the federal government had nothing extraordinary about it. It only registered an existing fact, that of a recognized power which had to be managed, not coerced.
ANOTHER DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE SENATE AND THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES.

The Senate named by the provincial legislatures. — The representatives, by the people. — Two stages of election for the former. — A single one for the latter. — Duration of the various mandates. — Powers.
The Senate differs from the other chamber not only in the very principle of representation, but also in the mode of election, in the length of the mandate, and in the diversity of its powers.
The House of Representatives is named by the people; the Senate, by the legislatures of each State.
The one is the product of direct election, the other of election in two stages.
The mandate of the representatives lasts only two years; that of the senators, six.

The House of Representatives has only legislative functions; it participates in the judicial power only by accusing public officers; the Senate concurs in the making of laws; it tries the political offenses referred to it by the House of Representatives; it is, moreover, the great executive council of the nation. The treaties concluded by the president must be ratified by the Senate; his appointments, to be final, require the approval of the same body[136].
THE EXECUTIVE POWER[137].

Dependence of the president. — Elective and responsible. — Free within his sphere, the Senate oversees him but does not direct him. — The president's salary fixed on his entry into office. — Suspensive veto.

The American legislators had a difficult task to perform: they wanted to create an executive power that would depend on the majority, and yet be strong enough in itself to act freely within its sphere.
The maintenance of the republican form required that the representative of the executive power be subject to the national will.

The president is an elective magistrate. His honor, his property, his liberty, his life, are at every moment answerable to the people for the good use he makes of his power. In exercising this power, moreover, he is not wholly independent: the Senate watches over him in his relations with foreign powers and in the distribution of offices, so that he can neither be corrupted nor corrupt.

The legislators of the Union recognized that the executive power could not fulfill its task with dignity and effect if they did not manage to give it more stability and more strength than had been granted to it in the individual States.
The president was appointed for four years, and could be re-elected. With a future before him, he had the courage to work for the public good, and the means to do so.

The president was made the sole and unique representative of the executive power of the Union. They took care not even to subordinate his will to that of a council: a dangerous expedient which, while weakening the action of the government, diminishes the responsibility of those who govern. The Senate has the right to render some of the president's acts sterile, but it cannot force him to act, nor share with him the executive power.
The action of the legislature on the executive power may be direct; we have just seen that the Americans had taken care that it should not be so. It can also be indirect.

The chambers, by depriving the public functionary of his salary, take from him part of his independence; mistresses of the laws, they may be feared to strip him gradually of the portion of power the constitution wished to preserve for him.

This dependence of the executive power is one of the vices inherent in republican constitutions. The Americans have not been able to destroy the slope that draws legislative assemblies into taking over the government, but they have made that slope less irresistible.

The president's salary is fixed, on his entry into office, for the whole duration of his magistracy. Moreover, the president is armed with a suspensive veto, which allows him to halt in their passage laws that might destroy the portion of independence the constitution has left him. There can nevertheless be only an unequal struggle between the president and the legislature, since the latter, by persisting in its designs, is always master of overcoming the resistance opposed to it; but the suspensive veto at least forces it to retrace its steps; it obliges it to consider the question again, and this time it can settle it only by a two-thirds majority of those voting. The veto, moreover, is a kind of appeal to the people. The executive power, which without this guarantee might have been oppressed in secret, then pleads its cause and makes its reasons heard.

But if the legislature persists in its designs, can it not always overcome the resistance opposed to it? To this I will reply that there is in the constitution of every people, whatever its nature, a point at which the legislator is obliged to rely on the good sense and virtue of the citizens. This point is nearer and more visible in republics, more distant and more carefully hidden in monarchies; but it is always to be found somewhere. There is no country where the law can foresee everything, and where institutions can take the place of reason and of mores.
HOW THE POSITION OF THE PRESIDENT IN THE UNITED STATES DIFFERS FROM THAT OF A CONSTITUTIONAL KING IN FRANCE.

The executive power in the United States, limited and exceptional like the sovereignty in whose name it acts. — The executive power in France extends to everything, as that sovereignty does. — The king is one of the authors of the law. — The president is only the executor of the law. — Other differences arising from the duration of the two powers. — The president constrained within the sphere of the executive power. — The king is free within it. — France, despite these differences, resembles a republic more than the Union does a monarchy. — Comparison of the number of officials who, in the two countries, depend on the executive power.
The executive power plays so great a role in the destiny of nations that I want to pause here for a moment, the better to make it understood what place it occupies among the Americans.
In order to form a clear and precise idea of the position of the president of the United States, it is useful to compare it with that of the king in one of the constitutional monarchies of Europe.
In this comparison, I shall pay little attention to the external signs of power; they deceive the observer's eye more than they guide it.

When a monarchy is gradually transformed into a republic, the executive power retains its titles, its honors, its marks of respect, and even its money, long after it has lost the reality of power. The English, after cutting off the head of one of their kings and driving another from his throne, still went down on their knees to speak to the successors of those princes.

On the other side, when republics fall under the yoke of one man, power continues to show itself simple, plain, and modest in its manners, as if it had not already risen above all others. When the emperors disposed despotically of the fortune and the life of their fellow citizens, they were still called Caesars when addressed, and they went off to dine familiarly with their friends.
One must therefore leave the surface and go deeper.

Sovereignty in the United States is divided between the Union and the States, whereas among us it is one and compact; from this arises the first and greatest difference I can see between the president of the United States and the king in France.
In the United States, the executive power is limited and exceptional, like the sovereignty itself in whose name it acts; in France it extends to everything, as that sovereignty does.
The Americans have a federal government; we have a national government.

That is a first cause of inferiority, arising from the very nature of things; but it is not the only one. The second in importance is this: one can, strictly speaking, define sovereignty as the right to make laws.
The king, in France, really constitutes a part of the sovereign, since laws do not exist if he refuses to sanction them; he is, moreover, the executor of the laws.

The president is likewise the executor of the law, but he does not really concur in making it, since by refusing his assent he cannot prevent it from existing. He is therefore not a part of the sovereign; he is only its agent.

Not only does the king in France form a portion of the sovereign; he also participates in the formation of the legislature, which is its other portion. He participates in it by appointing the members of one chamber, and by ending at will the term of the other. The president of the United States plays no part in the composition of the legislative body, and cannot dissolve it.
The king shares with the chambers the right to propose laws.
The president has no such initiative.
The king is represented within the chambers by a certain number of agents who set forth his views, defend his opinions, and make his maxims of government prevail.
The president has no entry to Congress; his ministers are excluded from it as he himself is, and it is only by indirect means that he can make his influence and his advice penetrate that great body.
The king of France thus marches as an equal alongside the legislature, which cannot act without him, just as he cannot act without it.
The president is placed beside the legislature as an inferior and dependent power.

In the exercise of the executive power properly so called — the point on which his position seems to come closest to that of the king in France — the president has several other very great causes of inferiority.

The king's power in France has, first of all, the advantage of duration over that of the president. Now, duration is one of the first elements of strength. Men love and fear only what is to exist for a long time.
The president of the United States is a magistrate elected for four years. The king, in France, is a hereditary chief.

In the exercise of the executive power, the president of the United States is continually subject to jealous oversight. He prepares treaties, but he does not make them; he designates men for offices, but he does not appoint them[138].
The king of France is absolute master within the sphere of the executive power.
The president of the United States is responsible for his acts. French law says that the person of the king of France is inviolable.

Yet above each of them stands a directing power, that of public opinion. This power is less defined in France than in the United States; less recognized, less formulated in the laws; but in fact it exists there. In America, it proceeds by elections and judgments; in France, by revolutions. France and the United States thus have in common, despite the diversity of their constitution, that public opinion is, in the end, the dominant power. The generative principle of the laws is therefore truly the same in the two peoples, though its workings are more or less free in each, and the conclusions drawn from it are often different. This principle, by its nature, is essentially republican. So I think that France, with its king, resembles a republic more than the Union, with its president, resembles a monarchy.

In everything that precedes, I have taken care to point out only the chief differences. If I had wished to enter into the details, the picture would have been still more striking. But I have too much to say not to want to be brief.

I have noted that the power of the president of the United States is exercised only within the sphere of a restricted sovereignty, whereas the power of the king in France acts within the sphere of a complete sovereignty.

I could have shown the governmental power of the king in France going even beyond its natural limits, extensive as they are, and penetrating in a thousand ways into the administration of individual interests.

To this cause of influence I could have added the one arising from the great number of public officials who almost all owe their position to the executive power. This number has exceeded among us all known bounds; it amounts to 138,000[139]. Each of these 138,000 appointments must be considered an element of strength. The president has no absolute right of appointment to public offices, and those offices hardly exceed 12,000[140].
ACCIDENTAL CAUSES THAT MAY INCREASE THE INFLUENCE OF THE EXECUTIVE POWER.

External security enjoyed by the Union. — Wait-and-see policy. — Army of 6,000 soldiers. — Only a few ships. — The president possesses great prerogatives that he has no occasion to use. — In what he has occasion to execute, he is weak.
If the executive power is less strong in America than in France, the cause must be attributed to circumstances perhaps even more than to laws.
It is chiefly in its dealings with foreigners that a nation's executive power finds occasion to display skill and strength.

If the life of the Union were constantly threatened, if its great interests were every day mixed with those of other powerful peoples, the executive power would be seen growing in opinion, both by what would be expected of it and by what it would carry out.

The president of the United States is, it is true, the head of the army, but this army is made up of 6,000 soldiers; he commands the fleet, but the fleet has only a few ships; he directs the affairs of the Union toward foreign peoples, but the United States has no neighbors. Separated from the rest of the world by the Ocean, still too weak to want to dominate the sea, they have no enemies, and their interests are only rarely in contact with those of the other nations of the globe.
This makes it plain that one must not judge the practice of government by the theory.

The president of the United States possesses almost royal prerogatives which he has no occasion to use, and the rights of which he can, so far, make use are very narrowly drawn: the laws permit him to be strong, circumstances keep him weak.
It is, on the contrary, circumstances, even more than the laws, that give the royal authority of France its greatest strength.

In France, the executive power struggles incessantly against immense obstacles, and has immense resources to overcome them. It grows by the greatness of the things it executes and the importance of the events it directs, without thereby modifying its constitution.
Had the laws made it as weak and as narrowly drawn as that of the Union, its influence would soon become much greater.
WHY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES DOES NOT NEED, IN ORDER TO CONDUCT AFFAIRS, TO HAVE A MAJORITY IN THE CHAMBERS.
It is an axiom established in Europe that a constitutional king cannot govern when the opinion of the legislative chambers is not in accord with his own.

We have seen several presidents of the United States lose the support of the majority in the legislative body without being obliged to give up power, and without any great harm to society resulting from it.

I have heard this fact cited as proof of the independence and strength of the executive power in America. A few moments' reflection is enough to see in it, on the contrary, the proof of its impotence.

A king in Europe needs the support of the legislative body to fulfill the task the constitution imposes upon him, because that task is immense. A constitutional king in Europe is not merely the executor of the law: the care of its execution is so completely devolved upon him that, if the law were unfavorable to him, he could paralyze its forces. He needs the chambers to make the law, the chambers need him to execute it: they are two powers that cannot live without each other; the machinery of government grinds to a halt the moment disagreement arises between them.

In America, the president cannot prevent the formation of laws; he cannot evade the obligation to execute them. His zealous and sincere cooperation is no doubt useful, but it is not necessary to the workings of government. In everything he does of any importance, he is subjected, directly or indirectly, to the legislature; where he is entirely independent of it, he can do almost nothing. It is therefore his weakness, not his strength, that allows him to live in opposition to the legislative power.
In Europe, there must be accord between the king and the chambers, because there can be serious struggle between them. In America, accord is not required, because struggle is impossible.
ON THE ELECTION OF THE PRESIDENT.

The danger of the system of election grows in proportion to the extent of the prerogatives of the executive power. — The Americans can adopt this system because they can do without a strong executive power. — How circumstances favor the establishment of the elective system. — Why the election of the president does not cause the principles of government to vary. — Influence that the election of the president exerts on the fate of subordinate officials.
The system of election, applied to the head of the executive power in a great people, presents dangers that experience and historians have sufficiently signaled.
For this reason I will speak of it only in relation to America.

The dangers feared from the system of election are greater or smaller according to the place the executive power occupies and its importance in the State, according to the mode of election, and according to the circumstances in which the electing people finds itself.

What is reproached, not without reason, in the elective system applied to the head of State is that it offers so great a lure to private ambitions, and fires them so strongly in the pursuit of power, that often, when legal means no longer suffice, they appeal to force when right fails them.

It is clear that the more prerogatives the executive power has, the greater the lure; and the more the ambition of the contenders is excited, the more it finds support in a crowd of secondary ambitions that hope to share in the power once their candidate has triumphed.
The dangers of the system of election thus grow in direct proportion to the influence exercised by the executive power on the affairs of the State.
The revolutions of Poland are to be attributed not only to the elective system in general, but to the fact that the elected magistrate was the head of a great monarchy.

Before discussing the absolute merits of the elective system, then, there is always a preliminary question to decide: whether the geographical position, the laws, the habits, the mores and the opinions of the people among whom one wishes to introduce it permit the establishment there of a weak and dependent executive power; for to wish at one and the same time that the representative of the State remain armed with vast power and be elected is, in my view, to express two contradictory wishes. For my part, I know of only one way to pass from hereditary royalty to an elective power: one must narrow its sphere of action in advance, gradually diminish its prerogatives, and accustom the people little by little to live without its help. But this is hardly what the republicans of Europe concern themselves with. As many of them hate tyranny only because they are exposed to its rigors, the extent of executive power does not offend them; they attack only its origin, without seeing the tight bond between these two things.

No one has yet been found who cared to risk his honor and his life to become president of the United States, because the president has only a temporary, limited, and dependent power. Fortune must put a huge stake into play for desperate gamblers to step into the lists. No candidate, so far, has been able to stir up in his favor ardent sympathies and dangerous popular passions. The reason is simple: once at the head of the government, he cannot distribute to his friends much power, much wealth, or much glory, and his influence in the State is too weak for factions to see their success or their ruin in his rise to power.

Hereditary monarchies have a great advantage: since the particular interest of a family is there continually bound up closely with the interest of the State, there is never a single moment when the latter is left to itself. I do not know whether in these monarchies affairs are better managed than elsewhere; but at least there is always someone who, well or badly, according to his capacity, attends to them.

In elective States, on the contrary, as the election approaches, and long before it arrives, the machinery of government runs, so to speak, only of itself. The laws may no doubt be so combined that the election, taking place in a single stroke and rapidly, never leaves the seat of executive power, as it were, vacant; but whatever one does, the void exists in people's minds in spite of the legislator's efforts.

As the election approaches, the head of the executive power thinks of nothing but the coming struggle; he no longer has a future; he can undertake nothing, and pursues only listlessly what another will perhaps complete. "I am so near the moment of my retirement," wrote President Jefferson on January 21, 1809 (six weeks before the election), "that I no longer take part in affairs except by expressing my opinion. It seems to me right to leave to my successor the initiative of the measures whose execution he will have to follow up and whose responsibility he will have to bear."
On its side, the nation has its eyes turned to a single point; it is occupied only with watching the labor of bringing forth that is being prepared.

The greater the place the executive power occupies in the direction of affairs, the greater and the more necessary its habitual action, the more dangerous such a state of things becomes. Among a people that has contracted the habit of being governed by the executive power — and still more, of being administered by it — election cannot fail to produce a profound disturbance.
In the United States, the action of the executive power may slacken with impunity, because that action is weak and narrowly drawn.
When the head of the government is elected, there almost always results an absence of stability in the State's internal and external policy. That is one of the principal vices of the system.

But this vice is more or less perceptible depending on the share of power granted to the elected magistrate. At Rome, the principles of government did not vary, although the consuls were changed every year, because the Senate was the directing power, and the Senate was a hereditary body. In most of the monarchies of Europe, if the king were elected, the kingdom would change its face with each new choice.

In America, the president exercises a fairly great influence on the affairs of the State, but he does not direct them; the preponderant power lies in the national representation as a whole. It is therefore the mass of the people that must be changed, and not just the president, for the maxims of policy to vary. So, in America, the system of election applied to the head of the executive power does not harm the stability of the government in any very perceptible way.
And besides, the lack of stability is an evil so inherent in the elective system that it still makes itself sharply felt within the president's sphere of action, narrowly drawn as that is.

The Americans have rightly thought that the head of the executive power, in order to fulfill his mission and bear the full weight of responsibility, should remain as free as possible to choose his own agents and to dismiss them at will; the legislative body watches over the president rather than directs him. It follows that at each new election the fate of all federal employees is held, as it were, in suspense.

In the constitutional monarchies of Europe, people complain that the destiny of obscure agents of the administration often depends on the fate of ministers. It is much worse still in States where the head of government is elected. The reason is simple: in constitutional monarchies, ministers succeed one another rapidly, but the chief representative of the executive power never changes, which keeps the spirit of innovation within certain limits. Administrative systems there vary in detail rather than in principle; one cannot abruptly substitute one for another without causing a kind of revolution. In America, this revolution takes place every four years in the name of the law.

As for the individual miseries that are the natural consequence of such a legislation, one must admit that the lack of stability in the fate of officials does not produce in America the evils that might be expected of it elsewhere. In the United States, it is so easy to make an independent existence for oneself that to take away an official's place is sometimes to remove from him ease of life, but never the means of sustaining it.

I said at the beginning of this chapter that the dangers of the elective mode applied to the head of the executive power are greater or smaller according to the circumstances in which the electing people finds itself.

In vain does one strive to diminish the role of the executive power; there is one thing on which this power exerts a great influence whatever place the laws have assigned it: foreign policy. A negotiation can hardly be begun and carried through to good effect except by a single man.

The more precarious and perilous a people's position, the more the need for continuity and stability makes itself felt in the conduct of foreign affairs, and the more the application of the system of election to the head of State becomes dangerous.
The policy of the Americans toward the rest of the world is simple; one might almost say that no one needs them, and that they need no one. Their independence is never threatened.
Among them, the role of the executive power is therefore restricted by circumstances as well as by the laws. The president can change his views frequently without the State suffering or perishing.

Whatever prerogatives the executive power may be vested with, one must always regard the time immediately preceding the election, and the time during which it takes place, as a period of national crisis.

The more troubled the internal situation of a country, and the greater its external perils, the more dangerous this moment of crisis is for it. Among the peoples of Europe, there are very few that would not have to fear conquest or anarchy each time they gave themselves a new chief.

In America, society is so constituted that it can sustain itself by itself and without help; external dangers there are never pressing. The election of the president is a cause of agitation, not of ruin.
MODE OF ELECTION.

Skill shown by the American legislators in the choice of the mode of election. — Creation of a special electoral body. — Separate vote of the special electors. — In what case the House of Representatives is called upon to choose the president. — What has occurred at the twelve elections that have taken place since the constitution has been in force.
Apart from the dangers inherent in the principle, there are many others that arise from the very forms of the election, and that can be avoided by the legislator's care.

When a people gathers in arms in the public square to choose its head, it exposes itself not only to the dangers presented by the elective system in itself, but also to all those of the civil war that arises from such a mode of election.
When the Polish laws made the king depend on the choice — the *veto* — of a single man, they invited the murder of that man, or constituted anarchy in advance.

As one studies the institutions of the United States and takes a closer look at the political and social situation of that country, one notices a marvelous agreement there between fortune and human effort. America was a new country; yet the people inhabiting it had already long made use of liberty elsewhere: two great causes of internal order. Moreover, America had no conquest to fear. The American legislators, taking hold of these favorable circumstances, had no trouble establishing a weak and dependent executive power; having created it as such, they could without danger make it elective.

It only remained for them to choose, among the various systems of election, the least dangerous; the rules they laid down in this regard admirably complete the guarantees that the physical and political constitution of the country already provided.

The problem to be solved was to find the mode of election that, while expressing the real will of the people, would arouse its passions little and keep it in suspense as little as possible. It was agreed first that a *simple* majority would carry the law. But it was still a very difficult thing to obtain that majority without having to fear the delays which, above all, they wanted to avoid.

It is rare, in fact, to see one man gathering at the first stroke the majority of votes among a great people. The difficulty grows still greater in a republic of confederated States, where local influences are much more developed and more powerful.
To get around this second obstacle, one means presented itself: to delegate the electoral powers of the nation to a body that would represent it.
This mode of election made a majority more probable; for the fewer the electors, the easier it is for them to agree. It also offered more guarantees of a good choice.

But should the right to elect be entrusted to the legislative body itself — the habitual representative of the nation — or should one, on the contrary, form an electoral college whose sole purpose would be to proceed with the nomination of the president?

The Americans preferred the latter course. They thought that the men sent to make the ordinary laws would represent only incompletely the wishes of the people concerning the election of its chief magistrate. Being moreover elected for more than one year, they might represent a will that had already changed. They judged that if the legislature were charged with electing the head of the executive power, its members would, long before the election, become the object of corrupting maneuvers and the plaything of intrigue; whereas the special electors, like jurors, would remain unknown in the crowd until the day they were to act, and would appear only for an instant to pronounce their verdict.

It was therefore established that each State would name a certain number of electors[141], who would in turn elect the president. And since it had been observed that, in elective countries, the assemblies charged with choosing the heads of government inevitably became hotbeds of passions and intrigue; that sometimes they seized powers not belonging to them; and that often their operations, and the uncertainty that followed, dragged on long enough to put the State in peril, it was decided that the electors would all vote on a fixed day, but without having gathered[142].
The mode of election in two stages made a majority probable, but did not assure it, for the electors might differ among themselves as their constituents would have done.

Should this case arise, one of three measures had necessarily to be taken: either new electors had to be named, or the ones already named consulted again, or, finally, the choice referred to a new authority.
The first two methods, quite apart from their being unsure, brought delays and perpetuated an always dangerous agitation.

They settled, then, on the third, and it was agreed that the votes of the electors would be transmitted sealed to the president of the Senate; that on a fixed day, in the presence of both chambers, he would count them. If no candidate had obtained the majority, the House of Representatives would immediately proceed to the election itself; but care was taken to limit its right. The representatives could elect only one of the three candidates who had received the most votes[143].

It is only, as one sees, in a rare case difficult to foresee in advance that the election is entrusted to the ordinary representatives of the nation; and even then they can choose only a citizen already designated by a strong minority of the special electors. A fortunate combination, which reconciles the respect due to the will of the people with rapid execution and the guarantees of order that the interest of the State requires. Moreover, by having the question decided by the House of Representatives in case of a tie, they did not yet arrive at a complete solution to all the difficulties; for the majority might in turn prove doubtful in the House of Representatives, and this time the constitution offered no remedy. But by establishing required candidacies, by restricting their number to three, by relying on the choice of a few enlightened men, it had smoothed over all the obstacles[144] over which it could have any power; the others were inherent in the elective system itself.
In the forty-four years that the federal constitution has existed, the United States has already elected its president twelve times.
Ten elections took place in an instant, by the simultaneous vote of the special electors placed at the various points of the territory.

The House of Representatives has so far made use only twice of the exceptional right with which it is vested in case of a tie. The first time, in 1801, in the election of Mr. Jefferson; and the second, in 1825, when Mr. Quincy Adams was named.
THE CRISIS OF THE ELECTION.

The moment of the president's election can be considered a moment of national crisis. — Why. — Passion of the people. — Preoccupation of the president. — Calm that follows the agitation of the election.

I have said in what favorable circumstances the United States found itself for the adoption of the elective system, and I have made known the precautions the legislators took to diminish its dangers. The Americans are accustomed to proceeding with all sorts of elections. Experience has taught them to what degree of agitation they may go and where they must stop. The vast extent of their territory and the dispersion of the inhabitants make a collision between the different parties less probable and less perilous there than anywhere else. The political circumstances amid which the nation has found itself at the time of the elections have so far presented no real danger.
And yet the moment of the election of the president of the United States may still be considered a period of national crisis.

The influence the president exercises on the course of affairs is no doubt weak and indirect, but it extends over the whole nation; the choice of the president matters only moderately to each citizen, but it matters to all citizens. Now, any interest, however small, takes on a great character of importance the moment it becomes a general interest.

Compared with a king of Europe, the president has, no doubt, few means of creating partisans for himself; yet the offices at his disposal are numerous enough that several thousand electors have a direct or indirect interest in his cause.

Moreover, parties in the United States, as elsewhere, feel the need to group themselves around a man, so as to reach the understanding of the crowd more easily. They therefore generally use the name of the presidential candidate as a symbol; they personify their theories in him. Thus, the parties have a great interest in deciding the election in their favor, not so much to make their doctrines triumph with the aid of the elected president, as to show, by his election, that those doctrines have gained the majority.

Long before the appointed moment arrives, the election becomes the greatest, and so to speak the sole, business that occupies minds. Factions then redouble their ardor; all the artificial passions that imagination can create in a happy and tranquil country are stirred up in the open at that moment.

On his side, the president is absorbed in the care of defending himself. He no longer governs in the interest of the State, but in the interest of his re-election; he bows down before the majority, and often, instead of resisting its passions as his duty obliges him to do, he runs to meet its caprices.

As the election approaches, intrigues become more active, agitation livelier and more widespread. The citizens divide into several camps, each taking the name of its candidate. The whole nation falls into a feverish state, the election becomes the daily theme of the public papers, the subject of private conversations, the goal of every undertaking, the object of every thought, the only interest of the present.

As soon, it is true, as fortune has pronounced, this ardor dissipates, everything calms down, and the river, which for a moment had overflowed, returns peacefully to its bed. But should one not be astonished that the storm could have arisen at all?
ON THE RE-ELECTION OF THE PRESIDENT.

When the head of the executive power is re-eligible, it is the State itself that intrigues and corrupts. — The desire to be re-elected dominates all the thoughts of the president of the United States. — Drawback of re-election peculiar to America. — The natural vice of democracies is the gradual enslavement of all powers to the slightest desires of the majority. — The re-election of the president favors this vice.
Were the legislators of the United States wrong or right to permit the re-election of the president?

To prevent the head of the executive power from being re-eligible seems, at first sight, contrary to reason. We know what influence the talents or character of a single man can have on the destiny of an entire people, especially in difficult circumstances and in times of crisis. Laws forbidding citizens to re-elect their chief magistrate would deprive them of the best means of making the State prosper or of saving it. One would arrive, moreover, at the strange result that a man would be excluded from government at the very moment when he had finished proving that he was capable of governing well.
These reasons are powerful, no doubt; yet can one not oppose to them others stronger still?

Intrigue and corruption are vices natural to elective governments. But when the head of the State can be re-elected, these vices extend indefinitely and compromise the very existence of the country. When a mere candidate seeks to rise by intrigue, his maneuvers can be exercised only over a circumscribed space. When, on the contrary, the head of State himself enters the lists, he borrows for his own use the strength of the government.
In the first case, it is a man with his feeble means; in the second, it is the State itself, with its immense resources, that intrigues and corrupts.

The ordinary citizen who employs blameworthy maneuvers to reach power can harm the public prosperity only indirectly; but if the representative of the executive power steps down into the lists, the care of government becomes for him a secondary interest; the principal interest is his election. Negotiations, like laws, are for him no more than electoral combinations; offices become the reward of services rendered, not to the nation, but to its head. Even if the action of government were not always contrary to the country's interest, at least it no longer serves it. And yet it is for his use alone that this action is taken.

It is impossible to consider the ordinary course of affairs in the United States without noticing that the desire to be re-elected dominates the president's thoughts; that the whole policy of his administration tends toward this point; that his slightest actions are subordinated to this object; that especially as the moment of crisis approaches, individual interest substitutes itself in his mind for the general interest.

The principle of re-election therefore makes the corrupting influence of elective governments more extensive and more dangerous. It tends to degrade the political morality of the people and to replace patriotism with skill.
In America, it strikes still closer to the sources of national existence.

Every government carries within itself a natural vice that seems attached to the very principle of its life; the genius of the legislator consists in discerning it well. A State may overcome many bad laws, and one often exaggerates the harm they cause. But any law whose effect is to develop this seed of death cannot fail, in the long run, to become fatal, even if its bad effects are not immediately perceptible.

The principle of ruin, in absolute monarchies, is the unlimited and unreasonable extension of royal power. A measure that removed the counterweights the constitution had left to that power would therefore be radically bad, even if its effects long appeared imperceptible.

In the same way, in countries where democracy governs and where the people draws everything constantly to itself, the laws that make its action more and more rapid and irresistible attack the existence of the government in a direct manner.
The greatest merit of the American legislators is to have clearly perceived this truth and to have had the courage to put it into practice.

They conceived that outside the people there had to be a certain number of powers that, without being completely independent of it, would nevertheless enjoy, within their sphere, a fairly great degree of liberty; so that, forced to obey the permanent direction of the majority, they could nevertheless struggle against its caprices and refuse its dangerous demands.

To this end, they concentrated all the executive power of the nation in a single hand; they gave the president extensive prerogatives, and armed him with the veto, to resist the encroachments of the legislature.
But by introducing the principle of re-election, they have destroyed in part their own work. They granted the president a great power, and took from him the will to use it.

Not re-eligible, the president was not independent of the people, for he did not cease to be responsible to it; but the favor of the people was not so necessary to him that he had to bow in everything to its will.

Re-eligible (and this is true above all in our day, when political morality has slackened and great characters are disappearing), the president of the United States is only a docile instrument in the hands of the majority. He loves what it loves, hates what it hates; he flies to meet its will, anticipates its complaints, bends to its slightest desires: the legislators wanted him to guide it, and he follows it.

Thus, in order not to deprive the State of the talents of one man, they have rendered those talents almost useless; and, in order to keep a resource in reserve for extraordinary circumstances, they have exposed the country to daily dangers.
THE FEDERAL COURTS[145].

Political importance of the judicial power in the United States. — Difficulty of treating this subject. — Usefulness of justice in confederations. — Which courts could the Union use? — Necessity of establishing federal courts of justice. — Organization of federal justice. — The Supreme Court. — How it differs from all the courts of justice we know.
I have examined the legislative power and the executive power of the Union. It remains for me to consider the judicial power.
Here I must lay my fears before the reader.

The judicial institutions exercise a great influence on the destiny of the Anglo-Americans; they hold a very important place among the political institutions properly so called. From this point of view they particularly deserve our attention.

But how is one to make the political action of the American courts understood without entering into some technical details about their constitution and their forms; and how is one to descend into the details without repelling the reader's curiosity by the natural aridity of such a subject? How can one remain clear without ceasing to be brief?

I do not flatter myself that I have escaped these various perils. Men of the world will still find me too long; jurists will think me too brief. But that is a drawback attached to my subject in general, and to the particular matter I am dealing with at this moment.
The greatest difficulty was not how to constitute the federal government, but how to make its laws obeyed.

Governments in general have only two means of overcoming the resistance offered to them by the governed: the material force they find within themselves; the moral force lent to them by the judgments of the courts.

A government that had only war to make its laws obeyed would be very near its ruin. Probably one of two things would happen to it: if it were weak and moderate, it would use force only in the last extremity, and would let pass unnoticed a host of partial disobediences; the State would then gradually fall into anarchy.

If it were bold and powerful, it would have recourse every day to the use of violence, and would soon be seen to degenerate into pure military despotism. Its inaction and its activity would be equally fatal to the governed.
The great object of justice is to substitute the idea of right for that of violence; to place intermediaries between the government and the use of material force.

It is a surprising thing, the power of opinion granted in general by men to the intervention of the courts. This power is so great that it still attaches to the judicial form when the substance no longer exists; it gives a body to a shadow.

The moral force with which the courts are clothed makes the use of material force infinitely rarer, by substituting itself for it in most cases; and when at last the latter must act, it doubles its power by joining itself to it.

A federal government must wish more than another to obtain the support of justice, because by its nature it is weaker, and resistance can more easily be organized against it[146]. If it always had, and from the outset, to come down to the use of force, it would not be equal to its task.
To make the citizens obey its laws, or to repel the attacks of which those laws were the object, the Union therefore had a particular need of the courts.

But which courts was it to use? Each State already had a judicial power organized within itself. Should it have recourse to those courts? Should a federal justice be created? It is easy to prove that the Union could not adapt to its use the judicial power established in the States.

It is no doubt important to each man's security and to the liberty of all that the judicial power be separated from all the others; but it is no less necessary to national existence that the various powers of the State have the same origin, follow the same principles, and act in the same sphere — in a word, that they be *correlative* and *homogeneous*. No one, I imagine, ever thought of having offenses committed in France judged by foreign courts in order to be more sure of the magistrates' impartiality.

The Americans form only one people in relation to their federal government; but in the midst of this people, political bodies have been left to subsist, dependent on the national government on some points, independent on all others; with their own particular origin, their own doctrines, and their own special means of acting. To entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to the courts established by these political bodies was to deliver the nation to foreign judges.
What is more, each State is not only a foreigner with respect to the Union, but also a daily adversary, since the sovereignty of the Union can lose only to the profit of that of the States.
In having the laws of the Union applied by the courts of the individual States, the nation was therefore delivered not only to foreign judges, but also to partial ones.
Moreover, it was not their character alone that made the State courts unfit to serve a national purpose; it was above all their number.

At the moment when the federal constitution was formed, there were already in the United States thirteen courts of justice judging without appeal. Today there are twenty-four. How is one to admit that a State can subsist when its fundamental laws can be interpreted and applied in twenty-four different ways at once! Such a system is as contrary to reason as to the lessons of experience.

The legislators of America therefore agreed to create a federal judicial power, to apply the laws of the Union, and to decide certain questions of general interest that were carefully defined in advance.

The whole judicial power of the Union was concentrated in a single court, called the Supreme Court of the United States. But, to facilitate the dispatch of business, inferior courts were added to it, charged with judging less important cases without appeal, or with ruling, in the first instance, on more serious disputes. The members of the Supreme Court were not elected by the people or the legislature; the president of the United States was to choose them after taking the advice of the Senate.
In order to make them independent of the other powers, they were made irremovable, and it was decided that their salary, once fixed, would escape the control of the legislature[147].
It was easy enough to proclaim in principle the establishment of a federal justice, but difficulties arose in throngs as soon as it came to fixing its powers.
MANNER OF FIXING THE JURISDICTION OF THE FEDERAL COURTS.

Difficulty of fixing the jurisdiction of the various courts in confederations. — The courts of the Union obtained the right to fix their own jurisdiction. — Why this rule attacks the portion of sovereignty the individual States had reserved to themselves. — The sovereignty of these States restricted by laws and by the interpretation of laws. — The individual States thus run a danger more apparent than real.

A first question presented itself: the constitution of the United States, setting two distinct sovereignties face to face, each represented in matters of justice by a different order of courts, however much care was taken to establish the jurisdiction of each of these two orders of courts, frequent collisions between them could not be prevented. Now, in this case, to whom should the right belong to settle jurisdiction?
Among peoples forming a single political society, when a question of jurisdiction arises between two courts, it is generally referred to a third that serves as arbiter.
This is done without difficulty, because among such peoples questions of judicial jurisdiction have no bearing on questions of national sovereignty.
But above the superior court of an individual State and the superior court of the United States, it was impossible to establish any court at all that would be neither the one nor the other.

It was therefore necessary to give one of the two courts the right to judge in its own cause, and to take or retain cognizance of the case it was contested. This privilege could not be granted to the various courts of the States; that would have destroyed the sovereignty of the Union in fact after establishing it in law; for interpretation of the constitution would soon have restored to the individual States the portion of independence that the terms of the constitution took from them.

In creating a federal court, the aim had been to take from the State courts the right to settle, each in its own way, questions of national interest, and thus to manage to form a uniform body of jurisprudence for the interpretation of the laws of the Union. The aim would not have been reached if the courts of the individual States, while abstaining from judging cases as federal, had been able to judge them by claiming they were not federal.
The Supreme Court of the United States was therefore vested with the right to decide all questions of jurisdiction[148].

That was the most dangerous blow struck at the sovereignty of the States. It was thus restricted not only by the laws, but also by the interpretation of the laws; by a known boundary and by another that was not known; by a fixed rule and by an arbitrary one. The constitution had set, it is true, precise limits on federal sovereignty; but each time that sovereignty is in competition with that of the States, a federal court must pronounce.
For the rest, the dangers with which this manner of proceeding seemed to threaten the sovereignty of the States were not in reality as great as they appeared.

We will see later that in America the real strength resides in the provincial governments more than in the federal government. The federal judges feel the relative weakness of the power in whose name they act, and they are more inclined to give up a right of jurisdiction in cases where the law gives it to them than to claim it illegally.
DIFFERENT KINDS OF JURISDICTION.

The matter and the person, bases of federal jurisdiction. — Suits against ambassadors. — Against the Union. — Against a particular State. — By whom judged. — Suits arising from the laws of the Union. — Why judged by the federal courts. — Suits relating to non-execution of contracts judged by federal justice. — Consequence of this.
After recognizing the means of fixing federal jurisdiction, the legislators of the Union determined the kinds of cases over which it was to be exercised.
It was agreed that there were certain litigants who could be judged only by the federal courts, whatever the object of the suit.
It was then established that there were certain suits that could be decided only by these same courts, whatever the quality of the litigants.
The person and the matter thus became the two bases of federal jurisdiction.

Ambassadors represent nations friendly to the Union; everything that concerns ambassadors concerns in some sense the whole Union. When an ambassador is a party to a suit, the suit becomes a matter touching the well-being of the nation; it is natural that a federal court should pronounce.

The Union itself may have suits: in this case it would have been contrary to reason, as well as to the usage of nations, to appeal to the judgment of courts representing another sovereignty than its own. It is for the federal courts alone to pronounce.

When two individuals belonging to two different States have a suit, they cannot be judged, without inconvenience, by the courts of one of the two States. It is safer to choose a court that can arouse the suspicions of neither party, and the court that presents itself most naturally is the one of the Union.

When the two litigants are no longer isolated individuals, but States, to the same reason of equity is added a political reason of the first order. Here the quality of the litigants gives a national importance to every suit; the slightest disputed question between two States concerns the peace of the whole Union[149].
Often the very nature of the suits had to serve as the rule for jurisdiction. Thus all questions relating to maritime commerce had to be decided by the federal courts[150].

The reason is easy to indicate: nearly all these questions come within the appreciation of the law of nations. In this respect, they essentially concern the whole Union in its relations with foreigners. Moreover, the sea being enclosed within no judicial district rather than another, only the national justice has a title to take cognizance of suits of maritime origin.
The constitution has enclosed within a single category nearly all the suits which by their nature must come under the federal courts.
The rule it indicates in this regard is simple, but it comprehends in itself a vast system of ideas and a multitude of facts.
The federal courts, it says, are to judge all suits that *arise under the laws of the United States*.
Two examples will make the legislator's thought perfectly clear.

The constitution forbids the States to make laws on the circulation of money; in spite of this prohibition, a State makes such a law. The interested parties refuse to obey, on the ground that it is contrary to the constitution. They must go before a federal court, because the means of attack is taken from the laws of the United States.

Congress establishes an import duty. Difficulties arise over the collection of this duty. Again, one must appear before the federal courts, because the cause of the suit lies in the interpretation of a law of the United States.
This rule is in perfect accord with the bases adopted for the federal constitution.

The Union, as it was constituted in 1789, has, it is true, only a restricted sovereignty; but it was intended that within this sphere it should form one and the same people[151]. Within this sphere it is sovereign. This point established and admitted, all the rest becomes easy; for if you recognize that the United States, within the limits set by their constitution, form a single people, you must grant them the rights belonging to all peoples.

Now, since the origin of societies men have agreed on this point: that every people has the right to have judged by its own courts all questions relating to the execution of its own laws. But the answer comes: The Union is in this singular position that it forms a people only with respect to certain objects; for all others, it is nothing. What follows from this? It follows that at least for all laws relating to those objects, it has the rights one would grant to a complete sovereignty. The real point of difficulty is to know what those objects are. Once that point is settled (and we have seen above, in dealing with jurisdiction, how it has been settled), there are, properly speaking, no more questions; for once it has been established that a suit was federal — that is, fell within the share of sovereignty reserved to the Union by the constitution — it naturally followed that only a federal court should pronounce.
Whenever, then, one wishes to attack the laws of the United States, or to invoke them in defense, one must turn to the federal courts.
Thus the jurisdiction of the courts of the Union expands or contracts as the sovereignty of the Union itself contracts or expands.

We have seen that the principal aim of the legislators of 1789 had been to divide sovereignty into two distinct shares. In the one they placed the direction of all the general interests of the Union; in the other, the direction of all the interests peculiar to some of its parts.
Their principal care was to arm the federal government with enough powers to defend itself, within its own sphere, against the encroachments of the individual States.
As for the States, the general principle adopted was to leave them free in theirs. The central government cannot direct them, nor even inspect their conduct.

I noted, in the chapter on the division of powers, that this last principle had not always been respected. There are certain laws an individual State cannot make, even though they appear to concern only itself.
When a State of the Union enacts a law of this nature, the citizens injured by the execution of that law can appeal to the federal courts.

Thus the jurisdiction of the federal courts extends not only to all suits taking their source in the laws of the Union, but also to all those arising from laws the individual States have made contrary to the constitution.
The States are forbidden to promulgate retroactive laws in criminal matters; the man condemned under a law of this kind can appeal to the federal justice.
The constitution has likewise forbidden the States to make laws that might destroy or alter rights acquired under a contract (*impairing the obligations of contracts*)[152].
The moment a private person believes he sees that a law of his State infringes a right of this kind, he can refuse to obey and appeal to the federal justice[153].
This provision strikes, it seems to me, more deeply than all the rest at the sovereignty of the States.

The rights granted to the federal government for evidently national purposes are defined and easy to understand. Those that the article I have just cited grants it indirectly are not easily grasped, and their limits are not clearly traced. There is in fact a multitude of political laws that bear upon the existence of contracts and that could thus furnish matter for an encroachment by the central power.
MANNER OF PROCEDURE OF THE FEDERAL COURTS.

Natural weakness of justice in confederations. — Efforts the legislators must make to place, as far as possible, only isolated individuals, and not States, before the federal courts. — How the Americans have succeeded in this. — Direct action of the federal courts on ordinary private persons. — Indirect attack against the States that violate the laws of the Union. — The decision of the federal justice does not destroy the provincial law; it weakens it.
I have made known what the rights of the federal courts are; it is no less important to know how they exercise them.

The irresistible force of justice in countries where sovereignty is not divided comes from the fact that, in those countries, the courts represent the entire nation in conflict with the single individual against whom the judgment has fallen. To the idea of right is joined the idea of the force that backs the right.

But in countries where sovereignty is divided, things are not always so. Justice there most often finds before it not an isolated individual, but a fraction of the nation. Its moral power and its material force are thereby diminished.
In federal States, justice is therefore naturally weaker and the litigant stronger.

The legislator, in confederations, must work without ceasing to give the courts a place analogous to the one they occupy among peoples that have not divided sovereignty; in other words, his most constant efforts must tend toward making the federal justice represent the nation, and the litigant a particular interest.
A government, of whatever nature, needs to act on the governed in order to force them to render it what is due to it; it needs to act against them to defend itself from their attacks.

As for the direct action of the government on the governed, to force them to obey the laws, the constitution of the United States arranged things (and this was its masterpiece) so that the federal courts, acting in the name of those laws, would never have to deal with anyone but individuals. Indeed, since it had been declared that the confederation formed only one and the same people within the circle drawn by the constitution, it followed that the government created by this constitution and acting within its limits was vested with all the rights of a national government, the chief of which is to make its commands reach the ordinary citizen without intermediary.
