Thus when the Union ordered the levy of a tax, for example, it was not to the States that it had to apply to collect it, but to each American citizen according to his assessment. The federal justice, in turn, charged with assuring the execution of this law of the Union, had to condemn not the recalcitrant State but the taxpayer. Like the justice of other peoples, it found before it only an individual.
Notice that here the Union has chosen its own adversary. It has chosen a weak one; it is altogether natural that he should give way.

But when the Union, instead of attacking, is itself reduced to defending itself, the difficulty grows. The constitution recognizes in the States the power to make laws. These laws may violate the rights of the Union. Here, necessarily, one finds oneself in conflict with the sovereignty of the State that made the law. The only thing left is to choose, among the means of action, the least dangerous. This means was indicated in advance by the general principles I have previously stated[154].

One can see that in the case I have just supposed, the Union could have summoned the State before a federal court, which would have declared the law null; this would have been to follow the most natural course of ideas. But in this way, the federal justice would have found itself directly facing a State, which was what they wished, as far as possible, to avoid.
The Americans thought it almost impossible that a new law would not, in its execution, injure some particular interest.

It is on this particular interest that the authors of the federal constitution rely to attack the legislative measure of which the Union may have cause to complain. It is to it that they offer a shelter.

A State sells lands to a company; a year later, a new law disposes of the same lands differently, and thus violates that part of the constitution forbidding the alteration of rights acquired by a contract. When the man who has bought under the new law presents himself to take possession, the possessor, who holds his rights from the old, brings him before the courts of the Union, and has his title declared null[155]. Thus, in reality, the federal justice finds itself at grips with the sovereignty of the State; but it attacks it only indirectly and on a particular application. It thus strikes the law in its consequences, not in its principle; it does not destroy it, it weakens it.
There remained, finally, one last hypothesis:
Each State formed a corporation with a separate existence and separate civil rights; consequently, it could sue or be sued before the courts. A State could, for example, prosecute another State.

In this case it was no longer a matter for the Union of attacking a provincial law, but of judging a suit in which a State was a party. It was a suit like any other; only the quality of the litigants was different. Here the danger pointed out at the beginning of this chapter still exists; but this time it cannot be avoided; it is inherent in the very essence of federal constitutions, whose result will always be to create within the nation private bodies powerful enough that justice can be exercised against them only with difficulty.
HIGH RANK OCCUPIED BY THE SUPREME COURT AMONG THE GREAT POWERS OF THE STATE.

No people has constituted so great a judicial power as the Americans. — Extent of its powers. — Its political influence. — The peace and the very existence of the Union depend on the wisdom of the seven federal judges.

When, after examining in detail the organization of the Supreme Court, one comes to consider as a whole the powers given to it, one easily discovers that never has a more immense judicial power been constituted in any people.
The Supreme Court is placed higher than any known court, both by the *nature* of its rights and by the *kind* of those who come before it.

Among all the civilized nations of Europe, the government has always shown great reluctance to let the ordinary courts settle questions in which it itself was interested. This reluctance is naturally greater the more absolute the government. As liberty grows, on the contrary, the range of the courts' powers steadily widens; but none of the European nations has yet thought that every judicial question, whatever its origin, could be left to the judges of the common law.
In America, this theory has been put into practice. The Supreme Court of the United States is the sole and unique tribunal of the nation.

It is charged with the interpretation of laws and of treaties; questions relating to maritime commerce, and all those in general that concern the law of nations, fall within its exclusive jurisdiction. One may even say that its powers are almost entirely political, although its constitution is entirely judicial. Its sole object is to have the laws of the Union executed, and the Union regulates only the relations of the government with the governed, and of the nation with foreigners; the relations of the citizens among themselves are nearly all governed by the sovereignty of the States.

To this first source of importance must be added another still greater. Among the nations of Europe, the courts have only private persons coming before them; but one may say that the Supreme Court of the United States summons sovereigns to its bar. When the bailiff, advancing on the steps of the court, comes to pronounce these few words, "The State of New York against that of Ohio," one feels that one is not within the precincts of an ordinary court of justice. And when one reflects that one of these litigants represents a million men, and the other two million, one is astonished at the responsibility that weighs on the seven judges whose decision is going to gladden or sadden so great a number of their fellow citizens.

In the hands of the seven federal judges rest unceasingly the peace, the prosperity, the very existence of the Union. Without them, the constitution is a dead work; it is to them that the executive power appeals to resist the encroachments of the legislative body; the legislature, to defend itself against the enterprises of the executive power; the Union, to make itself obeyed by the States; the States, to repel the exaggerated pretensions of the Union; the public interest against the private interest; the spirit of conservation against democratic instability. Their power is immense; but it is a power of opinion. They are all-powerful as long as the people consents to obey the law; they can do nothing the moment it scorns the law. Now, the power of opinion is the one most difficult to use, because it is impossible to say exactly where its limits lie. It is often as dangerous to fall short of them as to overstep them.

The federal judges must therefore not only be good citizens, learned and upright men — qualities necessary to all magistrates — they must also be statesmen; they must know how to discern the spirit of their age, how to face obstacles that can be overcome, and how to turn aside from the current when the flood threatens to carry away with them the sovereignty of the Union and the obedience due to its laws.

The president may err without the State suffering, because the president has only a limited power. Congress may err without the Union perishing, because above Congress lies the electoral body, which can change its spirit by changing its members.
But if the Supreme Court ever came to be composed of imprudent or corrupt men, the confederation would have anarchy or civil war to fear.

For the rest, make no mistake: the original cause of the danger is not in the constitution of the court, but in the very nature of federal governments. We have seen that nowhere is it more necessary to constitute the judicial power strongly than among confederated peoples, because nowhere are the individual existences that may struggle against the social body larger or better placed to resist the use of the government's material force.

Now, the more a power needs to be strong, the more extensive and independent it must be made. The more extensive and independent a power, the more dangerous the abuse that may be made of it. The origin of the evil therefore lies not in the constitution of this power, but in the very constitution of the State, which necessitates the existence of such a power.
HOW THE FEDERAL CONSTITUTION IS SUPERIOR TO THAT OF THE STATES.

How the constitution of the Union may be compared to that of the individual States. — The superiority of the constitution of the Union must be attributed particularly to the wisdom of the federal legislators. — The legislature of the Union less dependent on the people than that of the States. — The executive power freer within its sphere. — The judicial power less subjected to the will of the majority. — Practical consequences of this. — The federal legislators attenuated the dangers inherent in the government of democracy; the legislators of the States increased those dangers.

The federal constitution differs essentially from the constitution of the States in the aim it sets itself, but it comes very close to them as regards the means of attaining that aim. The object of government is different, but the forms of government are the same. From this particular point of view, they may usefully be compared.
I think that the federal constitution is superior to all the State constitutions. This superiority is due to several causes.
The present constitution of the Union was framed only after those of most of the States; so the experience already acquired could be drawn upon.

One will be convinced, however, that this cause is only a secondary one if one recalls that, since the establishment of the federal constitution, the American confederation has grown by eleven new States, and that these have nearly always exaggerated rather than attenuated the defects existing in the constitutions of their predecessors.
The great cause of the superiority of the federal constitution lies in the character of the legislators themselves.

At the time when it was framed, the ruin of the confederation seemed imminent; it was, so to speak, before everyone's eyes. In this extremity the people chose, not perhaps the men they loved best, but those they esteemed most.
I have already noted above that the legislators of the Union had nearly all been remarkable for their enlightenment, and still more remarkable for their patriotism.

They had all risen in the midst of a social crisis during which the spirit of liberty had continually had to struggle against a strong and dominating authority. The struggle ended, and while, as is usual, the excited passions of the crowd still clung to combating dangers that had long since ceased to exist, they had halted; they had cast a calmer and more penetrating gaze on their country; they had seen that a definitive revolution had been accomplished, and that henceforth the perils threatening the people could arise only from abuses of liberty. What they thought, they had the courage to say, because they felt in the depth of their hearts a sincere and ardent love for that same liberty; they dared speak of restricting it, because they were sure they did not want to destroy it[156].

Most of the State constitutions give the mandate of the House of Representatives a duration of only one year, and two years to that of the Senate. So that the members of the legislative body are constantly bound, in the most narrow way, to the slightest desires of their constituents.

The legislators of the Union thought that this extreme dependence of the legislature distorted the principal effects of the representative system, by placing in the people itself not only the origin of the powers, but also the government.
They increased the duration of the electoral mandate to leave the deputy a greater use of his free judgment.
The federal constitution, like the various State constitutions, divided the legislative body into two branches.

But, in the States, these two parts of the legislature were composed of the same elements and according to the same mode of election. As a result, the passions and the will of the majority found their way out with the same ease, and just as quickly found an organ and instrument in one chamber as in the other. This gave a violent and headlong character to the making of the laws.

The federal constitution also drew the two chambers from the votes of the people, but it varied the conditions of eligibility and the mode of election; so that, if, as in certain nations, one of the two branches of the legislature did not represent interests different from the other, it might at least represent a superior wisdom.
A mature age had to be reached to be a senator, and the body charged with electing was itself already chosen and small in number.

Democracies are naturally drawn to concentrate all social force in the hands of the legislative body. As it is the power that issues most directly from the people, it is also the one that partakes most of its omnipotence.
One therefore notices in it a habitual tendency to gather every kind of authority into itself.
This concentration of powers, at the same time as it singularly harms the good conduct of affairs, founds the despotism of the majority.
The legislators of the States have frequently surrendered to these instincts of democracy; those of the Union have always courageously struggled against them.

In the States, the executive power is placed in the hands of a magistrate apparently set beside the legislature, but who in reality is only a blind agent and a passive instrument of its will. Where would he draw his strength? From the duration of his functions? He is generally appointed for only a year. From his prerogatives? He has, so to speak, none. The legislature can reduce him to impotence by entrusting the execution of its laws to special commissions drawn from its own ranks. If it wished, it could in some sense annul him by cutting off his salary.

The federal constitution has concentrated all the rights of the executive power, as well as all its responsibility, in a single man. It has given the president four years of existence; it has assured him, throughout the duration of his magistracy, the enjoyment of his salary; it has given him a body of supporters, and armed him with a suspensive veto. In a word, after carefully tracing the sphere of the executive power, it has sought to give it, within that sphere, as strong and free a position as possible.
The judicial power is, of all powers, the one which, in the State constitutions, has remained least dependent on the legislative.
Yet, in all the States, the legislature has remained master of fixing the salaries of the judges, which necessarily subjects them to its immediate influence.
In certain States, the judges are appointed only for a fixed term, which takes from them still more a large part of their strength and their liberty.
In others, the legislative and judicial powers are entirely confounded. The Senate of New York, for example, forms for certain suits the superior court of the State.

The federal constitution, on the contrary, has taken care to separate the judicial power from all the others. It has, moreover, made the judges independent, by declaring their salary fixed and their functions irrevocable.

The practical consequences of these differences are easy to see. It is evident to every attentive observer that the affairs of the Union are infinitely better conducted than the private affairs of any State.

The federal government is more just and more moderate in its course than that of the States. There is more wisdom in its views, more duration and clever combination in its projects, more skill, persistence, and firmness in the execution of its measures.
A few words suffice to sum up this chapter.
Two principal dangers threaten the existence of democracies:
The complete enslavement of the legislative power to the will of the electoral body.
The concentration, in the legislative power, of all the other powers of the government.
The legislators of the States have favored the development of these dangers. The legislators of the Union have done what they could to make them less to be feared.
WHAT DISTINGUISHES THE FEDERAL CONSTITUTION OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA FROM ALL OTHER FEDERAL CONSTITUTIONS.

The American confederation resembles in appearance all other confederations. — Yet its effects are different. — Whence does this come? — In what way this confederation departs from all others. — The American government is not a federal government, but an incomplete national government.

The United States of America did not provide the first and only example of a confederation. Without speaking of antiquity, modern Europe has furnished several. Switzerland, the Germanic Empire, the Republic of the Netherlands have been or still are confederations.

When one studies the constitutions of these various countries, one notes with surprise that the powers conferred by them on the federal government are nearly the same as those granted by the American constitution to the government of the United States. Like the latter, they give the central power the right to make peace and war, the right to raise men and money, to provide for general needs and regulate the common interests of the nation.
Yet the federal government, among these various peoples, has almost always remained feeble and impotent, while that of the Union conducts affairs with vigor and ease.

More than that, the first American Union could not subsist, on account of the excessive weakness of its government, and yet that government, weak as it was, had received rights as extensive as the federal government of our day. One may even say that in certain respects its privileges were greater.
There are therefore in the present constitution of the United States some new principles that do not strike one at first, but whose influence is profoundly felt.

This constitution, which at first sight one is tempted to confuse with the federal constitutions that preceded it, rests in fact on an entirely new theory, which must be marked as a great discovery in the political science of our day.

In all the confederations that preceded the American confederation of 1789, the peoples that allied themselves for a common purpose agreed to obey the commands of a federal government; but they kept the right to order and supervise within their borders the execution of the laws of the Union.
The American States that joined in 1789 agreed not only that the federal government should dictate laws to them, but also that it should itself execute its laws.
In the two cases the right is the same; only the exercise of the right is different. But this single difference produces immense results.

In all the confederations that preceded the present American Union, the federal government, in order to provide for its needs, addressed itself to the particular governments. In the case where the prescribed measure displeased one of them, the latter could always evade the necessity of obeying. If it was strong, it appealed to arms; if it was weak, it tolerated resistance to the laws of the Union, which had become its own, pleaded impotence as a pretext, and resorted to the force of inertia.

And so one of these two things has constantly been seen to happen: the most powerful of the united peoples, taking into its own hands the rights of the federal authority, has dominated all the others in its name[157]; or the federal government has been left to its own forces, and then anarchy has set in among the confederates, and the Union has fallen into incapacity to act[158].

In America, the Union has for its governed not States, but ordinary citizens. When it wants to levy a tax, it does not address itself to the government of Massachusetts, but to every inhabitant of Massachusetts. The older federal governments had peoples facing them; that of the Union has individuals. It does not borrow its strength: it draws it from itself. It has its own administrators, its own courts, its own officers of justice, and its own army.

No doubt the national spirit, the collective passions, the provincial prejudices of each State still tend strongly to diminish the extent of the federal power thus constituted, and to create centers of resistance to its will; restricted in its sovereignty, it cannot be as strong as one that possesses sovereignty entire; but that is an evil inherent in the federative system.

In America, each State has far fewer occasions and temptations to resist; and if the thought of it comes to it, it cannot carry it out except by openly violating the laws of the Union, interrupting the ordinary course of justice, and raising the standard of revolt; it must, in a word, take an extreme step all at once, which men long hesitate to do.

In the older confederations, the rights granted to the Union were for it causes of war, not of strength, since these rights multiplied its demands without increasing its means of being obeyed. So one has almost always seen the real weakness of federal governments grow in direct ratio to their nominal power.
It is not so in the American Union; like most ordinary governments, the federal government can do everything it is given the right to execute.
The human mind invents things more easily than words: hence the use of so many improper terms and incomplete expressions.

Several nations form a permanent league and establish a supreme authority which, without acting on ordinary citizens as a national government might, nevertheless acts on each of the confederated peoples taken as a body.
This government, so different from all others, receives the name of federal.
One then discovers a form of society in which several peoples really merge into one with respect to certain common interests, and remain separate and only confederated for all the rest.

Here the central power acts without intermediary on the governed, administers and judges them itself, as national governments do, but it acts so only within a restricted sphere. Clearly this is no longer a federal government, but an incomplete national government. Thus a form of government has been found that was precisely neither national nor federal; but they stopped there, and the new word that must express the new thing does not yet exist.

It is for having failed to know this new species of confederation that all the Unions have come to civil war, to subjection, or to inertia. The peoples composing them have all lacked either the enlightenment to see the remedy for their ills, or the courage to apply it.
The first American Union had also fallen into the same defects.

But in America, the confederated States, before reaching independence, had long been part of the same empire; they had therefore not yet contracted the habit of governing themselves completely, and national prejudices had not been able to take deep root; more enlightened than the rest of the world, they were among themselves equal in enlightenment, and they felt only feebly the passions that, ordinarily, in peoples oppose the extension of federal power, and those passions were opposed by the greatest citizens. The Americans, at the same time as they felt the evil, faced the remedy firmly. They corrected their laws and saved the country.
ON THE ADVANTAGES OF THE FEDERAL SYSTEM IN GENERAL, AND ITS SPECIAL UTILITY FOR AMERICA.

Happiness and liberty enjoyed by small nations. — Power of large nations. — Great empires favor the development of civilization. — That strength is often for nations the first element of prosperity. — The aim of the federal system is to unite the advantages peoples derive from the largeness and the smallness of their territory. — Advantages the United States derives from this system. — The law bends to the needs of the populations, and the populations do not bend to the necessities of the law. — Activity, progress, taste and practice of liberty among the American peoples. — The public spirit of the Union is only the summing-up of provincial patriotism. — Things and ideas circulate freely on the territory of the United States. — The Union is free and happy like a small nation, respected like a great one.

In small nations, the eye of society penetrates everywhere; the spirit of improvement reaches down into the slightest details: the people's ambition being much tempered by its weakness, its efforts and its resources are turned almost entirely toward its internal well-being, and are not liable to be dissipated in the vain smoke of glory. Moreover, since each person's faculties are generally limited, his desires are equally so. The moderate fortunes there make conditions roughly equal; mores there have a simple and peaceful cast. Thus, all things considered, and allowing for varying degrees of morality and enlightenment, one ordinarily encounters in small nations more ease, more population, and more tranquility than in great ones.

When tyranny comes to be established within a small nation, it is more troublesome there than anywhere else, because, acting within a more restricted circle, it extends to everything within that circle. Unable to lay hold of any great object, it busies itself with a multitude of small ones; it shows itself at once violent and meddling. From the political world, which is, strictly speaking, its domain, it penetrates into private life. After actions, it aspires to govern tastes; after the State, it wants to govern families. But this happens rarely; liberty is, properly speaking, the natural condition of small societies. The government there offers too little lure to ambition, the resources of private persons are too limited, for the sovereign power to be concentrated easily in the hands of one man. Should the case arise, it is not difficult for the governed to unite and, by a common effort, to overthrow at the same time the tyrant and the tyranny.

Small nations have therefore been at all times the cradle of political liberty. It has happened that most of them have lost this liberty as they grew larger; which clearly shows that it pertained to the smallness of the people and not to the people itself.

The history of the world furnishes no example of a great nation that has long remained a republic[159], which has led people to say that the thing is impracticable. For my part, I think it very imprudent for man to wish to set bounds on the possible and to judge the future — man, to whom the real and the present escape every day, and who is constantly taken by surprise in the things he knows best. What one can say with certainty is that the existence of a great republic will always be infinitely more exposed than that of a small one.
All the passions fatal to republics grow with the extent of territory, while the virtues that serve as their support do not increase in the same measure.

The ambition of private persons grows with the power of the State; the strength of parties grows with the importance of the aim they propose to themselves; but love of country, which must struggle against these destructive passions, is no stronger in a vast republic than in a small one. It would even be easy to prove that it is less developed and less powerful there. Great wealth and deep misery, capital cities, the corruption of mores, individual selfishness, the complication of interests — these are so many perils that almost always arise from the greatness of the State. Several of these things do not harm the existence of a monarchy; some may even contribute to its duration. Moreover, in monarchies, the government has a strength of its own; it uses the people and does not depend on it; the larger the people, the stronger the prince. But republican government can oppose to these dangers only the support of the majority. Now, this element of strength is no more powerful, proportionally, in a vast republic than in a small one. Thus, while the means of attack constantly grow in number and in power, the force of resistance remains the same. One may even say that it diminishes, for the more numerous the people, and the more the nature of minds and interests diversifies, the more difficult it consequently is to form a compact majority.

It may be noted, moreover, that human passions gain in intensity not only by the greatness of the aim they wish to attain, but also by the multitude of individuals who feel them at the same time. There is no one who has not felt himself more moved in the midst of an agitated crowd that shared his emotion than if he had felt it alone. In a great republic, political passions become irresistible, not only because the object they pursue is immense, but also because millions of men feel them in the same way and at the same moment.
One may therefore say in a general way that nothing is so contrary to the well-being and the liberty of men as great empires.
Great States have nevertheless advantages peculiar to them which must be acknowledged.

Just as the desire for power is more ardent there than elsewhere among ordinary men, so the love of glory is more developed there in certain souls who find in the applause of a great people an object worthy of their efforts and capable of raising them, in a sense, above themselves. Thought there receives in every matter a swifter and more powerful impulse, ideas circulate more freely, capital cities are like vast intellectual centers where all the rays of the human mind come to shine and combine: this fact explains why great nations cause enlightenment and the general cause of civilization to advance more rapidly than small ones. To this it must be added that important discoveries often require a development of national strength of which the government of a small people is incapable; among great nations, the government has more general ideas, it frees itself more completely from the routine of precedent and the selfishness of localities. There is more genius in its conceptions, more boldness in its bearing.

Internal well-being is more complete and more widespread in small nations, as long as they keep at peace; but a state of war is more harmful to them than to great ones. With the latter, the remoteness of frontiers sometimes allows the mass of the people to remain for centuries far from danger. For them, war is rather a cause of malaise than of ruin.
There is presented, moreover, in this matter as in many others, a consideration that dominates all the rest: that of necessity.
If there were only small nations and no large ones, humanity would surely be more free and more happy; but one cannot prevent there being great nations.

This introduces into the world a new element of national prosperity, which is strength. What does it matter that a people offers the picture of ease and liberty if it sees itself exposed every day to being ravaged or conquered? What does it matter that it is manufacturing and commercial, if another dominates the seas and lays down the law in every market? Small nations are often wretched, not because they are small, but because they are weak; great ones prosper, not because they are great, but because they are strong. Strength is therefore often for nations one of the first conditions of happiness and even of existence. Hence, barring special circumstances, small peoples always end up either being violently united to large ones or uniting with them of their own accord. I know of no condition more deplorable than that of a people that can neither defend itself nor provide for itself.
It is to unite the various advantages that flow from the greatness and the smallness of nations that the federative system was created.
A glance at the United States is enough to perceive all the goods that flow to them from the adoption of this system.

In great centralized nations, the legislator is obliged to give the laws a uniform character that the diversity of places and mores does not admit; never informed of the particular cases, he can proceed only by general rules; men are then obliged to bend to the necessities of the legislation, for the legislation does not know how to accommodate itself to the needs and the mores of men; which is a great cause of troubles and miseries.
This drawback does not exist in confederations: Congress regulates the principal acts of social existence; all the details are left to the provincial legislations.

One can hardly imagine to what point this division of sovereignty serves the well-being of each of the States composing the Union. In these small societies, which are not preoccupied with the care of defending themselves or expanding, all the public power and all individual energy are turned toward internal improvements. The central government of each State, being placed right alongside the governed, is daily informed of the needs that make themselves felt: each year, then, one sees presented new plans which, discussed in the communal assemblies or before the State legislature, and reproduced afterward by the press, excite universal interest and the zeal of the citizens. This need to improve constantly stirs up the American republics without troubling them; the ambition for power yields there to the love of well-being, a more vulgar passion but a less dangerous one. It is an opinion widely held in America that the existence and the duration of republican forms in the New World depend on the existence and the duration of the federative system. A large part of the miseries into which the new States of South America are plunged is attributed to the wish to establish great republics there, instead of fractionating sovereignty.

It is in fact incontestable that in the United States the taste for and habit of republican government were born in the townships and in the heart of the provincial assemblies. In a small nation, like Connecticut, for example, where the great political business is the opening of a canal and the laying out of a road, where the State has no army to pay or war to sustain, and can give those who direct it neither great wealth nor great glory, one can imagine nothing more natural and better suited to the nature of things than the republic. Now, it is this same republican spirit, these mores and these habits of a free people, that, after having taken birth and developed in the various States, then apply themselves without difficulty to the whole country. The public spirit of the Union is itself, in a sense, only the summing-up of provincial patriotism. Every citizen of the United States transfers, so to speak, the interest his little republic inspires in him into love of the common fatherland. In defending the Union, he defends the increasing prosperity of his district, the right to direct its affairs, and the hope of having there those plans of improvement that must enrich him personally prevail: all things that, ordinarily, touch men more than the general interests of the country and the glory of the nation.

On the other hand, if the spirit and the mores of the inhabitants make them more apt than others to make a great republic prosper, the federative system has made the task far less difficult. The confederation of all the American States does not present the ordinary drawbacks of large agglomerations of men. The Union is a great republic in extent; but one might in a sense compare it to a small republic, on account of the few matters with which its government concerns itself. Its acts are important, but they are rare. As the sovereignty of the Union is constrained and incomplete, the use of this sovereignty is not dangerous to liberty. Nor does it stir up those immoderate desires for power and noise that are so fatal to great republics. As everything there does not necessarily end up at a common center, there are no vast capital cities, no immense wealth, no great misery, no sudden revolutions. The political passions, instead of spreading in an instant like a sheet of fire over the whole surface of the country, go and break against the interests and the individual passions of each State.

In the Union, however, as among one and the same people, things and ideas circulate freely. Nothing there checks the impulse of the spirit of enterprise. Its government draws to itself talents and enlightenment. Within the frontiers of the Union reigns a profound peace, as in the interior of a country subject to a single rule; outside, it ranks among the most powerful nations of the earth; it offers foreign commerce more than 800 leagues of coast; and holding in its hands the keys of a whole world, it makes its flag respected to the ends of the seas.
The Union is free and happy like a small nation, glorious and strong like a great one.
WHY THE FEDERAL SYSTEM IS NOT WITHIN THE REACH OF ALL PEOPLES, AND WHAT HAS PERMITTED THE ANGLO-AMERICANS TO ADOPT IT.

There are in every federal system inherent vices which the legislator cannot combat. — Complication of every federal system. — It requires the governed to make daily use of their intelligence. — Practical science of the Americans in matters of government. — Relative weakness of the government of the Union, another vice inherent in the federal system. — The Americans have made it less serious, but have not been able to destroy it. — The sovereignty of the individual States weaker in appearance, stronger in reality than that of the Union. — Why. — There must therefore exist, independent of the laws, natural causes of union among confederated peoples. — What these causes are among the Anglo-Americans. — Maine and Georgia, four hundred leagues apart, more naturally united than Normandy and Brittany. — That war is the principal pitfall of confederations. — This proved by the very example of the United States. — The Union has no great wars to fear. — Why. — Dangers that the peoples of Europe would run in adopting the federal system of the Americans.

The legislator sometimes succeeds, after a thousand efforts, in exerting an indirect influence on the destiny of nations, and then his genius is celebrated, while often the geographical position of the country, over which he has no power, a social state created without his concurrence, mores and ideas whose origin he does not know, a starting point of which he is unaware, impart to society irresistible movements against which he struggles in vain, and which carry him along in their turn.

The legislator resembles the man who traces his course in the middle of the seas. He can also steer the vessel that carries him, but he cannot change its structure, create the winds, or prevent the Ocean from rising beneath his feet.

I have shown what advantages the Americans derive from the federal system. It remains for me to make clear what has permitted them to adopt this system; for it is not given to every people to enjoy its benefits.

One finds in the federal system accidental vices that arise from the laws; these may be corrected by the legislators. One encounters others which, being inherent in the system, cannot be destroyed by the peoples that adopt it. Those peoples must therefore find within themselves the strength necessary to bear the natural imperfections of their government.

Among the vices inherent in every federal system, the most visible of all is the complication of the means it employs. This system necessarily places two sovereignties in confrontation. The legislator manages to make the movements of these two sovereignties as simple and equal as possible, and can enclose both within clearly drawn spheres of action; but he cannot make there be only one of them, nor prevent them from touching at some point.
The federative system therefore rests, whatever one does, on a complicated theory, the application of which requires of the governed a daily use of the lights of their reason.

In general, only simple conceptions take hold of the mind of the people. A false but clear and precise idea will always have more power in the world than a true but complex one. Hence parties, which are like small nations within a great one, always hasten to adopt as a symbol a name or a principle which, often, represents only very incompletely the aim they propose and the means they employ, but without which they could neither subsist nor move. Governments that rest on a single idea or on a single sentiment easy to define are perhaps not the best, but they are surely the strongest and the most durable.

When one examines the constitution of the United States, the most perfect of all the federal constitutions known, one is frightened, on the contrary, by the multitude of varied knowledge and the discernment it supposes in those it is to govern. The government of the Union rests almost entirely on legal fictions. The Union is an ideal nation that exists, so to speak, only in people's minds, and whose extent and limits are discerned only by the intelligence.

The general theory once well understood, there remain the difficulties of application; they are without number, for the sovereignty of the Union is so entangled with that of the States that it is impossible, at a first glance, to perceive their limits. Everything is conventional and artificial in such a government, and it can be suited only to a people long accustomed to directing its own affairs, and among whom political science has come down to the lowest ranks of society. I have never more admired the good sense and the practical intelligence of the Americans than in the way in which they escape the countless difficulties that arise from their federal constitution. I have hardly ever encountered an ordinary man in America who did not, with surprising ease, discern the obligations born of the laws of Congress and those whose origin is in the laws of his State, and who, after distinguishing the matters placed in the general powers of the Union from those that the local legislature must regulate, could not indicate the point where the jurisdiction of the federal courts begins and the limit where that of the State courts stops.
The constitution of the United States resembles those fine creations of human industry that bring glory and goods upon those who invent them, but remain sterile in other hands.
That is what Mexico has shown in our day.

The inhabitants of Mexico, wishing to establish the federative system, took as their model and copied almost entirely the federal constitution of the Anglo-Americans, their neighbors[160]. But while transporting to themselves the letter of the law, they could not at the same time transport the spirit that gives it life. They were therefore seen constantly entangling themselves amid the workings of their double government. The sovereignty of the States and that of the Union, going beyond the circle the constitution had drawn, penetrated each day into one another. Even now, Mexico is constantly carried from anarchy to military despotism, and from military despotism to anarchy.
The second and most fatal of all the vices that I regard as inherent in the federal system itself is the relative weakness of the government of the Union.

The principle on which all confederations rest is the fractionation of sovereignty. The legislators render this fractionation little perceptible; they even hide it for a time from view, but they cannot make it not exist. Now, a fractioned sovereignty will always be weaker than a complete one.

We have seen, in the exposition of the constitution of the United States, with what art the Americans, while enclosing the power of the Union within the restricted sphere of federal governments, have nevertheless managed to give it the appearance and, up to a certain point, the strength of a national government.
In acting thus, the legislators of the Union have diminished the natural danger of confederations; but they have not been able to make it disappear entirely.
The American government, it is said, does not address itself to the States: it sends its commands directly to the citizens, and bends them individually under the force of the common will.

But if the federal law clashed violently with the interests and prejudices of a State, would it not be feared that each citizen of that State would believe himself involved in the cause of the man who refuses to obey? All the citizens of the State, finding themselves thus injured at the same time and in the same way by the authority of the Union, in vain would the federal government seek to isolate them in order to fight them: they would feel instinctively that they ought to unite to defend themselves, and they would find an organization all ready in the portion of sovereignty that has been left to their State to enjoy. The fiction would then disappear to give way to reality, and one would see the organized power of one part of the territory in struggle with the central authority.

I will say as much of the federal justice. If, in a particular suit, the courts of the Union violated an important law of a State, the struggle, if not apparent at least real, would be between the injured State represented by a citizen, and the Union represented by its courts[161].

One must have very little experience of the things of this world to imagine that, after leaving men's passions a means of satisfying themselves, they will always be prevented, by means of legal fictions, from perceiving it and making use of it.
The American legislators, by making the struggle between the two sovereignties less probable, have therefore not destroyed its causes.
One may even go further, and say that they have not been able, in case of struggle, to assure the federal power the preponderance.
They gave the Union money and soldiers, but the States kept the love and the prejudices of the peoples.

The sovereignty of the Union is an abstract being which connects itself with only a small number of external objects. The sovereignty of the States falls under every sense; one understands it without trouble; one sees it act at every instant. The one is new, the other was born with the people itself.
The sovereignty of the Union is the work of art. The sovereignty of the States is natural; it exists by itself, without effort, like the authority of a father of a family.

The sovereignty of the Union touches men only through a few great interests; it represents an immense, distant whole, a vague and indefinite sentiment. The sovereignty of the States envelops each citizen, in a sense, and takes hold of him daily in detail. It is this sovereignty that takes charge of guaranteeing his property, his liberty, his life; it influences at every moment his well-being or his misery. The sovereignty of the States rests on memories, on habits, on local prejudices, on provincial and familial selfishness — in a word, on all the things that make the instinct of fatherland so powerful in the heart of man. How can one doubt its advantages?

Since legislators cannot prevent dangerous collisions from arising between the two sovereignties that the federal system sets in confrontation, particular dispositions must therefore be joined to their efforts to turn the confederated peoples away from war — dispositions that incline them to peace.

It follows that the federal pact cannot have a long existence if it does not encounter, in the peoples to whom it applies, a certain number of conditions of union that make this common life easy for them and facilitate the task of government.
Thus, for the federal system to succeed, it does not only need good laws; it also needs circumstances to favor it.
All the peoples that have been seen to confederate had a certain number of common interests, which formed, as it were, the intellectual bonds of the association.

But besides material interests, man has also ideas and sentiments. For a confederation to subsist for a long time, it is no less necessary that there be homogeneity in the civilization than in the needs of the various peoples composing it. Between the civilization of the canton of Vaud and that of the canton of Uri, there is as much difference as between the nineteenth century and the fifteenth: that is why Switzerland has, properly speaking, never had a federal government. The union among these different cantons exists only on the map; and one would be well aware of it if a central authority wished to apply the same laws to the whole territory.

There is a fact that admirably facilitates, in the United States, the existence of the federal government. The various States have not only roughly the same interests, the same origin, and the same language, but also the same degree of civilization; which nearly always makes accord between them an easy matter. I do not know whether there is a small European nation that does not present a less homogeneous aspect in its various parts than the American people, whose territory is as large as half of Europe. From the State of Maine to the State of Georgia is about four hundred leagues. Yet there is less difference between the civilization of Maine and that of Georgia than between the civilization of Normandy and that of Brittany. Maine and Georgia, placed at the two extremities of a vast empire, therefore find naturally more real facilities for forming a confederation than Normandy and Brittany, which are separated only by a stream.

To these facilities, which the mores and habits of the people offered the American legislators, were joined others arising from the geographical position of the country. It is principally to the latter that the adoption and the maintenance of the federal system must be attributed.
The most important of all the acts that can mark the life of a people is war. In war, a people acts as a single individual in relation to foreign peoples: it struggles for its very existence.

As long as it is only a question of maintaining peace within a country and favoring its prosperity, skill in the government, reason in the governed, and a certain natural attachment that men have almost always for their country may easily suffice; but for a nation to be in a state to make a great war, the citizens must impose on themselves numerous and painful sacrifices. To believe that a great number of men will be capable of submitting of their own accord to such social demands is to know humanity very ill.

Hence all the peoples that have had to make great wars have been led, almost in spite of themselves, to increase the strength of the government. Those that have not succeeded in this have been conquered. A long war almost always places nations in the sad alternative that their defeat hands them over to destruction, and their triumph to despotism.

It is therefore in general in war that the weakness of a government reveals itself in the most visible and most dangerous manner; and I have shown that the vice inherent in federal governments was to be very weak.

In the federative system, not only is there no administrative centralization, or anything approaching it, but governmental centralization itself exists only incompletely, which is always a great cause of weakness when one must defend oneself against peoples in whom it is complete.

In the federal constitution of the United States — the one of all federal constitutions in which the central government is vested with the most real strength — this evil still makes itself sharply felt.
A single example will allow the reader to judge.

The constitution gives Congress the right to call the militia of the various States into active service when it is a question of suppressing an insurrection or repelling an invasion; another article says that in this case the president of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the militia.

At the time of the War of 1812, the president gave the order to the militias of the North to advance toward the frontiers; Connecticut and Massachusetts, whose interests the war injured, refused to send their contingents.

The constitution, they said, authorizes the federal government to make use of the militias in case of *insurrection* and *invasion*; now there is at present neither insurrection nor invasion. They added that the same constitution that gave the Union the right to call the militias into active service left the States the right to name the officers; it followed, according to them, that even in war no officer of the Union had the right to command the militias, except the president in person. Now, it was a matter of serving in an army commanded by someone other than him.

These absurd and destructive doctrines received not only the sanction of the governors and the legislature, but also that of the courts of justice of these two States; and the federal government was forced to seek elsewhere the troops it lacked[162].
How is it, then, that the American Union, protected as it is by the relative perfection of its laws, does not dissolve in the midst of a great war? It is because it has no great wars to fear.
Placed at the center of an immense continent, where human industry can spread without bounds, the Union is almost as isolated from the world as if it were hemmed in on all sides by the Ocean.
Canada has only a million inhabitants; its population is divided into two enemy nations. The rigors of the climate limit the extent of its territory and close its ports for six months.
From Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, one still meets a few half-destroyed savage tribes which 6,000 soldiers push before them.

To the south, the Union touches at a single point the empire of Mexico; it is from there that great wars will probably one day come. But for a long time still, the little advanced state of civilization, the corruption of mores, and poverty will prevent Mexico from taking a high rank among nations. As for the powers of Europe, their distance makes them little to be feared (*O*).
The great good fortune of the United States, then, is not to have found a federal constitution that permits it to sustain great wars, but to be so situated that it has none to fear.

No one can appreciate the advantages of the federative system more than I do. I see in it one of the most powerful combinations in favor of the prosperity and the liberty of mankind. I envy the lot of the nations to which it has been allowed to adopt it. But I nevertheless refuse to believe that confederated peoples can struggle long, on equal terms of strength, against a nation where governmental power is centralized.

A people that, in the presence of the great military monarchies of Europe, came to fraction its sovereignty would seem to me to abdicate, by that act alone, its power, and perhaps its existence and its name.
Admirable position of the New World, where man has yet no enemies but himself! To be happy and free, he has only to will it.

Example: Congress has the right to make a general bankruptcy law; it does not make one: each State could make one in its own way. This is how the *Federalist*, in no. 45, explains this division of sovereignty between the Union and the individual States: "The powers which the constitution delegates to the federal government," he says, "are defined and few in number. Those that remain at the disposal of the individual States are, on the contrary, undefined and many in number. The first are exercised principally in external matters, such as peace, war, negotiations, commerce. The powers that the individual States reserve to themselves extend to all matters that follow the ordinary course of affairs, and concern the life, the liberty, and the prosperity of the State." I shall often have occasion to cite the *Federalist* in this work. When the draft law that later became the constitution of the United States was still before the people and submitted to its adoption, three men already famous, and who have since become even more so, John Jay, Hamilton, and Madison, joined together with the aim of bringing out to the nation the advantages of the project submitted to it. With this design, they published, in the form of a journal, a series of articles, the whole of which forms a complete treatise. They had given their journal the name *Federalist*, which has remained that of the work. The *Federalist* is a fine book which, though it is special to America, ought to be familiar to statesmen of every country.

Every ten years, Congress fixes anew the number of deputies that each State must send to the House of Representatives. The total number was 69 in 1789; in 1833 it was 240. (*American almanac*, 1834, p. 194.) The constitution had said that there would be no more than one representative per 30,000 persons; but it had set no lower limit. Congress has not thought it necessary to increase the number of representatives in proportion to the increase in population. By the first law passed on this subject, on April 14, 1792 (see *laws of the United States* by Story, vol. 1, p. 135), it was decided that there would be one representative per 33,000 inhabitants. The latest law, passed in 1832, set the number at one representative per 48,000 inhabitants. The population represented is composed of all free men and three-fifths of the number of slaves.

Each year there is published in the United States an almanac called *National calendar*; one finds in it the name of every federal functionary. It is the *National calendar* of 1833 that has furnished me the figure I give here. The electors of the same State assemble; but they transmit to the seat of the central government the list of individual votes, not the result of the majority vote.

In this circumstance, it is the majority of States, and not the majority of members, that decides the question. So that New York has no more influence on the deliberation than Rhode Island. Thus the citizens of the Union are first consulted as forming only one and the same people; and when they cannot agree, the division by State is revived, and each of the latter is given a separate and independent vote. This is yet another of the oddities the federal constitution presents, and one that only the clash of opposing interests can explain.
Jefferson, in 1801, was however appointed only on the thirty-sixth ballot.

See Chapter VI, entitled: *Of the Judicial Power in the United States.* That chapter sets forth the general principles of the Americans in matters of justice. See also the federal constitution, art. III. See the work entitled: *The Federalist*, no. 78–83 inclusive, *Constitutional law, being a view of the practice and jurisdiction of the courts of the United States, by Thomas Sergeant*. See *Story*, pp. 134–162, 439–511, 581, 668. See the organic law of September 24, 1789, in the collection entitled: *Laws of the United States*, by Story, vol. 1, p. 53.

It is federal laws that have the most need of courts, and yet it is they that have admitted them least. The reason is that most confederations have been formed by independent States that had no real intention of obeying the central government, and that, while giving it the right to command, carefully reserved to themselves the faculty of disobeying it.

The Union was divided into districts; in each of these districts, a federal judge was placed on permanent assignment. The court over which this judge presided was called the District Court (*district-court*). Moreover, each of the judges composing the Supreme Court was required to travel each year over a certain portion of the territory of the republic, in order to decide on the spot certain more important cases: the court presided over by this magistrate was designated as the Circuit Court (*circuit-court*). Finally, the most serious affairs were to come, either directly or on appeal, before the Supreme Court, at the seat of which all the circuit judges gathered once a year to hold a solemn session. The jury system was introduced into the federal courts in the same way as in the State courts, and for similar cases. There is almost no analogy, as one sees, between the Supreme Court of the United States and our Court of Cassation. The Supreme Court may be seized in first instance, whereas the Court of Cassation may be seized only at the second or third remove. The Supreme Court does in truth form, like the Court of Cassation, a single tribunal charged with establishing a uniform jurisprudence; but the Supreme Court judges the fact as well as the law, and pronounces *itself*, without remanding to another tribunal — two things the Court of Cassation cannot do. See the organic law of September 24, 1789, *Laws of the United States*, by Story, vol. 1, p. 53.

For the rest, to render these jurisdictional disputes less frequent, it was decided that, in a very large number of federal suits, the tribunals of the individual States would have the right to pronounce concurrently with those of the Union; but then the condemned party always had the faculty of appealing to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Supreme Court of Virginia contested the right of the Supreme Court of the United States to judge the appeal of its judgments, but in vain. See *Kent's commentaries*, vol. 1, pp. 300, 370 ff. See *Story's comm.*, p. 646, and the organic law of 1789; *Laws of the United States*, vol. 1, p. 53.

The constitution likewise says that suits that might arise between a State and the citizens of another State shall be within the jurisdiction of the federal courts. The question soon arose whether the constitution had meant to speak of all the suits that might arise between a State and the citizens of another State, whether the ones or the others were *plaintiffs*. The Supreme Court pronounced in the affirmative; but this decision alarmed the individual States, which feared being haled, in spite of themselves and on every occasion, before the federal justice. An amendment was therefore introduced into the constitution, under which the judicial power of the Union could not extend so far as to judge suits that had been *brought* against one of the United States by the citizens of another. See *Story's commentaries*, p. 624.
Example: all acts of piracy.

Some restrictions have indeed been brought to this principle by introducing the individual States as an independent power in the Senate, and by having them vote separately in the House of Representatives in case of a presidential election; but these are exceptions. The contrary principle is dominant.

"It is perfectly clear," says Mr. Story, p. 503, "that any law that extends, restricts, or in any way changes the intention of the parties, such as it results from the stipulations contained in a contract, alters (*impairs*) that contract." The same author carefully defines, in the same place, what federal jurisprudence means by a contract. The definition is very broad. A grant made by the State to a private person and accepted by him is a contract, and cannot be taken away by the effect of a new law. A charter granted by the State to a company is a contract, and is law for the State as well as for the grantee. The article of the constitution we are speaking of thus assures the existence of a large part of *acquired rights*, but not of all. I may quite legitimately possess a piece of property without its having passed into my hands by reason of a contract. Its possession is for me an acquired right, and this right is not guaranteed by the federal constitution.

Here is a remarkable example cited by Mr. Story, p. 508. Dartmouth College, in New Hampshire, had been founded by virtue of a charter granted to certain individuals before the American Revolution. Its administrators formed, by virtue of this charter, a constituted body, or, in the American expression, a *corporation*. The legislature of New Hampshire thought fit to change the terms of the original charter, and transferred to new administrators all the rights, privileges, and franchises that resulted from this charter. The former administrators resisted, and appealed to the federal court, which decided in their favor, on the ground that the original charter being a true contract between the State and the grantees, the new law could not change the provisions of this charter without violating rights acquired by virtue of a contract, and consequently violating article 1, section X, of the constitution of the United States.
See the chapter entitled: *Of the Judicial Power in America.*
See *Kent's commentaries*, vol. 1, p. 387.

At that time, the celebrated Alexander Hamilton, one of the most influential framers of the constitution, did not fear to publish the following in the *Federalist*, no. 71: "I know," he said, "that there are people to whom the executive power can recommend itself in no better way than by bending servilely to the desires of the people or of the legislature; but these seem to me to hold very crude notions about the object of all government, as well as the true means of producing public prosperity. That the opinions of the people, when reasoned and matured, should direct the conduct of those to whom it confides its affairs is what follows from the establishment of a republican constitution; but republican principles do not require that one let oneself be carried away by the slightest wind of popular passions, nor that one hasten to obey every momentary impulse the multitude may receive from the artful hand of men who flatter its prejudices in order to betray its interests. The people, most ordinarily, wish only to arrive at the public good; this is true; but they often deceive themselves in seeking it. If one came to tell them that they always judge soundly the means to employ to produce national prosperity, their good sense would make them scorn such flatteries; for they have learned by experience that they have happened sometimes to be mistaken; and what one should be astonished at is that they are not mistaken more often, pursued as they always are by the wiles of parasites and sycophants; surrounded by the snares that so many greedy and resourceless men are constantly setting for them, deceived every day by the artifices of those who possess their confidence without deserving it, or who seek rather to possess it than to make themselves worthy of it. When the true interests of the people are contrary to their desires, the duty of all those whom they have set as guardians of those interests is to combat the error of which they are momentarily the victim, in order to give them time to come to themselves and look at things in cold blood. And it has happened more than once that a people, thus saved from the fatal consequences of its own errors, has taken pleasure in raising monuments of its gratitude to the men who had had the magnanimous courage to expose themselves to its displeasure in order to serve it."

This is what was seen among the Greeks under Philip, when this prince took it upon himself to execute the decree of the Amphictyons. This is what happened to the republic of the Netherlands, where the province of Holland always made the law. The same thing happens still in our day in the Germanic body. Austria and Prussia make themselves the agents of the Diet, and dominate the entire confederation in its name.
It has always been so for the Swiss confederation. — For centuries Switzerland would have ceased to exist were it not for the jealousies of her neighbors.
I am not speaking here of a confederation of small republics, but of a great consolidated republic.
See the Mexican constitution of 1824.

Example: The constitution has given the Union the right to have unoccupied lands sold on its account. Suppose that Ohio claims this same right for the lands enclosed within its limits, on the pretext that the constitution meant to speak only of territory not yet subject to any State jurisdiction, and that in consequence it wishes to sell them itself. The judicial question would, it is true, arise between the purchasers who hold their title from the Union and the purchasers who hold their title from the State, and not between the Union and Ohio. But if the court of the United States ordered that the federal purchaser be put in possession, and the courts of Ohio maintained his competitor in his property, what would then become of the legal fiction?

*Kent's commentaries*, vol. 1, p. 244. Note that I have chosen the example cited above from times subsequent to the establishment of the present constitution. Had I wished to go back to the period of the first confederation, I could have pointed to facts far more conclusive still. At that time there reigned a real enthusiasm in the nation; the revolution was represented by an eminently popular man, and yet, at that time, Congress had, strictly speaking, nothing at its disposal. Men and money were lacking to it at every moment; the best-laid plans failed in execution, and the Union, constantly on the point of perishing, was saved far more by the weakness of its enemies than by its own strength.

items.title: Note A (page 31)
paragraphs: Voyez, sur tous les pays de l'ouest où les Européens n'ont pas encore pénétré, les deux voyages entrepris par le major Long, aux frais du congrès.

M. Long dit notamment, à propos du grand désert américain, qu'il faut tirer une ligne à peu près parallèle au 20e degré de longitude (méridien de Washington[163]), partant de la rivière Rouge et aboutissant à la rivière Plate. De cette ligne imaginaire jusqu'aux montagnes Rocheuses, qui bornent la vallée du Mississipi à l'ouest, s'étendent d'immenses plaines, couvertes en général de sable qui se refuse à la culture, ou parsemées de pierres granitiques. Elles sont privées d'eau en été. On n'y rencontre que de grands troupeaux de buffles et de chevaux sauvages. On y voit aussi quelques hordes d'Indiens, mais en petit nombre.

Le major Long a entendu dire qu'en s'élevant au-dessus de la rivière Plate dans la même direction, on rencontrait toujours à sa gauche le même désert; mais il n'a pas pu vérifier par lui-même l'exactitude de ce rapport. _Long's expedition_, vol. 2, p. 361.

Quelque confiance que mérite la relation du major Long, il ne faut pas cependant oublier qu'il n'a fait que traverser le pays dont il parle, sans tracer de grands zigzags au-dehors de la ligne qu'il suivait.
Le 20e degré de longitude, suivant le méridien de Washington, se rapporte à peu près au 99e degré suivant le méridien de Paris.

translation: See the two expeditions undertaken by Major Long, at the expense of Congress, on all the western territories into which Europeans have not yet penetrated.

Major Long notes, in particular, concerning the great American desert, that one should draw a line roughly parallel to the 20th degree of longitude (Washington meridian [163]), running from the Red River to the Platte River. From this imaginary line to the Rocky Mountains, which bound the Mississippi valley on the west, there extend immense plains, covered for the most part with sand that resists cultivation, or strewn with granite rocks. They are without water in summer. One encounters there only great herds of buffalo and wild horses. A few Indian bands are also seen, but in small numbers.

Major Long has heard it said that, following the Platte River upstream in the same direction, one would always find the same desert to one's left; but he was not able to verify the accuracy of this report himself. *Long's Expedition*, vol. 2, p. 361.
Whatever confidence Major Long's account deserves, one must not forget that he only crossed the territory he describes, without tracing any wide detours beyond the line he was following.

paragraphs: The 20th degree of longitude, measured from the Washington meridian, corresponds roughly to the 99th degree measured from the Paris meridian.

items.title: Note B (page 33)
paragraphs: L'Amérique du Sud, dans ses régions intertropicales, produit avec une incroyable profusion ces plantes grimpantes connues sous le nom générique de lianes. La flore des Antilles en présente à elle seule plus de quarante espèces différentes.

Parmi les plus gracieux d'entre ces arbustes se trouve la grenadille. Cette jolie plante, dit Descourtiz dans sa description du règne végétal aux Antilles, au moyen des vrilles dont elle est munie, s'attache aux arbres et y forme des arcades mobiles, des colonnades riches et élégantes par la beauté des fleurs pourpres variées de bleu qui les décorent, et qui flattent l'odorat par le parfum qu'elles exhalent; vol. 1, p. 265.
L'acacia à grandes gousses est une liane très grosse qui se développe rapidement, et, courant d'arbres en arbres, couvre quelquefois plus d'une demi-lieue; vol. 3, p. 227.

translation: In its intertropical regions, South America produces with incredible abundance those climbing plants known by the general name of lianas. The flora of the Antilles alone presents more than forty different species.

Among the most graceful of these shrubs is the passionflower. This pretty plant, says Descourtiz in his description of the plant kingdom in the Antilles, by means of the tendrils with which it is equipped, attaches itself to trees and forms moving arcades, rich and elegant colonnades adorned by the beauty of the purple flowers variegated with blue that decorate them, and that please the sense of smell with the perfume they exhale; vol. 1, p. 265.
The large-podded acacia is a very thick liana that grows rapidly and, running from tree to tree, sometimes covers more than half a league; vol. 3, p. 227.

items.title: Note C (page 56)
paragraphs: _Sur les langues américaines._

Les langues que parlent les Indiens de l'Amérique, depuis le pôle arctique jusqu'au cap Horn, sont toutes formées, dit-on, sur le même modèle, et soumises aux mêmes règles grammaticales; d'où on peut conclure avec une grande vraisemblance que toutes les nations indiennes sont sorties de la même souche.

Chaque peuplade du continent américain parle un dialecte différent; mais les langues proprement dites sont en très petit nombre, ce qui tendrait encore à prouver que les nations du Nouveau-Monde n'ont pas une origine fort ancienne.

Enfin les langues de l'Amérique sont d'une extrême régularité; il est donc probable que les peuples qui s'en servent n'ont pas encore été soumis à de grandes révolutions, et ne se sont pas mêlés forcément ou volontairement à des nations étrangères; car c'est en général l'union de plusieurs langues dans une seule qui produit les irrégularités de la grammaire.

Il n'y a pas long-temps que les langues américaines, et en particulier les langues de l'Amérique du Nord, ont attiré l'attention sérieuse des philologues. On a découvert alors, pour la première fois, que cet idiome d'un peuple barbare était le produit d'un système d'idées très compliquées et de combinaisons fort savantes. On s'est aperçu que ces langues étaient fort riches, et qu'en les formant on avait pris grand soin de ménager la délicatesse de l'oreille.
Le système grammatical des Américains diffère de tous les autres en plusieurs points, mais principalement en celui-ci.

Quelques peuples de l'Europe, entre autres les Allemands, ont la faculté de combiner au besoin différentes expressions, et de donner ainsi un sens complexe à certains mots. Les Indiens ont étendu de la manière la plus surprenante cette même faculté, et sont parvenus à fixer pour ainsi dire sur un seul point un très grand nombre d'idées. Ceci se comprendra sans peine à l'aide d'un exemple cité par M. Duponceau, dans les _Mémoires de la Société philosophique d'Amérique_.

Lorsqu'une femme delaware joue avec un chat ou avec un jeune chien, dit-il, on l'entend quelquefois prononcer le mot _kuligatschis_. Ce mot est ainsi composé: _K_ est le signe de la seconde personne, et signifie _tu_ ou _ton_; _uli_, qu'on prononce _ouli_, est un fragment du mot _wulit_, qui signifie _beau_, _joli_; _gat_ est un autre fragment du mot _wichgat_, qui signifie _patte_; enfin _schis_, qu'on prononce _chise_, est une terminaison diminutive qui apporte avec elle l'idée de la petitesse. Ainsi, dans un seul mot, la femme indienne a dit: Ta jolie petite patte.
Voici un autre exemple qui montre avec quel bonheur les sauvages de l'Amérique savaient composer leurs mots.
Un jeune homme en delaware se dit _pilapé_. Ce mot est formé de _pilsit_, chaste, innocent; et de _lénapé_, homme: c'est-à-dire l'homme dans sa pureté et son innocence.

Cette faculté de combiner entre eux les mots se fait surtout remarquer d'une manière fort étrange dans la formation des verbes. L'action la plus compliquée se rend souvent par un seul verbe; presque toutes les nuances de l'idée agissent sur le verbe et le modifient.
Ceux qui voudraient examiner plus en détail ce sujet, que je n'ai fait moi-même qu'effleurer très superficiellement, devront lire:

1º La Correspondance de M. Duponceau avec le révérend Hecwelder, relativement aux langues indiennes. Cette correspondance se trouve dans le 1er volume des _Mémoires de la Société philosophique d'Amérique_, publiés à Philadelphie, en 1819, chez Abraham Small, p. 356-464.
2º La grammaire de la langue delaware ou lenape, par Geiberger, et la préface de M. Duponceau, qui y est jointe. Le tout se trouve dans les mêmes collections, vol. 3.
3º Un résumé fort bien fait de ces travaux, contenu à la fin du volume 6 de l'_Encyclopédie américaine_.

translation: *On the languages of the Americans.*

The languages spoken by the Indians of the Americas, from the Arctic pole to Cape Horn, are all said to be formed on the same model and governed by the same grammatical rules — from which one may conclude, with considerable plausibility, that all the Indian nations spring from a single stock.

Each tribe of the American continent speaks a different dialect; but the languages properly so called are very few in number — which would tend further to prove that the nations of the New World are not of very ancient origin.

The languages of the Americas are, moreover, of extreme regularity; it is therefore probable that the peoples who use them have not yet been subjected to great upheavals, and have not — whether by force or by choice — mixed with foreign nations. It is, generally speaking, the fusion of several languages into one that produces grammatical irregularities.

It is only recently that the American languages, and in particular those of North America, have attracted the serious attention of philologists. It was then discovered, for the first time, that this idiom of a barbarian people was the product of a highly complex system of ideas and of very learned combinations. These languages were found to be extraordinarily rich, and it became clear that great care had been taken, in forming them, to preserve the delicacy of the ear.
The grammatical system of the Americans differs from all others in several respects, but chiefly in the following.

Certain peoples of Europe — the Germans among others — have the ability to combine different expressions as needed, thereby giving a complex meaning to certain words. The Indians have extended this same faculty in the most astonishing way, and have succeeded in concentrating, on a single point as it were, a very large number of ideas. This will be readily understood with the help of an example cited by Mr. Duponceau in the *Memoirs of the American Philosophical Society*.

When a Delaware woman plays with a cat or a young dog, he tells us, she can sometimes be heard to pronounce the word *kuligatschis*. The word is formed as follows: *K* is the sign of the second person, meaning *you* or *your*; *uli*, pronounced *ouli*, is a fragment of the word *wulit*, meaning *beautiful*, *pretty*; *gat* is another fragment of the word *wichgat*, meaning *paw*; and finally *schis*, pronounced *chise*, is a diminutive ending that carries with it the idea of smallness. In a single word, then, the Indian woman has said: *Your pretty little paw*.
Here is another example showing how happily the savages of America knew how to compose their words.
