It is not that they see the sufferings of the poor without pity; but they cannot feel his miseries as if they shared them themselves. Provided the people seem to put up with their lot, the aristocracy hold themselves satisfied and expect nothing more of government. The aristocracy dreams of maintaining rather than improving.
When, on the contrary, public power is in the hands of the people, the sovereign seeks everywhere for what is better, because he feels himself unwell.

The spirit of improvement then extends to a thousand different objects; it descends to infinite details, and above all it applies itself to the kinds of improvements that can be had only by paying for them; for it is a matter of making better the condition of the poor man who cannot help himself.

There exists, besides, in democratic societies, an agitation without precise aim; a kind of permanent fever reigns there which turns into innovation of every sort, and innovations are almost always costly.
In monarchies and aristocracies, the ambitious flatter the natural taste that draws the sovereign toward renown and power, and so push him often to great expenditures.
In democracies, where the sovereign is needy, his goodwill can scarcely be acquired except by increasing his well-being; and this can almost never be done except with money.

Moreover, when the people themselves begin to reflect on their position, a host of needs are born in them that they had not felt at first, and that can be satisfied only by recourse to the state's resources. From this it comes that, in general, public charges seem to grow with civilization, and one sees taxes rise as enlightenment spreads.

There is, finally, one last cause that often makes democratic government more expensive than another. Sometimes democracy wishes to economize in its expenses, but cannot manage to, because it has not the art of being economical.

Since it changes views frequently, and its agents more frequently still, it happens that its enterprises are ill-conducted or remain unfinished: in the first case, the state makes expenditures disproportionate to the size of the goal it aims at; in the second, it makes unproductive expenditures.
ON THE INSTINCTS OF AMERICAN DEMOCRACY IN FIXING THE SALARIES OF OFFICIALS.

In democracies, those who set high salaries have no chance of profiting from them. — Tendency of American democracy to raise the salaries of secondary officials and lower those of the principal. — Why this is so. — Comparative table of the salaries of public officials in the United States and in France.
There is one great reason that leads democracies in general to economize on the salaries of public officials.
In democracies, those who set salaries, being very numerous, have very little chance of ever drawing them.

In aristocracies, on the contrary, those who set high salaries almost always have the vague hope of profiting from them. They are capital they create for themselves, or at the very least resources they prepare for their children.
It must be admitted, however, that democracy shows itself very parsimonious only toward its principal agents.
In America, officials of a secondary order are better paid than elsewhere, but high officials are paid much less.

These contrary effects are produced by the same cause: the people, in both cases, fix the salaries of public officials; they think of their own needs, and this comparison enlightens them. Living themselves in great comfort, it seems natural to them that those they employ should share in it.[9] But when they come to fix the lot of the great officers of state, their rule escapes them, and they proceed only at random.

The poor man has no distinct idea of the needs the upper classes of society may feel. What would seem a modest sum to a rich man appears a prodigious sum to him who is content with necessities; and he reckons that the governor of the state, supplied with his two thousand crowns, ought yet to count himself happy and to excite envy.[10]

Try to make him understand that the representative of a great nation must appear with a certain splendor in the eyes of foreigners, and he will grasp it at once; but as soon as he comes to think of his simple dwelling and the modest fruits of his hard labor, and to muse on all that he himself could do with this same salary you judge insufficient, he will be surprised and as it were frightened by the sight of so much wealth.
Add to this that the secondary official is almost on a level with the people, whereas the other dominates them. The first can still excite their interest; the other begins to arouse their envy.
This is seen very clearly in the United States, where salaries seem in a way to decrease as the power of the officials grows greater.[11]

Under the rule of aristocracy, on the contrary, it happens that high officials receive very large emoluments, while petty ones often have barely enough to live on. The reason for this is easy to find in causes analogous to those indicated above.

If democracy does not conceive of the pleasures of the rich or envies them, the aristocracy, on its side, does not understand the miseries of the poor — or rather, it knows nothing of them. The poor man is not, properly speaking, the rich man's like; he is a being of another species. The aristocracy therefore concerns itself little with the lot of its inferior agents. It raises their wages only when they refuse to serve it at too low a price.
It is the parsimonious tendency of democracy toward its principal officials that has caused great economical leanings to be attributed to it which it does not have.

It is true that democracy hardly gives those who govern it enough to live honestly, but it spends enormous sums to relieve the needs or facilitate the enjoyments of the people.[12] That is a better employment of the proceeds of taxation, not an economy.
In general, democracy gives little to those who govern and much to the governed. The contrary is seen in aristocracies, where the state's money chiefly profits the class that conducts affairs.
DIFFICULTY OF DISCERNING THE CAUSES THAT LEAD THE AMERICAN GOVERNMENT TO ECONOMY.
He who seeks in the facts the real influence the laws exercise on the lot of humanity is exposed to great mistakes, for there is nothing so hard to appreciate as a fact.
One people is naturally frivolous and enthusiastic; another reflective and calculating. This is owing to its physical constitution itself, or to remote causes I do not know.
One sees peoples who love display, noise, and joy, and who do not regret a million spent in smoke. One sees others who prize only solitary pleasures and who seem ashamed to appear content.

In some countries, a high value is attached to the beauty of buildings. In some others, no value is set on objects of art, and what brings in nothing is despised. There are some, finally, where renown is loved, and others where money is placed before everything.
Independently of the laws, all these causes exert a very powerful influence on the conduct of the state's finances.
If it has never happened to the Americans to spend the people's money on public festivals, it is not only because, among them, the people vote the tax, but because the people do not like to rejoice.
If they reject ornaments in their architecture and prize only material and positive advantages, it is not only because they form a democratic nation, but also because they are a commercial people.
The habits of private life have carried over into public life; and among them one must carefully distinguish the economies that depend on institutions from those that flow from habits and mores.
CAN THE PUBLIC EXPENDITURES OF THE UNITED STATES BE COMPARED TO THOSE OF FRANCE?

Two points to establish in order to assess the extent of public charges: national wealth and the tax. — The wealth and charges of France are not exactly known. — Why one cannot hope to know the wealth and charges of the Union. — The author's researches into the amount of taxation in Pennsylvania. — General signs by which the extent of a people's charges may be recognized. — Result of this examination for the Union.

Much labor has lately been spent on comparing the public expenditures of the United States with our own. All this work has been without result, and a few words will suffice, I believe, to show why it had to be so.

In order to assess the extent of public charges among a people, two operations are necessary: one must first learn what the wealth of that people is, and then what portion of that wealth it devotes to the state's expenditures. He who sought the amount of taxes without showing the extent of the resources that must answer for them would be engaging in unproductive work; for it is not the expenditure, but the ratio of expenditure to revenue, that it is interesting to know.
The same tax that a wealthy taxpayer bears easily will finish by reducing a poor one to misery.
The wealth of peoples is composed of several elements: immovable property forms the first; movable goods constitute the second.

It is difficult to know the extent of the cultivable land a nation possesses and its natural or acquired value. It is more difficult still to estimate all the movable goods a people disposes of. These escape, by their diversity and number, almost every effort of analysis.
And so we see that the most anciently civilized nations of Europe, even those whose administration is centralized, have not yet established in any precise way the state of their wealth.

In America, the idea of attempting it has not even been conceived. And how could one flatter oneself with succeeding at it in that new country where society has not yet taken a tranquil and definitive form, where the national government does not have at its disposal, as ours does, a multitude of agents whose efforts it can command and direct simultaneously, where, finally, statistics is not cultivated because there is no one there with the means to gather documents or the time to peruse them?

Thus the constitutive elements of our calculations cannot be obtained. We do not know the comparative wealth of France and the Union. The wealth of the one is not yet known, and the means of establishing that of the other do not exist.

But I am willing to consent, for a moment, to set aside this necessary term of comparison; I give up trying to learn what the ratio of tax to revenue is, and confine myself to wishing to establish what the tax is.
The reader will recognize that in narrowing the circle of my researches I have not made my task any easier.

I have no doubt that the central administration of France, aided by all the officials at its disposal, would succeed in discovering exactly the amount of direct and indirect taxes that weigh on the citizens. But this work, which a private person cannot undertake, the French government itself has not yet completed, or at least it has not made its results known. We know what the charges of the state are; the total of departmental expenditures is known to us; we do not know what happens in the communes: no one, therefore, can say, as of now, to what sum public expenditures in France amount.

If I now return to America, I see the difficulties become more numerous and more insurmountable. The Union tells me exactly what the amount of its charges is; I can obtain the separate budgets of the twenty-four states of which it is composed; but who will tell me what the citizens spend for the administration of the county and the township?[13]

The federal authority cannot extend itself so far as to oblige the provincial governments to enlighten us on this point; and even if these governments themselves were willing to lend us their simultaneous cooperation, I doubt they would be able to satisfy us. Independently of the natural difficulty of the undertaking, the political organization of the country would still stand in the way of their success. The magistrates of the township and the county are not named by the state's administrators, and do not depend on them. One may therefore believe that if the state wanted to obtain the information we need, it would meet great obstacles in the negligence of the inferior officials it would be forced to employ.[14]
It is, moreover, useless to investigate what the Americans could do in such a matter, since it is certain that, up to now, they have done nothing.
There exists therefore today, in America or in Europe, not a single man who can tell us what each citizen of the Union pays annually to meet the charges of society.[15]

Let us conclude that it is as difficult to compare with profit the social expenditures of the Americans with our own as it is the wealth of the Union with that of France. I add that it would even be dangerous to attempt it. When statistics are not founded on rigorously true calculations, they mislead instead of guiding. The mind is easily taken in by the false air of exactness they preserve even in their wanderings, and rests untroubled on errors clothed before its eyes in the mathematical forms of truth.
Let us abandon figures, then, and try to find our proofs elsewhere.

Does a country present the aspect of material prosperity? After having paid the state, does the poor man preserve resources there and the rich man surplus? Do both seem satisfied with their lot, and do they seek each day to improve it further, so that capital never being lacking to industry, industry in turn is never lacking to capital? Such are the signs to which, for lack of positive documents, one may resort to know whether the public charges that weigh on a people are proportionate to its wealth.
The observer confining himself to these testimonies would no doubt judge that the American of the United States gives the state a smaller portion of his income than the Frenchman.
But how could it be conceived otherwise?

Part of the French debt is the result of two invasions; the Union has none to fear. Our position obliges us habitually to keep a large army under arms; the isolation of the Union allows it to have only 6,000 soldiers. We maintain nearly 300 vessels; the Americans have only 52.[16] How could the inhabitant of the Union pay the state as much as the inhabitant of France?
There is, then, no parallel to be drawn between the finances of countries so differently placed.
It is by examining what happens within the Union, and not by comparing the Union with France, that we can judge whether American democracy is truly economical.

I cast my eyes over each of the various republics that make up the confederation, and I discover that their governments often lack perseverance in their designs, and that they exercise no continuous oversight over the men they employ. I naturally draw from this the conclusion that they must often spend the taxpayers' money uselessly, or devote more to their undertakings than is necessary.

I see that, faithful to its popular origin, this government makes prodigious efforts to satisfy the needs of the lower classes of society, to open to them the paths of power, and to spread among them well-being and enlightenment. It supports the poor, distributes millions each year to the schools, pays for every service, and remunerates with generosity its least agents. If such a way of governing seems to me useful and reasonable, I am obliged to recognize that it is costly.

I see the poor man conducting public affairs and disposing of the national resources; and I cannot believe that, profiting from the state's expenditures, he does not often draw the state into new ones.

I conclude, then, without having recourse to incomplete figures and without seeking to draw hazardous comparisons, that the democratic government of the Americans is not, as is sometimes claimed, a cheap government; and I do not fear to predict that, if great difficulties were one day to assail the peoples of the United States, taxes would be seen to rise there as high as in most of the aristocracies or monarchies of Europe.
ON THE CORRUPTION AND VICES OF THE GOVERNORS IN A DEMOCRACY; AND ON THE EFFECTS THAT RESULT FROM THEM ON PUBLIC MORALITY.

In aristocracies, the governors sometimes seek to corrupt. — Often, in democracies, they show themselves corrupted. — In the first, vices attack the people's morality directly. — In the second, they exercise on it an indirect influence which is more to be feared.
Aristocracy and democracy reproach each other with making corruption easy; a distinction must be drawn.
In aristocratic governments, the men who come into office are wealthy and desire only power. In democracies, statesmen are poor and have their fortune to make.
It follows that, in aristocratic states, the governors are little accessible to corruption and have only a very moderate taste for money, whereas the contrary occurs among democratic peoples.

But in aristocracies, those who wish to come to the head of affairs disposing of great wealth, and the number of those who can bring them there being often restricted within certain limits, the government finds itself in some sort up for auction. In democracies, on the contrary, those who seek power are hardly ever rich, and the number of those who concur in bestowing it is very great. Perhaps in democracies there are no fewer men for sale, but there are almost no buyers there; and besides, one would have to buy too many people at once to reach the goal.

Among the men who have held power in France for the last forty years, several have been accused of having made their fortune at the expense of the state and its allies; a reproach rarely addressed to the public men of the old monarchy. But in France there is almost no example of an elector's vote being bought for money, whereas this is done notoriously and publicly in England.

I have never heard it said that in the United States wealth was used to win over the governed; but I have often seen the probity of public officials called into doubt. More often still I have heard their successes attributed to base intrigues or to culpable maneuvers.

If, then, the men who direct aristocracies sometimes seek to corrupt, the heads of democracies show themselves corrupted. In the one case, the people's morality is directly attacked; in the other, an indirect action is exercised on the public conscience which is to be feared still more.

Among democratic peoples, those at the head of the state, being almost always exposed to disagreeable suspicions, lend in some way the support of the government to the crimes of which they are accused. They thus present dangerous examples to a virtue still struggling, and furnish glorious comparisons to a vice that hides itself.

In vain might it be said that base passions are met with in every rank; that they often mount the throne by right of birth; and that thus one may find very contemptible men at the head of aristocratic nations as well as in the bosom of democracies.

This reply does not satisfy me. There is discovered, in the corruption of those who come to power by chance, something coarse and vulgar that makes it contagious for the crowd; there reigns, on the contrary, even in the depravity of great lords, a certain aristocratic refinement, an air of grandeur, that often prevents it from being communicated.

The people will never penetrate the obscure labyrinth of the courtly spirit; they will always have difficulty in discovering the baseness hidden beneath the elegance of manners, refinement of tastes, and graces of language. But to rob the public treasury, or to sell the state's favors for money — the lowest wretch understands that, and may flatter himself with doing as much in his turn.

What is to be feared, moreover, is not so much the sight of immorality among the great as the sight of immorality leading to greatness. In a democracy, ordinary citizens see a man emerge from their own ranks and rise in a few years to wealth and power; the spectacle excites their surprise and their envy; they look into how he who was their equal yesterday is today clothed with the right to direct them. To attribute his rise to his talents or his virtues is awkward, for that is to admit that they themselves are less virtuous and less able than he. They therefore place the principal cause in some of his vices, and often they are right to do so. There thus comes about some odious mixture between the ideas of baseness and power, of unworthiness and success, of usefulness and dishonor.
OF WHAT EFFORTS DEMOCRACY IS CAPABLE.

The Union has fought only once for its existence. — Enthusiasm at the beginning of the war. — Cooling at the end. — Difficulty of establishing in America conscription or naval registration. — Why a democratic people is less capable than another of great sustained efforts.
I warn the reader that I am speaking here of a government that follows the real will of the people, and not of a government that confines itself to commanding in the name of the people.

There is nothing so irresistible as a tyrannical power that commands in the name of the people, because, being clothed with the moral power that belongs to the will of the greatest number, it acts at the same time with the decision, promptness, and tenacity that would belong to a single man.
It is rather difficult to say of what degree of effort a democratic government is capable in time of national crisis.

No great democratic republic has yet been seen. It would be doing injury to republics to give that name to the oligarchy that ruled over France in 1793. The United States alone present this new spectacle.

Now, in the half-century since the Union was formed, its existence has been called into question only once, at the time of the War of Independence. At the beginning of that long war, there were extraordinary displays of enthusiasm for the service of the country.[17] But as the struggle was prolonged, individual selfishness reappeared: money no longer flowed into the public treasury; men no longer presented themselves at the army; the people still wanted independence, but they shrank from the means of obtaining it. "In vain have we multiplied taxes and tried new methods of levying them," says Hamilton in the *Federalist* (no. 12); "public expectation has always been disappointed, and the treasury of the states has remained empty. The democratic forms of administration, which are inherent in the democratic nature of our government, combined with the scarcity of specie produced by the languishing state of our commerce, have hitherto rendered useless all the efforts that could be made to raise considerable sums. The various legislatures have at last understood the folly of such attempts."
Since that time, the United States have not had a single serious war to sustain.

To judge what sacrifices democracies can impose on themselves, one must therefore wait for the time when the American nation will be obliged to put into its government's hands half of the income of its property, as England does, or to throw a twentieth of its population at once onto the battlefields, as France has done.

In America, conscription is unknown; men are enlisted for money. Forced recruitment is so contrary to the ideas, and so foreign to the habits, of the people of the United States that I doubt it would ever be dared to introduce it into the laws. What is called conscription in France is assuredly the heaviest of all our taxes; but without conscription how could we sustain a great continental war?

The Americans have not adopted the impressment of the English. They have nothing resembling our naval registration. The state's navy, like the merchant marine, is recruited by means of voluntary engagements.

Now, it is not easy to conceive how a people could sustain a great maritime war without having recourse to one of the two means indicated above; and so the Union, which has already fought on the sea with glory, has nevertheless never had numerous fleets, and the arming of its small number of vessels has always cost it very dearly.

I have heard American statesmen admit that the Union will have trouble maintaining its rank on the seas if it does not resort to impressment or to naval registration; but the difficulty is to oblige the people, who govern, to suffer impressment or naval registration.

It is incontestable that free peoples generally display, in times of danger, an energy infinitely greater than peoples who are not free; but I am led to believe that this is true above all of free peoples in whom the aristocratic element predominates. Democracy seems to me much better suited to directing a peaceful society, or to making at need a sudden and vigorous effort, than to braving for a long time the great storms of a people's political life. The reason is simple: men expose themselves to dangers and privations out of enthusiasm, but they remain long exposed to them only through reflection. There is, in what is called instinctive courage itself, more calculation than is thought; and although passions alone generally make one make the first efforts, it is in view of the result that one continues them. One risks a part of what is dear in order to save the rest.

Now, it is this clear perception of the future, founded on enlightenment and experience, that must often be lacking in democracy. The people feel far more than they reason; and if present evils are great, it is to be feared they will forget the still greater evils that perhaps await them in case of defeat.
There is yet another cause that must make the efforts of a democratic government less lasting than those of an aristocracy.

The people not only see less clearly than the upper classes what they may hope or fear from the future, they also suffer quite otherwise than they do from present evils. The noble, in exposing his person, runs as many chances of glory as of peril. In giving up to the state the greater part of his income, he deprives himself momentarily of some of the pleasures of wealth; but for the poor man, death has no prestige, and the tax that strains the rich man often attacks in him the sources of life.

This relative weakness of democratic republics in times of crisis is perhaps the greatest obstacle that stands in the way of such a republic being founded in Europe. For a democratic republic to subsist without difficulty among a European people, it would have to be established at the same time among all the others.

I believe that the government of democracy must, in the long run, increase the real strength of society; but it cannot bring together at once, at a given point and at a given time, as much force as an aristocratic government or an absolute monarchy. If a democratic country remained subject for a century to republican government, one may believe that at the end of the century it would be richer, more populous, and more prosperous than the despotic states around it; but during that century it would several times have run the risk of being conquered by them.
ON THE POWER AMERICAN DEMOCRACY GENERALLY EXERCISES OVER ITSELF.
That the American people only slowly, and sometimes refuses, to do what is useful to its well-being. — Faculty the Americans have of making reparable mistakes.
The difficulty democracy finds in conquering the passions and silencing the needs of the moment in view of the future is to be noticed in the United States in the smallest matters.

The people, surrounded by flatterers, has difficulty triumphing over itself. Every time it is asked to impose on itself a privation or an inconvenience, even for a goal its reason approves, it nearly always begins by refusing. The obedience the Americans give to the laws is rightly praised. One must add that in America legislation is made by the people and for the people. In the United States, the law thus shows itself favorable to those who, everywhere else, have the greatest interest in violating it. Thus one may believe that an inconvenient law whose present utility the majority did not feel would not be enacted, or would not be obeyed.

In the United States there is no legislation relating to fraudulent bankruptcies. Is it that there are no bankruptcies? No, on the contrary, it is because there are many. The fear of being prosecuted as a bankrupt outweighs, in the mind of the majority, the fear of being ruined by bankruptcies; and there forms in the public conscience a kind of culpable tolerance for the offense that every individual condemns.

In the new states of the Southwest, the citizens almost always take justice into their own hands, and murders constantly recur there. This comes from the people's habits being too rough, and enlightenment too little diffused in those wildernesses, for the usefulness of giving force to the law to be felt: duels are still preferred there to lawsuits.

Someone said to me one day in Philadelphia that almost all crimes in America were caused by abuse of strong liquors, which the common people could use at will, because they were sold to them at a low price. Why, I asked, don't you put a duty on brandy? — Our legislators, he replied, have often thought of it, but the undertaking is difficult. A revolt is feared; and besides, the members who voted such a law would be sure of not being reelected. — So, I went on, in your country drinkers are in the majority, and temperance is unpopular.

When one points such things out to statesmen, they confine themselves to answering: Let time do its work; the sense of the evil will enlighten the people and show them their needs. This is often true: if democracy has more chance of being mistaken than a king or a body of nobles, it has also more chance of coming back to the truth once the light reaches it, because there are not, in general, within it interests contrary to that of the greatest number which struggle against reason. But democracy can obtain truth only from experience, and many peoples cannot wait, without perishing, for the results of their errors.
The great privilege of the Americans is therefore not only to be more enlightened than others but to have the faculty of making reparable mistakes.
Add to this that, in order easily to profit from the experience of the past, democracy must already have arrived at a certain degree of civilization and enlightenment.

Peoples are seen whose first education has been so vicious, and whose character presents so strange a mixture of passions, ignorance, and erroneous notions of all things, that they cannot of themselves discern the cause of their miseries; they succumb to evils of which they know nothing.

I have traversed vast countries once inhabited by powerful Indian nations that today no longer exist; I have lived among tribes already mutilated who each day see their numbers shrink and the brilliance of their savage glory fade; I have heard these Indians themselves foresee the final destiny reserved for their race. There is no European, however, who does not see what would have to be done to preserve these unfortunate peoples from inevitable destruction. But they do not see it; they feel the evils that each year heap up on their heads, and they will perish to the last man rejecting the remedy. They would have to be compelled by force to live.

One is astonished to see the new nations of South America stirring, for the past quarter-century, in the midst of revolutions endlessly reborn, and each day one expects to see them return to what is called their *natural state*. But who can affirm that revolutions are not, in our time, the most natural state of the Spaniards of South America? In that country, society struggles at the bottom of an abyss from which its own efforts cannot draw it out.

The people who inhabit that fair half of a hemisphere seem stubbornly attached to tearing out their own entrails; nothing can turn them from it. Exhaustion makes them fall for an instant into repose, and repose soon gives them back to new furies. When I come to consider them in this alternating state of miseries and crimes, I am tempted to believe that for them despotism would be a blessing.
But these two words can never be united in my thought.
ON THE MANNER IN WHICH AMERICAN DEMOCRACY CONDUCTS THE FOREIGN AFFAIRS OF THE STATE.

Direction given to the foreign policy of the United States by Washington and Jefferson. — Almost all the natural defects of democracy are felt in the conduct of foreign affairs, and its qualities are little perceptible there.

We have seen that the federal constitution placed the permanent direction of the nation's external interests in the hands of the president and the Senate,[18] which puts the general policy of the Union, to a certain extent, beyond the direct and daily influence of the people. One cannot therefore say in any absolute way that it is democracy that, in America, conducts the foreign affairs of the state.
Two men gave American policy a direction that is still followed today: the first is Washington, and the second is Jefferson.
Washington said, in that admirable letter addressed to his fellow citizens which forms, as it were, the political testament of that great man:

"To extend our commercial relations with foreign peoples, and to form as few political ties as possible between them and us, must be the rule of our policy. We must fulfill faithfully the engagements already contracted, but we must guard against forming others.

"Europe has a certain number of interests of her own which have no relation, or only a very indirect relation, to ours; she must therefore find herself frequently engaged in quarrels naturally foreign to us. To attach ourselves by artificial ties to the vicissitudes of her policy, to enter into the various combinations of her friendships and her hatreds, and to take part in the struggles that result, would be to act imprudently.

"Our isolation and our distance from her invite us to follow a contrary course and allow us to follow it. If we continue to form a single nation, governed by a strong government, the time is not far off when we shall have nothing to fear from anyone. Then we may take an attitude that will make our neutrality respected; the belligerent nations, feeling the impossibility of acquiring anything from us, will fear to provoke us without motive; and we shall be in a position to choose peace or war, taking no other guides for our actions than our own interest and justice.

"Why should we abandon the advantages we can draw from so favorable a situation? Why should we leave a ground that is our own to go and establish ourselves on a ground foreign to us? Why, in short, by binding our destiny to that of any portion of Europe, should we expose our peace and prosperity to the ambition, the rivalries, the interests, or the caprices of the peoples that inhabit it?

"Our true policy is to contract no permanent alliance with any foreign nation; at least so far as we are still free not to do so, for I am far from wishing existing engagements to be broken. Honesty is always the best policy; a maxim that I hold equally applicable to the affairs of nations and to those of individuals. I think therefore that the engagements we have already contracted must be executed in their full extent; but I believe it useless and imprudent to contract others. Let us always place ourselves in such a way as to make our position respected, and temporary alliances will suffice to enable us to meet every danger."

Earlier Washington had expressed this fine and just idea: "The nation which gives way to habitual sentiments of love or hatred toward another becomes in some sense a slave. It is a slave to its hatred or its love."

Washington's political conduct was always directed by these maxims. He managed to keep his country at peace when all the rest of the world was at war, and he established as a point of doctrine that the well-understood interest of the Americans was never to take sides in the internal quarrels of Europe.

Jefferson went further still, and introduced into the policy of the Union this other maxim: "That the Americans must never ask privileges of foreign nations, so as not to be obliged themselves to grant any."
These two principles, whose obvious justness made them easily intelligible to the crowd, have extremely simplified the foreign policy of the United States.

The Union, not meddling in the affairs of Europe, has, so to speak, no external interests to debate, for it does not yet have powerful neighbors in America. Placed by its situation as much as by its will outside the passions of the Old World, it has no more to guard against them than to embrace them. As for those of the New World, the future still hides them.

The Union is free of prior engagements; it profits, then, from the experience of the old peoples of Europe, without being obliged, as they are, to draw on the past and accommodate it to the present; like them, it is not forced to accept an immense inheritance bequeathed by its fathers — a mixture of glory and misery, of national friendships and hatreds. The foreign policy of the United States is eminently a policy of waiting; it consists far more in abstaining than in doing.

It is therefore very hard to know, for the present, what ability American democracy will develop in the conduct of the state's foreign affairs. On this point, its adversaries as much as its friends must suspend their judgment.

As for myself, I shall not hesitate to say it: it is in the direction of society's external interests that democratic governments seem to me decidedly inferior to others. Experience, mores, and instruction almost always end by creating in democracy that sort of everyday practical wisdom, and that science of the small events of life, that is called good sense. Good sense suffices for the ordinary running of society; and among a people whose education is complete, democratic liberty applied to the internal affairs of the state produces more goods than the errors of the government of democracy can bring evils. But it is not always so in the relations of one people to another.

Foreign policy requires the use of almost none of the qualities proper to democracy, and on the contrary demands the development of almost all those it lacks. Democracy favors the growth of the state's internal resources; it spreads comfort, develops public spirit, strengthens respect for the law in the various classes of society — all things that have only an indirect influence on the position of one people with respect to another. But democracy can only with difficulty coordinate the details of a great enterprise, fix upon a design, and then follow it obstinately through obstacles. It is little capable of combining measures in secret and waiting patiently for their result. These are qualities that belong more particularly to a single man or to an aristocracy. Now, it is precisely these qualities by which, in the long run, a people, like an individual, ends by dominating.

If, on the contrary, you give attention to the natural defects of aristocracy, you will find that the effect they can produce is hardly perceptible in the direction of the state's foreign affairs. The capital vice reproached against aristocracy is that of working only for itself, and not for the mass. In foreign policy, it is very rare that an aristocracy has an interest distinct from that of the people.

The slope that draws democracy, in politics, to obey sentiments rather than reasoning, and to abandon a long-matured design for the satisfaction of a momentary passion, was clearly seen in America when the French Revolution broke out. The simplest lights of reason were enough then, as today, to make the Americans understand that their interest was not to engage in the struggle that was about to bloody Europe, and from which the United States could suffer no harm.

The people's sympathies for France declared themselves, nevertheless, with such violence that nothing less than the inflexible character of Washington and the immense popularity he enjoyed was needed to prevent war from being declared on England. And even then, the efforts of that great man's austere reason to struggle against the generous but unreflecting passions of his fellow citizens nearly cost him the one reward he had ever reserved for himself: the love of his country. The majority pronounced against his policy; now the entire people approves it.[19]
If the constitution and public favor had not given Washington the direction of the state's foreign affairs, it is certain that the nation would have done precisely then what it condemns today.

Almost all the peoples who have acted forcefully upon the world, who have conceived, pursued, and executed great designs, from the Romans to the English, were directed by an aristocracy, and how could one be surprised at it?

What is most fixed in its views in the world is an aristocracy. The mass of the people may be seduced by its ignorance or its passions; the mind of a king may be taken by surprise and made to waver in its projects; and besides, a king is not immortal. But an aristocratic body is too numerous to be suborned, too small to yield easily to the intoxication of unreflecting passions. An aristocratic body is a firm and enlightened man who never dies.

paragraphs: Letter to Madison, December 20, 1787, translated by M. Conseil.
I take the word *magistrates* here in its broadest acceptation: I apply it to all those charged with carrying out the laws.
See the law of February 27, 1813. *General Collection of the Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 2, p. 331. It should be added that the jurors are then drawn by lot from the lists.

Law of February 28, 1787. See *General Collection of the Laws of Massachusetts*, vol. 1, p. 302. Here is the text: "The *select-men* of each township shall have posted in the shops of tavern-keepers, innkeepers, and retailers a list of the persons reputed to be drunkards, gamblers, and in the habit of wasting their time and their fortune in these houses; and the master of the said houses who, after this warning, shall have allowed the said persons to drink and gamble in his dwelling, or shall have sold them spirituous liquors, shall be condemned to a fine."
It is needless to say that I am speaking here of democratic government applied to a people and not to a small tribe.

It will be understood that the word *poor* has here, as throughout the chapter, a relative and not an absolute meaning. The poor of America, compared to those of Europe, might often appear rich; one is nevertheless right to call them poor when one opposes them to those of their fellow citizens who are richer than they.

The comfort in which secondary officials in the United States live is owing to yet another cause, one foreign to the general instincts of democracy: every kind of private career is very productive there; the state would not find secondary officials if it did not consent to pay them well. It is therefore in the position of a commercial enterprise obliged, whatever its economical tastes, to sustain an onerous competition.
The state of Ohio, which has a million inhabitants, gives the governor only 1,200 dollars or 6,504 francs in salary.

To make this truth visible to the eye, it suffices to examine the salaries of some of the agents of the federal government. I thought it useful to set alongside them the salary attached in France to analogous functions, so that the comparison may complete the reader's enlightenment.
UNITED STATES. TREASURY DEPARTMENT.
                                                                            fr.
The doorkeeper (messenger)                                                3,734
The lowest-paid clerk                                                     5,420
The highest-paid clerk                                                    8,672
The chief clerk                                                          10,840
The secretary (of state)                                                 32,520
The head of government (the president)                                  135,000
FRANCE. MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
The minister's doorkeeper                                                 1,500
The lowest-paid clerk                                                 1,000–1,800
The highest-paid clerk                                                3,200–3,600
The chief clerk                                                          20,000
The minister                                                             80,000
The head of government (the king)                                    12,000,000
I have perhaps been wrong to take France as a point of comparison. In France, where democratic instincts penetrate further into the government every day, a strong tendency is already perceptible that leads the chambers to raise small salaries and especially to lower large ones. Thus the minister of finance, who in 1834 receives 80,000 fr., received 160,000 under the Empire; the directors general of finance, who receive 20,000, then received 50,000.

See, among other things, what it costs in American budgets to maintain the indigent and provide free instruction. In 1831 the state of New York spent, for the support of the indigent, the sum of 1,290,000 francs. And the sum devoted to public instruction is estimated to rise to at least 5,420,000 francs. (*William's New-York Annual Register*, 1832, pp. 205 and 243.) The state of New York had in 1830 only 1,900,000 inhabitants, which does not make twice the population of the department of the Nord.

The Americans, as is seen, have four kinds of budgets: the Union has its own; the states, the counties, and the townships likewise have theirs. During my stay in America I undertook great research to learn the amount of public expenditure in the townships and counties of the principal states of the Union. I could easily obtain the budget of the largest townships, but it was impossible for me to obtain that of the small ones. I cannot therefore form any exact idea of the township expenditures. As for the county expenditures, I possess some documents which, though incomplete, are perhaps such as to merit the reader's interest. I owe to the kindness of M. Richard, former mayor of Philadelphia, the budgets of thirteen counties of Pennsylvania for the year 1830. These are those of Lebanon, Centre, Franklin, Lafayette, Montgomery, Luzerne, Dauphin, Butler, Allegheny, Columbia, Northumberland, Northampton, and Philadelphia. They contained, in 1830, 495,207 inhabitants. If one casts an eye on a map of Pennsylvania, one will see that these thirteen counties are scattered in every direction and subject to all the general causes that can influence the state of the country; so that it would be impossible to say why they would not furnish an exact idea of the financial state of the counties of Pennsylvania. Now, these same counties spent during the year 1830 1,800,221 francs, which makes 3 fr. 64 cent. per inhabitant. I have calculated that each of these same inhabitants, during the year 1830, devoted 12 fr. 70 cent. to the needs of the federal Union, and 3 fr. 80 cent. to those of Pennsylvania; from which it results that in the year 1830 these same citizens gave to society, to provide for all the public expenditures (except township expenditures), the sum of 20 fr. 14 cent. This result is doubly incomplete, as is seen, since it applies only to a single year and to a part of the public charges; but it has the merit of being certain.

Those who have wished to establish a parallel between the expenditures of the Americans and our own have rightly felt that it was impossible to compare the total public expenditures of France with the total public expenditures of the Union; but they have sought to compare detached portions of these expenditures with one another. It is easy to prove that this second way of proceeding is no less defective than the first. With what, for example, shall I compare our national budget? With the budget of the Union? But the Union occupies itself with many fewer objects than our central government, and its charges must naturally be much smaller. Shall I oppose our departmental budgets to the budgets of the particular states of which the Union is composed? But in general the particular states watch over more important and more numerous interests than the administration of our departments does; their expenditures are therefore naturally greater. As for the budgets of the counties, our financial system contains nothing resembling them. Shall we include the expenditures they carry in the budget of the state or in that of the townships? Township expenditures exist in both countries, but they are not always analogous. In America the township takes on several cares that in France it leaves to the department or the state. What, moreover, must be understood by township expenditures in America? The organization of the township differs from state to state. Shall we take as our rule what occurs in New England or in Georgia, in Pennsylvania or in the state of Illinois? It is easy to perceive a kind of analogy between certain budgets of the two countries; but the elements that compose them always differing more or less, no serious comparison can be established between them.

Even if one succeeded in knowing the precise sum that each French or American citizen pours into the public treasury, one would still have only a part of the truth. Governments do not ask the taxpayers only for money, but for personal efforts that are appreciable in money. The state raises an army; independently of the pay which the whole nation undertakes to furnish, the soldier must also give his time, which has a greater or lesser value according to the employment he could make of it if he remained free. I would say as much of service in the militia. The man who is part of the militia momentarily devotes a precious time to public security, and really gives to the state what he himself fails to acquire. I have cited these examples; I could have cited many others. The governments of France and of America levy taxes of this nature: these taxes weigh on the citizens; but who can exactly appreciate their amount in the two countries? This is not the last difficulty that arrests you when you wish to compare the public expenditures of the Union with our own. The state in France assumes certain obligations that it does not impose on itself in America, and vice versa. The French government pays the clergy; the American government leaves that care to the faithful. In America, the state takes charge of the poor; in France, it leaves them to public charity. We give all our officials a fixed salary; the Americans permit them to collect certain fees. In France, payments in kind are made on only a small number of roads; in the United States, on almost all the highways. Our roads are open to travelers, who can use them without paying anything; in the United States one meets many toll roads. All these differences in the manner in which the taxpayer discharges the charges of society make the comparison between the two countries very difficult; for there are certain expenditures the citizens would not make, or which would be smaller, if the state did not act in their name.
See the detailed budgets of the ministry of the marine in France, and, for America, the *National Calendar* of 1833, p. 228.

One of the most singular, in my view, was the resolution by which the Americans momentarily renounced the use of tea. Those who know that men generally cling to their habits more than to their lives will no doubt be astonished at this great and obscure sacrifice obtained from an entire people.

"The president," says the constitution, art. II, sect. 2, § 2, "shall make treaties by the advice and with the consent of the Senate." The reader must not lose sight of the fact that the senators' mandate lasts six years, and that, being chosen by the legislators of each state, they are the product of an election in two stages.

See the fifth volume of Marshall's *Life of Washington*. "In a government constituted as is that of the United States," he says, p. 314, "the chief magistrate cannot, whatever his firmness, long oppose a dike to the torrent of popular opinion; and the opinion that then prevailed seemed to lead to war. In fact, in the session of Congress held at that time, it was very frequently noticed that Washington had lost the majority in the chamber of representatives." Outside, the violence of the language used against him was extreme: in a political gathering, it was not feared to compare him indirectly to the traitor Arnold (p. 265). "Those who held to the party of the opposition," Marshall further says (p. 355), "claimed that the partisans of the administration formed an aristocratic faction submissive to England, and which, wishing to establish monarchy, was consequently the enemy of France; a faction whose members constituted a kind of nobility, having for their titles the shares of the Bank, and which feared so greatly any measure that might affect the funds that it was insensible to the affronts which the honor and the interest of the nation equally commanded should be repelled."

items.title: QUELS SONT LES AVANTAGES RÉELS QUE LA SOCIÉTÉ AMÉRICAINE RETIRE DU GOUVERNEMENT DE LA DÉMOCRATIE
paragraphs: Avant de commencer le présent chapitre, je sens le besoin de rappeler au lecteur ce que j'ai déjà indiqué plusieurs fois dans le cours de ce livre.

La constitution politique des États-Unis me paraît l'une des formes que la démocratie peut donner à son gouvernement; mais je ne considère pas les institutions américaines comme les seules ni comme les meilleures qu'un peuple démocratique doive adopter.

En faisant connaître quels biens les Américains retirent du gouvernement de la démocratie, je suis donc loin de prétendre ni de penser que de pareils avantages ne puissent être obtenus qu'à l'aide des mêmes lois.
DE LA TENDANCE GÉNÉRALE DES LOIS SOUS L'EMPIRE DE LA DÉMOCRATIE AMÉRICAINE, ET DE L'INSTINCT DE CEUX QUI LES APPLIQUENT.

Les vices de la démocratie se voient tout d'un coup. -- Ses avantages ne s'aperçoivent qu'à la longue. -- La démocratie américaine est souvent inhabile, mais la tendance générale de ses lois est profitable. -- Les fonctionnaires publics, sous la démocratie américaine, n'ont point d'intérêts permanents qui diffèrent de ceux du plus grand nombre. -- Ce qui en résulte.

Les vices et les faiblesses du gouvernement de la démocratie se voient sans peine; on les démontre par des faits patents, tandis que son influence salutaire s'exerce d'une manière insensible, et pour ainsi dire occulte. Ses défauts frappent du premier abord, mais ses qualités ne se découvrent qu'à la longue.

Les lois de la démocratie américaine sont souvent défectueuses ou incomplètes; il leur arrive de violer des droits acquis, ou d'en sanctionner de dangereux: fussent-elles bonnes, leur fréquence serait encore un grand mal. Tout ceci s'aperçoit au premier coup d'oeil.
D'où vient donc que les républiques américaines se maintiennent et prospèrent?
On doit distinguer soigneusement, dans les lois, le but qu'elles poursuivent, de la manière dont elles marchent vers ce but; leur bonté absolue de celle qui n'est que relative.

Je suppose que l'objet du législateur soit de favoriser les intérêts du petit nombre aux dépens de ceux du grand; ses dispositions sont combinées de façon à obtenir le résultat qu'il se propose dans le moins de temps et avec le moins d'efforts possibles. La loi sera bien faite, et son but mauvais; elle sera dangereuse en proportion de son efficacité même.

Les lois de la démocratie tendent en général au bien du plus grand nombre, car elles émanent de la majorité de tous les citoyens, laquelle peut se tromper, mais ne saurait avoir un intérêt contraire à elle-même.
Celles de l'aristocratie tendent au contraire à monopoliser dans les mains du petit nombre la richesse et le pouvoir, parce que l'aristocratie forme toujours de sa nature une minorité.
On peut donc dire, d'une manière générale, que l'objet de la démocratie, dans sa législation, est plus utile à l'humanité que l'objet de l'aristocratie dans la sienne.
Mais là finissent ses avantages.

L'aristocratie est infiniment plus habile dans la science du législateur, que ne saurait l'être la démocratie. Maîtresse d'elle-même, elle n'est point sujette à des entraînements passagers; elle a de longs desseins qu'elle sait mûrir jusqu'à ce que l'occasion favorable se présente. L'aristocratie procède savamment; elle connaît l'art de faire converger en même temps, vers un même point, la force collective de toutes ses lois.
Il n'en est pas ainsi de la démocratie: ses lois sont presque toujours défectueuses ou intempestives.
Les moyens de la démocratie sont donc plus imparfaits que ceux de l'aristocratie: souvent elle travaille, sans le vouloir, contre elle-même; mais son but est plus utile.

Imaginez une société que la nature, ou sa constitution, ait organisée de manière à supporter l'action passagère de mauvaises lois, et qui puisse attendre sans périr le résultat de la _tendance générale_ des lois, et vous concevrez que le gouvernement de la démocratie, malgré ses défauts, soit encore de tous le plus propre à faire prospérer cette société.
C'est précisément là ce qui arrive aux États-Unis; je répète ici ce que j'ai déjà exprimé ailleurs: le grand privilége des Américains est de pouvoir faire des fautes réparables.
Je dirai quelque chose d'analogue sur les fonctionnaires publics.

Il est facile de voir que la démocratie américaine se trompe souvent dans le choix des hommes auxquels elle confie le pouvoir; mais il n'est pas aussi aisé de dire pourquoi l'État prospère en leurs mains.
Remarquez d'abord que si, dans un État démocratique, les gouvernants sont moins honnêtes ou moins capables, les gouvernés sont plus éclairés et plus attentifs.

Le peuple, dans les démocraties, occupé comme il l'est sans cesse de ses affaires, et jaloux de ses droits, empêche ses représentants de s'écarter d'une certaine ligne générale que son intérêt lui trace.
Remarquez encore que si le magistrat démocratique use plus mal qu'un autre du pouvoir, il le possède en général moins long-temps.
Mais il y a une raison plus générale que celle-là, et plus satisfaisante.

Il importe sans doute au bien des nations que les gouvernants aient des vertus ou des talents; mais ce qui, peut-être, leur importe encore davantage, c'est que les gouvernants n'aient pas d'intérêts contraires à la masse des gouvernés; car, dans ce cas, les vertus pourraient devenir presque inutiles, et les talents funestes.

J'ai dit qu'il importait que les gouvernants n'aient point d'intérêts contraires ou différents de la masse des gouvernés; je n'ai point dit qu'il importait qu'ils eussent des intérêts semblables à ceux de _tous_ les gouvernés, car je ne sache point que la chose se soit encore rencontrée.

On n'a point découvert jusqu'ici de forme politique qui favorisât également le développement et la prospérité de toutes les classes dont la société se compose. Ces classes ont continué à former comme autant de nations distinctes dans la même nation, et l'expérience a prouvé qu'il était presque aussi dangereux de s'en remettre complétement à aucune d'elles du sort des autres, que de faire d'un peuple l'arbitre des destinées d'un autre peuple. Lorsque les riches seuls gouvernent, l'intérêt des pauvres est toujours en péril; et lorsque les pauvres font la loi, celui des riches court de grands hasards. Quel est donc l'avantage de la démocratie? L'avantage réel de la démocratie n'est pas, comme on l'a dit, de favoriser la prospérité de tous, mais seulement de servir au bien-être du plus grand nombre.

Ceux qu'on charge, aux États-Unis, de diriger les affaires du public, sont souvent inférieurs en capacité et en moralité aux hommes que l'aristocratie porterait au pouvoir; mais leur intérêt se confond et s'identifie avec celui de la majorité de leurs concitoyens. Ils peuvent donc commettre de fréquentes infidélités et de graves erreurs, mais ils ne suivront jamais systématiquement une tendance hostile à cette majorité; et il ne saurait leur arriver d'imprimer au gouvernement une allure exclusive et dangereuse.

La mauvaise administration d'un magistrat, sous la démocratie, est d'ailleurs un fait isolé qui n'a d'influence que pendant la courte durée de cette administration. La corruption et l'incapacité ne sont pas des intérêts communs qui puissent lier entre eux les hommes d'une manière permanente.

Un magistrat corrompu, ou incapable, ne combinera pas ses efforts avec un autre magistrat, par la seule raison que ce dernier est incapable et corrompu comme lui, et ces deux hommes ne travailleront jamais de concert à faire fleurir la corruption et l'incapacité chez leurs arrière-neveux. L'ambition et les manoeuvres de l'un serviront, au contraire, à démasquer l'autre. Les vices du magistrat, dans les démocraties, lui sont en général tout personnels.

Mais les hommes publics, sous le gouvernement de l'aristocratie, ont un intérêt de classe qui, s'il se confond quelquefois avec celui de la majorité, en reste souvent distinct. Cet intérêt forme entre eux un lien commun et durable; il les invite à unir et à combiner leurs efforts vers un but qui n'est pas toujours le bonheur du plus grand nombre: il ne lie pas seulement les gouvernants les uns aux autres; ils les unit encore à une portion considérable de gouvernés; car beaucoup de citoyens, sans être revêtus d'aucun emploi, font partie de l'aristocratie.
Le magistrat aristocratique rencontre donc un appui constant dans la société, en même temps qu'il en trouve un dans le gouvernement.

Cet objet commun, qui, dans les aristocraties, unit les magistrats à l'intérêt d'une partie de leurs contemporains, les identifie encore et les soumet pour ainsi dire à celui des races futures. Ils travaillent pour l'avenir aussi bien que pour le présent. Le magistrat aristocratique est donc poussé tout à la fois vers un même point, par les passions des gouvernés, par les siennes, propres, et je pourrais presque dire par les passions de sa postérité.

Comment s'étonner s'il ne résiste point? Aussi voit-on souvent, dans les aristocraties, l'esprit de classe entraîner ceux mêmes qu'il ne corrompt pas, et faire qu'à leur insu ils accommodent peu à peu la société à leur usage, et la préparent pour leurs descendants.
Je ne sais s'il a jamais existé une aristocratie aussi libérale que celle d'Angleterre, et qui ait, sans interruption, fourni au gouvernement du pays des hommes aussi dignes et aussi éclairés.

Il est cependant facile de reconnaître que dans la législation anglaise le bien du pauvre a fini par être souvent sacrifié à celui du riche, et les droits du plus grand nombre aux priviléges de quelques uns: aussi l'Angleterre, de nos jours, réunit-elle dans son sein tout ce que la fortune a de plus extrême, et l'on y rencontre des misères qui égalent presque sa puissance et sa gloire.

Aux États-Unis, où les fonctionnaires publics n'ont point d'intérêts de classe à faire prévaloir, la marche générale et continue du gouvernement est bienfaisante, quoique les gouvernants soient souvent inhabiles, et quelquefois méprisables.

Il y a donc, au fond des institutions démocratiques, une tendance cachée qui fait souvent concourir les hommes à la prospérité générale, malgré leurs vices ou leurs erreurs, tandis que dans les institutions aristocratiques, il se découvre quelquefois une pente secrète qui, en dépit des talents et des vertus, les entraîne à contribuer aux misères de leurs semblables. C'est ainsi qu'il peut arriver que, dans les gouvernements aristocratiques, les hommes publics fassent le mal sans le vouloir, et que dans les démocraties ils produisent le bien sans en avoir la pensée.
DE L'ESPRIT PUBLIC AUX ÉTATS-UNIS.

Amour instinctif de la patrie. -- Patriotisme réfléchi. -- Leurs différents caractères. -- Que les peuples doivent tendre de toutes leurs forces vers le second quand le premier disparaît. -- Efforts qu'ont faits les Américains pour y parvenir. -- L'intérêt de l'individu intimement lié à celui du pays.

Il existe un amour de la patrie qui a principalement sa source dans ce sentiment irréfléchi, désintéressé et indéfinissable, qui lie le coeur de l'homme aux lieux où l'homme a pris naissance. Cet amour instinctif se confond avec le goût des coutumes anciennes, avec le respect des aïeux et la mémoire du passé; ceux qui l'éprouvent chérissent leur pays comme on aime la maison paternelle. Ils aiment la tranquillité dont ils y jouissent; ils tiennent aux paisibles habitudes qu'ils y ont contractées; ils s'attachent aux souvenirs qu'elle leur présente, et trouvent même quelque douceur à y vivre dans l'obéissance. Souvent cet amour de la patrie est encore exalté par le zèle religieux, et alors on lui voit faire des prodiges. Lui-même est une sorte de religion; il ne raisonne point, il croit, il sent, il agit. Des peuples se sont rencontrés qui ont, en quelque façon, personnifié la patrie, et qui l'ont entrevue dans le prince. Ils ont donc transporté en lui une partie des sentiments dont le patriotisme se compose; ils se sont enorgueillis de ses triomphes, et ont été fiers de sa puissance. Il fut un temps, sous l'ancienne monarchie, où les Français éprouvaient une sorte de joie en se sentant livrés sans recours à l'arbitraire du monarque, et disaient avec orgueil: «Nous vivons sous le plus puissant roi du monde.»

Comme toutes les passions irréfléchies, cet amour du pays pousse à de grands efforts passagers plutôt qu'à la continuité des efforts. Après avoir sauvé l'État en temps de crise, il le laisse souvent dépérir au sein de la paix.

Lorsque les peuples sont encore simples dans leurs moeurs et fermes dans leur croyance; quand la société repose doucement sur un ordre de choses ancien, dont la légitimité n'est point contestée, on voit régner cet amour instinctif de la patrie.

Il en est un autre plus rationnel que celui-là; moins généreux, moins ardent peut-être, mais plus fécond et plus durable; celui-ci naît des lumières; il se développe à l'aide des lois, il croît avec l'exercice des droits, et il finit, en quelque sorte, par se confondre avec l'intérêt personnel. Un homme comprend l'influence qu'a le bien-être du pays sur le sien propre; il sait que la loi lui permet de contribuer à produire ce bien-être, et il s'intéresse à la prospérité de son pays, d'abord comme une chose qui lui est utile, et ensuite comme à son ouvrage.

Mais il arrive quelquefois, dans la vie des peuples, un moment où les coutumes anciennes sont changées, les moeurs détruites, les croyances ébranlées, le prestige des souvenirs évanoui, et où, cependant, les lumières sont restées incomplètes, et les droits politiques mal assurés ou restreints. Les hommes alors n'aperçoivent plus la patrie que sous un jour faible et douteux; ils ne la placent plus ni dans le sol, qui est devenu à leurs yeux une terre inanimée, ni dans les usages de leurs aïeux, qu'on leur a appris à regarder comme un joug; ni dans la religion, dont ils doutent; ni dans les lois qu'ils ne font pas, ni dans le législateur qu'ils craignent et méprisent. Ils ne la voient donc nulle part, pas plus sous ses propres traits que sous aucun autre, et ils se retirent dans un égoïsme étroit et sans lumière. Ces hommes échappent aux préjugés sans reconnaître l'empire de la raison; ils n'ont ni le patriotisme instinctif de la monarchie, ni le patriotisme réfléchi de la république; mais ils se sont arrêtés entre les deux, au milieu de la confusion et des misères.

Que faire en un pareil état? Reculer. Mais les peuples ne reviennent pas plus aux sentiments de leur jeunesse, que les hommes aux goûts innocents de leur premier âge; ils peuvent les regretter, mais non les faire renaître. Il faut donc marcher en avant, et se hâter d'unir aux yeux du peuple l'intérêt individuel à l'intérêt du pays, car l'amour désintéressé de la patrie fuit sans retour.

Je suis assurément loin de prétendre que pour arriver à ce résultat on doive accorder tout-à-coup l'exercice des droits politiques à tous les hommes; mais je dis que le plus puissant moyen, et peut-être le seul qui nous reste, d'intéresser les hommes au sort de leur patrie, c'est de les faire participer à son gouvernement. De nos jours, l'esprit de cité me semble inséparable de l'exercice des droits politiques; et je pense que désormais on verra augmenter ou diminuer en Europe le nombre des citoyens, en proportion de l'extension de ses droits.

D'où vient qu'aux États-Unis, où les habitants sont arrivés d'hier sur le sol qu'ils occupent, où ils n'y ont apporté ni usages, ni souvenirs; où ils s'y rencontrent pour la première fois sans se connaître; où, pour le dire en un mot, l'instinct de la patrie peut à peine exister; d'où vient que chacun s'intéresse aux affaires de sa commune, de son canton, et de l'État tout entier comme aux siennes mêmes? C'est que chacun, dans sa sphère, prend une part active au gouvernement de la société.

L'homme du peuple, aux États-Unis, a compris l'influence qu'exerce la prospérité générale sur son bonheur, idée si simple et cependant si peu connue du peuple. De plus, il s'est accoutumé à regarder cette prospérité comme son ouvrage. Il voit donc dans la fortune publique la sienne propre, et il travaille au bien de l'État, non seulement par devoir ou par orgueil, mais j'oserais presque dire par cupidité.

On n'a pas besoin d'étudier les institutions et l'histoire des Américains pour connaître la vérité de ce qui précède, les moeurs vous en avertissent assez. L'Américain prenant part à tout ce qui se fait dans son pays, se croit intéressé à défendre tout ce qu'on y critique; car ce n'est pas seulement son pays qu'on attaque alors, c'est lui-même: aussi voit-on son orgueil national recourir à tous les artifices et descendre à toutes les puérilités de la vanité individuelle.

Il n'y a rien de plus gênant dans l'habitude de la vie que ce patriotisme irritable des Américains. L'étranger consentirait bien à louer beaucoup dans leur pays; mais il voudrait qu'on lui permît de blâmer quelque chose, et c'est ce qu'on lui refuse absolument.

L'Amérique est donc un pays de liberté, où, pour ne blesser personne, l'étranger ne doit parler librement ni des particuliers, ni de l'État, ni des gouvernés, ni des gouvernants, ni des entreprises publiques, ni des entreprises privées; de rien enfin de ce qu'on y rencontre, sinon peut-être du climat et du sol; encore trouve-t-on des Américains prêts à défendre l'un et l'autre, comme s'ils avaient concouru à les former.

De nos jours, il faut savoir prendre son parti, et oser choisir entre le patriotisme de tous et le gouvernement du petit nombre; car on ne peut réunir à la fois la force et l'activité sociales que donne le premier, avec les garanties de tranquillité que fournit quelquefois le second.
DE L'IDÉE DES DROITS AUX ÉTATS-UNIS.
Il n'y a pas de grands peuples sans idée des droits. -- Quel est le moyen de donner au peuple l'idée des droits. -- Respect des droits aux États-Unis. -- D'où il naît.

Après l'idée générale de la vertu, je n'en sais pas de plus belle que celle des droits, ou plutôt ces deux idées se confondent. L'idée des droits n'est autre chose que l'idée de la vertu introduite dans le monde politique.

C'est avec l'idée des droits que les hommes ont défini ce qu'étaient la licence et la tyrannie. Éclairé par elle, chacun a pu se montrer indépendant sans arrogance et soumis sans hardiesse. L'homme qui obéit à la violence se plie et s'abaisse; mais quand il se soumet au droit de commander qu'il reconnaît à son semblable, il s'élève en quelque sorte au-dessus de celui même qui lui commande. Il n'est pas de grands hommes sans vertu; sans respect des droits il n'y a pas de grand peuple: on peut presque dire qu'il n'y a pas de société; car qu'est-ce qu'une réunion d'êtres rationnels et intelligents dont la force est le seul lien?

Je me demande quel est, de nos jours, le moyen d'inculquer aux hommes l'idée des droits, et de le faire pour ainsi dire tomber sous leur sens; et je n'en vois qu'un seul, c'est de leur donner à tous le paisible exercice de certains droits: on voit bien cela chez les enfants, qui sont des hommes, à la force et à l'expérience près. Lorsque l'enfant commence à se mouvoir au milieu des objets extérieurs, l'instinct le porte à mettre à son usage tout ce qui se rencontre sous ses mains; il n'a pas d'idée de la propriété des autres, pas même de celle de l'existence; mais à mesure qu'il est averti du prix des choses, et qu'il découvre qu'on peut à son tour l'en dépouiller, il devient plus circonspect, et finit par respecter dans ses semblables ce qu'il veut qu'on respecte en lui.

Ce qui arrive à l'enfant pour ses jouets, arrive plus tard à l'homme pour tous les objets qui lui appartiennent. Pourquoi en Amérique, pays de démocratie par excellence, personne ne fait-il entendre contre la propriété en général ces plaintes qui souvent retentissent en Europe? Est-il besoin de le dire? c'est qu'en Amérique il n'y a point de prolétaires. Chacun ayant un bien particulier à défendre, reconnaît en principe le droit de propriété.

Dans le monde politique, il en est de même. En Amérique, l'homme du peuple a conçu une haute idée des droits politiques, parce qu'il a des droits politiques; il n'attaque pas ceux d'autrui pour qu'on ne viole pas les siens. Et tandis qu'en Europe ce même homme méconnaît jusqu'à l'autorité souveraine, l'Américain se soumet sans murmurer au pouvoir du moindre de ses magistrats.

Cette vérité paraît jusque dans les plus petits détails de l'existence des peuples. En France, il y a peu de plaisirs exclusivement réservés aux classes supérieures de la société; le pauvre est admis presque partout où le riche peut entrer: aussi le voit-on se conduire avec décence et respecter tout ce qui sert à des jouissances qu'il partage. En Angleterre, où la richesse a le privilége de la joie comme le monopole du pouvoir, on se plaint que quand le pauvre parvient à s'introduire furtivement dans le lieu destiné aux plaisirs du riche, il aime à y causer des dégâts inutiles: comment s'en étonner? on a pris soin qu'il n'ait rien à perdre.

Le gouvernement de la démocratie fait descendre l'idée des droits politiques jusqu'au moindre des citoyens, comme la division des biens met l'idée du droit de propriété en général à la portée de tous les hommes. C'est là un de ses plus grands mérites à mes yeux.
Je ne dis point que ce soit chose aisée que d'apprendre à tous les hommes à se servir des droits politiques; je dis seulement que, quand cela peut être, les effets qui en résultent sont grands.
Et j'ajoute que s'il est un siècle où une pareille entreprise doive être tentée, ce siècle est le nôtre.

Ne voyez-vous pas que les religions s'affaiblissent et que la notion divine des droits disparaît? Ne découvrez-vous point que les moeurs s'altèrent, et qu'avec elles s'efface la notion morale des droits?

N'apercevez-vous pas de toutes parts les croyances qui font place aux raisonnements, et les sentiments aux calculs? Si, au milieu de cet ébranlement universel, vous ne parvenez à lier l'idée des droits à l'intérêt personnel qui s'offre comme le seul point immobile dans le coeur humain, que vous restera-t-il donc pour gouverner le monde, sinon la peur?

Lors donc qu'on me dit que les lois sont faibles, et les gouvernés turbulents; que les passions sont vives, et la vertu sans pouvoir, et que dans cette situation il ne faut point songer à augmenter les droits de la démocratie; je réponds que c'est à cause de ces choses mêmes que je crois qu'il faut y songer; et, en vérité, je pense que les gouvernements y sont plus intéressés encore que la société, car les gouvernements périssent, et la société ne saurait mourir. Du reste, je ne veux point abuser de l'exemple de l'Amérique.

En Amérique, le peuple a été revêtu de droits politiques à une époque où il lui était difficile d'en faire un mauvais usage, parce que les citoyens étaient en petit nombre et simples de moeurs. En grandissant, les Américains n'ont point accru pour ainsi dire les pouvoirs de la démocratie; ils ont plutôt étendu ses domaines.
On ne peut douter que le moment où l'on accorde des droits politiques à un peuple qui en a été privé jusqu'alors, ne soit un moment de crise, crise souvent nécessaire, mais toujours dangereuse.

L'enfant donne la mort quand il ignore le prix de la vie; il enlève la propriété d'autrui avant de connaître qu'on peut lui ravir la sienne. L'homme du peuple, à l'instant où on lui accorde des droits politiques, se trouve, par rapport à ses droits, dans la même position que l'enfant vis-à-vis de toute la nature, et c'est le cas de lui appliquer ce mot célèbre: _Homo puer robustus._
Cette vérité se découvre en Amérique même. Les États où les citoyens jouissent le plus anciennement de leurs droits sont ceux où ils savent encore le mieux s'en servir.

On ne saurait trop le dire: il n'est rien de plus fécond en merveilles que l'art d'être libre; mais il n'y a rien de plus dur que l'apprentissage de la liberté. Il n'en est pas de même du despotisme. Le despotisme se présente souvent comme le réparateur de tous les maux soufferts; il est l'appui du bon droit, le soutien des opprimés et le fondateur de l'ordre. Les peuples s'endorment au sein de la prospérité momentanée qu'il fait naître; et lorsqu'ils se réveillent, ils sont misérables. La liberté, au contraire, naît d'ordinaire au milieu des orages, elle s'établit péniblement parmi les discordes civiles, et ce n'est que quand elle est déjà vieille qu'on peut connaître ses bienfaits.
DU RESPECT POUR LA LOI AUX ÉTATS-UNIS.
Respect des Américains pour la loi. -- Amour paternel qu'ils ressentent pour elle. -- Intérêt personnel que chacun trouve à augmenter la puissance de la loi.

Il n'est pas toujours loisible d'appeler le peuple entier, soit directement, soit indirectement, à la confection de la loi; mais on ne saurait nier que, quand cela est praticable, la loi n'en acquière une grande autorité. Cette origine populaire, qui nuit souvent à la bonté et à la sagesse de la législation, contribue singulièrement à sa puissance.

Il y a dans l'expression des volontés de tout un peuple une force prodigieuse. Quand elle se découvre au grand jour, l'imagination même de ceux qui voudraient lutter contre elle en est comme accablée.
La vérité de ceci est bien connue des partis.

Aussi les voit-on contester la majorité partout où ils le peuvent. Quand elle leur manque parmi ceux qui ont voté, ils la placent parmi ceux qui se sont abstenus de voter, et lorsque là encore elle vient à leur échapper, ils la retrouvent au sein de ceux qui n'avaient pas le droit de voter.

Aux États-Unis, excepté les esclaves, les domestiques et les indigents nourris par les communes, il n'est personne qui ne soit électeur, et qui à ce titre ne concoure indirectement à la loi. Ceux qui veulent attaquer les lois sont donc réduits à faire ostensiblement l'une de ces deux choses: ils doivent ou changer l'opinion de la nation, ou fouler aux pieds ses volontés.

Ajoutez à cette première raison cette autre plus directe et plus puissante, qu'aux États-Unis chacun trouve une sorte d'intérêt personnel à ce que tous obéissent aux lois; car celui qui aujourd'hui ne fait pas partie de la majorité, sera peut-être demain dans ses rangs; et ce respect qu'il professe maintenant pour les volontés du législateur, il aura bientôt occasion de l'exiger pour les siennes. Quelque fâcheuse que soit la loi, l'habitant des États-Unis s'y soumet donc sans peine, non seulement comme à l'ouvrage du plus grand nombre, mais encore comme au sien propre; il la considère sous le point de vue d'un contrat dans lequel il aurait été partie.
