OF THE ACCIDENTAL OR PROVIDENTIAL CAUSES WHICH CONTRIBUTE TO THE MAINTENANCE OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC IN THE UNITED STATES.

The Union has no neighbors. — No great capital. — The Americans have had on their side the chance of birth. — America is an empty country. — How this circumstance powerfully serves the maintenance of the democratic republic. — How the deserts of America fill up. — The eagerness of the Anglo-Americans to seize the solitudes of the New World. — The influence of material well-being on the political opinions of the Americans.

A thousand circumstances independent of human will make the democratic republic easy in the United States. Some of these are known; others can readily be made known. I shall restrict myself to setting out the principal ones.

The Americans have no neighbors, and so no great wars to fear, no financial crisis, no ravages, no conquest; they have no need of heavy taxes, of a large army, of great generals; they have almost nothing to fear from a scourge more terrible to republics than all of those put together: military glory.

How can one deny the unbelievable influence that military glory exerts on the mind of a people? General Jackson, whom the Americans have twice chosen to place at their head, is a man of violent character and middling ability; nothing in the whole course of his career had ever shown that he possessed the qualities required to govern a free people; and the majority of the enlightened classes of the Union has always been against him. Who then placed him in the president's chair and keeps him there still? The memory of a victory he won, twenty years ago, beneath the walls of New Orleans. Now, the victory of New Orleans is a very ordinary feat of arms, one that could be dwelt upon only in a country where battles are never fought; and the people who let themselves be carried away by the prestige of glory is, beyond doubt, the coldest, the most calculating, the least military, and — if I may put it this way — the most prosaic of all the peoples of the world.

America has no great capital[36] whose direct or indirect influence makes itself felt across the whole extent of the territory, which I regard as one of the foremost causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States. In cities, men cannot easily be prevented from concerting with one another, inflaming one another in common, taking sudden and passionate resolutions. Cities form, as it were, vast assemblies of which all the inhabitants are members. The people there exercise a prodigious influence over their magistrates, and often execute their will without any intermediary.

To subject the provinces to the capital is therefore to place the destiny of the entire empire not only in the hands of one portion of the people, which is unjust, but in the hands of the people acting on its own, which is highly dangerous. The preponderance of capitals does grave damage to the representative system. It makes the modern republics fall into the same defect as the republics of antiquity, which all perished for not having known that system.

It would be easy for me to enumerate here a great number of other secondary causes that have favored the establishment and ensure the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States. But among this crowd of fortunate circumstances I see two principal ones, and I hasten to point them out.

I have already said that I saw in the origin of the Americans — in what I have called their point of departure — the first and most effective of all the causes to which the present prosperity of the United States may be attributed. The Americans have had on their side the chance of birth: their fathers long ago imported onto the soil they now occupy equality of conditions and of minds, from which the democratic republic was bound one day to issue as from its natural source. And that is not all; along with a republican social state, they bequeathed to their descendants the habits, the ideas, and the mores most apt to make a republic flourish. When I think of what this original fact has produced, it seems to me that I see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on its shores, just as the whole human race was contained in the first man.

Among the fortunate circumstances that have further favored the establishment and that ensure the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States, the first in importance is the choice of the country itself which the Americans inhabit. Their fathers gave them the love of equality and of liberty; but it is God himself who, by delivering them a continent without limits, granted them the means of remaining equal and free for a long time to come.

General well-being favors the stability of all governments, but particularly of democratic government, which rests on the dispositions of the greatest number, and chiefly on the dispositions of those most exposed to want. When the people governs, it must be content, or it will overturn the State. Misery produces in the people what ambition produces in kings. Now, the material causes — independent of laws — that can bring about well-being are more numerous in America than they have been in any country in the world, at any epoch of history.
In the United States, it is not only legislation that is democratic; nature herself works for the people.
Where, in all the memory of man, can one find anything resembling what is taking place before our eyes in North America?

The famous societies of antiquity were all founded amid enemy peoples whom they had to conquer in order to take their place. Even the moderns have found, in some parts of South America, vast regions inhabited by peoples less enlightened than themselves but who had already appropriated the soil by cultivating it. To found their new States, they had to destroy or enslave large populations, and made civilization blush for its triumphs.

But North America was inhabited only by wandering tribes who took no thought of turning the natural riches of the soil to use. North America was still, properly speaking, an empty continent, a deserted land waiting for inhabitants.
Everything is extraordinary about the Americans, their social state as well as their laws; but what is more extraordinary still is the soil that bears them.

When the earth was delivered to men by the Creator, it was young and inexhaustible, but they were weak and ignorant; and by the time they had learned to turn to account the treasures it held in its bosom, they already covered its face, and soon had to fight in order to gain the right to possess an asylum upon it and to rest there in liberty.
It is then that North America is discovered, as if God had been holding it in reserve, and as if it were only just emerging from beneath the waters of the flood.

It offers, as on the first days of creation, rivers whose source never runs dry, green and humid solitudes, boundless fields the plowshare has never yet turned. In this state, it presents itself no longer to the isolated, ignorant, and barbarous man of the first ages, but to a man already master of the most important secrets of nature, united to his fellows, and instructed by an experience of fifty centuries.

At the moment I speak, thirteen million civilized Europeans are quietly spreading out into fertile deserts whose resources and extent they themselves do not yet know exactly. Three or four thousand soldiers drive the wandering race of natives before them; behind the armed men advance woodsmen who pierce the forests, drive off the wild beasts, explore the rivers, and prepare the triumphal march of civilization across the desert.

Often, in the course of this work, I have alluded to the material well-being the Americans enjoy; I have indicated it as one of the great causes of the success of their laws. This reason had already been given by a thousand others before me; it is the only one which, falling somehow within reach of Europeans' senses, has become popular among us. I shall not, then, dwell on a subject so often treated and so well understood; I shall only add a few new facts.

It is generally imagined that the deserts of America are being peopled with the help of European emigrants who come down each year on the shores of the New World, while the American population grows and multiplies on the soil its forefathers occupied: this is a great mistake. The European who lands in the United States arrives without friends and often without resources; in order to live, he is obliged to hire out his services, and it is rare that he goes beyond the great industrial belt that runs along the Ocean. One cannot clear the desert without capital or credit; before risking himself in the forests, a man's body must have grown used to the rigors of a new climate. It is therefore Americans who, abandoning each day the place of their birth, go off to create vast domains in the distance. So the European leaves his cottage to go and live on the transatlantic shores, and the American born on those very shores plunges in his turn into the solitudes of Central America. This double movement of emigration never stops: it begins in the depths of Europe, it continues across the great Ocean, it pursues itself across the solitudes of the New World. Millions of men march at once toward the same point on the horizon: their language, their religion, their mores differ; their aim is common. They have been told that fortune is to be found somewhere toward the west, and they hurry to meet it.

Nothing can compare with this continual displacement of the human species, except perhaps what occurred at the fall of the Roman Empire. Then, as today, men were seen rushing in crowds to the same point and meeting tumultuously in the same places; but the designs of Providence were different. Every newcomer dragged destruction and death in his wake; today each one brings with him a germ of prosperity and of life.

The remote consequences of this migration of the Americans toward the west are still hidden from us by the future, but the immediate results are easy to recognize: a portion of the old inhabitants moves away each year from the States where they were born, so that those States grow in population only very slowly, even as they age. Thus in Connecticut, which still counts only fifty-nine inhabitants per square mile, the population has grown by only a quarter in forty years, while in England it increased by a third during the same period. The emigrant from Europe therefore always lands in a country half full, where hands are wanting for industry; he becomes a comfortable workman; his son goes off to seek his fortune in an empty country, and becomes a wealthy landowner. The first accumulates the capital that the second turns to account, and there is no misery either among foreigners or among natives.

In the United States, legislation favors the division of property as much as possible; but a cause more powerful than legislation prevents property from being divided beyond measure[37]. One sees this clearly in the States that are at last beginning to fill up. Massachusetts is the most populous country in the Union; there are eighty inhabitants per square mile — infinitely fewer than in France, where one hundred sixty-two are crowded into the same space.
In Massachusetts, however, it is already rare for the small estates to be divided: the eldest generally takes the land; the younger sons go to seek their fortune in the desert.
The law has abolished primogeniture; but one may say that Providence has reestablished it without anyone's having cause to complain, and this time at least it does no violence to justice.

A single fact will allow one to judge the prodigious number of individuals who in this way leave New England to carry their hearths off to the desert. We have been assured that in 1830, among the members of Congress, thirty-six had been born in the small State of Connecticut. Connecticut's population, which forms only one forty-third part of that of the United States, was therefore furnishing one eighth of their representatives.

The State of Connecticut, however, sends only five deputies of its own to Congress; the thirty-one others appear there as representatives of the new States of the West. If these thirty-one individuals had stayed in Connecticut, it is likely that, instead of being wealthy landowners, they would have remained small farmers; that they would have lived in obscurity without being able to open up a political career to themselves; and that, far from becoming useful legislators, they would have been dangerous citizens.
These considerations escape the minds of the Americans no more than they do ours.

"There can be no doubt," says Chancellor Kent in his Treatise on American Law (vol. IV, p. 380), "that the division of estates must produce great evils when it is carried to excess, so that each portion of land can no longer maintain a family; but these drawbacks have never been felt in the United States, and many generations will pass before they are felt. The extent of our uninhabited territory, the abundance of lands adjoining ours, and the continual stream of emigration that, setting out from the shores of the Atlantic, moves ceaselessly toward the interior of the country, suffice and will for a long time still suffice to prevent the parceling out of inheritances."

It would be hard to depict the eagerness with which the American hurls himself upon this immense prey that fortune offers him. To pursue it, he braves without fear the arrow of the Indian and the diseases of the desert; the silence of the woods holds nothing to astonish him, the approach of wild beasts does not move him: a passion stronger than the love of life goads him on continually. Before him stretches an almost boundless continent, and one would say that, already afraid of running out of room there, he hurries on for fear of arriving too late. I have spoken of the emigration from the old States; but what shall I say of that from the new ones? It is not yet fifty years since Ohio was founded; most of its inhabitants were not born there; its capital is not thirty years old, and immense stretches of empty fields still cover its territory; and yet already the population of Ohio has set itself in motion toward the west: most of those who come down into the fertile prairies of Illinois are inhabitants of Ohio. These men left their first homeland to be well off; they leave the second to be better off still: almost everywhere they meet fortune, but not happiness. With them, the desire for well-being has become a restless and ardent passion that grows by being satisfied. Long ago they broke the bonds that attached them to their native soil; since then they have formed no others. For them emigration began as a need; today, in their eyes, it has become a kind of game of chance, whose excitements they love as much as the winnings.

Sometimes the man moves so fast that the desert reappears behind him. The forest has only bent under his feet; once he has passed, it rises again. It is not rare, as one travels through the new States of the West, to come upon dwellings abandoned in the middle of the woods; often one discovers the remains of a cabin in the deepest solitude, and is surprised in crossing scarcely begun clearings, which attest at once to the power and to the inconstancy of man. Among these forsaken fields, on these one-day ruins, the ancient forest is not slow to put forth new shoots; the animals retake possession of their empire: nature comes laughing to cover with green branches and flowers the vestiges of man, and hastens to make his ephemeral traces vanish.

I remember that, crossing one of the deserted districts that still cover the State of New York, I came upon the shores of a lake entirely surrounded by forests as at the beginning of the world. A small island rose in the middle of the waters. The wood that covered it, spreading its foliage all around, hid its banks entirely. On the lake's shores nothing announced the presence of man; only on the horizon could one make out a column of smoke that, rising perpendicularly from the tops of the trees toward the clouds, seemed to hang from heaven rather than to climb toward it.

An Indian canoe was drawn up on the sand; I took advantage of it to visit the island that had first drawn my attention, and soon after I had reached its shore. The entire island formed one of those delicious solitudes of the New World that almost make civilized man regret the savage life. A vigorous vegetation announced through its marvels the incomparable richness of the soil. There reigned there, as in all the deserts of North America, a deep silence broken only by the monotonous cooing of the wood pigeons or by the strokes of the green woodpecker on the bark of the trees. I was far from believing that this place had once been inhabited, so much did nature there seem still left to herself; but, reaching the center of the island, I thought suddenly that I encountered traces of man. I then examined carefully all the objects around me, and soon I no longer doubted that a European had come to seek refuge in this spot. But how much his work had changed face! The wood that long ago he had hastily cut to make himself a shelter had since put forth new shoots; his fences had become living hedges, and his cabin was transformed into a thicket. Among these saplings one could still make out a few stones blackened by fire, scattered around a small heap of ashes; this no doubt was where the hearth had stood: the chimney, in collapsing, had covered it with its debris. For a time I admired in silence the resources of nature and the weakness of man; and when at last I had to leave these enchanted places, I repeated again with sadness: What — ruins already!

In Europe, we are accustomed to regard as a great social danger restlessness of mind, immoderate desire for riches, the extreme love of independence. It is precisely all these things that guarantee the American republics a long and peaceful future. Without these restless passions, the population would concentrate around certain places, and would soon experience, as among us, needs hard to satisfy. Happy country, the New World, where the vices of man are nearly as useful to society as his virtues!

This exerts a great influence on the way human actions are judged in the two hemispheres. Often the Americans give the name of praiseworthy industry to what we call love of gain, and they see a certain cowardice of heart in what we regard as moderation of desires.

In France, simplicity of taste, tranquility of mores, family feeling, and love of one's birthplace are regarded as great guarantees of tranquility and happiness for the State; but in America, nothing seems more harmful to society than such virtues. The French of Canada, who have faithfully preserved the traditions of the old mores, are already finding it difficult to live on their territory, and this small people, just born, will soon be a prey to the miseries of old nations. In Canada, the men with the most enlightenment, patriotism, and humanity make extraordinary efforts to disgust the people with the simple happiness that still suffices them. They celebrate the advantages of wealth, just as among us they might perhaps extol the charms of an honest mediocrity, and they take more care to goad on human passions than elsewhere is spent in calming them. To exchange the pure and tranquil pleasures that the homeland offers even to the poor for the sterile enjoyments that well-being affords under a foreign sky; to flee the paternal hearth and the fields where one's ancestors rest; to abandon the living and the dead in order to run after fortune — nothing in their eyes deserves greater praise.
In our day, America offers men a fund always vaster than the industry that turns it to account.

In America, then, one cannot give too much enlightenment; for all enlightenment, while it may be useful to him who possesses it, turns also to the profit of those who do not. New needs are not to be feared there, since all needs are satisfied without trouble; one need not fear giving birth to too many passions, since all passions find easy and salutary nourishment; men cannot be made too free, because they are almost never tempted to make bad use of liberty.
The American republics of our day are like companies of merchants formed to exploit in common the deserted lands of the New World, and engaged in a flourishing trade.

The passions that most deeply stir the Americans are commercial passions, not political passions, or rather they carry into politics the habits of trade. They love order, without which business cannot prosper, and they particularly prize regularity of mores, on which good houses are founded; they prefer the good sense that creates great fortunes to the genius that often dissipates them; general ideas frighten their minds, which are accustomed to positive calculations, and among them practice is in greater honor than theory.

It is to America that one must go to understand what power material well-being exerts over political actions and even over opinions themselves, which should be subject only to reason. It is among foreigners that one discovers the truth of this most clearly. Most of the emigrants from Europe bring to the New World that savage love of independence and of change which is so often born in the midst of our miseries. I sometimes met in the United States Europeans who had once been forced to flee their country for political opinions. All of them astonished me with their talk; but one of them struck me more than any other. As I was crossing one of the most remote districts of Pennsylvania, night overtook me, and I went to ask shelter at the door of a wealthy planter: he was a Frenchman. He had me sit down beside his hearth, and we began to converse freely, as becomes people who meet again at the bottom of a forest two thousand leagues from the country that saw them born. I was well aware that my host had been a great leveler forty years before and an ardent demagogue. His name had remained in history.

I was therefore strangely surprised to hear him discuss the right of property as an economist might have done — I was almost going to say a landowner; he spoke of the necessary hierarchy that fortune establishes among men, of obedience to the established law, of the influence of good mores in republics, and of the aid that religious ideas lend to order and to liberty: he even happened, as if by inadvertence, to cite in support of one of his political opinions the authority of Jesus Christ.

Listening to him, I admired the imbecility of human reason. This is true or false: how is one to find out, amid the uncertainties of science and the divergent lessons of experience? A new fact comes along that removes all my doubts. I was poor, now I am rich: if only well-being, in acting on my conduct, left my judgment at liberty! But no — my opinions have in fact changed with my fortune, and in the happy event from which I profit I have really discovered the determining reason that had escaped me until then.

The influence of well-being is exercised even more freely upon the Americans than upon foreigners. The American has always seen order and public prosperity linked together before his eyes, marching in step; he does not imagine that they can live apart. He has nothing therefore to forget, and need not lose, as so many Europeans must, what he holds from his earliest upbringing.
OF THE INFLUENCE OF THE LAWS UPON THE MAINTENANCE OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC IN THE UNITED STATES.
Three principal causes of the maintenance of the democratic republic. — Federal form. — Township institutions. — Judicial power.

The principal aim of this book was to make known the laws of the United States; if this aim has been attained, the reader has already been able to judge for himself which among these laws really tend to maintain the democratic republic and which put it in danger. If I have not succeeded in the whole course of the book, I should succeed still less in a chapter.
I do not, therefore, want to retread ground I have already covered, and a few lines should suffice to sum up.
Three things seem to me to contribute more than all the others to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the New World:
The first is the federal form which the Americans have adopted, and which permits the Union to enjoy the power of a great republic and the security of a small one.
The second I find in the township institutions, which, by moderating the despotism of the majority, give the people at the same time the taste for liberty and the art of being free.

The third lies in the constitution of the judicial power. I have shown how greatly the courts serve to correct the deviations of democracy, and how, without ever being able to halt the movements of the majority, they manage to slow them and to direct them.
OF THE INFLUENCE OF *MORES* UPON THE MAINTENANCE OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC IN THE UNITED STATES.
I have said above that I considered mores as one of the great general causes to which the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States may be attributed.

I take the expression mores here in the sense the ancients attached to the word *mores*; I apply it not only to mores properly so called — what one might call the habits of the heart — but to the various notions men possess, the diverse opinions current among them, and the whole body of ideas of which the habits of the mind are formed.

I include under this word, then, the whole moral and intellectual state of a people. My aim is not to draw a picture of American mores; I confine myself for the moment to seeking out among them what is favorable to the maintenance of political institutions.
OF RELIGION CONSIDERED AS A POLITICAL INSTITUTION, AND HOW IT POWERFULLY SERVES THE MAINTENANCE OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC AMONG THE AMERICANS.
North America peopled by men who professed a democratic and republican Christianity. — The arrival of the Catholics. — Why in our day the Catholics form the most democratic and republican class.
Alongside every religion is found a political opinion which, by affinity, is joined to it.
Let the human mind follow its tendency, and it will regulate political society and the city of God in a uniform manner; it will seek, if I may dare say it, to *harmonize* earth with heaven.

The greater part of English America was peopled by men who, after having removed themselves from the authority of the pope, had submitted to no religious supremacy. They therefore brought to the New World a Christianity which I cannot better describe than by calling it democratic and republican: this remarkably favored the establishment of the republic and of democracy in public affairs. From the outset, politics and religion were found to be in agreement, and since then they have never ceased to be so.

It is about fifty years since Ireland began to pour into the United States a Catholic population. For its part, American Catholicism made converts: there are today in the Union more than a million Christians professing the truths of the Roman Church.

These Catholics show great fidelity in the practices of their worship, and are full of ardor and zeal for their beliefs; nevertheless they form the most republican and democratic class to be found in the United States. This fact surprises at first sight, but reflection easily uncovers its hidden causes.

I think one is wrong to regard the Catholic religion as a natural enemy of democracy. Among the various Christian doctrines, Catholicism seems to me, on the contrary, one of those most favorable to equality of conditions. Among Catholics, religious society is composed of only two elements: the priest and the people. The priest alone rises above the faithful: below him all is equal.

In matters of dogma, Catholicism places the same level on all intelligences; it binds to the same details of belief the learned and the ignorant, the man of genius as well as the common man; it imposes the same practices on the rich as on the poor, inflicts the same austerities on the powerful as on the weak; it makes no compromise with any mortal, and, applying the same measure to each of mankind, it loves to mingle all the classes of society at the foot of the same altar, as they are mingled in the eyes of God.

If Catholicism disposes the faithful to obedience, it does not therefore prepare them for inequality. I would say the contrary of Protestantism, which, in general, leads men far less toward equality than toward independence.
Catholicism is like an absolute monarchy. Remove the prince, and conditions there are more equal than in republics.

It has often happened that the Catholic priest has come out of the sanctuary to enter society as a power, and to take his seat there in the midst of the social hierarchy; sometimes then he has used his religious influence to secure the duration of a political order of which he was a part: at those times one has been able to see Catholics partisans of aristocracy out of religious sentiment.

But once priests are set apart from government, or set themselves apart, as they do in the United States, there are no men who by their beliefs are more disposed than Catholics to carry into the political world the idea of equality of conditions.

If, then, the Catholics of the United States are not violently drawn by the nature of their beliefs toward democratic and republican opinions, at least they are not naturally opposed to them, and their social position, as well as their small number, makes it a law for them to embrace them.

Most Catholics are poor, and they need all citizens to govern in order to reach the government themselves. The Catholics are in the minority, and they need all rights to be respected in order to be sure of the free exercise of their own. These two causes push them, even unawares, toward political doctrines they would perhaps adopt with less ardor if they were rich and predominant.

The Catholic clergy of the United States has not tried to fight against this political tendency; it seeks rather to justify it. The Catholic priests of America have divided the intellectual world into two parts: in the one they have left the revealed dogmas, to which they submit without discussion; in the other they have placed political truth, which they think God has abandoned to the free researches of men. Thus the Catholics of the United States are at once the most submissive of the faithful and the most independent of citizens.

One may say, then, that in the United States there is not a single religious doctrine that shows itself hostile to democratic and republican institutions. All the clergies there speak the same language; opinions there agree with the laws, and there reigns, so to speak, only a single current in the human mind.
I was staying briefly in one of the largest cities of the Union when I was invited to attend a political meeting whose purpose was to come to the aid of the Poles, and to send them arms and money.

I found two or three thousand people assembled in a vast hall that had been prepared to receive them. Soon afterward, a priest, in his ecclesiastical garments, advanced to the edge of the platform set aside for the speakers. The audience, having uncovered, stood in silence, and he spoke in these terms:

"Almighty God! God of armies! Thou who upheld the heart and guided the arm of our fathers when they defended the sacred rights of their national independence; Thou who made them triumph over a hateful oppression, and granted to our people the benefits of peace and liberty — O Lord! turn a favorable eye upon the other hemisphere; look in pity upon a heroic people that struggles today as we did long ago, and for the defense of the same rights! Lord, who created all men on the same model, do not allow despotism to deform Thy work and to maintain inequality on the earth. Almighty God! watch over the destinies of the Poles, render them worthy of being free; let Thy wisdom reign in their councils, let Thy strength be in their arms; spread terror over their enemies, divide the powers that plot their ruin, and do not allow the injustice that the world witnessed fifty years ago to be consummated today. Lord, who holdest in Thy powerful hand the hearts of peoples as well as those of men, raise up allies for the sacred cause of right; let the French nation at last arise, and, emerging from the rest in which its leaders are holding it, come once more to fight for the liberty of the world.
"O Lord! never turn Thy face from us; allow us to be always the most religious as well as the freest people.
"Almighty God, hear our prayer today; save the Poles. We ask this of Thee in the name of Thy well-beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who died on the cross for the salvation of all mankind. *Amen.*"
The whole assembly repeated *amen* with devotion.
INDIRECT INFLUENCE EXERCISED BY RELIGIOUS BELIEFS UPON POLITICAL SOCIETY IN THE UNITED STATES.

Morality of Christianity to be found in all the sects. — Influence of religion on the mores of the Americans. — Respect for the marriage bond. — How religion encloses the imagination of the Americans within certain limits and moderates among them the passion for innovation. — Opinion of the Americans on the political utility of religion. — Their efforts to extend and secure its empire.

I have just shown what the direct action of religion upon politics was in the United States. Its indirect action seems to me more powerful still, and it is when it does not speak of liberty that it best teaches the Americans the art of being free.

There is an innumerable multitude of sects in the United States. All differ in the worship they owe the Creator, but all agree on the duties of men toward one another. Each sect, then, worships God in its own way, but all sects preach the same morality in God's name. If it is of great importance to man as an individual that his religion be true, it is not the same for society. Society has nothing to fear and nothing to hope from the other life; and what matters most to it is not so much that all citizens profess the true religion, but that they profess a religion. Moreover, all the sects in the United States meet in the great Christian unity, and the morality of Christianity is everywhere the same.

It is permitted to think that a certain number of Americans follow, in the worship they render to God, their habits more than their convictions. In the United States, besides, the sovereign is religious, and consequently hypocrisy must be common. But America is nonetheless still the place in the world where the Christian religion has retained the most genuine power over souls; and nothing shows better how useful and natural it is to man, since the country where it exercises today the greatest empire is at the same time the most enlightened and the freest.

I have said that American priests pronounce themselves in general in favor of civil liberty, without excepting even those who do not admit religious liberty; however, they are not seen lending their support to any particular political system. They take care to remain outside of public business, and do not enter into the combinations of parties. One cannot say, then, that in the United States religion exercises an influence on the laws or on the detail of political opinions; but it directs mores, and it is by regulating the family that it works to regulate the State.

I do not doubt for a moment that the great severity of mores one notices in the United States has its first source in beliefs. Religion there is often powerless to hold back the man in the midst of the numberless temptations that fortune presents him. It cannot moderate in him the ardor to grow rich which everything serves to goad on; but it reigns sovereignly over the soul of the woman, and it is the woman who makes the mores. America is certainly the country in the world where the bond of marriage is most respected, and where the highest and most just idea of conjugal happiness has been conceived.

In Europe, almost all the disorders of society take their origin around the domestic hearth and not far from the nuptial bed. It is there that men conceive contempt for natural bonds and for permitted pleasures, the taste for disorder, the restlessness of heart, the instability of desires. Stirred by the tumultuous passions that have often troubled his own home, the European submits only with difficulty to the legislative powers of the State. When, after the agitations of the political world, the American returns to the bosom of his family, he meets there at once the image of order and of peace. There, all his pleasures are simple and natural, his joys innocent and tranquil; and as he arrives at happiness through the regularity of life, he grows used without effort to regulating his opinions as well as his tastes.
While the European seeks to escape his domestic sorrows by disturbing society, the American draws from his home the love of order, which he then carries into the affairs of the State.
In the United States, religion does not only regulate mores; it extends its empire even over intelligence.

Among the Anglo-Americans, some profess Christian dogmas because they believe in them, others because they fear not to appear to believe in them. Christianity therefore reigns without obstacle by everyone's admission; it follows, as I have already said elsewhere, that everything is certain and settled in the moral world, although the political world seems abandoned to the discussion and the experiments of men. Thus the human mind never sees before it a field without limits: however bold it may be, it feels from time to time that it must halt before insurmountable barriers. Before innovating, it is forced to accept certain first givens and to submit its boldest conceptions to certain forms that delay and arrest it.

The imagination of the Americans, in its greatest excursions, therefore proceeds only in a circumspect and uncertain way; its movements are constrained and its works incomplete. These habits of restraint are found again in political society and singularly favor the tranquility of the people, as well as the duration of the institutions it has given itself. Nature and circumstances had made the inhabitant of the United States a bold man; one can easily see this when one observes the manner in which he pursues fortune. If the spirit of the Americans were free of all restraint, one would soon meet among them the boldest innovators and the most implacable logicians in the world. But the revolutionaries of America are obliged to profess openly a certain respect for Christian morality and equity, which does not allow them easily to violate its laws when these stand in the way of carrying out their designs; and if they could raise themselves above their scruples, they would still feel checked by those of their partisans. Up to the present, no one has been found in the United States who has dared to advance this maxim: that everything is permitted in the interest of society. An impious maxim, which seems to have been invented in an age of liberty in order to legitimize all tyrants to come.
Thus, at the same time that the law permits the American people to do everything, religion prevents them from conceiving everything and forbids them to dare everything.

Religion, which among the Americans never mixes directly in the government of society, must therefore be considered as the first of their political institutions; for if it does not give them the taste for liberty, it singularly facilitates their use of it.

It is also from this point of view that the inhabitants of the United States themselves consider religious beliefs. I do not know whether all Americans have faith in their religion — for who can read the bottom of hearts? — but I am sure that they believe it necessary to the maintenance of republican institutions. This opinion does not belong to one class of citizens or to one party, but to the whole nation; one finds it again in every rank.

In the United States, when a political man attacks a sect, that is no reason for the partisans of that very sect not to support him; but if he attacks all the sects together, everyone flees him, and he stands alone.

While I was in America, a witness presented himself at the assizes of Chester county (State of New York), and declared that he did not believe in the existence of God and in the immortality of the soul. The presiding judge refused to receive his oath, on the grounds, he said, that the witness had destroyed in advance all the faith one could attach to his words[38]. The newspapers reported the fact without comment.

The Americans so completely confound in their minds Christianity and liberty that it is almost impossible to make them conceive of the one without the other; and this is not for them one of those sterile beliefs that the past bequeaths to the present, and that seem less to live than to vegetate at the bottom of the soul.

I have seen Americans band together to send priests to the new States of the West, and to found schools and churches there; they fear that religion may come to be lost in the depths of the woods, and that the people rising up may not be as free as the one from which it came. I have met wealthy inhabitants of New England who left the country of their birth in order to go and lay, on the banks of the Missouri or on the prairies of Illinois, the foundations of Christianity and of liberty. Thus in the United States religious zeal warms itself unceasingly at the hearth of patriotism. You may think that these men act solely with a view to the other life, but you would be mistaken: eternity is only one of their concerns. If you question these missionaries of Christian civilization, you will be surprised to hear them speak so often of the goods of this world, and to find politicians where you thought to see only churchmen. "All the American republics are bound up with one another," they will tell you; "if the republics of the West fell into anarchy or submitted to the yoke of despotism, the republican institutions that flourish on the shores of the Atlantic ocean would be in great peril; we have therefore an interest in the new States being religious, so that they may permit us to remain free."

Such are the opinions of the Americans; but their error is plain — for every day I am very learnedly shown that all is well in America, except precisely this religious spirit I admire; and I am informed that what the liberty and happiness of the human race lack, on the other side of the Ocean, is only to believe with Spinoza in the eternity of the world, and to maintain with Cabanis that the brain secretes thought. To that I have nothing to reply, in truth, except that those who hold this language have not been in America, and have not seen religious peoples any more than they have seen free ones. I shall wait, then, for their return.

There are people in France who consider republican institutions as the passing instrument of their own elevation. They measure with their eyes the immense space that separates their vices and their wretchedness from power and wealth, and they would like to heap up ruins in that abyss to try to fill it. These men stand to liberty as the free companies of the Middle Ages stood to kings; they wage war on their own account even while they wear its colors: the republic will always live long enough to draw them up out of their present baseness. It is not to them that I am speaking; but there are others who see in the republic a permanent and tranquil state, a necessary end toward which ideas and mores daily draw modern societies, and who would sincerely like to prepare men to be free. When these attack religious beliefs, they follow their passions and not their interests. It is despotism that can do without faith, but not liberty. Religion is much more necessary in the republic they espouse than in the monarchy they attack, and in democratic republics than in all others. How could society fail to perish if, while the political bond is loosened, the moral bond were not tightened? And what is to be done with a people master of itself, if it is not subject to God?
OF THE PRINCIPAL CAUSES THAT MAKE RELIGION POWERFUL IN AMERICA.

The care the Americans have taken to separate Church from State. — The laws, public opinion, the efforts of the priests themselves, all concur in this result. — It is to this cause that one must attribute the power religion exercises over souls in the United States. — Why. — What is in our day the natural state of men in matters of religion. — What particular and accidental cause stands in the way, in certain countries, of men conforming to that state.

The philosophers of the eighteenth century explained the gradual weakening of beliefs in a very simple manner. Religious zeal, they said, must die out as liberty and enlightenment increase. It is unfortunate that the facts do not accord with this theory.

There is a European population whose unbelief is equaled only by its brutishness and ignorance, while in America one sees one of the freest and most enlightened peoples in the world fulfill with ardor all the outward duties of religion.

On my arrival in the United States, it was the religious aspect of the country that first struck my gaze. As my stay lengthened, I perceived the great political consequences that flowed from these new facts.

I had seen among us the spirit of religion and the spirit of liberty almost always march in opposite directions. Here, I found them intimately united with one another: they reigned together over the same soil.
Each day I felt my desire grow to know the cause of this phenomenon.

To learn it, I questioned the faithful of every communion; I sought above all the society of the priests, who guard the deposit of the various beliefs and who have a personal interest in their endurance. The religion I profess brought me particularly close to the Catholic clergy, and I was not slow to form a sort of intimacy with several of its members. To each of them I expressed my astonishment and laid out my doubts: I found that all these men differed among themselves only on points of detail; but all attributed mainly to the complete separation of Church and State the peaceful empire that religion exercises in their country. I do not fear to affirm that during my stay in America I did not meet a single man, priest or layman, who did not agree on this point.

This led me to examine more attentively than I had done up to then the position the American priests occupy in political society. I recognized with surprise that they fill no public employment[39]. I saw not a single one in the administration, and I found that they were not even represented in the assemblies.
In several States the law had closed the political career to them[40]; in all the others, opinion had.

When at last I came to investigate what the spirit of the clergy itself was, I saw that most of its members seemed voluntarily to keep themselves away from power, and to take a kind of professional pride in remaining strangers to it.

I heard them anathematize ambition and bad faith, whatever the political opinions under which these took care to cloak themselves. But I learned, in listening to them, that men cannot be condemnable in the eyes of God on account of those very opinions, when they are sincere, and that there is no more sin in being mistaken in matters of government than in being mistaken about how to build one's dwelling or trace one's furrow.
I saw them carefully separate themselves from all parties, and shun contact with them with all the ardor of personal interest.

These facts completed the proof for me that I had been told the truth. Then I wanted to work back from the facts to their causes: I asked myself how it could come about that, in diminishing the apparent strength of a religion, one might come to increase its real power, and I believed it not impossible to discover the answer.

Never will the short span of sixty years contain the whole imagination of man; the incomplete joys of this world will never suffice for his heart. Alone among all beings, man shows a natural distaste for existence and an immense desire to exist: he despises life and fears nothingness. These different instincts ceaselessly drive his soul toward the contemplation of another world, and it is religion that leads him there. Religion is therefore only a particular form of hope, and it is as natural to the human heart as hope itself. It is by a kind of aberration of the intelligence, and with the help of a sort of moral violence done to their own nature, that men depart from religious beliefs; an invincible slope brings them back to them. Unbelief is an accident; faith alone is the permanent state of mankind.

Considering religions only from a purely human point of view, one may therefore say that all religions draw from man himself an element of strength that can never fail them, because it is rooted in one of the constitutive principles of human nature.

I know there are times when religion can add to this influence proper to itself the artificial power of the laws and the support of the material powers that direct society. Religions have been seen, intimately united with the governments of the earth, dominating souls at the same time by terror and by faith: but when a religion contracts such an alliance, I am not afraid to say, it acts as a man might act; it sacrifices the future in view of the present, and in obtaining a power not its due, it puts at risk its legitimate power.

When a religion seeks to found its empire only on the desire for immortality that torments equally the heart of all men, it can aim at universality; but when it comes to unite itself with a government, it must adopt maxims applicable only to certain peoples. Thus, in allying itself with a political power, religion increases its power over a few, and loses the hope of reigning over all.

So long as a religion rests only on those sentiments which are the consolation of all miseries, it can draw to itself the heart of the human race. Mingled with the bitter passions of this world, it is sometimes constrained to defend allies given to it by interest rather than by love; and it must repel as adversaries men who often still love it, even while it combats those with whom it has united. Religion cannot, then, share the material force of those who govern without taking on a part of the hatred they arouse.

The political powers that appear most firmly established have no guarantee of their duration but the opinions of a generation, the interests of a century, often the life of a man. A law can modify the social state that seems most settled and best secured, and with it everything changes.

The powers of society are all more or less fleeting, as are our years on the earth; they succeed one another rapidly like the various concerns of life; and no government has ever been seen to rest on an invariable disposition of the human heart, or that has been able to base itself on an immortal interest.

So long as a religion finds its strength in sentiments, instincts, passions that one sees reproduced in the same manner in every age of history, it defies the effort of time, or at least it can only be destroyed by another religion. But when religion tries to lean upon the interests of this world, it becomes almost as fragile as all the powers of the earth. Alone, it can hope for immortality; bound to ephemeral powers, it follows their fortune, and often falls with the passions of a day that sustain them.
In uniting itself with the different political powers, religion can therefore only contract a burdensome alliance. It does not need their help to live, and in serving them it may die.
The danger I have just pointed out exists at all times, but it is not always equally visible.
There are centuries when governments appear immortal, and others when one would say that the existence of society is more fragile than that of a man.
Certain constitutions maintain the citizens in a kind of lethargic sleep, and others deliver them up to a feverish agitation.
When governments seem so strong and the laws so stable, men do not perceive the danger religion may run by uniting itself with power.
When governments show themselves so weak and the laws so changeable, the peril strikes every gaze; but often by then it is too late to escape it. One must therefore learn to perceive it from afar.

As a nation takes on a democratic social state, and as societies are seen to incline toward the republic, it becomes more and more dangerous to unite religion to authority; for the times are approaching when power will pass from hand to hand, when political theories will succeed one another, when men, laws, even constitutions themselves will disappear or be modified every day, and this not for a time, but unceasingly. Agitation and instability belong to the nature of democratic republics, as immobility and sleep form the law of absolute monarchies.

If the Americans, who change the seat of the State every four years, who every two years choose new legislators, and who replace their provincial administrators every year — if the Americans, who have delivered the political world over to the experiments of innovators, had not placed their religion somewhere outside it, to what could it hold in the flux and reflux of human opinions? Amid the struggle of parties, where would be the respect owed to it? What would become of its immortality, when everything around it was perishing?

The American priests perceived this truth before all others, and they conform their conduct to it. They saw that they would have to renounce religious influence if they wished to acquire a political power, and they preferred to lose the support of power rather than to share its vicissitudes.

In America, religion is perhaps less powerful than it has been at certain times and among certain peoples, but its influence is more lasting. It has been reduced to its own forces, which no one can take from it; it acts only within a single circle, but it traverses it entire and dominates there without effort.
I hear in Europe voices raised on all sides; people deplore the absence of beliefs, and ask themselves what is the means of restoring to religion some remnant of its former power.

It seems to me that one must first investigate carefully what should be, in our day, the natural state of men in matters of religion. Knowing then what we can hope for and what we have to fear, we would clearly perceive the goal toward which our efforts should tend.
Two great dangers threaten the existence of religions: schisms, and indifference.

In ages of fervor, it sometimes happens that men abandon their religion, but they only escape its yoke to submit themselves to that of another. Faith changes its object; it does not die. The old religion then excites in every heart ardent loves or implacable hatreds; some leave it in anger, others cling to it with new fervor: beliefs differ, irreligion is unknown.
But it is not so when a religious belief is silently undermined by doctrines I shall call negative, since in affirming the falsity of one religion they establish the truth of no other.

Then prodigious revolutions take place in the human mind without man's appearing to assist them by his passions, and so to speak without his suspecting them. One sees men let slip, as if from forgetfulness, the object of their dearest hopes. Carried along by an imperceptible current against which they have not the courage to struggle, and to which nevertheless they yield with regret, they abandon the faith they love to follow the doubt that leads them to despair.

In the ages we have just described, men leave these beliefs out of coldness rather than out of hatred; they do not reject them, they let them slip away. Ceasing to believe the religion true, the unbeliever continues to judge it useful. Considering religious beliefs from a human aspect, he recognizes their empire over the affections, their influence on the laws. He understands how they can make men live in peace and prepare them gently for death. He therefore regrets the faith after having lost it, and deprived of a good whose full price he knows, he fears to take it away from those who still possess it.

For his part, he who continues to believe does not fear to expose his faith to every gaze. In those who do not share his hopes he sees unfortunates rather than adversaries; he knows he can win their esteem without following their example; he is therefore at war with no one; and not considering the society in which he lives as an arena where religion must constantly fight against a thousand relentless enemies, he loves his contemporaries even as he condemns their weaknesses and is grieved by their errors.

Those who do not believe hiding their unbelief, and those who believe showing their faith, there forms a public opinion in favor of religion; it is loved, supported, honored, and one must penetrate to the bottom of souls to discover the wounds it has received.

The mass of men, whom religious sentiment never abandons, then sees nothing that draws it away from established beliefs. The instinct for another life leads it easily to the foot of the altar and delivers up its heart to the precepts and consolations of the faith.
Why does this picture not apply to us?
I perceive among us men who have ceased to believe in Christianity without attaching themselves to any religion.
I see others who are halted in doubt, and who already pretend to believe no longer.
Further on, I meet Christians who still believe and dare not say so.

Amid these lukewarm friends and these ardent adversaries, I discover at last a small number of faithful ready to brave every obstacle and to scorn every danger for their beliefs. These have done violence to human weakness in order to raise themselves above common opinion. Carried along by that very effort, they no longer know precisely where they should stop. As they have seen that, in their country, the first use man has made of independence was to attack religion, they dread their contemporaries and recoil with terror from the liberty these are pursuing. Unbelief seeming to them something new, they wrap up in a single hatred all that is new. They are thus at war with their century and their country, and in each of the opinions professed there they see a necessary enemy of the faith.
Such ought not to be in our day the natural state of men in matters of religion.
There is therefore among us an accidental and particular cause that prevents the human mind from following its bent and pushes it beyond the limits at which it ought naturally to halt.
I am profoundly convinced that this particular and accidental cause is the intimate union of politics and religion.

The unbelievers of Europe pursue the Christians as political enemies rather than as religious adversaries: they hate the faith as the opinion of a party, far more than as a mistaken belief; and what they reject in the priest is less the representative of God than the friend of power.

In Europe, Christianity has permitted itself to be intimately united with the powers of the earth. Today these powers are falling, and it is as if buried beneath their debris. It is a living thing that has been tied to corpses: cut the bonds that hold it, and it will rise again.

I do not know what would have to be done to give Christianity in Europe back the energy of youth. God alone could do it; but at least it depends on men to leave the faith the use of all the forces it still retains.
HOW THE ENLIGHTENMENT, THE HABITS, AND THE PRACTICAL EXPERIENCE OF THE AMERICANS CONTRIBUTE TO THE SUCCESS OF DEMOCRATIC INSTITUTIONS.

What is to be understood by the enlightenment of the American people. — The human mind has received in the United States a less profound cultivation than in Europe. — But no one has remained in ignorance. — Why. — The rapidity with which thought circulates in the half-deserted States of the West. — How practical experience serves the Americans even more than literary knowledge.

In a thousand places in this work, I have pointed out to readers what influence the enlightenment and habits of the Americans exercise upon the maintenance of their political institutions. There remains for me now little new to say.

America has up to this point had only a very small number of remarkable writers; she has no great historians and does not count a single poet. Her inhabitants regard literature properly so called with a sort of disfavor; and there is many a third-rank European city that publishes each year more literary works than the twenty-four States of the Union taken together.

The American mind turns away from general ideas; it does not direct itself toward theoretical discoveries. Politics itself and industry cannot draw it that way. In the United States, new laws are constantly being made; but no great writers have yet appeared to seek out the general principles of laws.
The Americans have jurists and commentators; publicists they lack; and in politics they give the world examples rather than lessons.
It is the same with the mechanical arts.

In America, the inventions of Europe are sagaciously applied, and after being perfected they are admirably adapted to the needs of the country. The men there are industrious, but they do not cultivate the science of industry. Good workmen are to be found there, and few inventors. Fulton long peddled his genius among foreign peoples before he could devote it to his own country.

Anyone who wishes to judge what is the state of enlightenment among the Anglo-Americans is therefore liable to see the same object under two different aspects. If he pays attention only to the learned, he will be astonished at their small number; and if he counts the ignorant, the American people will seem to him the most enlightened on earth.
The whole population is placed between these two extremes: I have already said it elsewhere.

In New England, every citizen receives the elementary notions of human knowledge; he learns besides what the doctrines and proofs of his religion are; he is made acquainted with the history of his country and the principal features of the constitution that governs it. In Connecticut and Massachusetts, it is very rare to find a man who knows all these things only imperfectly, and one who is wholly ignorant of them is something of a phenomenon.

When I compare the Greek and Roman republics to these American republics — the manuscript libraries of the former, and their coarse populace, to the thousand newspapers that crisscross the latter and to the enlightened people that inhabits them — and when I think next of all the efforts still being made to judge the one by the other, and to predict, from what happened two thousand years ago, what will happen in our own day, I am tempted to burn my books, so as to apply only new ideas to a social state so new.

What I say of New England, moreover, should not be extended indiscriminately to the whole Union. The further one advances toward the west or toward the south, the more the instruction of the people diminishes. In the States that border the Gulf of Mexico, there are, as among us, a certain number of individuals who are strangers to the elements of human knowledge; but one would seek in vain in the United States a single district that had remained plunged in ignorance. The reason is simple: the peoples of Europe set out from darkness and barbarism to advance toward civilization and enlightenment. Their progress has been unequal: some have run along this course, others have done little more than walk it; several have stopped, and they sleep still on the road.
It has not been so in the United States.

The Anglo-Americans arrived already civilized on the soil their posterity occupies; they had nothing to learn — it was enough for them not to forget. Now, it is the sons of these same Americans who, each year, transport into the desert, with their dwelling, the knowledge already acquired and the esteem for learning. Education has made them feel the utility of enlightenment, and has placed them in a position to transmit that same enlightenment to their descendants. In the United States, therefore, society has no infancy; it is born in manhood.

The Americans make no use of the word peasant; they do not employ the word because they do not have the idea; the ignorance of the first ages, the simplicity of the fields, the rusticity of the village, have not been preserved among them, and they conceive neither the virtues nor the vices, neither the coarse habits nor the artless graces of a nascent civilization.

At the extreme limits of the confederated States, on the confines of society and the desert, lives a population of bold adventurers who, to flee the poverty ready to overtake them beneath the paternal roof, have not feared to plunge into the solitudes of America and to seek there a new homeland. Scarcely arrived at the place that is to serve him for asylum, the pioneer hastily fells a few trees and raises a cabin beneath the foliage. There is nothing that offers a more miserable aspect than these isolated dwellings. The traveler who approaches one of them toward evening sees, from far off, through the walls, the flame of the hearth glow; and at night, if the wind rises, he hears the roof of leaves stir noisily among the trees of the forest. Who would not believe that this poor cottage serves as a refuge for coarseness and ignorance? Yet one must establish no link between the pioneer and the place that gives him shelter. Everything is primitive and wild around him, but he himself is, so to speak, the result of eighteen centuries of labor and experience. He wears the clothing of cities, speaks their language; he knows the past, is curious about the future, argues about the present; he is a very civilized man, who for a time submits to living in the woods, and who plunges into the deserts of the New World with a Bible, an axe, and some newspapers.
It is difficult to imagine with what incredible rapidity thought circulates within the bosom of these deserts[41].
I do not believe that as great an intellectual movement takes place in the most enlightened and most populous cantons of France[42].

There can be no doubt that in the United States the instruction of the people serves powerfully to maintain the democratic republic. It will be so, I think, wherever instruction that enlightens the mind is not separated from the education that regulates mores.

I do not, however, exaggerate this advantage, and I am still further from believing, as a great many people in Europe do, that it suffices to teach men to read and write in order to make them, at once, citizens.

True enlightenment is born chiefly of experience, and if the Americans had not been accustomed gradually to govern themselves, the literary knowledge they possess would not today be of much help to them in succeeding at it.
I have lived much with the people in the United States, and I cannot say how much I admired their experience and their good sense.

Do not bring the American to speak of Europe; he will ordinarily show great presumption and a rather foolish pride. He will content himself with those general and indefinite ideas which, in every country, are of such great help to the ignorant. But question him about his own country, and you will see all at once the cloud that wrapped his intelligence dissipate: his language will become clear, precise, exact, like his thought. He will tell you what his rights are and what means he should employ to exercise them; he will know according to what practices the political world is conducted. You will see that the rules of administration are known to him, and that he has made the mechanism of the laws familiar. The inhabitant of the United States has not drawn this practical knowledge and these positive notions from books: his literary education may have prepared him to receive them, but it has not furnished them to him.

It is by taking part in legislation that the American learns to know the laws; it is by governing that he learns the forms of government. The great work of society is accomplished each day before his eyes and, so to speak, in his hands.

In the United States, the whole of men's education is directed toward politics; in Europe, its principal goal is to prepare them for private life. The action of the citizen in public affairs is too rare a fact to be foreseen.
As soon as one casts a glance at the two societies, these differences reveal themselves down to their outward aspect.

In Europe, we often bring the ideas and habits of private life into public life, and as it happens to us to pass suddenly from the interior of the family to the government of the State, we are often seen discussing the great interests of society as we converse with our friends.

On the contrary, it is the habits of public life that the Americans nearly always transport into private life. With them, the idea of the jury is found in the games of the schoolyard, and one finds parliamentary forms even in the arrangement of a banquet.
THAT THE LAWS SERVE THE MAINTENANCE OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC IN THE UNITED STATES MORE THAN PHYSICAL CAUSES, AND *MOEURS* MORE THAN THE LAWS.

All the peoples of America have a democratic social state. — Yet democratic institutions sustain themselves only among the Anglo-Americans. — The Spaniards of South America, as favored by physical nature as the Anglo-Americans, cannot bear the democratic republic. — Mexico, which has adopted the constitution of the United States, cannot bear it. — The Anglo-Americans of the West bear it with more difficulty than those of the East. — Reasons for these differences.
I have said that one had to attribute the maintenance of the democratic institutions of the United States to circumstances, to laws, and to mores[43].
Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and give it a preponderant importance it does not have.

It is true that the Anglo-Americans brought to the New World equality of conditions. Neither commoners nor nobles were ever to be found among them; prejudices of birth have always been as unknown there as prejudices of profession. The social state being thus democratic, democracy had no trouble establishing its empire.

But this fact is not peculiar to the United States; nearly all the colonies of America were founded by men equal among themselves, or who became so by inhabiting them. There is not a single part of the New World where Europeans were able to create an aristocracy.
Yet democratic institutions prosper only in the United States.
The American Union has no enemies to fight. It is alone in the midst of deserts, like an island in the bosom of the Ocean.

But nature had isolated the Spaniards of South America in the same way, and this isolation has not prevented them from maintaining armies. They have made war on one another when foreigners were lacking. Only Anglo-American democracy has, up to the present, been able to maintain itself in peace.

The territory of the Union offers a field without limits to human activity; it offers inexhaustible nourishment to industry and to labor. The love of riches therefore takes the place of ambition there, and well-being extinguishes party ardor.

But in what portion of the world does one find more fertile deserts, greater rivers, more intact and inexhaustible riches than in South America? Yet South America cannot bear democracy. If it sufficed for peoples to be happy that they should have been placed in a corner of the universe, and be able to spread out at will over uninhabited lands, the Spaniards of South America would have no cause to complain of their lot. And even if they did not enjoy the same happiness as the inhabitants of the United States, they should at least make themselves envied by the peoples of Europe. There are nevertheless no more wretched nations on the earth than those of South America.

Thus, not only can physical causes not produce analogous results among the Americans of the South and those of the North, but they cannot even produce among the former anything that is not inferior to what one sees in Europe, where they act in the contrary direction.
Physical causes therefore do not have as much influence on the destiny of nations as is supposed.

I have met men of New England prepared to leave a homeland where they could have found ease, in order to go and seek their fortune in the desert. Nearby, I saw the French population of Canada crowding into a space too narrow for it, while the same desert lay close at hand; and while the emigrant from the United States acquired, for the price of a few days' labor, a great domain, the Canadian paid for land as dearly as if he were still living in France.
Thus nature, in delivering up to Europeans the solitudes of the New World, offers them goods of which they do not always know how to make use.

I see among other peoples of America the same conditions of prosperity as among the Anglo-Americans, minus their laws and their mores; and these peoples are wretched. The laws and the mores of the Anglo-Americans constitute, then, the special reason of their greatness and the predominant cause I seek.

I am far from claiming an absolute goodness in American laws: I do not think them applicable to all democratic peoples; and among them there are several that, even in the United States, seem to me dangerous.
Nevertheless one cannot deny that the legislation of the Americans, taken as a whole, is well adapted to the genius of the people it must govern and to the nature of the country.

The American laws are therefore good, and one must attribute to them a large share in the success obtained in America by the government of democracy; but I do not think they are its principal cause. And while they seem to me to have more influence on the social happiness of the Americans than the nature of the country itself, on the other hand I see reasons to believe that they exercise less than do mores.
The federal laws certainly form the most important portion of the legislation of the United States.
Mexico, which is as happily situated as the Anglo-American Union, has appropriated to itself those same laws, and cannot accustom itself to the government of democracy.
There is, therefore, a reason independent of physical causes and of the laws, that makes democracy able to govern the United States.

But here is what proves still more. Almost all the men who inhabit the territory of the Union come from the same blood. They speak the same language, pray to God in the same manner, are subject to the same material causes, obey the same laws.
Whence then come the differences that one must observe among them?

Why, in the east of the Union, does republican government show itself strong and regular, and proceed with maturity and slowness? What cause imprints on all its acts a character of wisdom and of duration?
Whence comes it, on the contrary, that in the west the powers of society seem to march at random?
Why does there reign there, in the movement of affairs, something disordered, passionate, one might almost say feverish, that promises no long future?

I no longer compare the Anglo-Americans to foreign peoples; I now oppose the Anglo-Americans to one another, and I ask why they do not resemble one another. Here all the arguments drawn from the nature of the country and the difference of the laws fail me at the same time. Recourse must be had to some other cause; and that cause, where shall I find it, if not in mores?

It is in the east that the Anglo-Americans have had the longest practice of the government of democracy, and that they have formed the habits and conceived the ideas most favorable to its maintenance. Democracy has there penetrated little by little into customs, into opinions, into forms; one finds it in every detail of social life as in the laws. It is in the east that literary instruction and the practical education of the people have been most perfected and that religion has best intermingled itself with liberty. What are all these habits, these opinions, these usages, these beliefs, if not what I have called mores?

In the west, on the contrary, a part of those same advantages is still lacking. Many Americans of the western States were born in the woods, and they mingle with the civilization of their fathers the ideas and the customs of savage life. Among them, passions are more violent, religious morality less powerful, ideas less settled. The men there exercise no control over one another, for they hardly know one another. The nations of the West therefore show, up to a certain point, the inexperience and the disordered habits of nascent peoples. Nevertheless the societies of the West are formed of ancient elements; only the assembly is new.

It is therefore particularly mores that make the Americans of the United States, alone among all the Americans, capable of bearing the empire of democracy; and it is they too that make the various Anglo-American democracies more or less well regulated and prosperous.

Thus, in Europe the influence of the country's geographical position on the duration of democratic institutions is exaggerated. Too much importance is attributed to laws, too little to mores. These three great causes no doubt serve to regulate and to direct American democracy; but if one had to rank them, I would say that physical causes contribute to it less than the laws, and the laws infinitely less than mores.

I am convinced that the happiest situation and the best laws cannot maintain a constitution in spite of mores, while mores still turn the most unfavorable positions and the worst laws to account. The importance of mores is a common truth to which study and experience constantly lead back. It seems to me that I find it placed in my mind as a central point; I perceive it at the end of all my ideas.
I have only a word more to say on this subject.

If I have not succeeded in making the reader feel, in the course of this work, the importance I attributed to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions — in a word, to their mores — in the maintenance of their laws, I have missed the principal aim I proposed to myself in writing it.
WOULD LAWS AND *MOEURS* SUFFICE TO MAINTAIN DEMOCRATIC INSTITUTIONS ELSEWHERE THAN IN AMERICA?

The Anglo-Americans, transported to Europe, would be obliged to modify their laws there. — One must distinguish between democratic institutions and American institutions. — One can conceive of democratic laws better, or at least different, from those that American democracy has given itself. — The example of America proves only that one must not despair of being able, with the help of laws and mores, to regulate democracy.
I have said that the success of democratic institutions in the United States was due to the laws themselves and to mores more than to the nature of the country.

But does it follow that these same causes transported elsewhere would alone have the same power, and if the country cannot take the place of laws and mores, can laws and mores, in their turn, take the place of the country?

Here it will easily be conceived that the elements of proof fail us: one finds in the New World other peoples besides the Anglo-Americans, and these peoples being subject to the same material causes as the latter, I have been able to compare them with one another.
