Civilization is the result of a long social labor that takes place in one and the same locality, and that the various generations bequeath to one another in succession. The peoples among whom civilization most slowly establishes its empire are hunting peoples. Pastoral tribes change places, but in their migrations they always follow a regular order, and constantly return upon their tracks; the dwelling of the hunter varies like that of the animals he pursues.

Several attempts have been made to spread enlightenment among the Indians while leaving them their wandering mores; the Jesuits had undertaken this in Canada, the Puritans in New England[55]. Neither did anything that lasted. Civilization was born in the hut and went to die in the woods. The great fault of these legislators of the Indians was not to understand that, in order to civilize a people, it must first be brought to settle, and that it cannot settle unless it cultivates the soil; the first task, then, was to make farmers of the Indians.
Not only do the Indians not possess this indispensable preliminary of civilization, it is very difficult for them to acquire it.

Men who have once given themselves up to the idle and adventurous life of hunters feel an almost insurmountable disgust for the constant and regular labors that cultivation demands. One can see this in the heart of our own societies; but it is far more visible still among peoples for whom the habits of the chase have become national customs.
Independent of this general cause, there is one no less powerful and to be found only among the Indians. I have already indicated it; I believe I must return to it.
The natives of North America consider work not only an evil but a disgrace, and their pride struggles against civilization almost as obstinately as their laziness[56].

There is no Indian so wretched that, beneath his bark hut, he does not entertain a lofty idea of his individual worth; he considers the cares of industry as degrading occupations; he compares the cultivator to the ox that traces a furrow, and in each of our arts he sees only the labors of slaves. Not that he has not formed a very high idea of the power of the whites and of the greatness of their intelligence; but if he admires the result of our efforts, he despises the means by which we have obtained it, and even while submitting to our ascendancy, he still believes himself superior to us. The hunt and war seem to him the only cares worthy of a man[57]. The Indian, deep in the misery of his woods, harbors then the same ideas, the same opinions as the noble of the Middle Ages in his fortified castle, and to complete the resemblance he lacks only one thing: to become a conqueror. So, strange to say, it is in the forests of the New World, and not among the Europeans who people its shores, that the old prejudices of Europe are to be found today.

More than once in the course of this work I have tried to make plain the prodigious influence that the social state seems to me to exert on the laws and mores of men. Allow me to add a single word on this subject.

When I notice the resemblance between the political institutions of our forefathers the Germans and those of the wandering tribes of North America, between the customs described by Tacitus and those I have at times been able to witness, I cannot help thinking that the same cause has produced, in the two hemispheres, the same effects, and that amid the apparent diversity of human things it is not impossible to find a small number of generating facts from which all the others flow. In all that we call the Germanic institutions, then, I am tempted to see nothing but the habits of barbarians, and in what we call feudal ideas, the opinions of savages.
Whatever the vices and prejudices that prevent the Indians of North America from becoming cultivators and civilized, sometimes necessity compels them to it.

Several considerable nations of the South, among them the Cherokees and the Creeks[58], have found themselves, as it were, enveloped by the Europeans, who, landing on the shores of the Ocean, descending the Ohio, and ascending the Mississippi, arrived around them at the same time. They have not been driven from place to place, like the tribes of the North, but rather pressed gradually into limits too narrow, as hunters first make a ring around a thicket before penetrating it simultaneously. The Indians, placed then between civilization and death, found themselves reduced to live shamefully by their labor like the whites; they thus became cultivators, and without entirely giving up either their habits or their mores, sacrificed of them only what was absolutely necessary for their existence.

The Cherokees went further; they created a written language, established a fairly stable form of government; and, since in the New World everything moves at a precipitate pace, they had a newspaper[59] before they all had clothes.

What has singularly favored the rapid development of European habits among these Indians has been the presence of the mixed-bloods[60]. Sharing in his father's learning without entirely abandoning the savage customs of his maternal race, the mixed-blood forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism. Wherever mixed-bloods have multiplied, the savages have been seen gradually to modify their social condition and to change their *mores*[61].
The success of the Cherokees proves, then, that the Indians have the faculty of civilizing themselves, but it in no way proves that they can succeed in it.
This difficulty the Indians find in submitting to civilization arises from a general cause from which it is almost impossible for them to escape.
If one casts an attentive glance at history, one discovers that in general barbarous peoples have raised themselves little by little, by their own efforts, to civilization.
When they have gone to draw enlightenment from a foreign nation, they have occupied toward it the rank of conquerors, not the position of the conquered.

When the conquered people is enlightened and the conqueror half savage, as in the invasion of the Roman Empire by the nations of the North, or that of China by the Mongols, the power that victory secures to the barbarian suffices to keep him at the level of the civilized man and to allow him to walk as his equal until he becomes his rival; the one has force on his side, the other intelligence; the first admires the sciences and arts of the vanquished, the second envies the power of the victors. The barbarians end by bringing the civilized man into their palaces, and the civilized man in turn opens his schools to them. But when the one who possesses material force enjoys at the same time intellectual preponderance, it is rare that the conquered civilizes himself; he withdraws, or he is destroyed.
Thus one can say in general that savages go in search of enlightenment with weapons in hand, but that they do not receive it.

If the Indian tribes that now inhabit the center of the continent could find within themselves energy enough to undertake to civilize themselves, they might perhaps succeed. Then, being superior to the barbarous nations around them, they would gradually gain strength and experience, and when at last the Europeans appeared on their frontiers, they would be in a position, if not to maintain their independence, at least to have their right to the soil recognized and to incorporate themselves with the victors. But the misfortune of the Indians is to come into contact with the most civilized people, and I will add the most rapacious, on the globe, while they themselves are still half barbarous; to find masters in their instructors, and to receive at one and the same time oppression and enlightenment.

Living amid the liberty of the woods, the Indian of North America was wretched, but he felt himself inferior to no one; from the moment he wishes to enter into the social hierarchy of the whites, he can occupy only the lowest rank, for he comes ignorant and poor into a society where science and wealth reign. After leading a stormy life, full of hardships and dangers, but at the same time filled with emotions and grandeur[62], he must submit to a monotonous, obscure, and degraded existence. To earn by painful labor and in the midst of ignominy the bread that is to feed him: such, in his eyes, is the sole result of that civilization which is so vaunted to him.
And even this result he is not always sure of obtaining.

When the Indians undertake to imitate the Europeans, their neighbors, and to cultivate the land as the latter do, they at once expose themselves to the effects of a most disastrous competition. The white man is master of the secrets of agriculture. The Indian begins crudely in an art he does not know. The one easily raises great harvests, the other wrings fruit from the earth only with a thousand efforts.
The European is set in the midst of a population whose needs he knows and shares.

The savage is isolated in the midst of an enemy people whose mores, language, and laws he knows only imperfectly, and whom he yet cannot do without. Only by exchanging his products for those of the whites can he find any ease, for his countrymen are now of little help to him.

So when the Indian wishes to sell the fruits of his labor, he does not always find the buyer that the European cultivator finds without difficulty, and he cannot produce except at great cost what the other delivers at low cost.

The Indian, then, has escaped the evils to which barbarous nations are exposed only to submit to the greater miseries of civilized peoples, and he finds it almost as hard to live amid our abundance as in his forests.

And yet the habits of the wandering life are not yet destroyed in him. The traditions have not lost their power; the taste for the hunt is not extinguished. The savage joys he once experienced deep in the woods now paint themselves in livelier colors on his troubled imagination; the privations he endured there seem, by contrast, less terrible, the perils he met less great. The independence he enjoyed among his equals stands in contrast with the servile position he occupies in a civilized society.

On the other hand, the solitude in which he so long lived free is still near him; a few hours' march can give it back to him. From the half-cleared field, from which he scarcely draws enough to feed himself, the white men, his neighbors, offer him a price that seems to him high. Perhaps that money the Europeans hold out will allow him to live happy and at peace far from them. He drops the plow, takes up his weapons again, and returns forever to the wilderness[63].
The truth of this sad picture can be judged by what is happening among the Creeks and the Cherokees, whom I have cited.

In the little they have done, these Indians have certainly shown as much natural genius as the peoples of Europe in their vastest enterprises; but nations, like men, need time to learn, whatever their intelligence and their efforts.

While these savages worked to civilize themselves, the Europeans continued to envelop them on all sides and to confine them more and more. Today the two races have at last met; they are in contact. The Indian has already become superior to his father the savage, but he is still far inferior to the white man, his neighbor. With the help of their resources and their enlightenment, the Europeans were not slow to take for themselves most of the advantages that possession of the soil could give the natives; they settled in their midst, took the land or bought it at a low price, and ruined them by a competition the natives could in no way withstand. Isolated in their own country, the Indians have come to form only a small colony of troublesome strangers in the midst of a numerous and dominating people[64].
Washington had said, in one of his messages to Congress: "We are more enlightened and more powerful than the Indian nations; it is for our honor to treat them with kindness and even with generosity."
This noble and virtuous policy has not been followed.

To the greed of the settlers is ordinarily joined the tyranny of the government. Although the Cherokees and the Creeks are settled on the soil they inhabited before the arrival of the Europeans, although the Americans have often treated with them as with foreign nations, the States in the midst of which they find themselves have refused to recognize them as independent peoples, and have undertaken to subject these men, scarcely out of the forests, to their magistrates, customs, and laws[65]. Misery had pushed these unfortunate Indians toward civilization; oppression now drives them back toward barbarism. Many of them, abandoning their half-cleared fields, take up the habits of savage life again.

If one considers the tyrannical measures adopted by the legislators of the Southern States, the conduct of their governors, and the acts of their tribunals, one will easily be convinced that the complete expulsion of the Indians is the final aim toward which all their efforts tend simultaneously. The Americans of this part of the Union view with jealousy the lands the natives possess[66]; they sense that the latter have not yet completely lost the traditions of savage life, and before civilization has firmly attached them to the soil, they wish to reduce them to despair and force them to depart.

Oppressed by the particular States, the Creeks and the Cherokees have appealed to the central government. The latter is not insensible to their sufferings; it would sincerely save the remnants of the natives and assure them the free possession of the territory it has itself guaranteed them[67]; but when it tries to carry out this design, the particular States oppose a formidable resistance, and it then resolves without difficulty to let some savage tribes already half destroyed perish, rather than put the American Union in danger.
Powerless to protect the Indians, the federal government would at least soften their lot; to this end it has undertaken to transport them at its expense to other places.

Between the 33rd and 37th degrees of north latitude stretches a vast country that has taken the name of Arkansas, from the principal river that waters it. It borders on one side the frontiers of Mexico, on the other the banks of the Mississippi. A multitude of streams and rivers cut across it from all sides; its climate is mild and its soil fertile. It is inhabited only by a few wandering bands of savages. It is in the portion of this country closest to Mexico, and at a great distance from the American settlements, that the government of the Union wishes to transport the remnants of the native populations of the south.

At the end of 1831 we were assured that 10,000 Indians had already been landed on the banks of the Arkansas; others were arriving every day. But Congress has not yet been able to create a unanimous will among those whose fate it wishes to settle: some consent gladly to leave the seat of tyranny; the more enlightened refuse to abandon their nascent harvests and their new dwellings; they think that if the work of civilization is once interrupted, it will not be resumed; they fear that habits of settled life, scarcely contracted, will be lost forever in the midst of still savage countries, where nothing is prepared for the subsistence of a cultivating people; they know that they will find in these new wildernesses enemy tribes, and that to resist them they no longer have the energy of barbarism, while they have not yet acquired the strength of civilization. The Indians, moreover, easily see all that is provisional in the settlement proposed to them. Who will assure them that they can at last rest in peace in their new asylum? The United States pledges to maintain them there; but the territory they now occupy had once been guaranteed to them by the most solemn oaths[68]. Today the American government does not, it is true, take their lands from them, but it lets them be invaded. In a few years, no doubt, the same white population that now presses around them will be on their heels again in the solitudes of Arkansas; they will then find the same evils without the same remedies; and the land in time failing them, they will always have to resign themselves to dying.
There is less greed and violence in the Union's manner of acting toward the Indians than in the policy followed by the States; but both governments are equally lacking in good faith.

The States, in extending what they call the benefit of their laws over the Indians, count on the Indians' preferring to depart rather than submit to them; and the central government, in promising these unfortunates a permanent asylum in the West, is well aware that it cannot guarantee it[69].

Thus, the States by their tyranny force the savages to flee; the Union, by its promises and with the help of its resources, makes this flight easy. These are different measures tending to the same end[70].

"By the will of our Heavenly Father, who governs the universe," said the Cherokees in their petition to Congress[71], "the race of red men of America has become small; the white race has become great and renowned.

"When your ancestors arrived upon our shores, the red man was strong, and though he was ignorant and savage, he received them with kindness and allowed them to rest their weary feet on the dry land. Our fathers and yours took each other by the hand in token of friendship, and lived in peace.

"Whatever the white man asked to satisfy his needs, the Indian hastened to grant. The Indian was then the master, and the white man the suppliant. Today the scene is changed: the strength of the red man has become weakness. As his neighbors grew in number, his power diminished more and more; and now, of the many powerful tribes that covered the surface of what you call the United States, scarcely any remain that the universal disaster has spared. The tribes of the North, once so renowned among us for their power, have nearly disappeared. Such has been the destiny of the red man of America.
"Here we are, the last of our race; must we too die?

"From time immemorial, our common Father who is in heaven gave our ancestors the land we occupy; our ancestors transmitted it to us as their inheritance. We have preserved it with respect, for it contains their ashes. This inheritance — have we ever ceded it or lost it? Allow us to ask you humbly what better right a people can have to a country than the right of inheritance and immemorial possession. We know that the State of Georgia and the President of the United States now claim that we have lost this right. But this seems to us a gratuitous assertion. At what time did we lose it? What crime have we committed that could deprive us of our country? Are we reproached with having fought under the banners of the King of Great Britain during the war of independence? If that is the crime in question, why, in the first treaty that followed that war, did you not declare that we had lost the ownership of our lands? Why did you not then insert in that treaty an article worded thus: The United States are willing to grant peace to the Cherokee nation; but to punish them for having taken part in the war, it is declared that they will henceforth be considered only as tenants of the soil, and that they shall be required to depart when the States that surround them shall demand it? That was the moment to speak so; but no one then thought of it, and our fathers would never have consented to a treaty whose result would have been to deprive them of their most sacred rights and to take their country from them."
Such is the language of the Indians: what they say is true; what they foresee seems to me inevitable.

From whichever angle one envisages the destiny of the natives of North America, one sees only irremediable evils: if they remain savage, they are pushed onward as we advance; if they try to civilize themselves, the contact of men more civilized than themselves delivers them to oppression and misery. If they continue to wander from wilderness to wilderness, they perish; if they undertake to settle, they perish still. They can become enlightened only with the help of the Europeans, and the approach of the Europeans depraves them and pushes them back toward barbarism. As long as they are left in their solitudes, they refuse to change their mores, and it is no longer time to do so when they are at last forced to wish it.

The Spaniards let their dogs loose on the Indians as on wild beasts; they pillaged the New World as a city taken by storm, without discernment and without pity; but one cannot destroy everything; fury has a limit; the remnant of the Indian populations that escaped the massacre ended by mingling with the conquerors and adopting their religion and their mores[72].

The conduct of the Americans of the United States toward the natives, by contrast, breathes the purest love of forms and of legality. Provided the Indians remain in the savage state, the Americans do not meddle in their affairs and treat them as independent peoples; they do not permit themselves to occupy their lands without having duly acquired them through a contract; and if by chance an Indian nation can no longer live on its territory, they take it fraternally by the hand and lead it themselves to die outside the country of its fathers.

The Spaniards, by means of monstrosities without example, covering themselves with an indelible shame, were unable to exterminate the Indian race, or even to prevent it from sharing their rights; the Americans of the United States have achieved this double result with marvelous ease, tranquilly, legally, philanthropically, without spilling blood, without violating a single one of the great principles of morality[73] in the eyes of the world. It would be impossible to destroy men with greater respect for the laws of humanity.
POSITION OCCUPIED BY THE BLACK RACE IN THE UNITED STATES[74]: DANGERS THAT ITS PRESENCE POSES FOR THE WHITES.

Why it is harder to abolish slavery and to wipe out its trace among the moderns than among the ancients. — In the United States, the prejudice of the whites against the blacks seems to grow stronger as slavery is destroyed. — Situation of the negroes in the Northern and Southern States. — Why the Americans abolish slavery. — Servitude, which brutalizes the slave, impoverishes the master. — Differences to be observed between the right bank and the left bank of the Ohio. — To what they must be attributed. — The black race recedes toward the South, as does slavery. — How this is to be explained. — Difficulties the Southern States meet in abolishing slavery. — Dangers ahead. — Preoccupation of men's minds. — Founding of a black colony in Africa. — Why the Americans of the South, even as they are growing disgusted with slavery, increase its rigors.

The Indians will die in isolation as they have lived; but the destiny of the negroes is in a sense entwined with that of the Europeans. The two races are bound to each other without being merged; they find it as difficult to separate completely as to unite.

The most fearful of all the evils that threaten the future of the United States arises from the presence of the blacks upon their soil. When one looks for the cause of the present embarrassments and the future dangers of the Union, one almost always arrives at this first fact, whatever point one starts from.

Men generally need great and sustained efforts to create lasting evils; but there is one evil that comes into the world stealthily: at first one barely sees it amid the ordinary abuses of power; it begins with an individual whose name history does not preserve; it is laid like an accursed seed on some patch of the soil; it then feeds on itself, spreads without effort, and grows naturally with the society that has received it: that evil is slavery.

Christianity had destroyed servitude; the Christians of the sixteenth century reestablished it; yet they have never accepted it except as an exception in their social system, and they have taken care to restrict it to one only of the human races. They have thus given humanity a less wide wound, but one infinitely more difficult to heal.
Two things must be carefully distinguished: slavery in itself, and its consequences.

The immediate evils produced by slavery were about the same among the ancients as they are among the moderns, but the consequences of those evils were different. Among the ancients the slave was of the same race as his master, and often his superior in education and enlightenment[75]. Liberty alone separated them; once liberty was given, they merged easily.
The ancients thus had a very simple means of delivering themselves from slavery and its consequences; that means was emancipation, and as soon as they applied it on a large scale, they succeeded.
Not that, in antiquity, the traces of servitude did not subsist some time even after servitude itself was destroyed.

There is a natural prejudice that leads man to despise whoever has been his inferior, long after that person has become his equal; to the real inequality produced by fortune or by law there always succeeds an imaginary inequality rooted in mores. But among the ancients this secondary effect of slavery had a limit. The freedman so closely resembled men of free origin that it soon became impossible to distinguish him among them.
What was hardest among the ancients was to modify the law; among the moderns, it is to change the mores, and for us the real difficulty begins where antiquity saw it end.

This comes from the fact that among the moderns the immaterial and fleeting fact of slavery combines in the most disastrous way with the material and permanent fact of difference of race. The memory of slavery dishonors the race, and the race perpetuates the memory of slavery.

No African came freely to the shores of the New World; from which it follows that all those who are there today are slaves or freedmen. Thus the negro transmits, together with existence, to all his descendants the outward sign of his ignominy. The law can destroy servitude; but God alone can erase its trace.

The modern slave differs from his master not only in liberty, but also in origin. You can make the negro free, but you cannot prevent him from standing toward the European in the position of a stranger.

And that is not all: this man who was born in baseness, this stranger whom servitude has brought among us — we scarcely recognize in him the general features of humanity. His face appears to us hideous, his intelligence seems limited, his tastes are low; we come close to taking him for a being intermediate between brute and man[76].

The moderns, after abolishing slavery, still have to destroy three prejudices much more elusive and stubborn than slavery itself: the prejudice of the master, the prejudice of race, and lastly the prejudice of the white.

It is very difficult for us, who have had the good fortune to be born among men whom nature had made our likes and law our equals; it is very difficult, I say, to grasp what an unbridgeable distance separates the American negro from the European. But we can have a distant idea of it by reasoning by analogy.

We have known among ourselves great inequalities whose roots lay only in legislation. What more fictitious than a purely legal inferiority! What more contrary to man's instinct than permanent differences established between people obviously alike! These differences nevertheless subsisted for centuries; they subsist still in a thousand places; everywhere they have left imaginary traces which time can barely efface. If inequality created by law alone is so hard to root out, how is one to destroy that which seems, in addition, to have its immovable foundations in nature itself?

For my part, when I consider with what difficulty aristocratic bodies, of whatever nature they may be, come to merge with the mass of the people, and the extreme care they take to preserve for centuries the ideal barriers that separate them from it, I despair of seeing an aristocracy disappear that is founded on visible and imperishable marks.

Those who hope that the Europeans will one day merge with the negroes seem to me, then, to be cherishing an illusion. My reason does not lead me to believe it, and I see nothing in the facts to suggest it.

Up to now, wherever the whites have been the most powerful, they have held the negroes in degradation or in slavery. Wherever the negroes have been the strongest, they have destroyed the whites; that is the only reckoning that has ever been opened between the two races.

If I look at the United States today, I see clearly that in a certain part of the country the legal barrier that separates the two races tends to fall, but not the barrier of mores: I see slavery in retreat; the prejudice it has begotten is immovable.

In the portion of the Union where the negroes are no longer slaves, have they come closer to the whites? Anyone who has lived in the United States will have noticed that a contrary effect has been produced.

The prejudice of race appears to me stronger in the States that have abolished slavery than in those where slavery still exists, and nowhere does it show itself so intolerant as in the States where servitude has always been unknown.

True, in the North of the Union the law allows negroes and whites to contract lawful marriages; but opinion brands as infamous the white who would unite himself to a negro woman, and it would be very difficult to cite a single example of such a thing.

In nearly all the States where slavery is abolished, the negro has been given electoral rights; but if he comes to vote, he risks his life. Oppressed, he may complain, but he finds only whites among his judges. The law does open the jury box to him, but prejudice keeps him out. His son is excluded from the school where the descendants of the Europeans go to learn. In the theaters he cannot, at any price, buy the right to sit beside the man who was his master; in the hospitals he lies apart. The negro is allowed to entreat the same God as the whites, but not to pray to Him at the same altar. He has his own priests and his own temples. The gates of heaven are not closed to him: yet inequality scarcely stops at the edge of the next world. When the negro is no more, his bones are cast aside, and the difference of conditions is to be found even in the equality of death.

Thus the negro is free, but he can share neither the rights, nor the pleasures, nor the labors, nor the pains, nor even the grave of him to whom he has been declared an equal; he can meet him nowhere, neither in life nor in death.

In the South, where slavery still exists, the negroes are kept apart less carefully; they sometimes share the labors of the whites and their amusements; people consent up to a point to mix with them; legislation is harsher toward them; habits are more tolerant and gentler.

In the South the master does not fear to raise his slave up to his level, because he knows that, if he wishes, he can always cast him back into the dust. In the North the white no longer sees clearly the barrier that must separate him from a degraded race, and he keeps away from the negro all the more carefully because he fears that one day he may come to be confounded with him.

With the American of the South, nature now and then returning to her rights comes for a moment to restore equality between whites and blacks. In the North, pride silences even the most imperious passion of man. The American of the North would perhaps consent to make the negro woman the passing companion of his pleasures, if the legislators had declared that she should never aspire to share his bed; but since she may become his wife, he keeps away from her with a kind of horror.
Thus in the United States the prejudice that rejects the negroes seems to grow in proportion as the negroes cease to be slaves, and inequality engraves itself in mores as it is effaced from the laws.

But if the relative position of the two races inhabiting the United States is such as I have just shown, why have the Americans abolished slavery in the North of the Union, why do they preserve it in the South, and why do they aggravate its rigors?
The answer is easy. It is not in the interest of the negroes, but in that of the whites, that slavery is being destroyed in the United States.

The first negroes were imported into Virginia around the year 1621[77]. In America, as elsewhere on the globe, servitude was thus born in the South. From there it spread by degrees; but as slavery moved northward, the number of slaves diminished[78]; there have always been very few negroes in New England.

The colonies were founded; a century had passed, and an extraordinary fact began to strike every eye. The provinces that had, so to speak, no slaves were growing in population, in wealth, and in well-being more rapidly than those that had them.

Yet in the former, the inhabitant was obliged to cultivate the soil himself, or to hire the services of another; in the latter, he had at his disposal workers whose efforts he did not pay for. There was thus labor and expense on one side, leisure and economy on the other: yet the advantage remained with the first.

This result seemed all the more difficult to explain in that the emigrants, all belonging to the same European race, had the same habits, the same civilization, the same laws, and differed only by barely perceptible shadings.

Time continued to march on. Leaving the shores of the Atlantic, the Anglo-Americans pressed each day deeper into the solitudes of the West; they encountered new soils and climates; they had to overcome obstacles of every kind; their races mingled, men of the South moved north, men of the North descended south. Amid all these causes, the same fact reproduced itself at every step; and in general, the colony where there were no slaves became more populous and more prosperous than the one where slavery prevailed.
As one advanced, then, it began to be glimpsed that servitude, so cruel to the slave, was disastrous to the master.
But this truth received its final demonstration when one had reached the banks of the Ohio.

The river that the Indians named, by way of excellence, the Ohio, or the Beautiful River, waters with its waters one of the most magnificent valleys ever inhabited by man. On both banks of the Ohio stretch undulating lands, where the soil offers each day to the tiller inexhaustible treasures; on both banks the air is equally healthy and the climate temperate; each forms the extreme frontier of a vast State: the one that follows on the left the thousand windings the Ohio traces in its course is called Kentucky; the other has taken its name from the river itself. The two States differ in only one point: Kentucky has admitted slaves, the State of Ohio has expelled them all from its bosom[79].

The traveler who, placed in the middle of the Ohio, lets himself be carried by the current to the river's mouth at the Mississippi, navigates, so to speak, between liberty and servitude; and he has only to glance around him to judge in an instant which is the more favorable to humanity.

On the left bank of the river, the population is thinly scattered; from time to time one notices a band of slaves moving with a careless air through half-deserted fields; primeval forest constantly reappears; one would say society was asleep; man seems idle, only nature offers an image of activity and life.

From the right bank, on the contrary, rises a confused hum that proclaims from afar the presence of industry; rich harvests cover the fields; elegant dwellings announce the taste and the care of the tiller; on all sides comfort reveals itself; man appears rich and content: he works[80].

The State of Kentucky was founded in 1775, the State of Ohio only twelve years later: twelve years in America is more than half a century in Europe. Today the population of Ohio already exceeds that of Kentucky by 250,000 inhabitants[81].
These different effects of slavery and of liberty are easily understood; they suffice to explain many of the differences to be found between ancient civilization and our own.

On the left bank of the Ohio, labor is confounded with the idea of slavery; on the right bank, with the idea of well-being and progress; there it is degraded, here it is honored; on the left bank of the river one cannot find workers belonging to the white race, they would fear to resemble slaves; one must rely on the negroes' efforts; on the right bank one would search in vain for an idle man; the white extends his activity and intelligence to every kind of work.

Thus the men who in Kentucky are charged with exploiting the natural riches of the soil have neither zeal nor enlightenment; while those who could have these two things do nothing, or pass over into Ohio in order to put their industry to use and to be able to exercise it without shame.

It is true that in Kentucky the masters make the slaves work without being obliged to pay them; but they draw little fruit from their efforts, while the money they would give to free workers would come back to them with interest in the price of their work.

The free worker is paid, but he works faster than the slave, and the rapidity of execution is one of the great elements of economy. The white man sells his help, but it is bought only when it is useful; the black has nothing to demand as the price of his services, but he must be fed all the time; he must be supported in his old age as in his prime, in his unproductive childhood as during the fruitful years of his youth, in sickness as in health. Thus it is only by paying that the labor of either man is obtained: the free worker receives a wage; the slave, an education, food, care, clothing; the money the master spends on the upkeep of the slave flows out little by little and in small amounts; he scarcely notices it: the wage given to the worker is paid all at once, and seems to enrich only him who receives it; but in reality the slave has cost more than the free man, and his labor has been less productive[82].
The influence of slavery reaches further still; it penetrates even into the master's soul, and gives a particular direction to his ideas and his tastes.
On both banks of the Ohio, nature has given man an enterprising and energetic character; but on each side of the river he puts this common quality to a different use.

The white of the right bank, forced to live by his own efforts, has placed the chief end of his existence in material well-being; and as the country he inhabits offers his industry inexhaustible resources, and presents to his activity ever-renewing inducements, his desire to acquire has gone beyond the ordinary bounds of human cupidity: tormented by the longing for wealth, he is seen to enter boldly upon every path that fortune opens to him; he becomes indifferently a sailor, a pioneer, a manufacturer, a cultivator, bearing with equal steadfastness the labors or the dangers attached to these various professions; there is something marvelous in the resources of his genius, and a kind of heroism in his greed for gain.

The American of the left bank scorns not only labor but every undertaking that labor brings to success; living in an idle ease, he has the tastes of idle men; money has lost a part of its value in his eyes; he pursues less fortune than excitement and pleasure, and he carries to that side the energy his neighbor deploys elsewhere; he passionately loves the hunt and war; he delights in the most violent exercises of the body; he is at home with the use of arms, and from childhood he has learned to wager his life in single combat. Slavery, then, not only prevents the whites from making a fortune; it turns them from wanting to.

The same causes operating continually for two centuries in opposite directions in the English colonies of North America have ended by setting a prodigious difference between the commercial capacity of the man of the South and that of the man of the North. Today only the North has ships, factories, railroads, and canals.

This difference is noticed not only when one compares North and South, but when one compares the inhabitants of the South among themselves. Nearly all the men in the most southern States of the Union who engage in commercial enterprises and who try to make use of slavery have come from the North; every day people of the North spread into this part of the American territory where competition is less to be feared by them; they discover resources there that the inhabitants would not see, and bending themselves to a system of which they disapprove, they manage to draw a greater profit from it than those who still uphold it after having founded it.

If I wished to carry the parallel further, I could easily prove that almost all the differences to be remarked between the character of the Americans of the South and that of those of the North have arisen out of slavery; but that would take me from my subject: I am seeking at this moment, not what all the effects of servitude are, but what effects it produces upon the material prosperity of those who have admitted it.

This influence of slavery on the production of wealth could be only very imperfectly known in antiquity. Servitude existed then throughout the civilized universe, and the peoples who did not know it were barbarians.
Christianity, accordingly, destroyed slavery only by asserting the rights of the slave; in our day it can be attacked in the name of the master: on this point interest and morality are in agreement.
As these truths revealed themselves in the United States, slavery was seen to recede little by little before the light of experience.

Servitude had begun in the South and had then spread northward; today it is retreating. Liberty, starting from the North, descends without halting toward the South. Among the great States, Pennsylvania forms today the extreme limit of slavery toward the North, but within those very limits it is shaken; Maryland, immediately below Pennsylvania, prepares each day to do without it, and already Virginia, which follows Maryland, is debating its usefulness and its dangers[83].
No great change occurs in human institutions without one's discovering, among the causes of that change, the law of inheritance.

When inequality of partition reigned in the South, each family was represented by a rich man who felt neither the need nor the taste for labor; around him, in the same way, lived as so many parasitic plants the members of his family whom the law had excluded from the common inheritance; one then saw in every family of the South what one sees today in the noble families of certain countries of Europe, where the younger sons, without having the same wealth as the eldest, remain as idle as he. This similar effect was produced in America and in Europe by causes entirely analogous. In the South of the United States, the whole race of whites formed an aristocratic body at whose head stood a certain number of privileged individuals whose wealth was permanent and whose leisure was hereditary. These chiefs of the American nobility perpetuated, in the body they represented, the traditional prejudices of the white race, and maintained idleness in honor. Within this aristocracy one could meet poor men, but no workers; misery seemed there preferable to industry; black and slave workers thus found no competition, and whatever opinion one might have of the usefulness of their efforts, one had to employ them, since they were the only ones available.

From the moment the law of inheritance was abolished, all fortunes began to diminish at the same time, and all families drew nearer, by the same movement, to the condition in which labor becomes necessary to existence; many of them disappeared altogether; all foresaw the moment when each would have to provide for his own needs. Today there are still rich men, but they no longer form a compact, hereditary body; they have not been able to adopt a spirit, to persevere in it, and to make it penetrate every rank. So people began by common consent to abandon the prejudice that branded labor; the poor became more numerous, and the poor were able without shame to occupy themselves in earning their living. Thus one of the most immediate effects of equal partition has been to create a class of free workers. From the moment the free worker entered into competition with the slave, the inferiority of the latter made itself felt, and slavery was attacked in its very principle, which is the master's interest.
As slavery recedes, the black race follows it in its retrograde march, and goes back with it toward the tropics, from which it originally came.
This may appear extraordinary at first sight; it will soon be understood.
In abolishing the principle of servitude, the Americans do not set the slaves at liberty.

What follows might be hard to grasp, were I not to cite an example; I will choose that of the State of New York. In 1788 the State of New York forbids the sale of slaves within its borders. That was in a roundabout way to forbid their importation. From then on the number of negroes increases only by the natural increase of the black population. Eight years later, a more decisive measure is taken, and it is declared that from July 4, 1799, all children born of slave parents will be free. Every path of increase is then closed; there are still slaves, but one can say that servitude no longer exists.
From the time a Northern State thus forbids the importation of slaves, no more negroes are brought up from the South into its territory.

The moment a Northern State forbids the sale of negroes, the slave, no longer being able to leave the hands of his owner, becomes an inconvenient piece of property, and there is an interest in transporting him to the South.

The day a Northern State declares that the son of the slave shall be born free, the slave loses a great part of his market value, for his offspring can no longer enter the market, and there is still a great interest in transporting him to the South.
Thus the same law prevents the slaves of the South from coming to the North and drives those of the North toward the South.
But here is another cause more powerful than any I have just spoken of.

As the number of slaves diminishes in a State, the need of free workers is felt there. As free workers take possession of industry, the slave's labor being less productive, he becomes a mediocre or useless property, and there is still a great interest in exporting him to the South, where competition is not to be feared.
The abolition of slavery, then, does not bring the slave to liberty; it only makes him change masters: from the north, he passes to the south.

As for the emancipated negroes and those born after the abolition of slavery, they do not leave the North to go South, but they find themselves with respect to the Europeans in a position analogous to that of the natives; they remain half civilized and deprived of rights in the midst of a population infinitely superior to them in wealth and enlightenment; they are exposed to the tyranny of the laws[84] and to the intolerance of mores. In one respect more unhappy than the Indians, they have against them the memories of slavery, and they cannot claim possession of a single spot on the soil; many sink under their misery[85]; the others crowd into the cities, where, taking up the coarsest labors, they lead a precarious and wretched existence.

Even if the number of negroes were to continue to grow in the same way as in the time when they did not yet have liberty, the number of whites increasing with double speed after the abolition of slavery, the blacks would soon be, as it were, engulfed in the waves of a foreign population.

A country cultivated by slaves is generally less peopled than one cultivated by free men; moreover, America is a new country; at the moment, then, when a State abolishes slavery, it is still only half full. Scarcely is servitude destroyed there, and the need of free workers felt, when a crowd of bold adventurers comes streaming in from all parts of the country; they come to take advantage of the new resources industry is about to find there. The soil is divided among them; a family of whites settles on each portion and takes it over. It is also toward the free States that European emigration is directed. What would the poor man of Europe, who comes seeking ease and happiness in the New World, do if he went to live in a country where labor is stained with ignominy?

Thus the white population grows by its natural movement and at the same time by an immense emigration, while the black population receives no immigrants and grows weaker. Soon the proportion that had existed between the two races is reversed. The negroes no longer form anything but a wretched remnant, a small, poor, and nomadic tribe lost in the midst of an immense people, master of the soil; and one notices their presence only by the injustices and severities of which they are the objects.

In many of the States of the West, the negro race has never appeared; in all the States of the North it is disappearing. The great question of the future thus narrows into a small circle; it becomes thereby less formidable, but not easier to resolve.
As one descends toward the South, it becomes more difficult to abolish slavery to any useful purpose. This results from several material causes that must be set forth.

The first is the climate: it is certain that in proportion as Europeans approach the tropics labor becomes harder for them; many Americans even maintain that, under a certain latitude, it eventually becomes fatal to them, while the negro endures it without danger[86]; but I do not think that this idea, so favorable to the laziness of the man of the South, is founded on experience. It is not hotter in the south of the Union than in the south of Spain and Italy[87]. Why should the European not be able to do the same work there? And if slavery has been abolished in Italy and Spain without the masters perishing, why should not the same thing come to pass in the Union? I do not believe, then, that nature has forbidden the Europeans of Georgia or the Floridas, on pain of death, to draw their subsistence from the soil themselves; but their work would assuredly be more painful and less productive[88] than that of the inhabitants of New England. The free worker thus losing in the South a part of his superiority over the slave, it is less useful to abolish slavery.
All the plants of Europe grow in the North of the Union; the South has special products.

It has been observed that slavery is an expensive means of cultivating cereals. He who harvests wheat in a country where servitude is unknown ordinarily keeps in his service only a small number of workers; at harvest time, and during sowing, he gathers, it is true, many others; but those stay only briefly in his house.

To fill his barns or to sow his fields, the farmer who lives in a slave State is obliged to keep all year a great number of servants who are necessary to him only for a few days; for, unlike free workers, slaves cannot wait, working for themselves, until the moment when someone comes to hire their labor. They must be bought to be used.
Slavery, then, apart from its general disadvantages, is naturally less applicable to countries where cereals are cultivated than to those where other products are harvested.

The cultivation of tobacco, of cotton, and above all of sugar cane, on the contrary, demands continual care. Women and children can be employed in it who could not be used in the cultivation of wheat. Thus slavery is naturally better suited to the country from which the products I have just named come.

Tobacco, cotton, and sugar cane grow only in the South; they form there the principal sources of the country's wealth. By destroying slavery, the men of the South would find themselves in one of two alternatives: either they would be obliged to change their system of cultivation, and then they would enter into competition with the men of the North, more active and more experienced than themselves; or they would cultivate the same products without slaves, and then they would have to bear the competition of other Southern States that had preserved them.
Thus the South has particular reasons for keeping slavery, that the North does not have.

But here is another motive more powerful than all the others. The South could indeed, at a pinch, abolish servitude; but how would it rid itself of the blacks? In the North, slavery and the slaves are driven out together. In the South, this double result cannot be hoped for at the same time.

In showing that servitude was more natural and more advantageous in the South than in the North, I have sufficiently indicated that the number of slaves there must be much greater. It is into the South that the first Africans were brought; it is there that they have always arrived in greatest numbers. As one moves toward the South, the prejudice that keeps idleness in honor gains strength. In the States closest to the tropics, no white man works. Negroes are therefore naturally more numerous in the South than in the North. Every day, as I said above, they become more so; for in proportion as slavery is destroyed at one of the extremities of the Union, the negroes accumulate at the other. Thus the number of blacks grows in the South not only by the natural movement of population, but also by the forced emigration of negroes from the North. The African race has, for growing in this part of the Union, causes analogous to those which make the European race grow so fast in the North.

In the State of Maine, one counts one negro per 300 inhabitants; in Massachusetts, one per 100; in the State of New York, two per 100; in Pennsylvania, three; in Maryland, thirty-four; forty-two in Virginia, and finally fifty-five in South Carolina[89]. Such was the proportion of blacks to whites in the year 1830. But this proportion changes constantly: every day it becomes smaller in the North and greater in the South.

It is evident that in the most southern States of the Union, slavery cannot be abolished as it has been in the Northern States, without running very great dangers that the latter did not have to fear.

We have seen how the Northern States managed the transition between slavery and liberty. They keep the present generation in chains and emancipate future races; in this way, the negroes are introduced into society only little by little, and while keeping in servitude the man who might make ill use of his independence, they set free the one who, before becoming his own master, may still learn the art of being free.

It would be difficult to apply this method to the South. From the moment one declares that, beginning at a certain date, the son of the negro will be free, one introduces the principle and the idea of liberty into the very bosom of servitude: the blacks whom the legislator keeps in slavery and who see their sons leave it are astonished at this unequal division destiny makes between them; they grow uneasy and incensed. From that moment, slavery has lost in their eyes the kind of moral power that time and custom gave it; it is reduced to being no more than a visible abuse of force. The North had nothing to fear from this contrast, because in the North the blacks were few and the whites very numerous. But if this first dawn of liberty were to come and shine at one moment upon two million men, the oppressors should tremble.
After freeing the sons of their slaves, the Europeans of the South would soon be compelled to extend the same benefit to the whole black race.

In the North, as I said earlier, from the moment slavery is abolished, and even from the moment it becomes probable that the time of its abolition is approaching, a double movement takes place: the slaves leave the country to be transported farther south; the whites of the Northern States and emigrants from Europe flow in to take their place.

These two causes cannot operate in the same way in the most southern States. On the one hand, the mass of slaves there is too great for one to hope to make them leave the country; on the other, the Europeans and the Anglo-Americans of the North shrink from going to inhabit a country where labor has not yet been rehabilitated. Besides, they regard with reason as threatened by great misfortunes the States in which the proportion of negroes exceeds or equals that of the whites, and they refrain from bringing their industry that way.

Thus, in abolishing slavery, the men of the South would not succeed, as their brothers of the North have, in bringing the negroes gradually to liberty; they would not appreciably diminish the number of blacks, and they would remain alone to hold them in check. Within a few years, then, one would see a great people of free negroes set in the midst of a nation of whites approximately equal in number.

The same abuses of power that today maintain slavery would then become in the South the source of the greatest dangers the whites would have to fear. Today the descendant of the Europeans alone possesses the soil; he is absolute master of industry; he alone is rich, enlightened, armed. The black has none of these advantages; but he can do without them, he is a slave. Once free, charged with watching over his own fate, can he remain deprived of all these things without perishing? What constituted the white's strength when slavery existed thus exposes him to a thousand perils after slavery is abolished.

Leaving the negro in servitude, he can be kept in a state close to that of the brute; once free, he cannot be prevented from instructing himself enough to measure the extent of his ills and to glimpse the remedy. There is besides a singular principle of relative justice that one finds very deeply lodged in the human heart. Men are far more struck by the inequality that exists within a single class than by the inequalities to be observed between different classes. Slavery one can grasp; but how is one to grasp the existence of several million citizens eternally bent beneath infamy and given over to hereditary miseries? In the North, a population of emancipated negroes feels these evils and resents these injustices; but it is weak and reduced; in the South it would be numerous and strong.

From the moment one admits that the whites and the emancipated negroes are placed on the same soil as two alien peoples, one will see at once that there are only two chances in the future: the negroes and the whites must either merge entirely or separate.
I have already expressed above what my conviction is regarding the first[90]. I do not think that the white race and the black race will anywhere come to live on a footing of equality.

But I believe the difficulty will be far greater still in the United States than anywhere else. It happens that a man stands outside the prejudices of religion, country, and race, and if that man is a king, he can bring about astonishing revolutions in society: a whole people cannot, as it were, lift itself above itself in this way.

A despot bringing together the Americans and their former slaves under the same yoke might perhaps succeed in mixing them: as long as American democracy remains at the head of affairs, no one will dare to attempt such an undertaking, and one can foresee that the freer the whites of the United States are, the more they will try to keep themselves apart.[91]

I said elsewhere that the true link between the European and the Indian was the mixed-blood; in the same way the true transition between the white and the negro is the mulatto: wherever there are very many mulattoes, the fusion of the two races is not impossible.

There are parts of America where the European and the negro have crossed so completely that it is hard to meet a man who is wholly white or wholly black: at that point one can really say that the races are mingled; or rather, in their place a third has come into being that partakes of both without being precisely either.

Of all the Europeans, the English are those who have least mixed their blood with that of the negroes. One sees in the South of the Union more mulattoes than in the North, but infinitely fewer than in any other European colony; mulattoes are very few in number in the United States; they have no strength of their own, and in the quarrels of race they usually make common cause with the whites. So in Europe one often sees the lackeys of great lords playing the noble before the common people.

This pride of origin, natural to the Englishman, is still further heightened in the American by the individual pride that democratic liberty produces. The white man of the United States is proud of his race and proud of himself.

Moreover, since the whites and the negroes do not come to mix in the North of the Union, how should they mix in the South? Can one suppose for a moment that the American of the South, placed, as he always will be, between the white man, with all his physical and moral superiority, and the negro, could ever think of merging with the latter? The American of the South has two energetic passions that will always carry him to keep apart: he will fear to resemble the negro, his former slave, and to descend below the white, his neighbor.

If one absolutely had to foresee the future, I would say that, in the probable course of things, the abolition of slavery in the South will increase the repugnance the white population there feels for blacks. I base this opinion on what I have already noted as analogous in the North. I have said that the white men of the North keep away from negroes the more carefully as the legislator marks the less the legal separation that should exist between them: why should it not be so in the South? In the North, when the whites are afraid of coming to be confounded with the blacks, they fear an imaginary danger. In the South, where the danger would be real, I cannot believe the fear would be less.

If, on the one hand, it is acknowledged (and the fact is not in doubt) that in the southernmost extremity the blacks are constantly accumulating and growing more rapidly than the whites; and if, on the other, it is granted that it is impossible to foresee the time when blacks and whites will come to mingle and to draw the same advantages from the state of society — must one not conclude that, in the Southern States, blacks and whites will sooner or later end by coming into conflict?
What will be the final result of this struggle?

It will be readily understood that on this point one must shut oneself within the vagueness of conjecture. The human mind manages only with difficulty to trace, as it were, a great circle around the future; but within that circle moves chance, which escapes every effort. In the picture of the future, chance always forms the dark spot the eye of the intellect cannot penetrate. What may be said is this: in the Antilles, it is the white race that seems destined to succumb; on the continent, the black race.

In the Antilles, the whites are isolated in the midst of an immense population of blacks; on the continent, the blacks are placed between the sea and an innumerable people that already extends above them like a compact mass, from the ice of Canada to the frontiers of Virginia, from the banks of the Missouri to the shores of the Atlantic. If the whites of North America remain united, it is hard to believe that the negroes can escape the destruction that threatens them; they will succumb to the sword or to misery. But the black populations gathered along the Gulf of Mexico have a chance of safety if the struggle between the two races comes to be established at a time when the American confederation has been dissolved. Once the federal ring is broken, the men of the South would be wrong to count on lasting support from their brothers of the North. The latter know that the danger can never reach them; if a positive duty does not compel them to march to the aid of the South, one can foresee that the sympathies of race will be powerless.

Whatever the time of the struggle, however, the whites of the South, even if abandoned to themselves, will enter the lists with an immense superiority of enlightenment and resources; but the blacks will have on their side numbers and the energy of despair. These are great resources when one has arms in hand. Perhaps the white race of the South will then meet the fate that befell the Moors of Spain. After occupying the country for centuries, it will withdraw at last little by little toward the land from which its forefathers once came, leaving to the negroes possession of a country that Providence seems to have destined for them, since they live there without difficulty and work there more easily than the whites.

The danger, more or less distant, but inevitable, of a struggle between the blacks and the whites who people the south of the Union, presents itself constantly as a painful dream to the imagination of the Americans. The inhabitants of the North talk every day of these perils, although they have nothing directly to fear from them. They search in vain for a means of averting the misfortunes they foresee.

In the Southern States, people are silent; they do not speak of the future to strangers; they avoid explaining themselves about it among friends; each, so to speak, conceals it from himself. The silence of the South has something more frightening about it than the noisy fears of the North.
This general preoccupation has given rise to an undertaking, almost unknown, that can change the fate of part of the human race.

Fearing the dangers I have just described, a certain number of American citizens have joined together in a society for the purpose of transporting, at their own expense, to the coasts of Guinea, the free negroes who wish to escape the tyranny that weighs on them.[92]

In 1820 the society of which I speak succeeded in founding in Africa, on the 7th degree of north latitude, an establishment to which it gave the name of *Liberia*. The latest news reported that two thousand five hundred negroes had already gathered there. Transported into their ancient homeland, the blacks have introduced American institutions there. Liberia has a representative system, negro jurors, negro magistrates, negro priests; one sees there temples and newspapers, and by a strange turn of this world's vicissitudes, whites are forbidden to settle within its walls[93].

Here is surely a strange caprice of fortune. Two centuries have passed since the day when the inhabitant of Europe undertook to tear the negroes from their families and their country in order to transport them to the shores of North America. Today one sees the European busy carrying back across the Atlantic Ocean the descendants of those same negroes, in order to set them down again on the soil from which he had once torn their fathers. Barbarians have drawn the lights of civilization from the bosom of servitude, and have learned in slavery the art of being free.

Until our own day, Africa was closed to the arts and sciences of the whites. The lights of Europe, imported by Africans, will perhaps penetrate there. There is a fine and great idea in the founding of Liberia; but this idea, which may become so fruitful for the Old World, is sterile for the New.

In twelve years, the society for the colonization of the blacks has transported to Africa two thousand five hundred negroes. During the same span of time, about seven hundred thousand were born in the United States.

Even if the colony of Liberia were in a position to receive thousands of new inhabitants each year, and these were in a condition to be brought there usefully; even if the Union were to put itself in the society's place and apply each year its treasure[94] and its ships to exporting negroes to Africa, it could still not balance the mere natural increase of the black population; and removing each year fewer men than come into the world, it would not even succeed in halting the development of the evil that grows every day in its bosom.[95]

The negro race will not leave the shores of the American continent, to which the passions and the vices of Europe brought it; it will not disappear from the New World except by ceasing to exist. The inhabitants of the United States can push back the misfortunes they fear, but they cannot destroy the cause of those misfortunes today.
I am obliged to confess that I do not regard the abolition of servitude as a means of delaying, in the Southern States, the struggle of the two races.

The negroes can remain slaves a long time without complaining; but once they have entered the ranks of free men, they will soon grow indignant at being deprived of nearly all the rights of citizens; and being unable to become the equals of the whites, they will not be slow to show themselves their enemies.

In the North, it was all to the profit of the masters to emancipate the slaves: they thus rid themselves of slavery without having anything to fear from the free negroes. The latter were too few ever to claim their rights. It is not so in the South.

The question of slavery was for the masters, in the North, a commercial and manufacturing question; in the South, it is a question of life and death. One must not, then, confuse slavery in the North with slavery in the South.

God forbid that I should seek, as certain American authors do, to justify the principle of negro servitude; I say only that all those who have admitted that frightful principle in the past are not equally free today to depart from it.

I confess that, when I consider the state of the South, I find for the white race that inhabits those regions only two ways of acting: emancipate the negroes and merge them with itself; remain isolated from them and keep them as long as possible in slavery. The middle courses seem to me to lead very shortly to the most horrible of all civil wars, and perhaps to the ruin of one of the two races.
The Americans of the South view the question from this angle, and they act accordingly. Not wishing to merge with the negroes, they refuse to set them at liberty.

It is not that all the inhabitants of the South regard slavery as necessary to the master's wealth; on this point, many of them agree with the men of the North, and readily admit with them that servitude is an evil; but they think this evil must be preserved in order to live.

As enlightenment has grown in the South, it has made the inhabitants of that part of the territory perceive that slavery is harmful to the master, and this same enlightenment shows them, more clearly than they had seen until then, the near-impossibility of destroying it. Hence a singular contrast: slavery establishes itself more and more firmly in the laws as its usefulness is more contested; and while its principle is gradually abolished in the North, in the South harsher and harsher consequences are drawn from that same principle.

The legislation of the Southern States with respect to slaves presents today a kind of unheard-of atrocity, which by itself reveals some profound disturbance in the laws of humanity. It is enough to read the legislation of the Southern States to judge the desperate position of the two races that inhabit them.

It is not that the Americans of this part of the Union have precisely increased the rigors of servitude; on the contrary, they have softened the material lot of the slaves. The ancients knew only irons and death to maintain slavery; the Americans of the South have found more intellectual guarantees for the duration of their power. They have, if I may put it this way, spiritualized despotism and violence. In antiquity, the effort was to prevent the slave from breaking his chains; in our day, the effort has been to take from him the desire to do so.

The ancients chained the body of the slave, but they left his mind free and allowed him to enlighten himself. In this they were consistent with themselves; there was then a natural way out of servitude: from one day to the next the slave could become free and the equal of his master.

The Americans of the South, who do not believe that at any time the negroes will be able to merge with them, have forbidden, under severe penalties, teaching them to read or write. Not wishing to raise them to their level, they keep them as close as possible to the brute.
In all times the hope of liberty had been placed within slavery itself, to soften its rigors.

The Americans of the South have understood that emancipation always offers dangers, when the freedman cannot one day come to be assimilated to the master. To give a man liberty and to leave him in misery and ignominy — what is that but to furnish a future chief to a slave revolt? It had also long been observed that the presence of the free negro cast a vague unease into the soul of those who were not, and made the idea of their rights penetrate, like an uncertain glimmer. The Americans of the South have taken from the masters, in most cases, the faculty of emancipating.[96]

I met in the South of the Union an old man who had once lived in an unlawful commerce with one of his negresses. He had had several children by her who, on coming into the world, had become the slaves of their father. He had thought several times of bequeathing them at least their liberty, but years had passed before he could remove the obstacles set in the way of emancipation by the legislator. Meanwhile old age had come, and he was about to die. He saw before him his sons dragged from market to market, passing from paternal authority under the rod of a stranger. These horrible images threw his expiring imagination into delirium. I saw him in the throes of despair, and I understood then how nature knew how to avenge itself for the wounds the laws inflicted on it.
These evils are dreadful, no doubt; but are they not the foreseen and necessary consequence of the very principle of servitude among the moderns?

From the moment the Europeans took their slaves from within a race of men different from their own, that many of them considered as inferior to the other human races, and with which all of them view with horror the idea of ever being assimilated, they have supposed slavery eternal; for between the extreme inequality that servitude creates and the complete equality that independence naturally produces among men, there is no durable middle state. The Europeans have vaguely felt this truth, but without admitting it. Whenever it was a question of negroes, they were seen to obey now their interest or their pride, now their pity. They have violated, with regard to the black, every right of humanity, and then have instructed him in the value and inviolability of those rights. They have opened their ranks to their slaves, and when the latter tried to enter them, they have driven them out with ignominy. Wanting servitude, they have allowed themselves to be drawn, in spite of themselves or unawares, toward liberty, without having the courage to be either completely unjust or entirely just.

If it is impossible to foresee a time when the Americans of the South will mingle their blood with that of the negroes, can they, without exposing themselves to perish, allow the latter to attain liberty? And if they are obliged, to save their own race, to wish to keep them in chains, must they not be excused for taking the most effective means to do so?

What happens in the South of the Union seems to me at once the most horrible and the most natural consequence of slavery. When I see the order of nature overturned, when I hear humanity crying out and struggling in vain against the laws, I confess that I find no indignation with which to brand the men of our day, the authors of these outrages; but I gather all my hatred against those who, after more than a thousand years of equality, have brought servitude into the world again.

Whatever the efforts of the Americans of the South to preserve slavery, they will not always succeed. Slavery, confined to a single spot on the globe, attacked by Christianity as unjust, by political economy as disastrous; slavery, in the midst of democratic liberty and the enlightenment of our age, is not an institution that can endure. It will end through the act of the slave or through that of the master. In either case great misfortunes are to be expected.
If liberty is refused the negroes of the South, they will end by seizing it for themselves by violence; if it is granted them, they will not be slow to abuse it.
WHAT ARE THE CHANCES OF DURATION OF THE AMERICAN UNION, AND WHAT DANGERS THREATEN IT.

The preponderant force lies in the States rather than in the Union. — The confederation will last only as long as all the States that compose it wish to belong to it. — Causes that must lead them to remain united. — Usefulness of being united in order to resist foreigners and so as not to have foreigners in America. — Providence has not raised natural barriers between the different States. — There are no material interests that divide them. — Interest the North has in the prosperity and union of the South and West; the South in those of the North and West; the West in those of the two others. — Immaterial interests that unite the Americans. — Uniformity of opinions. — The dangers of the confederation are born of differences of character in the men who compose it, and of their passions. — Characters of the men of the South and the North. — The rapid growth of the Union is one of its greatest perils. — Movement of the population toward the Northwest. — Gravitation of power in that direction. — Passions to which these rapid movements of fortune give rise. — Does the government of the Union, while it lasts, tend to gain force or to weaken? — Various signs of weakening. — *Internal improvements.* — Vacant lands. — Indians. — The Bank affair. — The Tariff affair. — General Jackson.

The maintenance of what exists in each of the States composing it depends in part on the existence of the Union. One must, then, first examine what the probable fate of the Union is. But before all, it is well to settle one point: if the present confederation came to break up, it seems to me incontestable that the States that compose it would not return to their original individuality. In place of one Union, several would form. I do not intend to inquire on what bases these new Unions would come to be established; what I wish to show are the causes that may bring about the dismemberment of the present confederation.

To do so, I shall be obliged to retrace some of the paths I have already entered upon. I shall have to set before the eye several objects already known. I know that in so doing I expose myself to the reader's reproaches; but the importance of the matter still to be treated is my excuse. I prefer to repeat myself sometimes than not to be understood, and I would rather harm the author than the subject.
The legislators who framed the constitution of 1789 strove to give the federal power a separate existence and a preponderant force.

But they were bounded by the very conditions of the problem they had to solve. They had not been charged with constituting the government of a single people, but with regulating the association of several peoples; and whatever their wishes, they always had to come to share the exercise of sovereignty.
To grasp fully the consequences of this sharing, it is necessary to make a brief distinction among the acts of sovereignty.
