There are objects that are national by their nature, that is to say, that relate only to the nation taken as a body, and that can be entrusted only to the man or assembly that most completely represents the entire nation. Among these I would place war and diplomacy.
There are others that are provincial by their nature, that is to say, that relate only to certain localities, and can be properly treated only in the locality itself. Such is the municipal budget.

Lastly there are objects of a mixed nature: they are national in that they concern all the individuals composing the nation; they are provincial in that there is no necessity for the nation itself to provide for them. Such, for example, are the rights that regulate the civil and political state of the citizens. There is no social state without civil and political rights. These rights therefore concern every citizen equally; but it is not always necessary to the existence and prosperity of the nation that these rights be uniform, and consequently that they be regulated by the central power.

Among the objects with which sovereignty is concerned, there are two necessary categories; they are found in every well-constituted society, whatever the basis on which the social compact has been established.

Between these two extreme points are placed, like a floating mass, the general but not national objects that I have called mixed. These objects, being neither exclusively national nor entirely provincial, can be left for either the national or the provincial government to provide for, according to the agreement of those who associate, without the aim of the association ceasing to be attained.

Most often, simple individuals unite to form the sovereign, and their gathering composes a people. Below the general government they have given themselves, one finds then only individual forces or collective powers, each of which represents a very small fraction of the sovereign. In this case too it is the general government that is most naturally called upon to regulate, not only the objects national by their essence, but the greater part of the mixed objects of which I have already spoken. The localities are reduced to the portion of sovereignty indispensable to their well-being.

Sometimes, by a fact prior to the association, the sovereign happens to be composed of already organized political bodies; it happens then that the provincial government is charged with providing not only for objects exclusively provincial in their nature, but also for all or part of the mixed objects of which we have just spoken. For the confederated nations, which were themselves sovereigns before their union, and which continue to represent a very considerable fraction of the sovereign though they have united, have meant to yield to the general government only the exercise of the rights indispensable to the Union.

When the national government, independently of the prerogatives inherent in its nature, finds itself invested with the right to regulate the mixed objects of sovereignty, it possesses a preponderant force. Not only does it have many rights, but all the rights it does not have are at its mercy, and there is reason to fear that it may end by stripping the provincial governments of their natural and necessary prerogatives.

When, on the contrary, it is the provincial government that finds itself invested with the right to regulate the mixed objects, an opposite tendency prevails in society. The preponderant force then resides in the province, not in the nation; and one must fear that the national government may end by being stripped of the privileges necessary to its existence.
Single peoples, then, are naturally drawn toward centralization, and confederations toward dismemberment.
It only remains to apply these general ideas to the American Union.
To the particular States was necessarily left the right to regulate purely provincial objects.

Furthermore, these same States retained the right to fix the civil and political capacity of the citizens, to regulate the relations of men among themselves, and to render them justice; rights that are general by their nature, but that do not necessarily belong to the national government.

We have seen that to the government of the Union was delegated the power to give orders in the name of the whole nation in cases where the nation would have to act as a single individual. It represented it before foreigners; it directed against the common enemy the common forces. In a word, it concerned itself with the objects I have called exclusively national.
In this division of the rights of sovereignty, the share of the Union still seems at first glance greater than that of the States; a somewhat closer examination shows that in fact it is smaller.
The government of the Union carries out larger enterprises, but one rarely feels it act. The provincial government does smaller things, but it never rests and reveals its existence at every moment.
The government of the Union watches over the general interests of the country; but the general interests of a people have only a contestable influence on individual happiness.
The affairs of the province, on the contrary, visibly affect the well-being of those who inhabit it.

The Union secures the independence and greatness of the nation, things that do not immediately touch private men. The State maintains liberty, regulates rights, guarantees fortune, secures the life and the entire future of each citizen.

The federal government is placed at a great distance from its subjects; the provincial government is within reach of all. One has only to raise one's voice to be heard by it. The central government has on its side the passions of a few superior men who aspire to direct it: on the side of the provincial government is found the interest of men of the second rank, who hope to obtain power only in their State; and it is these who, placed near the people, exercise the most power upon them.

The Americans, then, have far more to expect and to fear from the State than from the Union; and, in keeping with the natural course of the human heart, they must attach themselves far more vividly to the first than to the second.
In this, habits and feelings agree with interests.

When a compact nation breaks up its sovereignty and arrives at the state of confederation, memories, usages, habits long struggle against the laws, and give the central government a force the laws refuse it. When confederated peoples unite themselves under a single sovereignty, the same causes work in the opposite direction. I do not doubt that if France were to become a confederated republic like that of the United States, the government would at first prove more energetic there than that of the Union; and if the Union were to constitute itself as a monarchy like France, I think the American government would remain for some time weaker than ours. At the time when national life was created among the Anglo-Americans, provincial existence was already long established; necessary relations had been established between the townships and the individuals of the same State; people there had grown accustomed to consider certain objects under a common viewpoint, and to occupy themselves exclusively with certain undertakings as representing a special interest.

The Union is an immense body that offers patriotism a vague object to embrace. The State has settled forms and circumscribed bounds; it represents a certain number of things known and dear to those who inhabit it. It is merged with the very image of the soil, identified with property, with family, with memories of the past, with the labors of the present, with dreams of the future. Patriotism, which most often is only an extension of individual egoism, has therefore remained in the State, and has not, so to speak, passed over to the Union.
Thus interests, habits, feelings combine to concentrate true political life in the State, and not in the Union.
One can easily judge the difference in strength between the two governments by watching each of them move within the circle of its power.

Whenever a State government addresses a man or an association of men, its language is clear and imperative; the same is true of the federal government when it speaks to individuals; but as soon as it finds itself face to face with a State, it begins to parley: it explains its motives, justifies its conduct; it argues, advises, hardly orders. If doubts arise about the limits of the constitutional powers of each government, the provincial government claims its right boldly, and takes prompt and energetic measures to support it. During this time the government of the Union reasons; it appeals to the good sense of the nation, to its interests, to its glory; it temporizes, it negotiates; it is only when reduced to the last extremity that it finally resolves to act. At first sight one might believe that it is the provincial government that is armed with the forces of the entire nation, and that Congress represents a State.

The federal government, in spite of the efforts of those who constituted it, is therefore, as I have already said elsewhere, by its very nature, a weak government, which more than any other needs the free concurrence of the governed to subsist.

It is easy to see that its purpose is to carry out with ease the wish of the States to remain united. This first condition being fulfilled, it is wise, strong, and agile. It has been organized so as to meet, ordinarily, only individuals before it, and to overcome easily the resistance opposed to the common will; but the federal government was not established on the supposition that the States, or several of them, would cease to wish to be united.

If the sovereignty of the Union were today to enter into a struggle with that of the States, it can readily be foreseen that it would succumb; I doubt even whether the combat would ever be seriously joined. Whenever an obstinate resistance is opposed to the federal government, it will be seen to yield. Experience has shown so far that whenever a State firmly willed a thing and resolutely demanded it, it never failed to obtain it; and that when it flatly refused to act[97], it was left free to do so.
Even if the government of the Union had a force of its own, the material situation of the country would make its use very difficult[98].

The United States cover an immense territory; long distances separate them; the population is scattered across regions still half wilderness. If the Union undertook to maintain the confederates in their duty by arms, its situation would be analogous to that of England during the war of independence.

Besides, a government, however strong, cannot easily escape the consequences of a principle once it has admitted that principle as the foundation of the public law that is to govern it. The confederation was formed by the free will of the States; in uniting, these did not lose their nationality, and they did not fuse into one and the same people. If today one of those same States were to wish to withdraw its name from the contract, it would be hard to prove that it could not do so. The federal government, to oppose it, would not visibly rest either on force or on right.

For the federal government to triumph easily over the resistance offered it by some of its subjects, it would be necessary that the particular interest of one or more of them be intimately bound to the existence of the Union, as has often been seen in the history of confederations.

Suppose that among the States the federal bond gathers there are a few that alone enjoy the principal advantages of union, or whose prosperity depends entirely on the fact of union; it is clear that the central power will find in these a very great support for keeping the others in obedience. But it will then draw its strength no longer from itself; it will draw it from a principle contrary to its nature. Peoples confederate themselves only to draw equal advantages from union, and in the case just cited, it is because inequality reigns among the united nations that the federal government is powerful.

Suppose again that one of the confederated States has acquired a preponderance great enough to take possession of the central power by itself; it will consider the other States as its subjects, and will make its own sovereignty respected in the pretended sovereignty of the Union. Great things will then be done in the name of the federal government, but, truly speaking, that government will exist no longer[99].
In both these cases, the power that acts in the name of the confederation becomes the stronger the more one departs from the natural state and the recognized principle of confederations.

In America, the present union is useful to all the States, but it is essential to none of them. Several States could break the federal tie without the lot of the others being compromised, though the sum of their happiness would be less. As there is no State whose existence or prosperity is entirely tied to the present confederation, none is disposed to make very great personal sacrifices to preserve it.

On the other side, one does not see a State which, at present, has any great interest of ambition in maintaining the confederation such as we see it in our day. All do not exercise, no doubt, the same influence in the federal councils, but none can flatter itself with dominating there, or can treat its confederates as inferiors or as subjects.

It seems to me certain, therefore, that if a portion of the Union seriously wished to separate from the other, not only could it not be prevented from doing so, but no attempt would even be made to prevent it. The present Union, then, will last only as long as all the States that compose it continue to wish to belong to it.
This point fixed, we are more at ease: it is no longer a question of inquiring whether the States now confederated could separate, but whether they will wish to remain united.
Among all the reasons that make the present union useful to the Americans, two principal ones stand out whose evidence readily strikes every eye.

Although the Americans are, so to speak, alone on their continent, commerce gives them as neighbors all the peoples with whom they trade. Despite their apparent isolation, the Americans have a need to be strong, and they cannot be strong except by all remaining united.

The States, by disuniting, would not only reduce their force against foreigners; they would create foreigners on their own soil. From then on they would enter into a system of internal customs: they would divide the valleys with imaginary lines; they would imprison the courses of the rivers, and hamper in every way the exploitation of the immense continent that God has given them for a domain.
Today they have no invasion to fear, consequently no armies to keep up, no taxes to levy; if the Union were to break up, the need for all these things would perhaps soon be felt.
The Americans, then, have an immense interest in remaining united.
On the other hand, it is almost impossible to discover what kind of material interest a portion of the Union would have, at present, in separating from the others.

When one casts the eye over a map of the United States and sees the chain of the Allegheny Mountains running from northeast to southwest, traversing the country over an extent of 400 leagues, one is tempted to think that the aim of Providence was to raise between the basin of the Mississippi and the shores of the Atlantic one of those natural barriers which, opposing themselves to lasting relations among men, form, as it were, the necessary limits of different peoples.

But the average height of the Alleghenies does not exceed 800 meters[100]. Their rounded summits and the spacious valleys they enclose in their windings offer in a thousand places easy access. Moreover, the chief rivers that come to pour their waters into the Atlantic Ocean — the Hudson, the Susquehanna, the Potomac[101] — have their sources beyond the Alleghenies, on an open plateau bordering on the basin of the Mississippi. Starting from this region[102], they force their way through the rampart that seemed bound to throw them back westward, and trace, in the heart of the mountains, natural roads always open to man.

No barrier, then, rises between the different parts of the country occupied today by the Anglo-Americans. Far from serving as limits to peoples, the Alleghenies do not even border on States. New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia enclose them within their limits, and stretch as far to the west as to the east of those mountains[103].

The territory occupied in our day by the twenty-four States of the Union and the three great districts not yet ranked among the States, although they already have inhabitants, covers a surface of 131,144 square leagues[104], that is to say, it already presents an area almost equal to five times that of France. Within these limits are found a varied soil, different temperatures, and very diverse products.

This great extent of territory occupied by the Anglo-American republics has given rise to doubts about the maintenance of their union. Here a distinction is necessary: contrary interests are sometimes created in the various provinces of a vast empire, and end by entering into conflict; it happens then that the greatness of the State is what most compromises its duration. But if the men who cover that vast territory have no interests among themselves opposed to one another, the very extent of the territory must serve their prosperity; for the unity of the government singularly favors the exchange that can be made of the various products of the soil, and by making their distribution easier, it increases their value.
Now, I see in the different parts of the Union different interests, but I do not discover any that are contrary to one another.

The Southern States are almost exclusively agricultural; the Northern States are particularly manufacturing and commercial; the Western States are at once manufacturing and agricultural. In the South, tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugar are grown; in the North and West, maize and wheat. Here are diverse sources of wealth; but to draw on those sources, there is a common means equally favorable to all: the Union.

The North, which carries the wealth of the Anglo-Americans into all parts of the world and the wealth of the universe into the bosom of the Union, has an obvious interest in the confederation's subsisting as it is today, so that the number of American producers and consumers it is called to serve may remain as large as possible. The North is the most natural intermediary between the South and the West of the Union, on the one hand, and the rest of the world on the other; the North, then, must wish that the South and the West remain united and prosperous, so that they may furnish raw materials to its factories and freight to its ships.

The South and the West, for their part, have a still more direct interest in the preservation of the Union and the prosperity of the North. The products of the South are exported, for the most part, overseas; the South and the West therefore need the commercial resources of the North. They must wish the Union to have a great maritime power to be able to protect them effectively. The South and the West must contribute willingly to the costs of a navy, although they have no ships of their own; for if the fleets of Europe came to blockade the ports of the South and the delta of the Mississippi, what would become of the rice of the Carolinas, the tobacco of Virginia, the sugar and cotton that grow in the valleys of the Mississippi? There is not a portion of the federal budget that does not serve a material interest common to all the confederates.
Independent of this commercial usefulness, the South and the West of the Union find a great political advantage in remaining united with each other and with the North.
The South contains within itself an immense population of slaves, a population threatening in the present, still more threatening in the future.

The Western States occupy the bottom of a single valley. The rivers that water the territory of these States, starting from the Rocky Mountains or the Alleghenies, all come to mingle their waters with those of the Mississippi, and to roll with it toward the Gulf of Mexico. The Western States are entirely cut off, by their position, from the traditions of Europe and the civilization of the Old World.

The inhabitants of the South, then, must wish to preserve the Union so as not to remain alone facing the blacks, and the inhabitants of the West, so as not to find themselves shut up in the middle of Central America without free communication with the world.
The North, for its part, must wish that the Union not be divided, so as to remain the ring that joins this great body to the rest of the world.
There exists, then, a close link between the material interests of all the parts of the Union.
I would say as much for the opinions and sentiments one might call man's immaterial interests.

The inhabitants of the United States talk a great deal of their love of country; I confess I do not trust this calculated patriotism which is founded on interest and which interest, by changing its object, may destroy.
Nor do I attach great importance to the language of the Americans when they daily express the intention of preserving the federal system their fathers adopted.

What keeps a great number of citizens under the same government is far less a reasoned will to remain united than the instinctive and, as it were, involuntary accord that results from the similarity of feelings and the resemblance of opinions.

I will never agree that men form a society for the mere fact that they recognize the same head and obey the same laws; there is society only when men view a great number of objects in the same light; when, on a great number of subjects, they have the same opinions; when, finally, the same facts produce in them the same impressions and the same thoughts.

Anyone who, viewing the question from this angle, were to study what passes in the United States would discover without trouble that their inhabitants, divided as they are into twenty-four distinct sovereignties, nevertheless constitute a single people; and he might even come to think that the state of society exists more truly within the Anglo-American Union than among certain nations of Europe that have, after all, only a single legislation and submit to a single man.
Though the Anglo-Americans have several religions, they all have the same way of viewing religion.

They do not always agree on the means to take in order to govern well, and they vary on some of the forms it is fitting to give to government; but they agree on the general principles that must regulate human societies. From Maine to the Floridas, from Missouri to the Atlantic Ocean, it is believed that the origin of all legitimate powers is in the people. They have the same ideas about liberty and equality; they profess the same opinions on the press, the right of association, the jury, the responsibility of the agents of power.
If we pass from political and religious ideas to the philosophical and moral opinions that regulate the daily actions of life and direct conduct as a whole, we shall observe the same agreement.

The Anglo-Americans[105] place moral authority in universal reason, as they place political power in the universality of citizens, and they hold that it is the sense of all that one must rely on to discern what is allowed or forbidden, what is true or false. Most of them think that the knowledge of one's well-understood interest suffices to lead man toward what is just and honest. They believe that each man on coming into the world has received the faculty of governing himself, and that no one has the right to force his fellow to be happy. All have a vivid faith in human perfectibility; they judge that the diffusion of enlightenment must necessarily produce useful results, and ignorance bring about disastrous effects; all consider society as a body in progress; humanity as a changing picture, in which nothing is, or ought to be, fixed forever, and they admit that what seems good to them today may tomorrow be replaced by the better that is still hidden.
I do not say that all these opinions are correct, but they are American.
At the same time as the Anglo-Americans are thus united among themselves by common ideas, they are separated from all other peoples by a feeling of pride.

For fifty years it has not ceased to be repeated to the inhabitants of the United States that they form the only religious, enlightened, and free people. They see that with them up to now democratic institutions are prospering, while they fail in the rest of the world; they thus have an immense opinion of themselves, and they are not far from believing that they form a species apart within the human race.

Thus the dangers with which the American Union is threatened arise no more from the diversity of opinions than from that of interests. They must be sought in the variety of characters and in the passions of the Americans.

The men who inhabit the immense territory of the United States are almost all descended from a common stock; but over time the climate, and above all slavery, have introduced marked differences between the character of the English of the South of the United States and that of the English of the North.

It is generally believed among us that slavery gives one part of the Union interests contrary to those of the other. I have not observed this to be the case. Slavery has not created in the South interests contrary to those of the North; but it has modified the character of the inhabitants of the South and given them different habits.
I have made known elsewhere what influence servitude has exercised on the commercial capacity of the Americans of the South; this same influence extends equally to their mores.

The slave is a servant who does not argue and who submits to everything without a murmur. Sometimes he assassinates his master, but he never resists him. In the South there are no families so poor that they do not have slaves. The American of the South, from his birth, is invested with a kind of domestic dictatorship; the first notions he receives of life teach him that he was born to command, and the first habit he contracts is that of dominating without effort. Education thus tends powerfully to make of the American of the South a haughty man, prompt, irascible, violent, ardent in his desires, impatient of obstacles; but easily discouraged if he cannot triumph at the first stroke.

The American of the North does not see slaves running about his cradle. He does not even see free servants there, for most often he must himself provide for his needs. Scarcely is he in the world when the idea of necessity comes from all sides to present itself to his mind; he therefore learns early to know exactly by himself the natural limit of his power; he does not expect to bend by force the wills that will be opposed to his own, and he knows that to obtain the support of his fellows he must above all win their favor. He is therefore patient, reflective, tolerant, slow to act, and persevering in his designs.

In the southern States the most pressing needs of man are always satisfied. Thus the American of the South is not preoccupied with the material cares of life; someone else attends to them for him. Free on this point, his imagination is directed toward other objects, larger and less precisely defined. The American of the South loves grandeur, luxury, glory, noise, pleasures, and idleness above all; nothing constrains him to make efforts to live, and since he has no necessary labor, he sleeps, and undertakes nothing useful either.

Since equality of fortunes reigns in the North, and slavery no longer exists there, man finds himself, as it were, absorbed by those same material cares that the white of the South disdains. From his childhood he busies himself with combating poverty, and he learns to place comfort above all the joys of mind and heart. Concentrated on the small details of life, his imagination dies out, his ideas are less numerous and less general, but they become more practical, clearer, and more precise. Since he directs toward the single study of well-being all the efforts of his intelligence, he is not slow to excel in it; he knows admirably how to make use of nature and of men to produce wealth; he understands wonderfully the art of making society conspire toward the prosperity of each of its members, and of extracting from individual egoism the happiness of all.
The man of the North has not only experience but also knowledge; yet he does not prize science as a pleasure, he values it as a means, and seizes eagerly only its useful applications.
The American of the South is more spontaneous, more spirited, more open, more generous, more intellectual, and more brilliant.
The American of the North is more active, more reasonable, more enlightened, and more skillful.
The one has the tastes, the prejudices, the weaknesses, and the grandeur of all aristocracies.
The other, the qualities and defects that characterize the middle class.

Bring two men together in society, give those two men the same interests and in part the same opinions; if their character, their enlightenment, and their civilization differ, there are great chances they will not agree. The same remark applies to a society of nations.
Slavery, then, does not attack the American confederation directly through interests, but indirectly through mores.

The States that adhered to the federal pact in 1790 numbered thirteen; the confederation counts twenty-four today. The population, which stood at nearly four million in 1790, had quadrupled in a span of forty years; in 1830 it had risen to nearly thirteen million[106].
Such changes cannot occur without danger.
For a society of nations as for a society of individuals, there are three main chances of duration: the wisdom of the associates, their individual weakness, and their small number.

The Americans who leave the shores of the Atlantic to plunge into the West are adventurers impatient of every kind of yoke, greedy for wealth, often cast out by the States that saw their birth. They arrive in the midst of the wilderness without knowing one another. They find there nothing to contain them, neither traditions, nor family spirit, nor examples. Among them the empire of laws is weak, and that of mores weaker still. The men who fill each day the valleys of the Mississippi are therefore inferior in every respect to the Americans who inhabit within the old limits of the Union. Yet they already exercise a great influence in its councils, and come to the government of common affairs before having learned to govern themselves[107].

The weaker the associates are individually, the greater chance the society has of lasting, for then they have security only in remaining united. When in 1790 the most populous of the American republics did not have 500,000 inhabitants[108], each of them felt its insignificance as an independent people, and this thought made obedience to federal authority easier. But when one of the confederated States counts 2,000,000 inhabitants like the State of New York, and covers a territory equal to a fourth of that of France[109], it feels itself strong by itself, and even if it continues to desire union as useful to its well-being, it no longer regards it as necessary to its existence; it can do without it; and while consenting to remain in it, it is not slow to wish to predominate in it.

The mere multiplication of the members of the Union would already tend powerfully to break the federal bond. All men placed at the same point of view do not view the same objects in the same way. It is so all the more when the point of view is different. As the number of American republics grows, then, the chance of bringing them all to assent to the same laws diminishes.

Today the interests of the various parts of the Union are not contrary to one another; but who could foresee the various changes that a near future will produce in a country where each day creates cities and each five years nations?

Since the founding of the English colonies, the number of inhabitants there has doubled about every twenty-two years; I see no causes that should arrest this progressive movement of the Anglo-American population from now to the end of a century. Before a hundred years have passed, I think the territory occupied or claimed by the United States will be covered by more than a hundred million inhabitants and divided into forty States[110].

Grant that these hundred million men have no differing interests; grant them all, on the contrary, an equal advantage in remaining united; I say that, by the mere fact that they are a hundred million forming forty distinct nations of unequal power, the maintenance of the federal government will be no more than a happy accident.

I am willing to credit human perfectibility; but until men have changed their nature and have transformed themselves completely, I shall refuse to believe in the durability of a government whose task is to hold together forty diverse peoples spread over a surface equal to half of Europe[111], to avoid among them rivalries, ambition, and strife, and to unite the action of their independent wills toward the accomplishment of the same designs.
But the greatest peril the Union runs as it grows comes from the continual displacement of forces that takes place within it.

From the shores of Lake Superior to the Gulf of Mexico, as the crow flies, one counts about four hundred French leagues. Along this immense line winds the frontier of the United States; sometimes it falls back within these limits, more often it penetrates far beyond them into the wilderness. It has been calculated that along this whole vast front the whites advance, on average, seven leagues every year[112]. From time to time an obstacle is met: an unproductive district, a lake, an Indian nation unexpectedly across the way. The column halts then for a moment; its two extremities curve inward upon themselves, and once they have joined again, the advance is resumed. There is something providential in this gradual and continuous march of the European race toward the Rocky Mountains: it is like a deluge of men rising without ceasing, lifted each day by the hand of God.

Within this first line of conquerors cities are built and vast States are founded. In 1790 only a few thousand pioneers were scattered through the valleys of the Mississippi; today those same valleys contain as many men as the whole Union contained in 1790. The population there rises to nearly four million inhabitants[113]. The city of Washington was founded in 1800, at the very center of the American confederation; now it finds itself placed at one of its extremities. The representatives of the farthest western States[114], in order to take their seats in Congress, are already obliged to make as long a journey as the traveler who would go from Vienna to Paris.
All the States of the Union are being drawn at the same time toward fortune; but all cannot grow and prosper in the same proportion.

In the north of the Union, branches detached from the chain of the Alleghenies, reaching as far as the Atlantic Ocean, form spacious roads and ports always open to the largest vessels. From the Potomac southward, on the contrary, following the coasts of America to the mouth of the Mississippi, one finds only a flat and sandy terrain. In this part of the Union the outlets of nearly all the rivers are obstructed, and the ports that open here and there in the midst of these lagoons do not offer to ships the same depth, and present commerce with facilities much smaller than those of the North.
To this first inferiority arising from nature there is added another that comes from the laws.
We have seen that slavery, abolished in the North, still exists in the South, and I have shown the disastrous influence it exercises on the well-being of the master himself.
The North, then, must be more commercial[115] and more industrious than the South. It is natural that the population and the wealth move there more rapidly.

[Note B: *View of the United States*, by Darby.]

The States situated on the shore of the Atlantic are already half peopled. Most of the lands have an owner; they cannot, then, receive the same number of emigrants as the Western States, which still offer industry a boundless field. The basin of the Mississippi is infinitely more fertile than the coast of the Atlantic. This reason, joined to all the others, pushes the Europeans energetically toward the West. This can be rigorously demonstrated by figures.

If we operate on the United States as a whole, we find that, for the past forty years, the number of inhabitants has nearly tripled. But if we consider only the basin of the Mississippi, we discover that, in the same span of time, the population[116] has become thirty-one times greater[117].

Each day, the center of federal power shifts. Forty years ago, the majority of the citizens of the Union were on the shore of the sea, in the neighborhood of the place where Washington stands today; now it is found further inland and further north; one cannot doubt that within twenty years it will be on the other side of the Alleghenies. If the Union lasts, the basin of the Mississippi, by its fertility and its extent, is necessarily called to become the permanent center of federal power. In thirty or forty years the basin of the Mississippi will have taken its natural rank. It is easy to calculate that then its population, compared with that of the States placed on the shores of the Atlantic, will be in the proportion of about 40 to 11. A few more years and the direction of the Union will thus escape completely from the States that founded it, and the population of the valleys of the Mississippi will dominate in the federal councils.

This continual gravitation of federal forces and influence toward the Northwest is revealed every ten years, when, after a general census of the population, the number of representatives that each State must send to Congress is again fixed[118].

In 1790 Virginia had nineteen representatives in Congress. This number continued to grow until 1813, when it reached twenty-three. From that time on, it began to diminish. In 1833 it was no more than twenty-one[119]. During this same period, the State of New York followed an opposite progression: in 1790 it had ten representatives in Congress; in 1813, twenty-seven; in 1823, thirty-four; in 1833, forty. Ohio had only one representative in 1803; in 1833 it counted nineteen.

It is difficult to conceive of a lasting union between two peoples of whom one is poor and weak, the other rich and strong, even when it should be proved that the strength and wealth of the one were not the cause of the weakness and poverty of the other. Union is harder still to maintain at the time when one is losing strength and the other is in the process of acquiring it.

This rapid and disproportionate growth of certain States threatens the independence of the others. If New York, with its two million inhabitants and its forty representatives, wished to lay down the law in Congress, it might succeed. But even if the most powerful States did not seek to oppress the lesser ones, the danger would still exist, for it lies in the possibility of the fact almost as much as in the fact itself.

The weak rarely have confidence in the justice and reason of the strong. The States that grow less rapidly than the others therefore cast looks of distrust and envy upon those whom fortune favors. Hence the deep malaise and the vague uneasiness one observes in one part of the Union, which contrast with the well-being and confidence that reign in the other. I believe the hostile attitude the South has taken has no other cause.

The men of the South are, of all Americans, those who should hold most strongly to the Union, for they are above all the ones who would suffer most by being abandoned to themselves; yet they are the only ones who threaten to break the bundle of the confederation. Whence comes this? It is easy to say: the South, which has furnished four presidents to the confederation[120], which today knows that federal power is escaping from it, which every year sees the number of its representatives in Congress diminish and those of the North and West grow; the South, peopled by ardent and irascible men, grows irritated and uneasy. It turns its glance ruefully upon itself; questioning the past, it asks itself each day whether it is not oppressed. If it discovers that some law of the Union is not evidently favorable to it, it cries out that there is an abuse of force at its expense; it complains ardently, and if its voice is not heeded, it grows indignant and threatens to withdraw from a society in which it has the burdens without having the profits.

"The tariff laws," said the inhabitants of Carolina in 1832, "enrich the North and ruin the South; for without that, how could one conceive that the North, with its inhospitable climate and arid soil, should constantly increase its riches and power, while the South, which forms as it were the garden of America, falls rapidly into decadence[121]?"

If the changes I have spoken of were taking place gradually, so that each generation might at least have the time to pass with the order of things of which it had been the witness, the danger would be less; but there is something precipitate, I might almost say revolutionary, in the progress that society makes in America. The same citizen has been able to see his State at the head of the Union, and then become powerless in the federal councils. There is an Anglo-American republic that has grown as fast as a man, and that was born, grew up, and reached maturity in thirty years.

It must not be imagined, however, that the States that lose power are losing inhabitants or withering away; their prosperity does not halt; they grow even more rapidly than any kingdom in Europe[122]. But it seems to them that they are growing poor, because they do not enrich themselves as fast as their neighbor, and they believe themselves to be losing their power because they suddenly come into contact with a power greater than their own[123]: it is therefore their feelings and their passions that are wounded, more than their interests. But is that not enough to put the confederation in peril? If, since the beginning of the world, peoples and kings had had in view only their real utility, one would hardly know what war among men is.

Thus the greatest danger that threatens the United States arises from its very prosperity; it tends to create in some of the confederates the intoxication that accompanies the rapid increase of fortune, and in others the envy, the distrust, and the regrets that most often follow its loss.

The Americans rejoice as they contemplate this extraordinary movement; it seems to me that they should view it with regret and with fear. The Americans of the United States, whatever they do, will become one of the greatest peoples of the world; they will cover with their offshoots nearly all of North America; the continent they inhabit is their domain, it cannot escape them. Who, then, presses them to take possession of it from this very day? Wealth, power, and glory cannot fail to be theirs one day, and they rush toward this immense fortune as if they had only a moment left to seize it.

I believe I have shown that the existence of the present confederation depends entirely on the agreement of all the confederates in wishing to remain united; and starting from this datum I have inquired what were the causes that might lead the various States to wish to separate. But there are two ways for the Union to perish: one of the confederated States may wish to withdraw from the compact, and thus break the common bond violently; most of the remarks I have made above relate to this case. Or the federal government may lose its power gradually, by a simultaneous tendency of the united republics to resume the use of their independence. The central power, successively stripped of all its prerogatives, reduced by tacit agreement to impotence, would become unable to fulfill its object, and the second Union would perish, like the first, by a kind of senile imbecility.

The gradual weakening of the federal bond, which leads finally to the annulment of the Union, is moreover in itself a distinct fact that may bring about many other less extreme results before producing that one. The confederation might still exist, while the weakness of its government had already reduced the nation to impotence, caused anarchy within, and slowed the general prosperity of the country.

After inquiring what leads the Anglo-Americans to disunite, it is therefore important to examine whether, the Union subsisting, their government is enlarging the sphere of its action or narrowing it, whether it is becoming more energetic or weaker.

The Americans are evidently preoccupied by a great fear. They perceive that in most of the peoples of the world the exercise of the rights of sovereignty tends to concentrate itself in few hands, and they are alarmed at the idea that it will end by being so with them. Statesmen themselves feel these terrors, or at least pretend to feel them; for in America centralization is not popular, and one cannot court the majority more skillfully than by railing against the alleged encroachments of the central power. The Americans refuse to see that in the countries in which this centralizing tendency they fear shows itself one meets only a single people, while the Union is a confederation of different peoples; a fact that suffices to upset all forecasts founded on analogy.

I confess that I regard these fears of a great number of Americans as entirely imaginary. Far from fearing with them the consolidation of sovereignty in the hands of the Union, I believe the federal government is visibly weakening.
To prove what I advance on this point, I shall not resort to ancient facts, but to those I have been able to witness or that have occurred in our own time.

When one looks attentively at what is happening in the United States, one discovers without trouble the existence of two contrary tendencies; they are like two currents running through the same bed in opposite directions.

In the forty-five years that the Union has existed, time has dispatched a host of provincial prejudices that originally militated against it. The patriotic feeling that attached each American to his State has become less exclusive. As the various parts of the Union have come to know one another better, they have drawn closer. The post, that great bond of minds, today reaches into the depths of the wilderness[124]; steamboats every day put every point on the coast in communication with one another. Commerce descends and ascends the rivers of the interior with a speed without precedent[125]. To these facilities that nature and art have created are added the instability of desires, the restlessness of mind, the love of wealth, which, ceaselessly driving the American from his dwelling, place him in communication with a great number of his fellow citizens. He travels through his country in every direction; he visits all the populations that inhabit it. There is not a province of France whose inhabitants know one another so thoroughly as the 13,000,000 men who cover the surface of the United States.

At the same time as the Americans mingle, they assimilate; the differences that climate, origin, and institutions had set between them diminish. They all come closer and closer to a common type. Each year thousands of men setting out from the North spread into all parts of the Union: they bring with them their beliefs, their opinions, their mores; and since their enlightenment is superior to that of the men among whom they go to live, they are not slow to take possession of affairs and modify society to their profit. This continual emigration from the North to the South favors in a singular way the fusion of all the provincial characters into a single national character. The civilization of the North seems destined, then, to become the common measure on which all the rest must one day be regulated.

As the industry of the Americans makes progress, one sees the commercial bonds that unite all the confederated States grow tighter, and union enters into habits after having been in opinions. Time, in passing, brings about the disappearance of a host of fantastic terrors that tormented the imagination of the men of 1789. The federal power has not become oppressive; it has not destroyed the independence of the States; it does not lead the confederates to monarchy; with the Union, the small States have not fallen into dependence on the great. The confederation has continued to grow without ceasing in population, wealth, and power.
I am convinced, then, that in our day the Americans have fewer natural difficulties in living united than they had in 1789; the Union has fewer enemies than then.
And yet, if we wish to study with care the history of the United States over forty-five years, we shall easily be convinced that the federal power is declining.
It is not difficult to indicate the causes of this phenomenon.

At the time when the constitution of 1789 was promulgated, all was perishing in anarchy; the Union that succeeded this disorder excited much fear and hatred, but it had ardent friends, because it was the expression of a great need. Although more attacked then than it is today, the federal power therefore quickly attained the maximum of its power, as ordinarily happens with a government that triumphs after exalting its strength in the struggle. At that period, the interpretation of the constitution seemed to extend rather than to restrict federal sovereignty, and the Union presented in several respects the spectacle of a single people, directed at home as abroad by a single government.
But to arrive at this point, the people had, as it were, lifted themselves above themselves.

The constitution had not destroyed the individuality of the States, and all bodies, whatever they be, have a secret instinct that draws them toward independence. This instinct is more pronounced still in a country like America, where every village forms a kind of republic accustomed to governing itself.

There was therefore an effort on the part of the States that submitted to federal preponderance. And every effort, even one crowned with great success, cannot fail to weaken along with the cause that gives it birth.

As the federal government consolidated its power, America was resuming her rank among nations; peace was reborn on the frontiers; public credit was rising; to confusion succeeded a settled order that allowed individual industry to follow its natural course and to develop in liberty.

It was this very prosperity that began to make people lose sight of the cause that had produced it; the peril passed, the Americans no longer found in themselves the energy and patriotism that had helped to avert it. Freed from the fears that had preoccupied them, they easily fell back into the course of their habits, and gave themselves up without resistance to the ordinary tendency of their inclinations. From the moment a strong government no longer seemed necessary, they began again to think it irksome. Everything prospered with the Union, and the Union was not abandoned; but they wanted to feel the action of the power that represented it as little as possible. In general, they wanted to remain united, and in each particular instance they tended to become independent again. The principle of confederation was each day more readily admitted and less applied; thus the federal government, in creating order and peace, brought about its own decline.
As soon as this disposition of mind began to manifest itself, the men of party, who live off the passions of the people, set about exploiting it for their profit.
The federal government thus found itself in a very critical position; its enemies had popular favor, and it was by promising to weaken it that one obtained the right to direct it.

From that time on, whenever the government of the Union has entered the lists against that of the States, it has almost never ceased to retreat. When the terms of the federal constitution have had to be interpreted, the interpretation has most often been unfavorable to the Union and favorable to the States.

The constitution charged the federal government with providing for the national interests: it had been thought that it was for it to undertake or to favor, within the country, the great enterprises whose nature was to increase the prosperity of the whole Union (*internal improvements*), such, for example, as canals.

The States grew alarmed at the idea of seeing any authority other than their own dispose in this way of a portion of their territory. They feared that the central power, acquiring in this way within their own borders a redoubtable patronage, would come to exercise there an influence they wished to reserve entirely for their own agents.

The democratic party, which has always been opposed to every development of federal power, raised its voice; Congress was accused of usurpation, the head of state of ambition. The central government, intimidated by these clamors, ended by recognizing its error itself, and by confining itself strictly within the sphere drawn for it.

The constitution gives the Union the privilege of treating with foreign peoples. The Union had generally considered under this rubric the Indian tribes that border on its territory. As long as these savages consented to flee before civilization, federal right was not contested; but from the day an Indian tribe undertook to fix itself on a point of the soil, the surrounding States claimed a right of possession over those lands, and a right of sovereignty over the men who lived on them. The central government hastened to recognize both, and after having treated with the Indians as with independent peoples, it delivered them up like subjects to the legislative tyranny of the States[126].

Among the States that had formed on the shore of the Atlantic, several extended indefinitely to the west into wilderness areas where the Europeans had not yet penetrated. Those whose limits were irrevocably fixed viewed with a jealous eye the immense future opened before their neighbors. The latter, in a spirit of conciliation, and in order to facilitate the act of Union, consented to set themselves limits, and abandoned to the confederation all the territory that might be found beyond[127].

Since that time, the federal government has become the proprietor of all the uncultivated land that is to be found outside the thirteen States originally confederated. It is the federal government that takes charge of dividing and selling it, and the money that comes from it is paid exclusively into the treasury of the Union. With the help of this revenue, the federal government buys their lands from the Indians, opens roads in the new districts, and there facilitates with all its power the rapid development of society.

Now it has come to pass that in these same wildernesses ceded long ago by the inhabitants of the shores of the Atlantic, new States have in time been formed. Congress has continued to sell, for the profit of the whole nation, the uncultivated lands these States still contain within them. But now those States claim that, once constituted, they ought to have the exclusive right to apply the proceeds of these sales to their own use. The demands having become more and more menacing, Congress thought it must take from the Union a part of the privileges it had enjoyed until then, and at the end of 1832 it passed a law by which, without ceding to the new republics of the West the ownership of their uncultivated lands, it nevertheless applied to their profit alone the greater part of the revenue drawn from them[128].

It is enough to travel through the United States to appreciate the advantages the country draws from the Bank. These advantages are of several kinds; but there is one above all that strikes the foreigner: the notes of the Bank of the United States are received on the frontier of the wilderness for the same value as at Philadelphia, where the seat of its operations is[129].

The Bank of the United States is nevertheless the object of great hatreds. Its directors have pronounced themselves against the president, and they are accused, not without probability, of having abused their influence to obstruct his election. The president, therefore, attacks the institution they represent with all the ardor of a personal enmity. What has encouraged the president to pursue his vengeance in this way is that he feels himself supported by the secret instincts of the majority.

The Bank forms the great monetary tie of the Union as Congress is its great legislative tie, and the same passions that tend to make the States independent of the central power tend to the destruction of the Bank.

The Bank of the United States always holds in its hands a great number of notes belonging to the provincial banks; it can every day oblige these to redeem their notes in specie. For itself, on the contrary, such a danger is not to be feared; the magnitude of its available resources allows it to meet every demand. Thus threatened in their existence, the provincial banks are forced to use restraint and to put into circulation only a number of notes proportionate to their capital. The provincial banks bear this salutary control only impatiently. The newspapers that have been bought by them, and the president whom his interest has made their organ, therefore attack the Bank with a kind of fury. They rouse against it local passions and the blind democratic instinct of the country. According to them, the directors of the Bank form an aristocratic and permanent body whose influence cannot fail to make itself felt in the government, and must sooner or later corrupt the principles of equality on which American society rests.

The struggle of the Bank against its enemies is but an incident in the great combat that in America the provinces wage against the central power; the spirit of independence and democracy, against the spirit of hierarchy and subordination. I do not pretend that the enemies of the Bank of the United States are precisely the same individuals who, on other points, attack the federal government; but I say that the attacks against the Bank of the United States are the product of the same instincts that militate against the federal government, and that the great number of the enemies of the first is an unhappy symptom of the weakening of the second.
But never did the Union show itself feebler than in the famous affair of the tariff[130].

The wars of the French revolution and that of 1812, by preventing free communication between America and Europe, had created factories in the North of the Union. When peace had reopened to European products the road to the New World, the Americans thought they had to establish a system of customs that would at once protect their nascent industry and pay off the debts the war had made them contract.
The Southern States, which have no factories to encourage, and which are only agricultural, were not slow to complain of this measure.
I do not pretend to examine here what there could be of imaginary or real in their complaints; I state the facts.

As early as the year 1820, South Carolina, in a petition to Congress, declared the tariff law *unconstitutional*, *oppressive*, and *unjust*. Since then, Georgia, Virginia, North Carolina, the State of Alabama, and that of Mississippi made more or less energetic remonstrances in the same sense.
Far from taking these murmurs into account, Congress, in the years 1824 and 1828, raised the tariff duties still higher and again consecrated its principle.
Then there was produced, or rather recalled, in the South a famous doctrine that took the name of *nullification*.

I have shown in its place that the aim of the federal constitution was not to establish a league, but to create a national government. The Americans of the United States, in all the cases foreseen by their constitution, form a single people. On all these points, the national will is expressed, as in all constitutional peoples, by means of a majority. Once the majority has spoken, the duty of the minority is to submit.
Such is the legal doctrine, the only one in accord with the text of the constitution and the known intention of those who established it.

The *nullifiers* of the South claim, on the contrary, that the Americans, in uniting, did not intend to merge into one and the same people, but only meant to form a league of independent peoples; from which it follows that each State, having preserved its complete sovereignty, if not in action at least in principle, has the right to interpret the laws of Congress, and to suspend within its borders the execution of those that seem to it contrary to the constitution or to justice.
The whole doctrine of nullification is summed up in a sentence pronounced in 1833 before the Senate of the United States by Mr. Calhoun, the avowed leader of the Southern nullifiers.

"The constitution," he said, "is a contract in which the States have appeared as sovereigns. Now, whenever a contract is made between parties that recognize no common arbiter, each of them retains the right to judge for itself the extent of its obligation."
It is manifest that such a doctrine destroys in principle the federal bond, and brings back in fact the anarchy from which the constitution of 1789 had delivered the Americans.

When South Carolina saw that Congress turned a deaf ear to its complaints, it threatened to apply the nullifiers' doctrine to the federal tariff law. Congress persisted in its system; at last the storm broke.

In the course of 1832, the people of South Carolina[131] nominated a national convention to consider the extraordinary measures that remained to be taken; and on November 24 of the same year, this convention published, under the name of an ordinance, a law that struck the federal tariff law with nullity, forbade the levying of the duties it imposed, and forbade the reception of any appeals that might be made to the federal tribunals[132]. This ordinance was to take effect only in the following February, and it was indicated that if Congress modified the tariff before that time, South Carolina might consent to take its threats no further. Later it was expressed, but in a vague and indeterminate manner, the desire to submit the question to an extraordinary assembly of all the confederated States.
Meanwhile, South Carolina was arming its militia and preparing for war.

What did Congress do? Congress, which had not listened to its subjects when they entreated, lent its ear to their complaints as soon as it saw them in arms[133]. It made a law[134] by which the duties of the tariff were to be reduced progressively over ten years, until they were brought down so as not to exceed the needs of the government. Thus Congress completely abandoned the principle of the tariff. To a duty protective of industry it substituted a purely fiscal measure[135]. To disguise its defeat, the government of the Union had recourse to an expedient much in use with weak governments: while yielding on the facts, it showed itself inflexible on the principles. At the same time that Congress changed the tariff legislation, it passed another law by virtue of which the president was invested with an extraordinary power to overcome by force the resistances which by then were no longer to be feared.

South Carolina did not even consent to leave the Union these feeble appearances of victory; the same national convention that had struck the tariff law with nullity having assembled again, it accepted the concession offered to it; but at the same time it declared that it persisted only with greater force in the doctrine of nullifiers, and to prove it, it annulled the law that conferred extraordinary powers on the president, although it was quite certain that they would not be used.

Nearly all the acts I have just spoken of took place under the presidency of General Jackson. It cannot be denied that, in the tariff affair, the latter upheld the rights of the Union with skill and vigor. Yet I think one must place among the dangers the federal power runs today the very conduct of the man who represents it.
Some people in Europe have formed, on the influence General Jackson can exercise in the affairs of his country, an opinion that seems quite extravagant to those who have seen things close up.

One has heard that General Jackson had won battles, that he was an energetic man, drawn by character and habit to the use of force, eager for power and despotic by taste. All this is perhaps true, but the consequences drawn from these truths are great errors.

It has been imagined that General Jackson wished to establish a dictatorship in the United States, that he was going to bring about the reign of the military spirit, and to give the central power an extension dangerous to provincial liberties. In America the time for such undertakings and the age for such men have not yet come: if General Jackson had wished to dominate in this way, he would assuredly have lost his political position and compromised his life; nor has he been imprudent enough to attempt it.

Far from wishing to extend federal power, the present president represents, on the contrary, the party that wishes to restrict that power to the clearest and most precise terms of the constitution, and that does not admit that interpretation can ever be favorable to the government of the Union; far from presenting himself as the champion of centralization, General Jackson is the agent of provincial jealousies; it is the *decentralizing* passions (if I may put it so) that have brought him to the sovereign power. It is by flattering these passions every day that he maintains himself and prospers there. General Jackson is the slave of the majority: he follows it in its wishes, in its desires, in its half-disclosed instincts, or rather he divines it and runs to place himself at its head.

Every time that the governments of the States enter into conflict with that of the Union, it is rare that the president is not the first to doubt his right; he almost always anticipates the legislative power; when there is occasion to interpret the extent of federal power, he ranges himself, as it were, against himself; he diminishes himself, he veils himself, he effaces himself. It is not that he is naturally weak or hostile to the Union; when the majority pronounced itself against the claims of the Southern nullifiers, he was seen to place himself at its head, to formulate with clearness and energy the doctrines it professed, and to appeal first to force. General Jackson, to use a comparison borrowed from the vocabulary of American parties, seems to me *federal* by taste and *republican* by calculation.

After having thus lowered himself before the majority to win its favor, General Jackson rises again; he then marches toward the objects it itself pursues, or those it does not view with a jealous eye, overturning before him every obstacle. Strong in a support his predecessors did not have, he tramples his personal enemies underfoot wherever he finds them, with an ease no president has met with; he takes upon his responsibility measures no one before him had ever dared to take; he even comes to treat the national representation with a kind of almost insulting disdain; he refuses to sanction the laws of Congress, and often omits to answer that great body. He is a favorite who sometimes treats his master roughly. The power of General Jackson, then, grows without ceasing; but that of the president diminishes. In his hands, the federal government is strong; it will pass enervated to his successor.

Either I am strangely mistaken, or the federal government of the United States tends each day to grow weaker; it withdraws successively from affairs, it narrows more and more the circle of its action. Naturally weak, it abandons even the appearances of strength. On the other hand, I thought I saw that in the United States the feeling of independence was becoming livelier and livelier in the States, the love of provincial government more and more pronounced.

The Union is wanted, but reduced to a shadow: it is wanted strong in certain cases and weak in all others; it is claimed that in time of war it should be able to gather in its hands the national forces and all the resources of the country, and that in time of peace it should, so to speak, not exist; as if this alternation of debility and vigor were in the nature of things.

I see nothing that could, at present, arrest this general movement of minds; the causes that gave it birth do not cease to operate in the same direction. It will therefore continue, and one can predict that, if some extraordinary circumstance does not intervene, the government of the Union will grow weaker each day.

I believe, however, that we are still far from the time when the federal power, incapable of protecting its own existence and of giving peace to the country, will, as it were, die out by itself. The Union is in the mores; it is desired; its results are evident, its benefits visible. When it is perceived that the weakness of the federal government compromises the existence of the Union, I do not doubt that one will see a movement of reaction in favor of strength arise.

The government of the United States is, of all federal governments that have been established up to our day, the one most naturally destined to act: as long as it is attacked only in an indirect way through the interpretation of its laws, as long as its substance is not profoundly altered, a change of opinion, an internal crisis, a war, could suddenly give it back all the vigor it needs.

What I have wished to establish is only this: many people among us think that in the United States there is a movement of minds favorable to the centralization of power in the hands of the president and of Congress. I maintain that one sees there, on the contrary, a clearly opposite movement. Far from the federal government becoming, as it grows older, stronger and threatening the sovereignty of the States, I say that it tends each day to weaken, and that the sovereignty of the Union alone is in peril. This is what the present reveals. What will be the final result of this tendency, what events may arrest, retard, or hasten the movement I have described? The future hides them, and I do not claim to be able to lift its veil.
OF REPUBLICAN INSTITUTIONS IN THE UNITED STATES, AND WHAT THEIR CHANCES OF DURATION ARE.

The Union is only an accident. — Republican institutions have more future. — The republic is, at present, the natural state of the Anglo-Americans. — Why. — To destroy it, one would have to change all the laws at once and modify all the mores. — Difficulties the Americans meet in creating an aristocracy.

The dismemberment of the Union, by introducing war among the States now confederated, and with it standing armies, dictatorship, and taxes, might in the long run compromise the fate of republican institutions there.
One must not, however, confuse the future of the republic with that of the Union.

The Union is an accident that will last only as long as circumstances favor it; but the republic seems to me the natural state of the Americans; and only the continuous action of contrary causes acting always in the same direction could substitute monarchy for it.
The Union exists chiefly in the law that created it. A single revolution, a change in public opinion, can shatter it forever. The republic has deeper roots.

What is meant by a republic in the United States is the slow and tranquil action of society upon itself. It is a regular state founded really on the enlightened will of the people. It is a conciliating government, where resolutions ripen at length, are discussed slowly, and are carried out with maturity.

The republicans in the United States prize mores, respect beliefs, recognize rights. They profess this opinion: that a people must be moral, religious, and moderate in proportion as it is free. What is called the republic in the United States is the tranquil reign of the majority. The majority, after having had the time to recognize itself and to ascertain its existence, is the common source of powers. But the majority itself is not all-powerful. Above it, in the moral world, are found humanity, justice, and reason; in the political world, acquired rights. The majority recognizes these two barriers, and if it happens to overstep them, it is because it has passions, like every man, and that, like them, it can do evil while discerning good.
But we have in Europe made strange discoveries.

The republic, according to some among us, is not the rule of the majority, as has been believed until now; it is the rule of those who declare themselves vouchers for the majority. It is not the people who govern in such governments, but those who know the greatest good of the people: a happy distinction that allows one to act in the name of nations without consulting them, and to demand their gratitude while trampling them underfoot. The republican government, moreover, is the only one to which the right to do everything must be granted, and which may despise what men have until now respected, from the highest laws of morality down to the common rules of common sense.

It had been thought, until us, that despotism was odious, whatever its forms. But in our day it has been discovered that there were in the world legitimate tyrannies and holy injustices, provided they were exercised in the name of the people.

The ideas that the Americans have formed of the republic singularly facilitate their use of it and ensure its duration. With them, if the practice of republican government is often bad, at least the theory is good, and the people end always by conforming their acts to it.

It was impossible at the outset, and would still be very difficult, to establish in America a centralized administration. Men are dispersed over too great a space and separated by too many natural obstacles for one alone to undertake to direct the details of their existence. America is therefore par excellence the country of provincial and communal government.
To this cause, whose action was felt equally on all the Europeans of the New World, the Anglo-Americans added several others that were peculiar to them.

When the colonies of North America were established, municipal liberty had already penetrated into English law as well as into English mores, and the English emigrants adopted it not only as a thing necessary, but as a good whose full value they knew.

We have seen, moreover, in what manner the colonies had been founded. Each province, and so to speak each district, was peopled separately by men strangers to one another, or associated for different purposes.

The English of the United States have thus found themselves, from the start, divided into a great number of small distinct societies that connected themselves to no common center, and it was necessary that each of these small societies occupy itself with its own affairs, since nowhere did one perceive a central authority that ought naturally and could easily provide for them.

Thus the nature of the country, the very manner in which the English colonies were founded, the habits of the first emigrants — all combined to develop there to an extraordinary degree communal and provincial liberties.

In the United States, then, the whole set of the country's institutions is essentially republican; to destroy in a lasting way the laws that found the republic there, one would have to abolish, as it were, all the laws at once.

If, in our day, a party undertook to found monarchy in the United States, it would find itself in a still more difficult position than one that wished to proclaim the republic in France right now. Royalty would not find legislation prepared in advance for it, and it would then really be a monarchy surrounded by republican institutions.
The monarchical principle would also penetrate with difficulty into the mores of the Americans.

In the United States, the dogma of the sovereignty of the people is not an isolated doctrine that connects neither with habits nor with the whole of dominant ideas; on the contrary, it can be viewed as the last link in a chain of opinions that envelops the whole Anglo-American world. Providence has given to each individual, whoever he be, the degree of reason necessary for him to direct himself in the things that concern him exclusively. Such is the great maxim on which, in the United States, civil and political society rests: the father of the family applies it to his children, the master to his servants, the township to those it administers, the province to the townships, the State to the provinces, the Union to the States. Extended to the whole nation, it becomes the dogma of the sovereignty of the people.

Thus, in the United States, the generative principle of the republic is the same as that which regulates most human actions. The republic therefore penetrates, if I may put it so, into the ideas, the opinions, and all the habits of the Americans at the same time as it is established in their laws; and to manage to change the laws, they would have to come to change themselves, as it were, entirely. In the United States, the religion of the greater number is itself republican; it submits the truths of the other world to individual reason, as politics leaves to the good sense of all the care of the interests of this one, and it consents that each man take freely the path that is to lead him to heaven, in the same manner as the law recognizes in each citizen the right to choose his government.
Evidently, only a long succession of facts all tending in the same direction could substitute, for this whole of laws, opinions, and mores, a whole of mores, opinions, and laws contrary to it.

If republican principles are to perish in America, they will succumb only after a long social labor, frequently interrupted, often resumed; several times they will seem to be reborn, and they will disappear without return only when an entirely new people has taken the place of the one that exists in our day. Now, nothing can presage such a revolution; no sign announces it.

What strikes you most when you arrive in the United States is the kind of tumultuous movement amid which political society finds itself placed. The laws change without ceasing, and at first sight it seems impossible that a people so unsure of its wishes should not soon substitute an entirely new form of government for the present one. Such fears are premature. In matters of political institutions there are two species of instability that must not be confused: the one attaches to secondary laws; that one can reign for a long time at the heart of a well-settled society; the other constantly shakes the very foundations of the constitution and attacks the generative principles of laws; that one is always followed by troubles and revolutions; the nation that suffers it is in a violent and transitory state.
