Experience teaches that these two species of legislative instability have no necessary connection with each other, for they have been seen to exist jointly or separately, depending on the times and places. The first is found in the United States, but not the second. The Americans change their laws frequently, but the foundation of the constitution is respected.

In our day, the republican principle reigns in America as the monarchical principle prevailed in France under Louis XIV. The French of that time were not only friends of the monarchy, they could not imagine putting anything in its place; they accepted it as they accept the course of the sun and the vicissitudes of the seasons. Among them, royal power had no more advocates than it had opponents.
It is thus that the republic exists in America, without combat, without opposition, without proof, by a tacit agreement, a kind of *consensus universalis*.
Yet I think that, by changing their administrative procedures as often as they do, the inhabitants of the United States compromise the future of republican government.

Constantly hampered in their plans by the continual versatility of the legislation, it is to be feared that men will end by viewing the republic as an inconvenient way of living in society; the evil arising from the instability of the secondary laws would then bring into question the existence of the fundamental laws, and bring about indirectly a revolution; but that time is still very far from us.

What can be foreseen from now on is that, on leaving the republic, the Americans would pass rapidly to despotism, without lingering very long in monarchy. Montesquieu said that there is nothing more absolute than the authority of a prince who succeeds the republic, since the indefinite powers that had been entrusted without fear to an elective magistrate then find themselves placed in the hands of a hereditary chief. This is true in general, but particularly applicable to a democratic republic. In the United States, the magistrates are not elected by a particular class of citizens, but by the majority of the nation; they immediately represent the passions of the multitude, and depend entirely on its wishes; they therefore inspire neither hatred nor fear: so I noted earlier how little care had been taken to limit their power by tracing bounds for its action, and how immense a part had been left to their arbitrary discretion. This order of things has created habits that would survive it. The American magistrate would keep his indefinite power while ceasing to be responsible, and it is impossible to say where tyranny would stop then.
There are people among us who expect to see aristocracy be born in America, and who already foresee with exactitude the time when it must seize power.
I have already said, and I repeat that the present movement of American society seems to me more and more democratic.

Yet I do not claim that one day the Americans will not come to restrict among themselves the circle of political rights, or to confiscate these same rights to the profit of one man; but I cannot believe that they will ever entrust the exclusive use of them to a particular class of citizens, or, in other terms, that they will found an aristocracy.

An aristocratic body is composed of a certain number of citizens who, without being placed very far from the crowd, rise nevertheless in a permanent manner above it; whom one touches and cannot strike; with whom one mingles every day, and with whom one cannot be merged.

Nothing more contrary to nature and to the secret instincts of the human heart can be imagined than a subjection of this kind: left to themselves, men will always prefer the arbitrary power of a king to the regular administration of nobles.

An aristocracy, to last, needs to found inequality on principle, to legalize it in advance, and to introduce it into the family at the same time as it spreads it through society; all things that so strongly repel natural equity that they can be obtained from men only by constraint.

Since human societies have existed, I do not believe one can cite the example of a single people that, left to itself and by its own efforts, has created an aristocracy in its midst. All the aristocracies of the Middle Ages are daughters of conquest. The victor was the noble, the vanquished the serf. Force then imposed inequality, which, once entered into mores, maintained itself and passed naturally into the laws.

Societies have been seen which, as a result of events prior to their existence, were, as it were, born aristocratic, and which each century brought back toward democracy. Such was the fate of the Romans, and that of the barbarians who established themselves after them. But a people that, starting from civilization and democracy, drew nearer by degrees to inequality of conditions, and ended by establishing within itself inviolable privileges and exclusive categories — this would be something new in the world.
Nothing indicates that America is destined to give the first such spectacle.
SOME CONSIDERATIONS ON THE CAUSES OF THE COMMERCIAL GREATNESS OF THE UNITED STATES.

The Americans are called by nature to be a great maritime people. — Extent of their shores. — Depth of the ports. — Greatness of the rivers. — Yet it is much less to physical causes than to intellectual and moral ones that the commercial superiority of the Anglo-Americans must be attributed. — Reason for this opinion. — Future of the Anglo-Americans as a commercial people. — The ruin of the Union would not check the maritime expansion of the peoples that compose it. — Why. — The Anglo-Americans are naturally called to serve the needs of the inhabitants of South America. — They will become, like the English, the carriers of a great part of the world.
From the Bay of Fundy to the Sabine River in the Gulf of Mexico, the coast of the United States stretches over a length of about 900 leagues.
These shores form a single unbroken line; they are all placed under the same domination.
There is no people in the world that can offer commerce ports deeper, vaster, and safer than the Americans.

The inhabitants of the United States compose a great civilized nation that fortune has placed in the midst of the wilderness, 1,200 leagues from the principal seat of civilization. America therefore has a daily need of Europe. With time, the Americans will doubtless succeed in producing or manufacturing at home most of the objects necessary to them, but the two continents will never be able to live entirely independent of each other: there are too many natural ties between their needs, their ideas, their habits, and their mores.

The Union has products that have become necessary to us, and that our soil either refuses to furnish at all, or can give only at great expense. The Americans consume only a very small portion of these products; they sell us the rest.

Europe is therefore the market for America, as America is the market for Europe; and maritime commerce is as necessary to the inhabitants of the United States, to bring their raw materials to our ports, as to transport our manufactured goods to them.

The United States, then, had to furnish a great fund to the industry of maritime peoples, if they themselves renounced commerce, as the Spaniards of Mexico have done up to the present; or to become one of the first maritime powers of the globe: this alternative was inevitable.

The Anglo-Americans have at all times shown a decided taste for the sea. Independence, by breaking the commercial ties that united them to England, gave their maritime genius a new and powerful impulse. Since that time, the number of the Union's vessels has grown in a progression almost as rapid as the number of its inhabitants. Today it is the Americans themselves who carry to their shores nine-tenths of the products of Europe[136]. It is again Americans who bring to European consumers three-fourths of the exports of the New World[137].
The ships of the United States fill the ports of Le Havre and Liverpool. One sees only a small number of English or French vessels in the port of New York[138].
Thus, not only does the American merchant brave competition on his own soil, but he also fights with advantage against foreigners on theirs.

This is easily explained: of all the vessels in the world, those of the United States cross the seas the most cheaply. As long as the merchant marine of the United States preserves this advantage over others, it will not only keep what it has conquered, but it will increase its conquests every day.

It is a difficult problem to know why the Americans navigate at a lower price than other men: at first one is tempted to attribute this superiority to some material advantages that nature has placed within their reach alone, but this is not so.
American vessels cost almost as much to build as ours[139]; they are not better constructed, and in general they last less long.
The wages of the American sailor are higher than those of the European sailor; what proves it is the great number of Europeans one meets in the merchant marine of the United States.
Whence comes it, then, that the Americans navigate more cheaply than we do?
I think one would search in vain for the causes of this superiority in material advantages; it depends on purely intellectual and moral qualities.
Here is a comparison that will clarify my thought:

During the wars of the Revolution, the French introduced into the art of war a new tactic that confounded the oldest generals and nearly destroyed the most ancient monarchies of Europe. They undertook for the first time to do without a host of things that until then had been judged indispensable to war; they demanded of their soldiers new efforts that the civilized nations had never asked of theirs; they were seen to do everything at a run, and to risk men's lives without hesitating in view of the result to be obtained.

The French were less numerous and less rich than their enemies; they had infinitely fewer resources; nevertheless they were constantly victorious until the latter had made up their minds to imitate them.
The Americans have introduced something analogous into commerce. What the French did for victory, they do for cheapness.

The European navigator ventures only with prudence onto the seas; he leaves only when the weather invites him; if an unforeseen accident befalls him, he returns to port; at night he furls part of his sails, and when he sees the ocean whiten at the approach of land, he slows his course and observes the sun.

The American neglects these precautions and braves these dangers. He sets out while the storm still rumbles; at night as by day, he abandons all his sails to the wind; in motion he repairs his ship, fatigued by the gale, and when at last he nears the end of his journey, he continues to fly toward the shore as if he already saw the port.
The American is often shipwrecked; but there is no navigator who crosses the seas as rapidly as he does. Doing the same things as another in less time, he can do them at less cost.

Before reaching the end of a long voyage, the navigator of Europe thinks it necessary to put in several times along his route. He loses precious time looking for a port of call or waiting for an opportunity to leave it, and pays each day for the right to remain there.

The American navigator sets out from Boston to go buy tea in China. He arrives at Canton, remains there a few days, and returns. He has covered in less than two years the entire circumference of the globe, and he has seen land only once. Through a crossing of eight or ten months he has drunk brackish water and lived on salt meat; he has fought ceaselessly against the sea, against sickness, against boredom; but on his return he can sell the pound of tea one penny cheaper than the English merchant: the aim is reached.
I cannot better express my thought than by saying that the Americans put a kind of heroism into their manner of doing commerce.

It will always be very difficult for the European merchant to follow his American competitor in the same career. The American, in acting as I have described above, does not merely follow a calculation: he obeys above all his nature.

The inhabitant of the United States feels all the needs and all the desires that an advanced civilization gives rise to, and he does not find around him, as in Europe, a society skillfully organized to satisfy them; he is therefore often obliged to procure for himself the various objects that his education and his habits have made necessary to him. In America it sometimes happens that the same man tills his field, builds his dwelling, makes his tools, makes his shoes, and weaves with his own hands the coarse cloth that is to cover him. This is detrimental to the perfecting of industry, but it serves powerfully to develop the workman's intelligence. There is nothing that tends more than the great division of labor to materialize man and to take from his works even the trace of soul. In a country like America, where specialists are so rare, one cannot demand a long apprenticeship of each of those who take up a profession. Americans therefore find great ease in changing trades, and they take advantage of it according to the needs of the moment. One meets some who have been successively lawyers, farmers, merchants, evangelical ministers, doctors. If the American is less skillful than the European in each separate industry, there is scarcely one entirely foreign to him. His capacity is more general, the circle of his intelligence wider. The inhabitant of the United States, then, is never stopped by any axiom of his trade; he escapes all the prejudices of profession; he is no more attached to one system of operation than to another; he feels no more bound to an old method than to a new one; he has formed no habit, and easily withdraws from the empire that foreign habits might exercise over his mind, for he knows that his country resembles no other, and that his situation is new in the world.

The American inhabits a land of marvels; around him everything stirs without ceasing, and each movement seems a progress. The idea of the new is thus intimately joined in his mind with the idea of the better. Nowhere does he perceive the limit that nature may have set to man's efforts; in his eyes, what is not is what has not yet been tried.

This universal movement that reigns in the United States, these frequent reverses of fortune, this unforeseen displacement of public and private wealth — all combine to keep the soul in a kind of feverish agitation that disposes it admirably to every effort, and maintains it, so to speak, above the common level of humanity. For an American, all of life passes like a round of play, a time of revolution, a day of battle.

These same causes, operating at the same time on all individuals, end by imprinting an irresistible impulse on the national character. The American taken at random must therefore be a man ardent in his desires, enterprising, adventurous, above all an innovator. This spirit is found, indeed, in all his works; he carries it into his political laws, into his religious doctrines, into his theories of social economy, into his private industry; he carries it everywhere with him, into the depths of the woods as well as into the cities. It is this same spirit which, applied to maritime commerce, makes the American navigate faster and more cheaply than all the merchants of the world.

As long as the sailors of the United States keep these intellectual advantages and the practical superiority that derives from them, not only will they continue to provide themselves for the needs of the producers and consumers of their country, but they will tend more and more to become, like the English[140], the carriers of other peoples.

This is beginning to come about under our eyes. Already we see American navigators introducing themselves as intermediary agents into the commerce of several nations of Europe[141]; America offers them a still greater future.

The Spaniards and the Portuguese founded in South America great colonies that have since become empires. Civil war and despotism today desolate these vast regions. The growth of population has been arrested there, and the small number of men who inhabit them, absorbed in the care of defending themselves, scarcely feel the need to improve their lot.

But it cannot always be so. Europe, left to itself, has managed by its own efforts to pierce the darkness of the Middle Ages; South America is Christian like us; it has our laws, our customs; it contains all the germs of civilization that have developed within the European nations and their offshoots; South America has, moreover, what we did not have — our example: why should it remain forever barbarous?
The question is evidently only one of time: a more or less distant period will doubtless come when the Americans of the South will form flourishing and enlightened nations.

But when the Spaniards and Portuguese of southern America begin to feel the needs of civilized peoples, they will still be far from being able to satisfy them themselves; the youngest born of civilization, they will be subject to the superiority already acquired by their elders. They will be agriculturalists long before being manufacturers and merchants, and they will need the intermediation of foreigners to sell their products overseas and to procure in exchange the objects whose new necessity will be felt.

There can be no doubt that the Americans of the North of America are called one day to provide for the needs of the Americans of the South. Nature has placed them near them. It has thus given them great facilities for knowing and appreciating the needs of the latter, for forming with these peoples lasting relations and gradually taking possession of their market. The merchant of the United States could lose these natural advantages only if he were much inferior to the merchant of Europe, and he is, on the contrary, superior to him on several points. The Americans of the United States already exercise a great moral influence over all the peoples of the New World. From them goes forth the light. All the nations that inhabit the same continent are already accustomed to regarding them as the most enlightened, most powerful, and richest offshoots of the great American family. They therefore turn their gaze ceaselessly toward the Union, and they assimilate themselves, as far as is in their power, to the peoples that compose it. Each day they come to draw at the United States political doctrines and to borrow laws.

The Americans of the United States find themselves toward the peoples of South America precisely in the same situation as their fathers the English toward the Italians, the Spaniards, the Portuguese, and all those peoples of Europe who, being less advanced in civilization and industry, receive from their hands most of the objects of consumption.

England is today the natural center of the commerce of nearly all the nations that approach her; the American Union is called to play the same role in the other hemisphere. Every people that is born or grows up in the New World therefore is born and grows up there, as it were, for the profit of the Anglo-Americans.

If the Union came to dissolve, the commerce of the States that have formed it would no doubt be slowed for a time in its expansion, less so, however, than is thought. It is clear that, whatever happens, the commercial States will remain united. They all adjoin one another; there is between them perfect identity of opinions, interests, and mores, and they alone can compose a very great maritime power. Even were the South of the Union to become independent of the North, it would not follow that it could do without it. I have said that the South is not commercial; nothing indicates yet that it must become so. The Americans of the South of the United States will therefore be obliged for a long time to have recourse to foreigners to export their products and to bring them the objects that are necessary to their needs. Now, of all the intermediaries they could take, their neighbors of the North are surely those who can serve them most cheaply. They will therefore serve them, for cheapness is the supreme law of commerce. There is no sovereign will or national prejudice that can long fight against cheapness. One could not see a hatred more envenomed than that which exists between the Americans of the United States and the English. In spite of these hostile feelings, the English nevertheless furnish the Americans with most manufactured objects, for the sole reason that they sell them cheaper than other peoples. The growing prosperity of America thus turns, in spite of the Americans' wishes, to the profit of the manufacturing industry of England.
Reason indicates and experience proves that there is no commercial greatness that is durable, if it cannot unite itself, at need, with a military power.
This truth is as well understood in the United States as anywhere else. The Americans are already in a position to have their flag respected; soon they will be able to make it feared.

I am convinced that the dismemberment of the Union, far from diminishing the naval forces of the Americans, would strongly tend to increase them. Today, the commercial States are tied to those that are not, and the latter often lend themselves only with reluctance to increasing a maritime power from which they profit only indirectly.

If, on the contrary, all the commercial States of the Union formed one and the same people, commerce would become for them a national interest of the first order; they would therefore be disposed to make very great sacrifices to protect their ships, and nothing would prevent them from following their wishes on this point.

I think that nations, like men, almost always indicate from their early days the principal traits of their destiny. When I see in what spirit the Anglo-Americans conduct commerce, the facilities they find in doing so, the successes they obtain, I cannot help believing that they will one day become the first maritime power of the globe. They are driven to take possession of the seas, as the Romans were to conquer the world.
CONCLUSION.
I now approach the end. Up to now, in speaking of the future destiny of the United States, I have striven to divide my subject into different parts, in order to study each of them with greater care.

I would now like to gather them all into a single point of view. What I shall say will be less detailed, but more sure. I shall perceive each object less distinctly; I shall embrace with more certainty the general facts. I shall be like the traveler who, on leaving the walls of a vast city, climbs the nearby hill. As he moves away, the men he has just left vanish from his eyes; their dwellings merge; he no longer sees the public squares; he can scarcely make out the lines of the streets; but his eye follows more easily the contours of the city, and for the first time he grasps its shape. It seems to me that I likewise discover before me the whole future of the English race in the New World. The details of this immense picture remain in shadow; but my glance takes in the whole, and I conceive a clear idea of all.
The territory occupied or possessed in our day by the United States of America forms about one twentieth of the inhabited lands.
However extensive these limits may be, one would be wrong to believe that the Anglo-American race will remain confined to them forever; it is already stretching far beyond.

There was a time when we too could have created in the American wilderness a great French nation and balanced with the English the destinies of the New World. France once possessed in North America a territory almost as vast as all of Europe. The three greatest rivers of the continent then flowed entirely under our laws. The Indian nations who inhabit from the mouth of the Saint Lawrence to the delta of the Mississippi heard only our language; all the European settlements scattered over this immense expanse recalled the memory of our country: they were Louisbourg, Montmorency, Duquesne, Saint Louis, Vincennes, New Orleans — all names dear to France and familiar to our ears.

But a concurrence of circumstances that it would take too long to enumerate[142] has deprived us of this magnificent inheritance. Wherever the French were few in number and ill-established, they have disappeared. The rest has gathered into a small space and has passed under other laws. The four hundred thousand Frenchmen of Canada today are like the remnants of an ancient people lost in the midst of the waves of a new nation. Around them the foreign population grows without cease; it stretches on every side; it penetrates even into the ranks of the former masters of the soil, dominates in their cities, and denatures their language. This population is identical to that of the United States. I am therefore right to say that the English race does not stop at the limits of the Union, but advances far beyond them toward the Northeast.
To the Northwest one encounters only a few Russian settlements of no importance; but to the Southwest, Mexico presents itself before the steps of the Anglo-Americans like a barrier.
Thus, truly speaking, there are now only two rival races sharing the New World between them: the Spaniards and the English.
The limits that are to separate these two races have been fixed by a treaty. But however favorable this treaty may be to the Anglo-Americans, I do not doubt that they will soon come to break it.

Beyond the frontiers of the Union, on the side of Mexico, stretch vast provinces that still lack inhabitants. The men of the United States will penetrate into these solitudes before even those who have the right to occupy them. They will appropriate the soil, they will establish themselves in society there, and when the legitimate proprietor at last appears, he will find the wilderness made fertile and strangers tranquilly seated in his inheritance.
The land of the New World belongs to the first occupant, and empire there is the prize of the race.
The already peopled countries will themselves have difficulty in protecting themselves against invasion.

I have already spoken earlier of what is happening in the province of Texas. Each day, the inhabitants of the United States introduce themselves bit by bit into Texas, they acquire lands there, and while submitting to the laws of the country, they found there the empire of their language and their mores. The province of Texas is still under the domination of Mexico; but soon one will find there, so to speak, no more Mexicans. The like is occurring at every point where the Anglo-Americans come into contact with populations of another origin.

One cannot conceal from oneself that the English race has acquired an immense preponderance over all the other European races of the New World. It is far superior to them in civilization, in industry, and in power. As long as it has only deserted or thinly inhabited countries before it, as long as it does not meet on its way agglomerated populations through which it is impossible to clear a passage, it will be seen to spread without cease. It will not halt at the lines drawn in treaties, but will overflow in every direction those imaginary dikes.
What further facilitates marvelously this rapid development of the English race in the New World is the geographical position it occupies there.

When one rises northward above its northern frontiers, one meets the polar ice; and when one descends a few degrees below its southern limits, one enters into the fires of the equator. The English of America are therefore placed in the most temperate zone and the most habitable portion of the continent.

It is imagined that the prodigious movement noticeable in the growth of the population of the United States dates only from independence: this is an error. The population grew as quickly under the colonial system as in our own day; it doubled likewise in about twenty-two years. But one was then operating on thousands of inhabitants; one now operates on millions. The same fact that passed unnoticed a century ago today strikes every mind.
The English of Canada, who obey a king, increase in number and spread almost as quickly as the English of the United States, who live under a republican government.
During the eight years that the war of independence lasted, the population did not cease to grow according to the ratio previously indicated.

Although there then existed, on the western frontiers, great Indian nations leagued with the English, the movement of emigration toward the West, so to speak, never slackened. While the enemy ravaged the shores of the Atlantic, Kentucky, the western districts of Pennsylvania, the State of Vermont, and that of Maine were filling with inhabitants. The disorder that followed the war did not prevent the population from growing either, and did not arrest its progressive march into the wilderness. Thus the difference of laws, the state of peace or war, of order or anarchy, have had only an imperceptible influence on the successive development of the Anglo-Americans.

This is easily understood: there are no causes general enough to make themselves felt at once on every point of so immense a territory. Thus there is always a large portion of country where one is sure of finding shelter from the calamities that strike the other, and however great the evils, the remedy offered is always greater still.

One must not believe, then, that it is possible to arrest the expansion of the English race of the New World. The dismemberment of the Union, by bringing war upon the continent, the abolition of the republic, by introducing tyranny there, may slow its development, but cannot prevent it from attaining the necessary completion of its destiny. There is no power on earth that can close before the steps of the emigrants those fertile wildernesses open on every side to industry and that offer an asylum to every misery. Future events, whatever they may be, will take from the Americans neither their climate, nor their inland seas, nor their great rivers, nor the fertility of their soil. Bad laws, revolutions, and anarchy could not destroy among them the taste for well-being and the spirit of enterprise that seems the distinctive character of their race, nor extinguish altogether the enlightenment that illumines them.

Thus, amid the uncertainty of the future, there is at least one event that is certain. At a time we may call near, since here it is a question of the life of peoples, the Anglo-Americans alone will cover all the immense space lying between the polar ice and the tropics; they will spread from the shores of the Atlantic to those of the South Sea.

I think that the territory over which the Anglo-American race must one day extend equals three quarters of Europe[143]. The climate of the Union is, all things considered, preferable to that of Europe; its natural advantages are as great; it is evident that its population cannot fail to be one day proportional to ours.

Europe, divided among so many diverse peoples; Europe, through ceaselessly recurring wars and the barbarism of the Middle Ages, has managed to have four hundred and ten inhabitants[144] per square league. What cause so powerful could prevent the United States from having as many one day?

Many centuries will pass before the various offshoots of the English race of America cease to present a common physiognomy. One cannot foresee the time when man will be able to establish in the New World the permanent inequality of conditions.

Whatever, then, the differences that peace or war, liberty or tyranny, prosperity or misery, may one day set in the destiny of the various offshoots of the great Anglo-American family, they will all preserve at least an analogous social state, and they will have in common the customs and the ideas that derive from the social state.

The single bond of religion sufficed in the Middle Ages to bring together within a common civilization the diverse races that peopled Europe. The English of the New World have between them a thousand other bonds, and they live in an age when all is seeking to be made equal among men.

The Middle Ages was an age of fragmentation. Each people, each province, each city, each family then strongly tended to individualize itself. In our day, a contrary movement is felt; peoples seem to be marching toward unity. Intellectual bonds unite the most distant parts of the earth, and men cannot remain a single day strangers to one another, or ignorant of what is happening in any corner of the universe: thus one notices today less difference between the Europeans and their descendants in the New World, despite the ocean that divides them, than between certain cities of the thirteenth century separated only by a river.
If this movement of assimilation draws strange peoples nearer, it opposes still more strongly the offshoots of the same people becoming strangers to one another.

The time will come, then, when one shall be able to see in North America one hundred and fifty million men[145] equal among themselves, who all will belong to the same family, who will have the same starting point, the same civilization, the same language, the same religion, the same habits, the same mores, and through whom thought will circulate in the same form and paint itself in the same colors. All the rest is doubtful, but this is certain. Now, here is a fact entirely new in the world, the bearing of which the imagination itself cannot grasp.
There are today two great peoples on earth who, starting from different points, seem to be advancing toward the same goal: the Russians and the Anglo-Americans.

Both have grown up in obscurity; and while men's gazes were occupied elsewhere, they have placed themselves all at once in the first rank of nations, and the world has learned of their birth and their greatness almost at the same time.

All the other peoples seem to have reached approximately the limits drawn by nature, and to have nothing left to do but to preserve; but they are still growing[146]: all the others have halted or advance only with a thousand efforts; they alone walk with an easy and rapid step along a road whose end the eye cannot yet perceive.

The American struggles against the obstacles that nature opposes to him; the Russian is at grips with men. The one combats the wilderness and barbarism; the other, civilization clothed in all her arms: so the conquests of the American are made with the laborer's plow, those of the Russian with the soldier's sword.
To reach his aim, the first relies on personal interest, and lets the strength and reason of individuals act without directing them.
The second concentrates, as it were, in one man all the power of society.
The one has as his principal means of action liberty; the other, servitude.
Their starting point is different, their paths are diverse; nevertheless, each of them seems called by a secret design of Providence to hold one day in his hands the destinies of half the world.

paragraphs: See the map at the end of the first volume.

The native of North America preserves his opinions and even the least details of his habits with an inflexibility that has no example in history. For more than two hundred years that the wandering tribes of North America have had daily relations with the white race, they have, so to speak, borrowed from it neither an idea nor a usage. The men of Europe have nevertheless exercised a very great influence on the savages. They have made the Indian character more disordered, but they have not made it more European. Finding myself in the summer of 1831 behind Lake Michigan, in a place called Green Bay, which serves as the extreme frontier of the United States on the side of the Indians of the Northwest, I made the acquaintance of an American officer, Major H., who one day, after speaking to me at length of the inflexibility of the Indian character, told me the following: "I once knew," he said, "a young Indian who had been raised in a New England college. He had had great success there, and had taken on all the outward aspect of a civilized man. When war broke out between us and the English in 1810, I saw this young man again; he was then serving in our army, at the head of the warriors of his tribe. The Americans had admitted Indians to their ranks only on condition that they abstain from the horrible custom of scalping the vanquished. On the evening of the battle of ***, C... came to sit beside our bivouac fire; I asked him what had happened to him during the day; he told me, and warming by degrees to the memory of his exploits, he ended by half-opening his coat and saying to me: 'Do not betray me, but look!' I saw indeed," added Major H., "between his body and his shirt, the scalp of an Englishman still all dripping with blood."
In the thirteen original States, only 6,373 Indians remain. (See *Legislative Documents*, 20th Congress, no. 117, p. 20.)

Messrs. Clark and Cass, in their report to Congress, February 4, 1829, p. 23, said: "The time is already long past when the Indians could procure the objects necessary for their food and clothing without recourse to the industry of civilized men. Beyond the Mississippi, in a country where immense herds of buffalo are still to be met with, there live Indian tribes that follow these wild animals in their migrations; the Indians we speak of still find the means of living by conforming to all the usages of their fathers; but the buffalo retreat without ceasing. The wild beasts of the smaller species, such as the bear, the deer, the beaver, the muskrat, which particularly furnish the Indians with what is necessary to sustain life, can now be reached only with rifles or traps. It is chiefly in the Northwest that the Indians are obliged to give themselves up to excessive labor to feed their family. Often the hunter devotes several days in succession to pursuing game without success; during this time, his family must feed on bark and roots, or perish: thus many die of hunger each winter." The Indians do not want to live like the Europeans; yet they cannot do without the Europeans, nor live entirely like their fathers. This may be judged by this one fact, the knowledge of which I likewise draw from an official source. Men belonging to an Indian tribe on the banks of Lake Superior had killed a European; the American government forbade trading with the tribe to which the guilty men belonged, until the latter had been delivered up to it: which was done.

"Five years ago," says Volney in his *Tableau des États-Unis*, p. 370, "in going from Vincennes to Kaskaskias, a territory now included in the State of Illinois, then entirely savage (1797), one did not cross a prairie without seeing herds of four or five hundred buffalo: today there are none left; they have swum across the Mississippi, importuned by hunters, and especially by the bells of the American cattle."

One can convince oneself of the truth of what I advance here by consulting the general table of the Indian tribes contained within the limits claimed by the United States. (*Legislative Documents*, 20th Congress, no. 117, pp. 90–105.) It will be seen that the tribes of the center of America are rapidly decreasing, although the Europeans are still very far from them.

"The Indians," say Messrs. Clark and Cass in their report to Congress, p. 15, "hold to their country by the same feeling of affection that ties us to ours; and, moreover, they attach to the idea of alienating the lands that the Great Spirit gave to their ancestors certain superstitious ideas that exercise great power over the tribes that have not yet ceded anything, or that have ceded only a small portion of their territory to the Europeans. 'We do not sell the place where rest the ashes of our fathers,' is the first answer they always give to anyone who proposes to buy their fields."

See in the *Legislative Documents of Congress*, doc. 117, the account of what passes in these circumstances. This curious piece is found in the report already cited, made by Messrs. Clark and Lewis Cass to Congress on February 4, 1829. Mr. Cass is today Secretary of State for War. "When the Indians arrive at the place where the treaty is to be made," say Messrs. Clark and Cass, "they are poor and almost naked. There they see and examine a great number of objects precious in their eyes, which the American merchants have taken care to bring. The women and children, who wish to have their needs provided for, then begin to torment the men with a thousand importunate demands, and use all their influence over the latter so that the sale of the lands may take place. The improvidence of the Indians is habitual and invincible. To provide for one's immediate needs and to gratify one's present desires is the irresistible passion of the savage: the expectation of future advantages acts only feebly on him; he easily forgets the past, and does not occupy himself with the future. One would ask the Indians in vain for the cession of part of their territory if one were not in a state to satisfy their needs on the spot. When one considers with impartiality the situation in which these unfortunate people find themselves, one is not astonished at the eagerness with which they obtain some relief from their ills."

On May 19, 1830, Mr. Edward Everett affirmed before the House of Representatives that the Americans had already acquired by treaty, east and west of the Mississippi, 230,000,000 acres. In 1808 the Osages ceded 48,000,000 acres for an annuity of 1,000 dollars. In 1818 the Quapaws ceded 20,000,000 acres for 4,000 dollars; they had reserved for themselves a territory of 1,000,000 acres in order to hunt there. It had been solemnly sworn that it would be respected; but it has not been slow to be invaded like the rest. "In order to appropriate to ourselves the deserted lands the Indians claim as property," said Mr. Bell, reporter of the committee on Indian affairs to Congress on February 24, 1830, "we have adopted the usage of paying the Indian tribes what their *hunting-ground* is worth after the game has fled or been destroyed. It is more advantageous and certainly more in conformity with the rules of justice and more humane to act thus, than to seize by force of arms the territory of the savages." "The usage of buying from the Indians their title of property is thus nothing other than a new mode of acquisition that humanity and *expediency* have substituted for violence, and which must equally render us masters of the lands we claim by virtue of discovery, and which is besides assured to us by the right that civilized nations have to settle on the territory occupied by savage tribes." "Up to this day, several causes have not ceased to diminish in the eyes of the Indians the price of the soil they occupy, and then the same causes have led them to sell it to us without difficulty. The usage of buying from the savages their *right of occupancy* has therefore never been able to retard, to any perceptible degree, the prosperity of the United States." (*Legislative Documents*, 21st Congress, no. 227, p. 6.)

This opinion has appeared to us, moreover, to be that of almost all the American statesmen. "If one judges the future by the past," said Mr. Cass to Congress, "one must foresee a progressive diminution in the number of the Indians, and expect the final extinction of their race. So that this event might not occur, our frontiers would have to cease extending, and the savages to settle beyond them; or else there would have to come about a complete change in our relations with them, which it would be unreasonable to expect."

See among others the war undertaken by the Wampanoags and the other confederated tribes, under the leadership of Metacom, in 1675, against the colonists of New England, and the one the English had to sustain in 1622 in Virginia.
See the various historians of New England. See also the *History of New France*, by Charlevoix, and the *Lettres édifiantes*.

"In all the tribes," says Volney in his *Tableau des États-Unis*, p. 423, "there still exists a generation of old warriors who, on seeing the hoe handled, do not cease to cry out against the degradation of ancient mores, and who claim that the savages owe their decadence only to these innovations, and that, in order to recover their glory and power, it would suffice for them to return to their primitive mores."

There is found in an official document the following picture: "Until a young man has been at grips with the enemy, and can boast of some prowess, he is held in no consideration: he is regarded almost as a woman. At their great war dances, the warriors come, one after another, to strike the post, as they call it, and recount their exploits. On this occasion, their audience is composed of the relatives, friends, and companions of the narrator. The deep impression his words produce on them appears clearly in the silence with which he is listened to, and manifests itself loudly in the applause that accompanies the end of his accounts. The young man who has nothing to tell in such gatherings considers himself very unfortunate, and it is not without example that young warriors whose passions had been thus excited have suddenly left the dance and, going off alone, have gone in search of trophies they could show and adventures they might glory in."

These nations are today included within the States of Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. There were formerly in the South (one sees the remnants) four great nations: the Choctaws, the Chickasaws, the Creeks, and the Cherokees. The remnants of these four nations still formed in 1830 about 75,000 individuals. It is reckoned that there are at present, in the territory occupied or claimed by the Anglo-American Union, about 300,000 Indians. (See *Proceedings of the Indian Board in the City of New York*.) The official documents furnished to Congress put this number at 313,130. The reader curious to know the name and strength of all the tribes who inhabit Anglo-American territory should consult the documents I have just indicated. (*Legislative Documents*, 20th Congress, no. 17, pp. 90–105.)
I have brought back to France one or two copies of this singular publication.

See, in the report of the committee on Indian affairs, 21st Congress, no. 227, p. 23, what has caused the mixed-bloods to multiply among the Cherokees; the principal cause goes back to the war of independence. Many Anglo-Americans of Georgia, having taken the part of England, were compelled to withdraw among the Indians, and married there.

Unfortunately, mixed-bloods have been fewer in number, and have exercised less influence in North America than anywhere else. Two great nations of Europe peopled this portion of the American continent: the French and the English. The first did not delay in contracting unions with native daughters; but the misfortune was that there was found a secret affinity between the Indian character and their own. Instead of giving the barbarians the taste and habits of civilized life, they themselves often attached themselves with passion to savage life: they became the most dangerous inhabitants of the wilderness, and won the friendship of the Indian by exaggerating his vices and his virtues. M. de Senonville, governor of Canada, wrote to Louis XIV in 1685: "It has long been believed that the savages had to be brought close to us in order to Frenchify them; we have every reason to recognize that we were mistaken. Those who have come near us have not become French, and the French who have frequented them have become savages. They affect to dress like them, to live like them." (*History of New France*, by Charlevoix, vol. II, p. 345.) The Englishman, on the contrary, remaining obstinately attached to the opinions, the customs, and the least habits of his fathers, has remained in the midst of the American wilderness what he was in the heart of the cities of Europe; he therefore would not establish any contact with savages he despised, and carefully avoided mingling his blood with that of the barbarians. Thus, while the Frenchman exercised no salutary influence on the Indians, the Englishman always remained a stranger to them.

There is in the adventurous life of hunting peoples some irresistible attraction that seizes the heart of man and draws him along in spite of his reason and his experience. One can convince oneself of this truth by reading the *Memoirs* of Tanner. Tanner is a European who was carried off at the age of six by the Indians, and who remained thirty years in the forests with them. It is impossible to see anything more dreadful than the miseries he describes. He shows us tribes without chiefs, families without nations, isolated men, mutilated remnants of powerful tribes, wandering at random amid the ice and through the desolate solitudes of Canada. Famine and cold pursue them; each day life seems ready to leave them. Among them mores have lost their hold, traditions are without power. Men become more and more barbarous. Tanner shares all these evils; he knows his European origin; he is not held by force away from the whites; he comes on the contrary each year to trade with them, traverses their dwellings, sees their comfort; he knows that from the day he wishes to return to civilized life, he can easily do so, and yet he remains thirty years in the wilderness. When at last he returns to civilized society, he confesses that the existence whose miseries he has described has for him secret charms he cannot define; he goes back to it ceaselessly after leaving it; he tears himself only with a thousand regrets from so many ills; and when he is finally fixed among the whites, several of his children refuse to come share with him his tranquility and his comfort. I myself met Tanner at the entrance of Lake Superior. He seemed to me to resemble much more a savage than a civilized man. In Tanner's work, one finds neither order nor taste; but the author, even without knowing it, paints there a vivid picture of the prejudices, passions, vices, and above all the miseries of those among whom he had lived. M. le Vicomte Ernest de Blosseville, author of an excellent work on the penal colonies of England, has translated Tanner's *Memoirs*. M. de Blosseville has joined to his translation notes of great interest, which will allow the reader to compare the facts told by Tanner with those already related by a great number of ancient and modern observers. All who wish to know the present state and foresee the future destiny of the Indian races of North America must consult M. de Blosseville's work.

This destructive influence that highly civilized peoples exercise on those that are less so is to be remarked even among Europeans themselves. Frenchmen had founded, nearly a century ago, in the midst of the wilderness, the city of Vincennes on the Wabash. They lived there in great abundance until the arrival of the American emigrants. The latter at once began to ruin the older inhabitants by competition; they then bought up their lands at a low price. At the moment when M. de Volney, from whom I borrow this detail, crossed Vincennes, the number of Frenchmen was reduced to about a hundred individuals, most of whom were preparing to pass over to Louisiana and Canada. These Frenchmen were honest men, but without enlightenment and without industry; they had contracted part of the savage habits. The Americans, who were perhaps inferior to them from the moral point of view, had over them an immense intellectual superiority: they were industrious, instructed, rich, and accustomed to govern themselves. I myself have seen in Canada, where the intellectual difference between the two races is far less pronounced, the Englishman, master of commerce and industry in the country of the Canadian, spreading on every side and confining the Frenchman within limits too narrow. Similarly, in Louisiana, almost all commercial and industrial activity is concentrated in the hands of the Anglo-Americans. Something even more striking is happening in the province of Texas; the State of Texas forms, as is known, part of Mexico, and serves as its frontier on the side of the United States. For some years the Anglo-Americans have been penetrating individually into this still ill-peopled province, buying the lands, taking possession of industry, and rapidly substituting themselves for the original population. One can foresee that, if Mexico does not hasten to arrest this movement, Texas will not be slow to escape from her. If a few comparatively imperceptible differences in European civilization bring about such results, it is easy to understand what must happen when the most perfected civilization of Europe comes into contact with Indian barbarism.

See, in the legislative documents, 21st Congress, no. 89, the excesses of every kind committed by the white population on the territory of the Indians. Sometimes the Anglo-Americans settle on part of the territory, as if there were a lack of land elsewhere, and the troops of Congress must come to expel them; sometimes they carry off livestock, burn the houses, cut the fruit of the natives, or do violence to their persons. It results from all these pieces the proof that the natives are each day victims of the abuse of force. The Union habitually maintains among the Indians an agent charged with representing it; the report of the agent of the Cherokees is among the pieces I cite: the language of this official is almost always favorable to the savages. "The intrusion of the whites upon the territory of the Cherokees," he says, p. 12, "will cause the ruin of those who inhabit it, and who lead there a poor and inoffensive existence." Further on, one sees that the State of Georgia, wishing to narrow the limits of the Cherokees, proceeded to a boundary; the federal agent remarks that the boundary, having been made only by the whites, and not contradictorily, has no value.

In 1829 the State of Alabama divides the territory of the Creeks into counties, and submits the Indian population to European magistrates. In 1830 the State of Mississippi assimilates the Choctaws and the Chickasaws to the whites, and declares that those of them who take the title of chief shall be punished with a fine of 1,000 dollars and a year of prison. When the State of Mississippi thus extended its laws over the Choctaw Indians inhabiting within its limits, the latter assembled; their chief made known to them what the whites' claim was, and read to them some of the laws to which they were to be subjected: the savages declared with one voice that it was better to plunge again into the wilderness. (*Mississippi papers*.)

The Georgians, who find themselves so inconvenienced by the proximity of the Indians, occupy a territory that does not yet count more than seven inhabitants per square mile. In France, there are one hundred and sixty-two individuals in the same space.

In 1818 Congress ordered that the territory of Arkansas should be visited by American commissioners, accompanied by a deputation of Creeks, Choctaws, and Chickasaws. This expedition was commanded by Messrs. Kennerly, McCoy, Wash Hood, and John Bell. See the various reports of the commissioners and their journal in the Congress papers, no. 87, *House of Representatives*.

In the treaty made with the Creeks in 1790, one finds this clause: "The United States solemnly guarantee to the nation of the Creeks all the lands it possesses within the territory of the Union." The treaty concluded in July 1791 with the Cherokees contains the following: "The United States solemnly guarantee to the nation of the Cherokees all the lands which it has not previously ceded. If it should come to pass that a citizen of the United States, or any individual other than an Indian, should come to settle on the territory of the Cherokees, the United States declares that it withdraws from this citizen its protection, and that it delivers him up to the nation of the Cherokees to be punished as it shall see fit." Art. 8.

Which does not prevent it from promising it to them in the most formal manner. See the letter from the president addressed to the Creeks on March 23, 1829: (*Proceedings of the Indian Board in the City of New York*, p. 5) "Beyond the great river (the Mississippi)," he says, "your father has prepared, to receive you there, a vast country. There, your brothers the whites will not come to disturb you; they will have no rights over your lands; you will be able to live there, you and your children, in the midst of peace and abundance, as long as the grass grows and the streams flow; they will *belong to you forever*." In a letter written to the Cherokees by the Secretary of the Department of War, on April 18, 1829, this official declares to them that they should not flatter themselves to retain the enjoyment of the territory they then occupy, but he gives them this same positive assurance for the time when they will be on the other side of the Mississippi (same work, p. 6): as if the power which he lacks now should not lack him as well then!

To form an exact idea of the policy followed by the particular States and by the Union toward the Indians, one must consult: 1st, the laws of the particular States relating to the Indians (this collection is found in the legislative documents, 21st Congress, no. 319); 2nd, the laws of the Union relating to the same object, and in particular that of March 30, 1802 (these laws are found in the work by M. Story entitled: *Laws of the United States*); 3rd, finally, to know what is the present state of the relations of the Union with all the Indian tribes, see the report made by M. Cass, Secretary of State for War, on November 29, 1823.
On November 19, 1829. This piece is translated word for word.

The credit for this result is not, moreover, to be given to the Spaniards. If the Indian tribes had not already been fixed to the soil by agriculture at the moment of the Europeans' arrival, they would doubtless have been destroyed in South America as in North America.

See among others the report made by Mr. Bell in the name of the committee on Indian affairs on February 24, 1830, in which it is established, p. 5, by very logical reasons, and where it is proved most doctrinally that: "The fundamental principle, that the Indians had no right by virtue of their ancient possession either of soil, or sovereignty, has never been abandoned either expressly or by implication." That is to say that *the Indians, by virtue of their ancient possession, have acquired no right of property or of sovereignty: a fundamental principle that has never been abandoned, either expressly or tacitly*. On reading this report, drawn up moreover by a skillful hand, one is astonished at the facility and ease with which, from the very first words, the author rids himself of the arguments founded on natural right and reason, which he calls abstract and theoretical principles. The more I think on it, the more I think that the only difference that exists between the civilized man and the one who is not, in respect of justice, is this: the one contests with justice rights that the other contents himself with violating.

Before treating this matter, I owe a notice to the reader. In a book of which I have already spoken at the beginning of this work, and which is about to appear, M. Gustave de Beaumont, my traveling companion, has had as his principal aim to make known in France what the position of the negroes is in the midst of the white population of the United States. M. de Beaumont has treated thoroughly a question that my subject only allowed me to touch upon. His book, the notes of which contain a great number of legislative and historical documents, very precious and entirely unknown, presents in addition pictures whose energy could only be equaled by their truth. It is M. de Beaumont's work that those who wish to understand to what excesses of tyranny men are gradually pushed once they have begun to depart from nature and humanity must read.

It is known that several of the most celebrated authors of antiquity were, or had been, slaves: Aesop and Terence are of this number. The slaves were not always taken from among barbarous nations: war put very civilized men into servitude.

For the whites to give up the opinion they have formed of the intellectual and moral inferiority of their former slaves, the negroes would have to change, and they cannot change as long as this opinion subsists.

See the *History of Virginia* by Beverley. See also, in Jefferson's *Memoirs*, curious details on the introduction of the negroes into Virginia, and on the first act that prohibited their importation in 1778.

The number of slaves was less great in the North, but the advantages resulting from slavery were no more contested there than in the South. In 1740 the legislature of the State of New York declares that the direct importation of slaves must be encouraged as much as possible, and that smuggling must be severely punished, as tending to discourage the honest merchant. (*Kent's commentaries*, vol. 2, p. 206.) There are found in the Historical Collection of Massachusetts, vol. 4, p. 193, curious researches of Belknap on slavery in New England. It results from them that, as early as 1630, negroes were introduced, but that already then legislation and mores showed themselves opposed to slavery. See also in this place the manner in which public opinion, and then the law, succeeded in destroying servitude.
Not only does Ohio not admit slavery, but it prohibits the entry of free negroes onto its territory, and forbids them to acquire anything there. See the statutes of Ohio.

It is not only the individual man that is active in Ohio; the State itself undertakes immense enterprises: the State of Ohio has established, between Lake Erie and the Ohio, a canal by means of which the valley of the Mississippi communicates with the Hudson River. Thanks to this canal, the goods of Europe that arrive in New York can descend by water to New Orleans, across more than five hundred leagues of continent.
Exact figure according to the census of 1830. Kentucky, 688,844. Ohio, 937,669.

Independent of these causes, which, wherever free workers abound, make their labor more productive and more economical than that of slaves, there must be pointed out another peculiar to the United States: on the whole surface of the Union, it has so far been found possible to cultivate the sugar cane successfully only on the banks of the Mississippi, near the mouth of that river, in the Gulf of Mexico. In Louisiana, the cultivation of the cane is extremely advantageous: nowhere does the cultivator derive so great a price from his labors; and as there is always established a certain relation between the costs of production and the products, the price of slaves is very high in Louisiana. Now Louisiana being among the confederated States, slaves can be transported there from all parts of the Union; the price given for a slave in New Orleans therefore raises the price of slaves in all the other markets. The result is that, in countries where the land yields little, the costs of cultivation by slaves continue to be very considerable, which gives a great advantage to the competition of free workers.

There is a particular reason that completes the detachment from the cause of slavery of the two last States I have just named. The ancient wealth of this part of the Union was principally founded on the cultivation of tobacco. Slaves are particularly suited to this cultivation: now it has come about that for many years tobacco has been losing its market value; meanwhile the value of slaves remains always the same. Thus the relation between the costs of production and the products is changed. The inhabitants of Maryland and Virginia therefore feel themselves more disposed than they were thirty years ago either to do without slaves in the cultivation of tobacco, or to abandon both the cultivation of tobacco and slavery together.

The States in which slavery is abolished ordinarily apply themselves to making residence on their territory disagreeable to free negroes; and as there is established on this point a kind of emulation between the different States, the unhappy negroes can only choose among evils.

There is a great difference between the mortality of whites and that of blacks in the States where slavery is abolished: from 1820 to 1831, only one white in forty-two individuals belonging to the white race died at Philadelphia, while one negro in twenty-one individuals belonging to the black race died there. The mortality is not nearly so great among slave negroes. (See *Emerson's Medical Statistics*, p. 28.)

This is true in places where rice is cultivated. Rice fields, which are unhealthy in every country, are particularly dangerous in those struck by the burning sun of the tropics. The Europeans would have great difficulty in cultivating the land in this part of the New World, if they wished to insist on having it produce rice. But cannot one do without rice fields?
These States are nearer the equator than Italy and Spain, but the continent of America is infinitely colder than that of Europe.

Spain once had transported into a district of Louisiana called Attakapas a certain number of peasants from the Azores. Slavery was not introduced among them; it was a trial. Today these men still cultivate the land without slaves; but their industry is so languid that it scarcely furnishes their needs.

One reads in the American work entitled *Letters on the Colonization Society*, by Carey, 1833, the following: "In South Carolina, for the last forty years, the black race has grown faster than that of the whites. Taking the population as a whole of the five Southern States that first had slaves," M. Carey further says, "Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia, one discovers that from 1790 to 1830 the whites have increased in the ratio of 80 per 100." In the United States, in 1830, the men belonging to the two races were distributed as follows: States in which slavery is abolished, 6,565,434 whites, 120,520 negroes. States in which slavery still exists, 3,960,814 whites, 2,208,102 negroes.

This opinion, moreover, is supported by authorities far weightier than my own. One reads among others in the *Memoirs* of Jefferson: "Nothing is more clearly written in the book of fates than the emancipation of the blacks, and it is quite as certain that the two races equally free could not live under the same government. Nature, habit, and opinion have established between them insurmountable barriers." (See *Extract from the Memoirs of Jefferson*, by M. Conseil.)
If the English of the Antilles had governed themselves, one can count that they would not have granted the Act of Emancipation that the mother country has just imposed.

This society took the name of Society for the Colonization of the Blacks. See its annual reports, and notably the fifteenth. See also the pamphlet already indicated entitled *Letters on the Colonization Society and on its probable results*, by M. Carey. Philadelphia, April 1833.

This last rule was traced by the founders themselves of the establishment. They feared that something analogous to what is happening on the frontiers of the United States might happen in Africa, and that the negroes, like the Indians, coming into contact with a race more enlightened than their own, might be destroyed before being able to civilize themselves.

There would be many other difficulties still in such an enterprise. If the Union, in order to transport the negroes from America to Africa, were to undertake to buy the blacks from those whose slaves they are, the price of negroes, growing in proportion to their scarcity, would soon rise to enormous sums, and it is not credible that the States of the North would consent to making such an expenditure, the fruits of which they should not gather. If the Union were to seize by force or acquire at a low price fixed by it the slaves of the South, it would create an insurmountable resistance among the States situated in this part of the Union. On both sides one ends in the impossible.

There were in 1830 in the United States 2,010,327 slaves, and 319,439 freedmen; in all 2,329,766 negroes; which formed a little more than a fifth of the total population of the United States at the same period.
Emancipation is not forbidden, but submitted to formalities that make it difficult.

See the conduct of the Northern States in the war of 1812. "During this war," says Jefferson in a letter of March 17, 1817 to General Lafayette, "four of the Eastern States were no more linked to the rest of the Union than corpses to living men." — (*Correspondence of Jefferson*, published by M. Conseil.)

The state of peace in which the Union finds itself gives it no pretext for having a permanent army. Without a permanent army, a government has nothing prepared in advance to take advantage of the favorable moment, overcome resistance, and seize the sovereign power by surprise.

It is thus that the province of Holland, in the Republic of the Netherlands, and the emperor, in the Germanic Confederation, have sometimes placed themselves in the place of the Union, and exploited in their particular interest the federal power.

Average height of the Alleghenies, according to Volney (*Tableau des États-Unis*, p. 33), 700 to 800 meters; 5,000 to 6,000 feet, according to Darby: the greatest height of the Vosges is 1,400 meters above sea level.
See the map at the end of the first volume.
See *View of the United States*, by Darby, pp. 64 and 79.

The chain of the Alleghenies is no higher than that of the Vosges, and offers no more obstacles to the efforts of human industry than the latter. The countries situated on the eastern slope of the Alleghenies are therefore as naturally linked to the valley of the Mississippi as Franche-Comté, upper Burgundy, and Alsace are linked to France.
1,002,600 square miles. See *View of the United States*, by Darby, p. 435.

I do not need, I think, to say that by these expressions, *the Anglo-Americans*, I mean to speak only of the great majority of them. Apart from this majority there are always a few isolated individuals.
This is, it is true, but a passing peril. I do not doubt that with time society will come to be settled and ordered in the West as it already has been on the shores of the Atlantic.
Pennsylvania had 431,373 inhabitants in 1790.
Surface area of the State of New York, 6,213 square leagues (500 square miles.) See *View of the United States*, by Darby, p. 435.

If the population continues to double every twenty-two years, for another century, as it has for two hundred years, in 1852 there will be twenty-four million inhabitants in the United States, forty-eight in 1874, and ninety-six in 1896. It would be so even if there were to be encountered on the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains lands that would refuse cultivation. The lands already occupied can very easily contain this number of inhabitants. One hundred million men spread over the soil now occupied by the twenty-four States and the three territories of which the Union is composed would give only 762 individuals per square league, which would still be far below the average population of France, which is 1,006; that of England, which is 1,457; and which would even remain below the population of Switzerland. Switzerland, despite its lakes and mountains, counts 783 inhabitants per square league. See Malte-Brun, vol. 6, p. 92.
The territory of the United States has a surface area of 295,000 square leagues; that of Europe, according to Malte-Brun, vol. 6, p. 4, is 500,000.
See *Legislative Documents*, 20th Congress, no. 117, p. 105.
From Jefferson, the capital of the State of Missouri, to Washington, one counts 1,019 miles, or 420 post leagues. (*American Almanac*, 1831, p. 48.)

To judge of the difference that exists between the commercial movement of the South and that of the North, it suffices to cast one's eyes on the following table: In 1829, the vessels of the great and small commerce belonging to Virginia, the two Carolinas, and Georgia (the four great States of the South), gauged only 5,243 tons. In the same year, the ships of the single State of Massachusetts gauged 17,322 tons[A]. Thus the State of Massachusetts alone had three times more vessels than the four above-named States. Yet the State of Massachusetts has only 959 square leagues of surface area (7,335 square miles) and 610,014 inhabitants, while the four States I speak of have 27,304 square leagues (210,000 miles) and 3,047,767 inhabitants[B]. Thus the area of the State of Massachusetts is only a thirtieth of the area of the four States, and its population is five times smaller than theirs. Slavery harms in several ways the commercial prosperity of the South: it diminishes the spirit of enterprise among the whites, and it prevents them from finding at their disposal the sailors they would need. The navy is generally recruited only from the last class of the population. Now, in the South, it is the slaves who form this class, and it is difficult to put them to use at sea: their service would be inferior to that of the whites, and there would always be the fear that they might revolt in the middle of the Ocean, or take flight on touching foreign shores.
*View of the United States*, by Darby, p. 444.

Note that, when I speak of the basin of the Mississippi, I do not include the portion of the States of New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia placed to the west of the Alleghenies, although they ought also to be considered as part of it.

One then realizes that, during the last ten years, one State has increased its population in the proportion of 5 to 100, like Delaware; another in the proportion of 250 to 100, like the territory of Michigan. Virginia discovers that, during the same period, it has increased the number of its inhabitants in the ratio of 13 to 100, while the bordering State of Ohio has increased the number of its own in the ratio of 61 to 100. See the general table contained in the *National Calendar*: you will be struck by the inequality in the fortune of the different States.

It will be seen further on that, during the last period, the population of Virginia grew in the proportion of 13 to 100. It is necessary to explain how the number of a State's representatives can decrease when the population of the State, far from decreasing itself, is on the increase. I take Virginia, which I have already cited, as the object of comparison. The number of Virginia's deputies in 1823 was in proportion to the total number of the Union's deputies; the number of Virginia's deputies in 1833 is likewise in proportion to the total number of the Union's deputies in 1833, and in proportion to the rate of its population, grown during these ten years. The ratio of the new number of Virginia's deputies to the old will therefore be proportional, on the one hand to the ratio of the new total number of deputies to the old, and on the other hand to the ratio of the proportions of growth of Virginia and of the whole Union. Thus, for the number of Virginia's deputies to remain stationary, it suffices that the ratio of the proportion of growth of the small country to that of the large be the inverse of the ratio of the new total number of deputies to the old; and however slightly this proportion of growth of the Virginia population is in a weaker ratio to the proportion of growth of the entire Union, than the new number of the Union's deputies is to the old, the number of Virginia's deputies will be diminished.
Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe.
See the report made by its committee to the Convention, which proclaimed nullification in South Carolina.

The population of a country forms surely the first element of its wealth. During this same period from 1820 to 1832, during which Virginia lost two deputies to Congress, its population grew in the proportion of 13.7 to 100; that of the Carolinas in the ratio of 15 to 100, and that of Georgia in the proportion of 51.5 to 100. (See *American Almanac*, 1832, p. 162.) Now, Russia, which is the country of Europe where the population grows the most quickly, increases its inhabitants in ten years only in the proportion of 9.5 to 100; France in that of 7 to 100, and Europe en masse in that of 4.7 to 100. (See Malte-Brun, vol. 6, p. 95.)

It must be admitted, however, that the depreciation that has come about in the price of tobacco for fifty years has notably diminished the ease of the cultivators of the South; but this fact is independent of the will of the men of the North as of theirs.

In 1832, the district of Michigan, which has only 31,639 inhabitants, and still forms only a barely cleared wilderness, presented the development of 940 miles of post roads. The almost entirely savage territory of Arkansas was already crossed by 1,738 miles of post roads. See *the Report of the Postmaster General*, November 30, 1833. The carriage alone of newspapers throughout the whole Union brings in each year 254,796 dollars.

In the course of ten years, from 1821 to 1831, 271 steamboats were launched on the rivers alone that water the valley of the Mississippi. In 1829, there existed in the United States 256 steamboats. See *Legislative Documents*, no. 240, p. 274.

See in the legislative documents, which I have already cited in the chapter on the Indians, the letter from the president of the United States to the Cherokees, his correspondence on this subject with his agents, and his messages to Congress.

The first act of cession was made on the part of the State of New York in 1780; Virginia, Massachusetts, Connecticut, South Carolina, North Carolina, followed this example at different periods; Georgia was the last; its act of cession dates only from 1803.
The president refused, it is true, to sanction this law, but he completely admitted its principle. See *Message of December 8, 1833*.

The present Bank of the United States was created in 1816, with a capital of 35,000,000 dollars (185,500,000 francs): its charter expires in 1836. Last year, Congress passed a law to renew it; but the president refused his sanction. The struggle is today engaged on both sides with extreme violence, and it is easy to predict the imminent fall of the Bank.
See principally, for the details of this affair, the *Legislative Documents*, 22nd Congress, 2nd session, no. 30.

That is to say a majority of the people; for the opposing party, called the *Union Party*, always counted a very strong and very active minority in its favor. South Carolina may have about 47,000 electors; 30,000 were favorable to nullification, and 17,000 contrary.

This ordinance was preceded by the report of a committee charged with preparing its drafting: this report contains the exposition and the aim of the law. One reads there, p. 34: "When the rights reserved to the various States by the constitution are violated deliberately, the right and the duty of these States is to intervene, in order to halt the progress of the evil, to oppose the usurpation, and to maintain within their respective limits the powers and privileges that belong to them as *independent sovereigns*. If the States did not possess this right, in vain would they claim to be sovereign. South Carolina declares that it recognizes on earth no tribunal placed above it.
